Sports.title: Jude Bellingham joins exclusive five-man club after scooping individual honour
Sports.content:
Jude Bellingham has become the fifth player in history to be named the England Men's Senior Player of the Year in successive seasons.

He joins a legendary list of back-to-back winners including Wayne Rooney, Bukayo Saka, Frank Lampard, and Harry Kane.

2 Bellingham rounded off England's third-place play-off win by breaking England's World Cup goal record Credit: Getty

The 23-year-old's second consecutive award comes on the back of a historic summer in which he scored seven goals at the 2026 World Cup.

His seven goals this summer broke the record for the most scored at a single World Cup by an Englishman.

Bellingham famously scored a brace in England's 3-2 win over Mexico, and he registered a double again against Norway in the quarterfinal.

The midfielder's goals played a key role as England recorded their best international tournament finish since lifting the trophy in 1966.

Jude Bellingham reacts to latest award

"It feels great," Bellingham said upon receiving the honour.

"Obviously, a huge honour to be recognised by the fans again. It’s not something you think about when you play for your country, but it's obviously a beautiful little addition to the great summer we had."

England boss Thomas Tuchel added: "I think he was one of the players of the tournament, not only for us but for the whole tournament.

"He lived up to his full potential; you could just see what a competitor and what a machine he is.

"He just thrives under pressure, he just loves these moments, he loves these stages and it brings out the very best in him."

Bellingham's goal haul wasn't the only record he set this summer, either.

2 Bellingham scored twice in the heroic win over Mexico Credit: Getty

He became the youngest European player to feature at four major tournaments this summer, at the age of 22 years and 353 days.

Six days later, he followed that up by becoming the youngest Three Lions player to reach 50 caps - against Ghana.

Additionally, Bellingham was also gifted the FIFA Bronze Boot, yet he had no idea he could pick up an award for finishing third among the top scorers.

The Los Blancos player said: "The World Cup Bronze Boot... I didn't even know it existed, but thanks anyway."

When is Jude Bellingham next in action for England?

England will take on world champions Spain in a heavyweight clash at Wembley Stadium on Saturday in the UEFA Nations League and will be live on talkSPORT.

The contest is scheduled to kick off at 7:45pm.

Sports.title: Manchester City found guilty of almost all Premier League financial breaches
Sports.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty on almost all of the charges relating to breaches of the Premier League’s financial regulations.

City were first charged with 115 breaches of these rules in February 2023.

6 Man City's long-standing case finally looks to be reaching its conclusion Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

But the Citizens have now been found guilty on a significant amount of charges.

The sanctions have not been decided, with all possibilities remaining on the table.

talkSPORT also understands Premier League clubs both past and present are considering collective legal action against City for compensation.

Club officials have already discussed action which would come after the case, and any appeal is resolved. This could take the form of lost trophies, prize money and include relegated teams who claim City losing to rivals affected the league table.

This potential new action stems from teams calculating what seasons with City results expunged might look like.

talkSPORT understands City will appeal once it is confirmed the charges have gone against them.

A Premier League spokesperson told talkSPORT that the league process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality.

As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023.

In 2023, the club said it was 'surprised' by the charges and it 'welcomes the review of this matter by an independent commission, to impartially consider the comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of its position'.

A Premier League spokesperson has now said: "The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."

6 Manchester City have dominated English football over the last 15 years, but their achievements could now be tarnished Credit: Getty

What do Man City's charges relate to?

City were first charged following an investigation into alleged breaches between 2009 and 2018.

The investigation began after German newspaper Der Spiegel published leaked financial documents from City in November 2018.

The case was referred to an independent commission to adjudicate over the charges.

According to the Times, Premier League clubs were informed of the outcome of Man City's charges after a meeting on Thursday.

City have won a total of eight league titles, four FA Cups, seven League Cups and one Champions League under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour - who bought the club in 2008.

Six of those honours have come since the charges were brought forward.

6 Enzo Maresca is tasked with overseeing his Man City squad in the wake of huge news Credit: Getty

How could they be punished?

The potential consequences of Manchester City's guilty charges could be massive.

If they were given a points deduction, this could either be from when the decision is made or possibly retrospectively – raising the question of whether the club could stripped of their titles.

City won the Premier League in 2011/12, 2013/14 and 2017/18, with Manchester United were runners up in the first and last of those title wins, while Liverpool came second in 2013/14.

What now for Manchester City?

Reacting to the huge news live on air, talkSPORT's Ben Jacobs confirmed Man City will only appeal once the Premier League have decided on their punishment.

Jacobs told talkSPORT: "The independent panel ruling on Manchester City's 115 charges have found the club guilty on all but one.

"When we say all but one, we don't necessarily mean 114 out of 115 because these charges, broadly speaking, are in different kinds of buckets that were then repeated year on year on year.

6 Elliot Anderson joined Manchester City for £116million this summer, one of two nine-figure transfers alongside Ayyoub Bouaddi Credit: Getty

"But the vast majority of the charges against Manchester City are deemed to be enforceable and, as a consequence, the independent panel are now moving from guilt to sanctions. It's an ongoing process.

"Manchester City are waiting to see, following being found guilty, what the exact punishment is going to be and then from there, they are expected to appeal."

Jacobs added: "City still point to the fact that, originally, UEFA had found them guilty of certain elements, and they were able to overturn that case as well [in 2020]."

When will Man City learn their punishment?

While news of City's charges has sent shockwaves across English football, Jacobs revealed it could be months before we discover their exact punishment.

He pointed to Everton's initial 10 point deduction for breaching the Premier League's profit and sustainability rules in the 2021/22 season, which was then implemented during the 2023/24 campaign, with the penalty reduced to six points upon appeal..

Jacobs explained: "Due to the strict confidentiality, the sanctions can be passed down to the club or, alternatively, the guilt can be found first.

6 Manchester City are top of the Premier League after the first five games of the 2026/27 season Credit: Getty

"And then the process still has to understand what exactly the final punishment will be. We saw this with slightly smaller cases like Everton and Nottingham Forest, where the Premier League pushed for a certain points deduction and it got scaled back.

"My expectation is there'll still be an element of back and forth and it could take several weeks, if not months, to get a final resolution.

If City appeal, it's going to be longer.

"Could they go to the Premier League in light of the vast majority of these charges being upheld and ask for a more amicable settlement? Possibly as well, but I'm not expecting this to resolve itself in its full entirety in a matter of days or during the international break, maybe even not during this season as well."

Man City in 'very serious trouble'

In the wake of Man City's guilty verdict, football finance expert Stefan Borson has warned the club faces a strong chance that their appeal will be rejected by the Premier League.

Reacting to the news on air, he said: “With City being found guilty of more or less everything, the decision itself will be scathing in terms of the club's conduct, the conduct of individuals, the behaviour of individuals in the hearing itself in terms of their credibility.

“And there won't be any hiding place when that decision is published, because the language that will be used in there will not be kind, I think is the best way to describe it. "

6 Pep Guardiola oversaw the bulk of Man City's success in the period that their charges apply to Credit: PA

On their appeal chances, he explained: “There are cases in English law where delays of this type of duration, so 22 months, 23 months, have given rise to effectively the need for a re-hearing of the entire case.

“But all of those sorts of arguments - be it bias, be it something procedural, all of them are very unlikely to succeed. And overturning factual findings, again, is just very, very unlikely.

“I think ultimately, City are going to have to now take the punishment, which will come down the line.

"And it will be severe - there's no question, having been found guilty of everything, that the punishment will be absolutely severe."

Chelsea recently reached a £10million settlement and were given a suspended two-window registration ban over breaches of FA rules surrounding their dealings with agents and other third parties.

But Borson warned Manchester City won't be able to strike up a similar deal, given their continued denial of their charges.

He continued: “This will not be a Chelsea situation. Chelsea did a wonderful job in negotiating a deal with the Premier League and ended up with an incredibly lenient approach. They did a very similar thing with the FA.

"We are not in this situation with Manchester City. Manchester City have denied everything all the way through.

“They've gone through a process that may have cost as much as £100 million between the two parties, and they've been found to have breached everything.

"They are in very, very serious trouble.”

Sports.title: Danny Ings set for immediate debut after agreeing shock deal to join League One side
Sports.content:
Danny Ings set for immediate debut after agreeing shock deal to join League One side

Wycombe Wanderers have confirmed the signing of former Liverpool and West Ham United striker Danny Ings.

The 34-year-old has been without a club since leaving Sheffield United over the summer.



3 Former Premier League striker Ings left West Ham in 2025 and has recently been at Sheffield United Credit: Getty

And the League One side have won the race to land the experienced hitman, who was linked with a move to Leicester City earlier in the year.

Wycombe statement

"Former England international Danny Ings has joined Wycombe Wanderers," a statement read on the club's official website.

Ings has also signed in time to make his debut for Wycombe this weekend against Reading.



"And he could feature in the League One clash with Reading at Adams Park on Saturday," the club continued.

"The 34-year-old striker is a free agent after leaving Sheffield United in the summer and arrives in Wycombe with a wealth of experience including 240 appearances in the top flight with Burnley alongside Chairboys coach Sam Vokes, as well as Southampton, West Ham, Aston Villa and Liverpool.



"He’s netted more than 120 professional goals, including one for England in a friendly against Wales in 2020, and has trained with the Chairboys over the past week before putting pen to paper on a deal this morning.

"His move remains subject to EFL and FA approval, and he’ll wear squad number 28."



“We are excited to welcome Danny Ings to Wycombe Wanderers," Director of Football Strategy and Data Intelligence Tom Stockwell said.

"Danny is an attacking player with top quality and a huge amount of experience at the top of the game. We believe Danny can help the team on and off the pitch.

3 Wycombe's new striker could make his Chairboys debut this weekend Credit: Getty

"He joined up with the team Friday last week and has trained with the group since, so we know he’s fit and sharp, and ready to have an immediate impact."



Wycombe v Reading goes ahead

Reading's trip to Adams Park will go ahead as planned after Reading turned down the chance to postpone the fixture.

Andy Rinomhota, Jeriel Dorsett and Charlie Savage all received international call-ups from from Zimbabwe, Montserrat and Wales, respectively, earlier this month.

And EFL rules state that clubs are eligible to request a postponement if three or more of their players are selected for international duty.

The Royals had the chance to delay the clash, but opted to proceed with the fixture.



3 Reading's meeting with Wycombe goes ahead as scheduled Credit: Getty

"First of all, congratulations to the three lads who received international call-ups," Reading head coach Leam Richardson said.

"It’s a fantastic achievement for them and a proud moment for the club.

"We considered the circumstances carefully and, on this occasion, felt it was right to play the game.



"Football is a squad game and we have confidence in the players available to us, while keeping the fixture in place also helps us avoid adding another game to an already busy schedule.

"It’s better for the supporters too. Saturday afternoon is the ideal time to play football whenever circumstances allow, so we were pleased to keep this one in place."

Sports.title: Ex-Tottenham Hotspur and Newcastle United star Sebastien Bassong is accused of 'dodging £7 Tube fare with expired travelcard'
Sports.content:
Former Tottenham Hotspur star Sebastien Bassong has been accused of dodging a £7 Tube fare after allegedly using an invalid travel pass and following another passenger through a London Underground barrier, it has been reported.

The ex-Premier League defender, who also played for Newcastle United, is allegedly being prosecuted by Transport for London (TfL) after a revenue officer stopped him on the network.

Bassong, 39, has insisted he did not realise the pass he had been given was not valid, telling The Sun that he had been handed the card by somebody else.

'I didn't know about the prosecution and I haven't received a letter. I was using a card given to me, and I was stopped, and I didn't know it wasn't good enough. I use the Tube every day. I'm a good citizen.'

The case centres on an alleged incident in which Bassong is said to have attempted to use an Oyster card before entering the compulsory ticket area without a valid ticket.

In a witness statement, TfL employee Adebukola Anifowose said: 'I observed Mr Bassong pretend to tap an Oyster card enclosed in a white wallet before tailgating through the wide-aisle gate behind another male.

'When requested to produce the card used at the barrier, Mr Bassong presented a Transport for London Staff Nominee Pass without the required accompanying photocard.

'System checks later confirmed that the pass did not belong to him and had last been used in October 2025.'

Sebastien Bassong pictured after scoring for Tottenham Hotspur against Liverpool in 2009

The witness said checks established that the pass had been registered to an acquaintance.

Mr Anifowose added: 'No valid ticket was shown for being in the compulsory ticket area. The fare avoided was £7.'

Bassong, who lives in north London, was reportedly required to respond to the charge by September 15 but has failed to do so.

The allegations come years after Bassong made a name for himself in the Premier League, having moved to Newcastle from French club Metz in 2008.

He moved to Tottenham the following year in a deal reported at the time to be worth £8million and became part of the Spurs side that qualified for the Champions League.

The Cameroon international scored on his Tottenham debut against Liverpool and later netted in the club's Champions League qualifying victory over Swiss team Young Boys.

Bassong made 71 appearances for Tottenham before leaving for Norwich City in 2012.

He also spent time on loan at Wolves and Watford before establishing himself at Norwich, where he spent five years and captained the Canaries.

Bassong later joined Peterborough United in 2018 before moving to Greek side Volos, where his playing career ended later that year.

His career included 19 appearances for Cameroon, and he has since worked as a football pundit.

The Daily Mail has approached Bassong for further comment. TfL declined to comment.

Sports.title: Pep Guardiola was convinced Man City were innocent and used that sense of injustice to motivate his stars. Now he will have some awkward questions to ask his bosses with doubts being raised over his era of dominance, writes JACK GAUGHAN
Sports.content:
Pep Guardiola was convinced Man City were innocent and used that sense of injustice to motivate his stars. Now he will have some awkward questions to ask his bosses with doubts being raised over his era of dominance, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Pep Guardiola always counted the Community Shield as a trophy and for that there was only one reason. It’s legacy. His legacy in English football. His legacy at Manchester City.

There will be mounting questions and debate about what that means and looks like now, in the wake of the extraordinary verdict handed down by an independent commission.

For a large majority, City’s defeat in their case with the Premier League means more than just an asterisk next to any achievement over a nine-year period from 2009. It will mean that the trophies simply are not recognised, whether City are ultimately stripped of them or not.

And it doesn’t stop there. While the charges cover up to 2018, the wider argument is that Guardiola’s dominance was built on cheating. Cheating he will not have been privy to but a financial leg-up of attracting better players under Roberto Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini that in turn accelerated the football club and allowed the Catalan to prosper.

Without the early trophies, the 2012 title, it’s arguable whether even Txiki Begiristain could have convinced Guardiola to join.

So the whole lot will be lumped in. The six Guardiola league titles, the Champions League, three FA Cups, five Carabaos, a Club World Cup, a Super Cup and yes, those three Community Shields.

Pep Guardiola won the lot with Manchester City - but his achievements will now forever be tarnished

Guardiola has always publicly insisted City's innocence, based on conversations with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak

That is irrespective of the appeal that City will launch and its end result. City and Guardiola’s success has always been muddy in the court of public opinion and Friday’s news only solidifies that further.

Whatever happens from here, there is no coming back from the entrenched viewpoints, no grey area. The success will be forever tarnished for those who always believed in their guilt.

Guardiola’s next move will be fascinating, in what he says and where he’s spotted. There is a stand named after him at the Etihad Stadium, a statue on its way. He is a City Football Group ambassador and one who has always publicly insisted their innocence.

Insisted it based on conversations with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and chief executive Ferran Soriano – the latter's family are understood to have moved back to Spain earlier this year.

These are people he likes, people he trusts. People who convinced him to stay in Manchester far longer than initially planned. In an ironic twist, the charges actually helped in that regard, elongating their partnership.

The battles with the Premier League and before that, UEFA, had Guardiola subscribing to the world according to City and produced moments that spoke to that – like in February 2023, when the charges dropped, quoting Julius Caesar to underline what he felt was a betrayal by other top-flight clubs and claiming that the club had already been condemned.

He fumed at the assumption of guilt, he name-checked Daniel Levy, he sarcastically said they’d bring Paul Dickov and Mike Summerbee out of retirement when relegated.

‘It’s the same as with UEFA,’ Guardiola said. ‘The same articles, the same accusations. You need to go to League One. No, no, League One is too much. League Two. Or maybe the Conference. We were in Maine Road, we are not with a history of lots of titles. We’ve been in those divisions, we will be back there.’

Listening to Guardiola in those moments was like listening to any executive at City. And he’s not one to toe the party line if he doesn’t believe in it – as evidenced amid fan protests against ticket prices in recent years.

While the developments had no bearing on his players, he used this sense of perceived injustice to motivate himself to reel in Arsenal to win that title, to do the Treble.

He fumed at the assumption of guilt, he name-checked Daniel Levy, he sarcastically said they’d bring Paul Dickov and Mike Summerbee out of retirement when relegated

‘I’m not moving from this seat,’ he said – almost chillingly – that afternoon. ‘I… can… assure… you. More than ever I want to stay.’

Eventually he did, claiming a lack of energy and the realisation that City needed fresh ideas.

In fairness to him, he had remained in situ waiting for an outcome for more than long enough. He will believe that nothing happening away from the pitch should impact the glory constructed by his players, by Kevin De Bruyne and David Silva and Vincent Kompany and Erling Haaland but equally he knows that it must.

Guardiola initially insisted that he would walk if it transpired that City’s hierarchy had lied to him but behind the scenes he had quickly become convinced that they would have little to answer in front of legal experts. What the brushes did was bind Guardiola and City even tighter.

It formed a militance within Guardiola, who had been incandescent on the day of their 2019 FA Cup final victory at a question effectively alleging that he had received off-the-book payments from his employers.

This is a guy who once privately told his players that Europe’s referees were all against them in the Champions League to provoke a response, so the idea he used the boardroom pitchforks as motivation to slowly raise a big middle finger is only logical.

City certainly do not rewrite history in lifting four consecutive league titles without Guardiola. They likely do not complete the Treble without Guardiola. He would not have stayed to see out a decade, either.

City certainly do not rewrite history in lifting four consecutive league titles without Guardiola. They likely do not complete the Treble without Guardiola

No manager who coaches footballers to play in the way City did for so many years ought to be at the centre of such murk. And yet, here they are

But he will have questions of those he has formed bonds with within the hierarchy, whose own reputations will be sullied by this affair. Even as recently as last week, those right at the top, led by Al Mubarak and Soriano, were projecting an air of calm.

‘Once we have a ruling, believe me, we're going to have a wonderful sit down together and I'll say everything I've wanted to say for the last three years,’ Al Mubarak said in an interview at the end of last season. Not exactly the words of a man worried for the immediate future.

There will be awkward conversations going on about the last 10 years. It’s leaving supporters in a state of flux and should have the most decorated manager in their history feeling conflicted too.

No manager who coaches footballers to play in the way City did for so many years ought to be at the centre of such murk. And yet, here they are.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel raps Cole Palmer for 'missing way too many camps': Three Lions boss casts doubt on Chelsea star's desire to play for his country after latest withdrawal
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel raps Cole Palmer for 'missing way too many camps': Three Lions boss casts doubt on Chelsea star's desire to play for his country after latest withdrawal

Thomas Tuchel has cast doubt on Cole Palmer’s desire to play for his country.

Tuchel said ahead of Saturday's Nations League game against world champions Spain at Wembley ‘everybody is desperate to come’ and represent England.

But when it was suggested that Palmer’s decision to withdraw from the squad despite playing 90 minutes for Chelsea last Friday appeared to suggest otherwise, Tuchel said: ‘It’s hard to argue against what you are saying.’

Asked where it leaves Palmer and what advice he would give him were he his friend, Tuchel added: ‘It leaves us with Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers, Morgan Gibbs-White and Eberechi Eze in that position.

‘All in camp. All desperate to be here. All available. And all ready to go, ready to stop a holiday [like Gibbs-White] after one day in Dubai.

‘I am not his friend. I am his national team coach and I can only judge him on what he is delivering for the national team and he is just missing too many opportunities.’

England manager Thomas Tuchel (right) has berated Cole Palmer (left) for missing 'too many camps' with the Three Lions

Palmer is one of five players to withdraw from Tuchel’s squad ahead of a four-game fortnight that also sees England face Czechia home and away and Croatia away.

The England coach does not doubt that Palmer is carrying an injury, as are Declan Rice and Manchester United duo Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo.

Tuchel also stressed that the door is not closed on any player, saying he was ‘not worried’ about the issue.

Equally, he pulled no punches when it comes to the Chelsea player’s future opportunities.

‘My understanding is that Cole plays with discomfort and pain and he cannot compete on the highest level with discomfort and pain, so he withdrew and informed us and Chelsea informed us,’ Tuchel explained.

‘He misses too many opportunities, and I don't blame him for it. It's just the fact. He misses way too many camps with injuries and I only want to rely on what I personally witness and what I see within my team, and for that you have to be in camp.

‘If you're not in camp, there's a next level to impress that you cannot achieve because you only can do it when you're actually with me on the pitch and with us on the pitch so, yeah, it is a missed opportunity.

‘What sticks with me is the week that I have with the others.

Tuchel stressed that Palmer is missing too many opportunities, while acknowledging that he is carrying an injury

‘They [the absentees] lose that. That sticks. It sticks because we create something.

‘We actually work off the field, on the field, about our principles, on how to be in.

‘This brotherhood is so important and you miss out if you’re not there.’

Tuchel’s England face a huge test against the world and European champions on Saturday night and knows he needs a good performance from his team after the disappointment of the semi-final defeat to Argentina in the summer’s World Cup.

But he has questioned the wisdom of the four-game international break imposed by world governing body FIFA, suggesting it will ask too much of players not yet fully recovered from the World Cup.

‘I am not in favour of it,’ he said.

‘After a long tournament, to have another long period together is very demanding emotionally and physically for the players. They played the tournament until the very last day and struggled to decompress and then have no pre-season,

‘I think the players would have loved three short windows as normal. I really struggle.

‘I can hardly think of a period in club football where you have matches and a turnaround like we have now.

The England boss confirmed the recalled Trent Alexander-Arnold is fighting with Jarrell Quansah to start at right back

‘We have Saturday-Tuesday and then another Saturday-Tuesday, so only two days twice in between each game. That sounds just too condensed.

‘I watched yesterday a match between Netherlands and Germany and I think after 36 minutes there were already three players injured.’,

Tuchel will field his strongest possible team tonight as he will throughout the next week and a half.

With Real Madrid defender Trent Alexander-Arnold back in the squad for the first time in a year, Tuchel said he is in a straight fight with former Liverpool team-mate Jarell Quansah – now at Bayer Leverkusen – for a start at right-back.

‘He fights with Jarell for the position,’ he said.

‘Jarell played for us in the USA so that’s the competition.

‘Trent is up for it. We have had some very good training sessions and he has very much been part of that.

‘He will get his chance to take back the shirt.’

With so much talk about style of play in the days since Tuchel announced his squad, the German tried to simplify it ahead of tonight’s game. If his players can take their training performances on to the field of play, he believes they can compete with anybody.

‘If you remember my interview after the Norway game at the World Cup, I'm the first advocate to say we need to play better and I don't say it just to be grumpy or make a point,’ Tuchel said.

‘I say it because I see us. I see us train, I see the quality, I see the build-up play in training through the World Cup and I see yesterday,

‘So, yeah, we're working on that translation onto the pitch. I get it, it's training and then it's matches. It takes another step to get there.

‘We need a complete performance and we want to prove a point.

‘I don’t see the point of trying to copy Spain. The copy can’t be better than the original.

‘But that doesn’t mean we can’t learn from them.’

Sports.title: Man City face RELEGATION 'nuclear option' and appeal 'highly unlikely to succeed', says their former financial advisor, as they are found guilty of 114 Premier League charges
Sports.content:
Former Manchester City financial advisor Stefan Borson has claimed 'anything is possible,' including the nuclear option of relegation, after the club were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. The Premier League accused the club of widespread financial cheating over an era of sustained success – with an independent panel hearing concluding in 2024. There has since been a frustrating wait for a verdict but Daily Mail Sport sources have disclosed that clubs have been informed that the panel has now reached a decision – and there is a belief it's a win for the top flight. City are understood to have been found guilty on all but one of their 115 rule-break charges concerning the Premier League’s financial regulations. Borson, who advised Man City between 2002 and 2007, was asked by talkSPORT whether the nuclear option of relegation from the Premier League was on the table as a possible punishment following the decision. 'Anything is possible and all hell is now going to break loose, as this is going to go on for weeks and weeks and weeks,' Borson said. Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of their 115 Premier League rule-break charges Former Man City financial advisor Stefan Borson believes 'anything is possible' regarding the club's potentinal punishments and that an appeal is 'hihgly unlikely to succeed' The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation 'It is going to be very hard for City to say anything or to contain the fallout from this scenario and that is without being able to see what is in this decision. 'We will almost certainly soon see the decision of the independent commission laid out in great detail, it will give people huge ammunition to attack those individuals and the club. 'Then we will go into the process, which will be behind closed doors, around the sanction. 'Man City have denied everything all the way through, they have gone through a process that may have cost more than £100m between the two parties and they have been found to have breached everything. 'They are in very, very serious trouble.' An appeal from Man City is considered inevitable with the club having always strongly denied wrongdoing, since they were charged in February 2023 by the Premier League. A Manchester City spokesperson said: 'The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023. 'The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.' Borson claimed an appeal from Man City is 'highly unlikely to succeed' and suggested their statement indicated their likely arguments in an attempt to overturn the verdict. 'An appeal on the facts is highly unlikely to succeed,' he said. The club have maintained that they are innocent throughout the process and are expected to appeal 'Where we are now with City being found guilty of more or less everything, the decision itself will be scathing in terms of the club’s conduct, the conduct of individuals, the behaviour of individuals and the hearing itself in terms of their credibility. There won’t be any hiding place when that decision is published. 'To then have to present that to an appeal that does not have the benefit of listening to the whole case all over again, in terms of witness evidence, seeing all the documentation again, it is going to be extremely difficult for City to overturn those factual findings. ‘City have hinted in the last paragraph of their statement, I think their suggestion is that the process and panel itself was in some way partial and biased and that they will in some way challenge the length of time it has taken for the decision to come out. 'All of those sorts of arguments, be it bias or something procedural, all of them are very unlikely to succeed. Overturning factual findings I would say is very, very unlikely. 'Ultimately now I think City will have to take their punishment and it will be severe.' The Premier League accused Man City of multiple breaches of financial rules and of failing to co-operate with a subsequent investigation. The alleged rule breaking was claimed to have taken place over a 14-year period. A three-man panel was tasked with considering the evidence, with the initial expectation a verdict would have been reached on the case within months. It has since taken three-and-a-half years. The original 115 charges were extended to a total of 130 after an administration issue in what is the most expensive and wide-ranging case in English football history. Eight Premier League titles, three FA Cups, six League Cups and one Champions League have all been won by the club in the modern era City remained steadfast in maintaining their innocence over more than 115 alleged breaches across eight years, some including the start of the Pep Guardiola era. The club were accused of failing to report accurate financial information for nine seasons stretching from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as failing to provide full details of former manager Roberto Mancini’s pay between 2009-10 and 2012-13. They were also alleged to have failed to provide full details of money paid to players between 2010-11 and 2015-16 and failing to co-operate with the probe from 2018 to 2023. Between the years mentioned, Manchester City won eight Premier League titles, a Champions League, four FA Cups, and seven EFL Cups. City vehemently denied any breaches of financial rules but the investigation started in December 2018 after German website Der Spiegel published documents from a Football Leaks cache which had originated from Portuguese hacker Rui Pinto. It alleged that City had overstated sponsorship income with money paid from the club's owners instead of sponsors linked to Abu Dhabi. Roberto Mancini's wages were said to have doubled via a secret contract with an Abu Dhabi club when he was at Man City, while they were also alleged to have broken rules over approaching young players. The Mail on Sunday has led the way on reporting the story. In July 2021, they reported on emails that appeared to suggest that Man City had millions funnelled into the club by Abu Dhabi to help inflate their income. Back in February 2020, the club were banned from the Champions League and fined £25million after they were found to have seriously misled European footballing governing body UEFA and broken financial fair play rules. This was then lifted by the Court of Arbitration for Sport which also reduced the club's fine to £9million.

Sports.title: Morgan Rogers jokes he is glad to have a 'break' from Cole Palmer after Chelsea team-mate withdrew from England squad - as £117m man targets 'bigger stamp' on Three Lions games
Sports.content:
Morgan Rogers jokes he is glad to have a 'break' from Cole Palmer after Chelsea team-mate withdrew from England squad - as £117m man targets 'bigger stamp' on Three Lions games

While Thomas Tuchel is frustrated that Cole Palmer is missing for England, Morgan Rogers is relieved, joking it is nice that his Chelsea mate is not burdening him with his company for once.

‘I'm all right having the break from him, to be honest,’ Rogers says, smiling upon the mention of Palmer. ‘Being around him 24-7 can be quite tough, so having the break is quite nice.’

He is kidding, of course. He and Palmer are best pals, share the same celebration, and have been combining for fun for Chelsea, albeit not for England against Spain at Wembley on Saturday.

‘I love playing with Cole,’ Rogers continues on Palmer, who withdrew from England duty citing a minor muscular complaint. ‘I love being around him. Unfortunately, he couldn't be here, but he's got to focus on his body. He needs to be in a good physical state.

‘Obviously, as a nation, you want Cole Palmer and players like that in an English shirt, but it's not what is possible with the games and what we've got coming up. You have to manage yourself, especially after what he went through last year, he doesn't want to go through that again.’

Rogers wants to show England why they can rely on him at least, with the 24-year-old aiming to prove he can be a £117million player for his country as well as his club. That record-breaking transfer fee for a British player came with an immediate increase in expectations.

Morgan Rogers joked he was happy to have a few days after from Chelsea team-mate and best friend Cole Palmer, who pulled out of the England squad with a minor muscle problem

For Chelsea, he says it has been a ’10 out of 10’ start in how he is feeling.

‘Ten!’ Rogers says when asked for a rating. ‘I've enjoyed it. I'm happy. I'm enjoying my football. I'm feeling as good as I've ever felt playing, contributing, scoring, assisting, creating chances. I feel as good as I ever have done so far in my career. So why would it not be a 10?

‘It's been challenging at times. Obviously, a good start, and then it tailed off a bit at the end, which is disappointing. But that's football, and I just can't wait to get going and keep going.’

For England, he realises fans may desire more from him. Rather than leaving it to Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham, one of Rogers’ aims is to show he is reliable in front of goal, too.

‘People are going to look at me differently,’ he says of his £117m move to Chelsea. ‘People are going to judge me on probably a higher pedestal of what I'm delivering.

‘For me, I can't get too bogged down in that. I can't control how people view me. I just want to give positive performances for my country and to achieve something special with my country, which is something I've wanted to do ever since I started playing football, and to be here now, I don't want that to pass me by. I want to show what I'm about. That comes with a bit of pressure.

‘I think I'm definitely in a better stead now to make a bigger stamp on England games and be more important in England games and in big games.'

Rogers still speaks of his love for Villa. Explaining why he chose to sign for Chelsea, he says: ‘I feel like I want to be seen as one of the best players in the Prem, one of the best players in the world, and I feel like to do so, I needed to take that next step and that next chapter.

Rogers is determined to become more influential in England matches after his big money move to Chelsea

'I need to play with the best players in the world and compete with the best players in the world and be on that bigger stage. I just feel Chelsea brings that different level of pressure of having to win and having to perform each game. When they come in and there is an opportunity for me to go there, it's mind-boggling to think that I can be part of that history of that club. I'm so excited by the prospect of doing something special at that club.’

As well as Palmer, Declan Rice is not in this England camp, though Rogers says there is no bad blood between them after what happened during Arsenal’s 2-1 Premier League win over Chelsea. Rice got away with tripping Rogers rather cynically. Rogers was booked for his angry reaction.

‘It's just competitors competing and wanting to win,’ he says. ‘London derby, me getting absolute dog’s abuse by the fans doesn’t help! All emotions come into one at that moment, but Dec and I are fine. We spoke about it after the game. We're completely fine.

'It's actually a good thing – showing that we put friendships aside and just want to win for our clubs and do what it takes. Sometimes tempers rise a little, but it's all good.'

Sports.title: OLIVER HOLT: Strip Man City of ALL eight of their Premier League titles and relegate them for their defrauding of Man United and Liverpool's history. English football is broken irretrievably and will never be the same again
Sports.content:
Nothing will ever be quite the same again in English football. On the last Friday in September 2026, something broke irretrievably in our game. Something was ruined. Something was lost. Please don't laugh too bitterly at this, but this was the day when the last of our innocence slunk away into the corner and stood against the wall, its head bowed.

When the news emerged that Manchester City had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations, it plunged the game into a pit of fire and a world of recriminations and repercussions that may redraw much of the recent history of the top flight.

This is our Calciopoli Scandal that rocked Italian football in 2006 and relegated the mighty Juventus to Serie B, this is our equivalent of the bribery and match fixing scandal that defrocked Marseille in 1993, this is our Black Sox Scandal that surrounded the fixing of the 1919 World Series. It is a bleak, bleak day for the English game.

Say it Ain't So, Pep. Say that none of this is true. Because, one of the greatest sadnesses of all in these guilty verdicts is that they tarnish the achievements in this country of Pep Guardiola, one of the greatest coaches that has ever lived. They tarnish everything that City have achieved since they were taken over by Abu Dhabi. They have brought the whole edifice crumbling down.

But it is not the greatest sadness. The greatest sadness is in the cost to fans of so many other rival clubs who were cheated of what they should have won. City's dishonesty robbed them of moments that would have lasted a lifetime. It robbed them of celebrations with friends that they would never have forgotten. It robbed them of days out that would have been forever bathed in sunshine.

Sir Alex Ferguson would have won 14 league titles, not 13, if City had not evaded the rules. Steven Gerrard's domestic career with Liverpool would not have been defined by that slip against Chelsea in 2013-14 because Liverpool would have won the title. Manchester United would not still be wandering in a post-Ferguson wasteland because they would have won the title in 2017-18 under Jose Mourinho.

Pep Guardiola and Man City club chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak celebrate their 2024 title

Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool were among those beaten by City in the wake of their dishonesty

And Liverpool, not City, would have won one of the greatest title races of all time in 2018-19. And Jurgen Klopp and not Guardiola would have emerged victorious in that battle and history may have come to regard him as the greatest manager of the era that followed Ferguson instead.

Klopp's Liverpool came second to City in both the 18-19 and 21-22 title races by a solitary point. When he was asked after his departure in 2024 about the possibility of City being stripped of those titles, Klopp said: 'If you organise a bus parade, I am in. How long it takes I don't care.' That day may be coming sooner than he thought.

So the heartbreak lies in what others have lost as much as in the iniquity of what City gained. It lies in the defrauding of history and the way we were manipulated. City were a magnificent team to watch under Guardiola. Perhaps the best our league has ever seen. But that doesn't count for much anymore. Our eyes might as well have been scratched out. Our memories mean nothing now.

Some will say it is a great victory for the Premier League and, yes, it has established its authority over its member clubs and, yes, the alternative to winning this legal battle was unthinkable for it.

But the 'triumph' should make it question its direction of travel. This is a win for the Premier League in one way but in another, it is a catastrophic loss. City, and Guardiola, were its standard-bearers. They were its best team. They set new standards for beauty and quality. Now, it turns out, that was all built on sand. It may be that the league has won a battle but lost a wider war. City are part of the Premier League, too. The league is eating its own.

Everything that City have won since the Abu Dhabi takeover is discredited. Everything feels sullied. All the titles and trophies that were won between 2009 and 2018 are most at risk. The 'Aguerooo' moment from 2012 when City won their first top flight title for 44 years with a last-gasp winner from Sergio Aguero at the Etihad? That is tainted. That is spoiled. That is undermined.

The 'Aguerooo' moment from 2012 when City won their first top flight title is tainted

Jose Mourinho and Manchester United missed out on titles at the hands of Man City

Martin Tyler's greatest moment of commentary has been muted. The greatest moment in Premier League history? Not any more, it isn't. It may, in fact, come to be seen as a symbol of one of the most cursed eras in our national sport.

The guilty verdicts mean that City were playing by different rules to everybody else. And whatever you think of the rules, others respected them and so City should have done. The verdicts say they ignored the rules, that they manipulated the funds available to them unfairly. The verdicts say they had an unfair advantage. The verdicts say they cheated.

And so everything they achieved in those years is invalidated. And because those years provided the foundation upon which everything else was built, then everything that followed in the unparalleled success of the Pep Guardiola years is besmirched, too. No one is saying Guardiola knew what had passed before, of course, but he was an unwitting beneficiary of it.

And so what do we say now of the four top flight titles in a row that Guardiola's side won between 2020-21 and 2023-24? No other had done that in the long history of English football. That should have been Guardiola's greatest legacy but it turns out it was built on the shifting sands of the dishonesty of those that came before him. In a way, he too has been betrayed.

What now? Asterisks are not enough. The very least that should happen is that City be stripped of the titles they won in 2012, 2014, 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024. That scenario is said to be 'unlikely'. It should not be. The very least that should happen is that they be relegated from the Premier League and made to start next season in the Championship.

They will appeal, of course, and so that will protect their participation in the Premier League for the rest of this season and perhaps beyond. But if that appeal is unsuccessful, they should be cast out of the top flight. The entire credibility of English football is at stake here. If they escape with a lesser punishment, credibility will be lost.

The unparalleled success of the Pep Guardiola years at Man City is besmirched, too

The guilty verdicts should also make English football pause and take a long, hard look at itself. The Premier League can celebrate its victory but it has become a place where owners have declared war on clubs' long-standing fans in their desire to maximise revenue and destroy tradition.

It should make the league look again at its willingness to allow nation-states to own its football clubs, as is currently the case with City and Newcastle United. The power that they wield and the fabulous riches they command and the arrogance that seeps from them led directly to the entire 115 charges farrago.

This may be just the beginning for City, too. It is a bleak day for them but it may get worse. The verdict could be a gateway for City's rivals each to claim more than £100million in compensation. I spoke to one high-ranking official at a rival Premier League club recently and he predicted an avalanche of law-suits against City if they were found guilty of the most serious charges.

Anyone who missed out on a Champions League spot because City occupied one of the places, for instance, would be keen to seek redress, he said. A team that finished eighth, say, would want their prize money adjusted to the total it would have been if they had finished seventh. City may be entering a world of pain.

Guardiola was a human shield for the club while he was there because all recognised his talent and the beauty of the teams he produced. Now, when the storm breaks, Guardiola is gone and City are even more defenceless. Some, too, will seek to settle old scores.

Away from the pitch, City have ruled with a mixture of intimidation, obfuscation, charm and public relations expertise. They have sought to bully some sports journalists for reporting the truth. It is not a modus operandi peculiar to them but they have pursued it with vigour and relish.

The verdict could be a gateway for City's rivals each to claim more than £100million in compensation. Liverpool missed out on the title to City in 2014 when Steven Gerrard slipped

Their public relations tactics have been extremely effective. I have spoken to several high-ranking executives at other Premier League clubs who have been bitterly amused by the idea, which City have managed to promulgate, that they are disadvantaged outsiders fighting against a football establishment.

City, we were told, had been targeted by a supposed 'Red Cartel' of Manchester United, Arsenal and Liverpool, so that they could be kept with their noses pressed against the glass. We were told that Financial Fair Play and, later, Squad Cost Ratio rules baked in the superiority of United, Arsenal and Liverpool.

Well, if City are victims, they have been prosperous victims indeed. They have won eight league titles since 2011-12 and one Champions League. They are the fifth most valuable football club in the world. Their majority owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan is the UAE Vice President and Deputy Prime Minister. Outsiders? All these years? Please. Pull the other one.

Outsiders now? It is hard to see how it could be otherwise, for some time at least. City will be regarded as pariahs in the Premier League and beyond. They were, we thought, the best of our game. But now we know that was just an illusion.

Sports.title: Manchester City found guilty on vast majority of their 115 Premier League rule break charges - and could be kicked out of the top flight or face huge points deduction
Sports.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of their rule-break charges concerning the Premier League’s financial regulations, Daily Mail Sport understands.

The competition accused the club of widespread financial cheating over an era of sustained success – with an independent panel hearing concluding in 2024.

There has since been a frustrating wait for a verdict but sources have disclosed that clubs have been informed that the panel has now reached a decision – and there is a belief it's a win for the top flight.

The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation.

Points deductions could even be applied onto previous seasons, raising the chance that City will be stripped of their Premier League titles.

It is inevitable that they will appeal.

Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of their 115 Premier League rule-break charges

The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation

Staff at the City Football Academy learned of the news via Daily Mail Sport and other media reports. There was no official email, with some initially left fearing for their jobs and asking senior managers for an explanation.

'It felt like the club was completely blindsided,' one employee, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told this newspaper.

A Manchester City spokesperson said: 'The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023.

'The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.'

Man City, who have always strongly denied wrongdoing, were charged in February 2023 by the Premier League with a hearing concluding in December 2024.

Their statement that February insisted that they were 'surprised' by the charges.

The Premier League accused Man City of multiple breaches of financial rules and of failing to co-operate with a subsequent investigation. The alleged rule breaking was claimed to have taken place over a 14-year period.

A three-man panel was tasked with considering the evidence, with the initial expectation a verdict would have been reached on the case within months. It has since taken three-and-a-half years.

The original 115 charges were extended to a total of 130 after an administration issue in what is the most expensive and wide-ranging case in English football history.

Manchester United legend Rio Ferdinand was quick to stick the boot in on social media, writing on X: 'Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet.'

The charges stretch from the years 2009 to 2023, encompassing much of the Pep Guardiola era

He was part of the United team who were famously pipped to the title by City on the final day of the 2011-12 season.

City remained steadfast in maintaining their innocence over more than 115 alleged breaches across eight years, some including the start of the Pep Guardiola era.

The club were accused of failing to report accurate financial information for nine seasons stretching from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as failing to provide full details of former manager Roberto Mancini’s pay between 2009-10 and 2012-13.

They were also alleged to have failed to provide full details of money paid to players between 2010-11 and 2015-16 and failing to co-operate with the probe from 2018 to 2023.

Between the years mentioned, Manchester City won eight Premier League titles, a Champions League, four FA Cups, and seven EFL Cups.

In 2022, Guardiola said he would quit the club if he felt the club's hierarchy had ever lied to him. The next year, he said he would not walk out on his deal, even if he was relegated to League One.

Guardiola always insisted he was 'fully convinced' that the club is innocent and said in May: 'I trust them, I trust them. Because I spoke with them and I trust how they behave and how they did.'

City vehemently denied any breaches of financial rules but the investigation started in December 2018 after German website Der Spiegel published documents from a Football Leaks cache which had originated from Portuguese hacker Rui Pinto.

The club have maintained that they are innocent throughout the process and are expected to appeal

It alleged that City had overstated sponsorship income with money paid from the club's owners instead of sponsors linked to Abu Dhabi.

Roberto Mancini's wages were said to have doubled via a secret contract with an Abu Dhabi club when he was at Man City, while they were also alleged to have broken rules over approaching young players.

The Mail on Sunday has led the way on reporting the story. In July 2021, they reported on emails that appeared to suggest that Man City had millions funnelled into the club by Abu Dhabi to help inflate their income.

Back in February 2020, the club were banned from the Champions League and fined £25million after they were found to have seriously misled European footballing governing body UEFA and broken financial fair play rules.

This was then lifted by the Court of Arbitration for Sport which also reduced the club's fine to £9m.

City spent £440million over the summer, equalling the British transfer record by signing Enzo Fernandez for £125million, and their former chairman David Bernstein claimed that 'makes a mockery' of the Premier League's regulation of the top division.

Writing in the Sunday Times, Bernstein said: 'The fact they have done this (transfer spend) against the background of the 115 Premier League charges is extraordinary and makes a mockery of regulation in England's top division, supposedly the best-run league in the world.'

It was a bumper summer for City after the exit of Guardiola. They also signed Elliot Anderson (£116m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£86m), Iliman Ndiaye (£60m), Allan and Geronimo Rulli.

Enzo Maresca insisted that he was not worried about the situation when he became their manager in the summer

Other marquee signings down the years have included Jack Grealish for £100m, Erling Haaland for £51.2m, Josko Gvardiol for £77.6m, and Riyad Mahrez for £60m.

Four Premier League sides had reserved the right to seek compensation in the event City were found guilty.

Speaking to the BBC in August, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters described the case as 'hugely complex' as he defended the length of time taken to reach a conclusion.

'I do accept it is taking longer than expected and I understand that people want to find out as soon as possible what's going on, but I simply can't provide that,' he said.

'The process is the process,' he said. 'It will resolve itself. But as you know, I literally can't say a thing about it. There's only one available option, which is to allow the process to reach its natural conclusion. I can't talk about the substance of the case. I can't talk about the timing of the case. Our rules are very clear about that. I understand that people are frustrated but it will take as long as it takes.'

When Enzo Maresca, Guardiola's former assistant, took the managerial reins in the summer, he insisted that he wasn't worried about the situation.

He said: 'No, no, to be honest (they're not a concern.

'The only thing I can say is that three years ago, the treble season, I was here. And there were the same words about this kind of problem,” Maresca explained.

City spent £440m on players this summer, including a British record-equalling £125m on Enzo Fernandez to secure him from Chelsea

'In three years, it’s still the same, so nothing happened. I don’t have anything to say because it’s something that is there.'

The club have made a stunning start to the season, sitting top of the Premier League with five wins from as many games.

It is perhaps merciful that this decision has arrived towards the start of a three-week international break rather than during the cut and thrust of the domestic season.

The Premier League's latest domestic broadcast deal has seen the amount paid per game fall by around £2.5m.

Some have wondered if that is an indicator that fans are getting fed up of various litigations, with Nottingham Forest, Everton and Leicester City docked points in recent times.
