Federal law enforcement arrested a Senegalese immigrant in New Jersey accused of illegally voting in multiple elections, injecting a new flashpoint into Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill's escalating fights with Washington over immigration enforcement and election integrity.

The case comes as Washington and Trenton battle over immigration enforcement and election administration, with the Trump administration challenging Sherrill over state policies affecting federal law enforcement while also pressing New Jersey for access to its voter rolls.

Sanata Coulibaly, a Senegalese national, was arrested when DHS and FBI agents jointly executed a criminal warrant in Hudson County, which stretches from West New York to Bayonne across the Hudson River from Manhattan.

FOUR NONCITIZENS CHARGED WITH ILLEGALLY VOTING IN 2020, 2022 AND 2024 FEDERAL ELECTIONS IN NEW JERSEY

"This alien from Senegal has been charged with procurement of citizenship or naturalization unlawfully and voting by an alien after allegedly voting in three general elections in New Jersey," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

"Sanctuary politicians can try to claim that this kind of voter fraud isn’t happening, but it’s very real and is a serious threat to our country."

WATCH: TRUMP DOJ VOWS TO PURSUE ‘EVERY SINGLE’ VOTING VIOLATION AFTER NJ ROLL SHOCKER

Mullin said DHS and the Trump administration would continue efforts to protect election integrity.

The arrest comes after Sherrill revealed in July that a software error in New Jersey's motor vehicle system had improperly registered roughly 6,600 people who identified themselves as noncitizens. The state later determined that fewer than 400 of those newly registered because of the error had voted.

After that revelation, New Jersey resisted federal demands to turn over voter rolls while pursuing its own investigation.

Fox News Digital reached out to Sherrill for comment.

According to the criminal complaint, Coulibaly cast ballots in the November 2018 midterm election, the July 2020 primary, the November 2020 general election and the 2024 general election while she was not a U.S. citizen.

Coulibaly registered through a paper application submitted to the Hudson County superintendent of elections in Jersey City, falsely certifying that she was a U.S. citizen, the complaint said.

She first came to the U.S. from Senegal on a B-1 nonimmigrant visa in approximately 1993 and later became a lawful permanent resident, according to the Justice Department.

World.title: Indiana coach Curt Cignetti has message for antsy Hoosiers fans: 'Don’t b---- about a 38-0 win'
World.content:
The natives are starting to get restless in Bloomington, Indiana.

You read that right, folks. Fans of the Indiana Hoosiers, a program that came from literally nothing to reach the pantheon of college football, are a little miffed with how the team has performed early in the season.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The defending national champions have gotten off to a 3-0 start, but the first quarter of their season has been marred by sleepy first half performances against "lesser competition," to put it mildly.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S AP TOP 25 IS OUT: WHO’S OVERRATED, UNDERRATED AND FLAT-OUT SNUBBED?

Wins against North Texas, Howard, and Western Kentucky probably don't move the needle all that much, but the clumsy starts have the Hoosier faithful getting a little antsy as their team heads into Big Ten conference play.

Head coach Curt Cignetti has taken note of this, and decided to issue a personal statement on the matter during his weekly radio hit on Thursday.

"It was hot, and I was hot on the sideline," Cignetti admits when discussing the fans not staying in their seats for the entirety of Indiana's 38-0 win over the Hilltoppers on Saturday.

"What are we, 29-2? When we came, I saw the picture, 10,000 fans in the stands," he fired back. "Don't b---- about a 38-0 win."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

His response elicited plenty of laughs from those in attendance, but Cignetti, as is usually the case, was being dead serious.

And I can't say I blame him.

It's one thing for Alabama fans in year eight or nine of the Nick Saban dynasty to have gotten a little pissy about winning by 38 instead of 58, but this is Indiana we are talking about here.

Three years ago, this fanbase would have thrown a parade for going 8-4 and getting an invite to the Gator Bowl.

COCKY CURT CIGNETTI CALLED OUT THE SEC, BUT HE SHOULD GOOGLE INDIANA'S LAUGHABLE SCHEDULE FIRST

Now we're going to get our red and white striped overalls in a bunch over a 14-0 halftime lead against Western Kentucky?

I get it, that's not where you want to be, and if you play like that against Ohio State or Oregon you are going to get exposed, but have a little faith in The Cig, will you?

If anyone can get things cleaned up, it's him.

I've written exhaustively about how Cignetti is basically the closest thing we have in the game right now to prime Saban, and I mean it.

What he has done and is continuing to do at Indiana is unprecedented.

The Hoosiers are bored and they're playing with their food right now.

That's not something you want to see long term, but if anyone can coach that out of them, it's the man who barely cracked a smile after beating the tar out of everyone in his path en route to a national championship just nine months earlier.

And show a little respect to the man as well.

He's already the greatest coach to ever roam the sidelines of Memorial Stadium by a wide margin, and he's not going to be around forever, so just enjoy the time you have with the guy.

Take it from someone who didn't cherish a legend while he was coaching his team. Someday Cig will retire, and then you will be dreaming of 38-0 wins.

World.title: ‘Wave of freedom’ sweeps Latin America as Trump ally takes fight to Marxist terror group
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

UNITED NATIONS — Colombian Vice President José Manuel Restrepo said his country is embracing President Donald Trump’s push for a new security alliance across the Western Hemisphere, but drew a clear line on the role American forces would play inside Colombia, telling Fox News Digital that Colombian troops — not U.S. forces — will carry out operations against the country’s armed groups.

Restrepo spoke with Fox News Digital in an on-camera interview days after joining Trump and other regional leaders at a Shield of the Americas meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where Trump called the initiative the "largest and most powerful alliance for economic and national security ever to convene in the Western Hemisphere."

Trump urged members to treat what he called "narco terrorists" as common threats and impose sanctions on U.S.-designated terrorist organizations.

Restrepo said he personally discussed the region’s changing political and security landscape with Trump. The shift in Colombia comes amid a broader political realignment across Latin America, with De La Espriella’s June victory adding Colombia to a group of countries including Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia and Panama that have moved to the right, fueled in part by voter concerns over crime, economic weakness and political instability.

TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT

"There is a wave of freedom, a wave of democracy, a wave of free market. … There is a new momentum for the region and we have to take advantage of that momentum. That's what I said to President Trump," Restrepo told Fox News Digital. "If we want to keep and preserve democracy in the region, the Shield of the Americas is going to be the best opportunity to do it."

Asked what Trump told him, Restrepo said the president agreed and expressed respect for Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella.

"Colombia is a new partner. In my opinion, it's one of the most important partners for the United States in the region," Restrepo said.

That partnership is already being tested in the fight against drug trafficking and armed groups.

WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES

In August, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Colombia had authorized "joint military operations to destroy terrorists and terror networks" and told reporters that Washington had discussed possible joint strikes against groups including the National Liberation Army, or ELN, which the U.S. designates as a terrorist organization, and remnants of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia.

"Designated terrorist organizations, with partnered governments, will be legitimate targets of the United States government," including in Colombia, Hegseth said when asked whether such operations were expected, according to Reuters.

But when pressed by Fox News Digital on whether joint U.S.-Colombian strikes remained an option, Restrepo appeared to narrow the scope of direct American involvement.

"The United States helps us on security, helps us information, helps us on technology, but the public forces of Colombia are those who are going to act in those places," he said.

US FORCES OBLITERATE SUSPECTED 'NARCO-TERRORIST' VESSEL IN LETHAL EASTERN PACIFIC STRIKE, KILLING 3

Asked specifically whether Colombia would have the "boots on the ground," Restrepo replied: "We will have our group, our public forces on the ground."

The tougher posture comes as Colombia confronts renewed violence from armed and drug-trafficking groups. This week, De La Espriella ordered the military into Santa Marta after the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada, an illegal armed group involved in drug trafficking, responded to the killing of one of its senior leaders with an "armed strike," threats, roadblocks and attacks that left businesses shuttered and public transportation disrupted. More than 500 soldiers and 600 police officers were deployed, according to the Colombian presidency.

The new government is also seeking to reverse former President Gustavo Petro’s "total peace" policy, which pursued negotiations with several armed organizations. Before taking office, De La Espriella announced that he would dismantle key elements of the policy and reactivate arrest warrants against members of illegal armed groups.

Restrepo went further, accusing the former government of creating "the idea of impunity" and saying the new administration instead intends to confront groups it considers terrorists.

US, SHIELD OF THE AMERICAS CONDEMN 'ONGOING EFFORTS' TO OVERTHROW BOLIVIA'S ELECTED PRESIDENT AMID UNREST

He said that when the new government took office, "around 30%" of Colombia’s regions lacked effective territorial control — a figure Fox News Digital has not independently verified — and said the administration was seeking to regain those areas through stronger security forces, intelligence gathering, drug eradication and extraditions.

Restrepo also argued that the same security debate should extend to the United Nations, where Colombia used its General Assembly address this week to call for reforms and an international definition of terrorism. The UN has had a global counterterrorism strategy since 2006, but member states have for decades failed to agree on a comprehensive international convention defining terrorism.

Colombia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Thursday also announced that the country was suspending all diplomatic relations with Iran.

"This sovereign decision aligns with the pillars guiding the Government's foreign policy regarding national and hemispheric security, as well as the fight against transnational crime, taking into account alleged links between the Iranian government and international terrorist groups and other narcoterrorist groups that threaten the country's security," the Ministry wrote in a statement posted to X.

MELANIA TRUMP’S HOME-COUNTRY LEADER RIPS UN ‘DOUBLE STANDARDS’ AS TRUMP PROMISE IS REVEALED

"I think this is a moment in which the United Nations have to reflect on its own future," Restrepo told Fox News Digital, calling for greater efficiency and effectiveness as well as international agreement on terrorism.

"The only way to attain peace, which is one of the main objectives of the UN, is through confronting terrorism," he said, arguing that countries need greater intelligence sharing, judicial cooperation and coordination.

With Secretary-General António Guterres set to leave office at the end of the year, Restrepo said the transition could offer the institution an opportunity to change.

"I think that the UN has a new moment and the UN has to take advantage of that opportunity," he said.

Restrepo added that the institution also needed to address what he described as the inconsistent application of human rights standards.

"Human rights should apply to all, regardless of political considerations," Restrepo said. "Ideology cannot decide to whom we are going to apply or not human rights."

World.title: Cooper Flagg rookie card makes eye-popping record sale, but is it actually a good investment?
World.content:
Dallas Mavericks forward Cooper Flagg is a superstar, the reigning NBA Rookie of the Year, and his sports card market has been booming. Ever since he burst on the scene at Duke, following being the No. 1 overall high school prospect and a McDonald's All-American, sports fans and media knew he was going to be special.

I, for one, did not believe he was so special that his most sought-after rookie card, the Topps Chrome Update Rookie Debut Patch Auto 1-of-1 in a PSA Gem-Mint 10 grade for both the card and the auto, would become the sixth-most expensive trading card of all time.

The card sold in Fanatics Collect’s September Premier Auction for $8.04 million, amassing 83 bids. The auction ran from September 10 through September 24. A bidding war took place into the early hours of Friday morning, with the card going from $3.5 million to $8.04 million from 9 p.m. ET on Thursday to 2 a.m. ET on Friday. That sale was historic because it became the highest recorded sale for a basketball card featuring a single player.

According to a Fanatics spokesperson, "This is the first class of NBA Debut Patch cards, which saw each rookie wear a patch on their jersey sleeve during their first game which was removed following the game and put into a trading card and signed." The Debut Patch was first introduced in 2021 in Major League Baseball, garnering massive sales like the 2024 Paul Skenes Debut Patch Auto selling for $1.11 Million. It's easily been the most innovative concept the hobby has seen since the logo man, which is a patch of the respective league's logo from a game-worn jersey. It's among the rarest collectibles in the sports card market.

Flagg's card became the 3rd-highest NBA card sale ever, trailing only a pair of dual logoman cards, the 2006–07 Upper Deck Exquisite Collection Dual Logoman Autographs 1-of-1 Michael Jordan and LeBron James, which sold in a private sale for $10 Million and the 2007–08 Upper Deck Exquisite Collection Dual Logoman Autographs 1-of-1 Michael Jordan and Kobe Bryant, which sold in August of 2025 for $12,932,000.

AN ULTRA-RARE COOPER FLAGG TRADING CARD HAS BEEN FOUND, AND THE MAVERICKS ARE PREPARED TO GIVE A LOT FOR IT

It also ranks as the fifth-highest sports card sale, according to Card Ladder. A Mickey Mantle 1952 Topps card sold for $12.6 million at a Heritage auction in 2022, and an ungraded Shohei Ohtani 2026 Topps Chrome Gold Logoman patch autograph card, famously fetched $11 million on July 30 in a private sale to Kevin O'Leary and the investment group Secure Collectibles.

In a statement by Fanatics, the company said, "The Cooper Flagg card was famously pulled in a break done by Rhody Breakers in Rhode Island, and belonged to collector Jason Williams of South Carolina."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Jason Williams, 50, acquired the card after spending only $515 to land a spot on Rhody Breakers. For those who don't know, buying a spot in a "break" is where a customer purchases a team and/or player (spot) for an amount set by the specific breaker on a livestream, where the retailer opens a box(es) of sports cards, with the customer hoping to pull a life-changing card, an auto, or numbered card. It's a gamble. There was no guarantee Williams would even get a card(s) totaling that $515 spot purchase.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Speaking of gambles, this is the biggest gamble I have ever seen in the hobby (as the sports card collecting market is affectionately known). Is Cooper Flagg a generational talent? In some ways, yes, but the jury is still out and only time will tell if he is truly one of the greatest basketball players of all time. He's a No. 1 overall pick, fresh off a solid rookie season, but in my opinion, he's going to need to win an MVP and a championship soon if this buyer wants to see a solid return on the investment.

Many of the biggest names in the NBA, who have a proven track record, have cards I would find much more enticing to purchase. I believe Steph Curry is undervalued, LeBron James is a certified NBA legend, who owns many NBA records, with cards I'd happily purchase over this.

If I had $8 Million, here's what I would buy instead:

1909-11 T206 Honus Wagner

2003-04 Exquisite LeBron James RPA /23

1952 Topps Mickey Mantle PSA 9

2009-10 National Treasures Stephen Curry Logoman Auto 1/1

1998 Pikachu Illustrator PSA 9

1999 1st Edition Charizard PSA 10

1997 Upper Deck Ultimate Collection Ultimate Logos Auto 1/1

A few 1986 Fleer Michael Jordan rookie cards PSA 10

I could put a long list together, but I would much rather spend money on a tried and true sports legend, or a vintage Pokemon card, rather than gamble with losing millions on a potential NBA legend. But hey, I'm not the one with $8 million to blow, so to the buyer, this could just be pocket change.



Either way, this sale is a great thing for Flagg's card market, shows that sports cards are becoming more enticing than stocks in many ways, and the additional sales of debut patch autos, including San Antonio Spurs star Dylan Harper’s card selling for $2.88 million and Hornets' sharpshooter Kon Knueppel’s Debut Patch card selling for $2.34 million, are incredibly impressive as well.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

More than anything, congratulations to Jason Williams on the life-changing payday.

World.title: Michigan college president urges 'it's incumbent upon' higher education leaders to lower tuition every year
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Higher education leaders must lower tuition costs as Syracuse University faces questions over its nearly $100,000 annual cost of attendance, Adrian College President Dr. Jeffrey Docking told Fox News Digital.

"I think it's incumbent upon us as college presidents and institutions to say, 'Can we start to turn the dial back and lower costs every year for students?' And I think we can do that if we work together," Docking told Fox News Digital.

"The Syracuse University situation is simply a bellwether for the structural crisis facing higher education nationally," Docking said. "It's no different than at most private institutions — many regional publics as well."

Docking, who has served as president of Michigan-based Adrian College for more than 20 years, previously made headlines when he testified before Congress about innovation and lowering costs in higher education. He co-authored the book "Crisis in Higher Education: A Plan to Save Small Liberal Arts Colleges in America" and is credited with doubling Adrian College's enrollment since taking the helm in 2005.

ICE DROPS ‘UNCONTROLLED’ FRAUD BOMBSHELL INVOLVING THOUSANDS OF FOREIGN STUDENTS, ‘PHANTOM EMPLOYEES’

Docking was reacting to a Wall Street Journal report detailing Syracuse University's steep enrollment and financial challenges. The Central New York-based institution is saddled with nearly $500 million in debt tied to new residence halls and is facing a 1.5% budget shortfall as it struggles to attract enough students to cover its operational costs.

"The problem with Syracuse is that the school thinks of itself as like an Ivy, but it’s not," former Syracuse University Center for International Services Director Juan Tavares told The Wall Street Journal.

The Journal reported that in 2025, those underlying weaknesses collided with a high-profile federal crackdown on student visas, causing Syracuse's international enrollment numbers for both undergraduate and graduate programs to plummet by half. Syracuse also failed to meet its overall enrollment targets, forcing the school to issue emergency financial-aid packages to attract incoming freshmen.

FOX NEWS POLL: FAITH IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE US IS COLLAPSING

As students and families increasingly question the return on investment of a college degree, Syracuse increased its tuition to $69,180 for the current academic year—up from $40,458 in the 2013-14 school year. When factoring in room, board, fees and other expenses, the university's total cost of attendance can reach $98,544.

Fox News Digital reached out to Syracuse University for comment.

Rising college costs have coincided with total U.S. student loan balances reaching $1.65 trillion, according to data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

SKIP TWO YEARS OF COLLEGE DEBT AND GIVE YOUR FAMILY A LIFETIME OF WEALTH

Docking called for a total "re-engineering of higher education" to address the crisis.

"[Syracuse is] falling victim to the perfect storm that's out there with international enrollment being down, people questioning the value of higher education, and the fact that many schools are dealing with declining high school graduation rates — especially in northern states," Docking said.

"There's nothing wrong with Syracuse University. It's a fantastic place and will remain fantastic," he added. "But they are just victims of what needs to be a re-engineering of American higher education in the years ahead."

Syracuse University Chancellor and President J. Michael Haynie acknowledged the shortfall, insisting that higher ed leaders must re-evaluate their value proposition to students and families.

I’M A UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT. TRUMP IS RIGHT TO MAKE COLLEGES DELIVER FOR STUDENTS

Docking also co-founded Rize Education, a course-sharing platform that allows smaller colleges to collaborate and offer online classes without incurring massive overhead expenses. Through its partnership with Rize, Adrian College has added 27 majors, 13 minors, and eight certificates in high-demand fields like business, technology, engineering, and healthcare.

His efforts earned him an invitation to testify before the House Education and Workforce Committee and helped Adrian College earn a spot among U.S. News & World Report’s "Most Innovative Regional Universities in the Midwest" for three consecutive years.

Docking argued that soaring tuition is driven by operational inefficiency and an insular culture that prevents institutions from working together like private-sector businesses. By sharing faculty across institutions via course-sharing, schools can bypass the hefty costs of hiring new full-time faculty.

"Higher education institutions traditionally have been very inefficient. They've been very insular. They've not worked well together to drive down costs," Docking concluded. "The re-engineering has to be a massive effort to bring efficiency to existing institutions."

World.title: Conflicting court rulings leave Missouri’s congressional map in limbo
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A fast-moving fight over whether Missouri Republicans can use a redrawn congressional map for this fall’s midterm elections was cast into chaos on Tuesday with two different courts issuing conflicting rulings.

In one, the U.S. Supreme Court, in an order issued by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, left in place a Missouri Supreme Court ruling from last week that said the map could not be used while a ballot initiative that could lead to voters rejecting the newly drawn district lines moves forward. Kavanaugh handles emergency requests that arise from Missouri.

But soon after, a federal judge in Missouri ruled in favor of two GOP congressional candidates who argue that the new map, which was in place for the August primaries, must be used in November in order to avoid federal constitutional violations. That case could also quickly face U.S. Supreme Court scrutiny with time running out for the map to be finalized. The state’s deadline to finalize ballots was 5 p.m local time, and first ballots are set to go out Sept. 19.

Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe and Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, both Republicans, said on X Tuesday evening that the redrawn map would be used for the November election.

The two cases raise different legal issues, with the Missouri Supreme Court focused only on state law while the federal case raises questions under the U.S. Constitution.

The 2025 Republican redistricting plan, part of a wave prompted by President Donald Trump, was designed to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

If the Missouri Supreme Court ruling remains in effect, a map drawn in 2022, with six Republican-held seats and two Democratic-held seats, would be in place for the general election.

The new lawsuit was filed by Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the district currently held by Cleaver, as well as Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo. and two voters.

The legal clash erupted after the 2025 redistricting plan was enacted.

A group called People Not Politicians Missouri, led by Richard von Glahn, gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would veto the Legislature’s map and put it on hold for the 2026 election.

But Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, refused to put the measure on the ballot, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to being overturned by voters.

The Missouri Supreme Court found that Hoskins should not have rejected the plan, unanimously concluding there is nothing in state law that says redistricting plans are exempt from the referendum process.

The referendum petition was “legal, sufficient and timely,” the court found.

Under state law, whenever a proposed ballot initiative that overrides the Legislature is deemed valid, the law is automatically put on hold until after the people vote on it.

The court also said any confusion caused by its ruling was a result of Hoskins’ delay in deciding whether the referendum could move forward. Hoskins waited until the last minute to reject the proposal ahead of an Aug. 4 deadline and broke with the state’s typical process of putting a law facing a veto referendum on hold when enough signatures are submitted.

In the separate federal case, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, ruled that the state must use the map that people voted in during the primary. Using the old map would violate the rights of candidates under the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause and the provision of the Constitution that outlines how members of the House are elected, he found.

Hoskins argued at the Supreme Court that the state court ruling violated the U.S. Constitution’s elections clause, which he said delegates significant powers to state legislatures in overseeing elections. The Supreme Court rejected a similar argument in a redistricting case from North Carolina in 2023.

Hoskins’ lawyers told the justices that the state court ruling had created chaos because the new map was used in this year’s primary election. If the state has to revert to the old map, “hundreds of thousands of Missourians will see their votes in the primary election rendered pointless,” they wrote.

Lawyers for the referendum supporters said in court filings that Hoskins was seeking at the Supreme Court a “political victory to which he was never entitled under the Missouri Constitution.”

In May, the Supreme Court rejected a similar attempt by Democrats in Virginia who sought to revive their own congressional map that had been approved by voters. The Virginia Supreme Court had found legal flaws in the process that led to the referendum.

World.title: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use expanded database for potential voter purges
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday permitted the Trump administration to use an expanded federal database containing citizenship information, as the president encourages states to purge people from voter rolls.

The justices, divided 6-3 on ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, granted an emergency request filed by the government after lower courts ruled that the Trump administration’s changes to the database were likely unlawful.

Critics have said the data is unreliable and could lead to U.S. citizens being kicked off the voter rolls.

But the court noted in its unsigned ruling that the National Voter Registration Act bars the broad purging of voter rolls in the weeks leading up to an election, which “limits the potential impact” of the decision this year. States can still make individualized queries about voters.

On the broader legal questions raised in the case, the court said that federal law requires the government to respond to requests from states for information about citizenship.

The lower court injunction “prevents the federal government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court said.

In dissent, liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the government had not done enough to show that the lower court ruling needed to be blocked.

In her view, “the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” she added.

Various groups challenging the plan, led by the League of Women Voters, have argued that it violates several laws, including the Social Security Act and the Privacy Act.

The Supreme Court decision “puts millions of Americans at risk for being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database,” the groups said in a statement.

Conservative who have backed the administration’s efforts to tighten voting laws, welcomed the decision.

The ruling “just makes it easier for states to get federal citizenship data to help them clean up voter rolls,” Jason Snead, executive director of the Honest Elections Project, said in a statement.

The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, known as SAVE, was set up by Congress in 1986 so that government agencies could quickly determine someone’s immigration status when they applied for benefits like Social Security.

The Trump administration expanded SAVE after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in March 2025 that required agencies to take steps to better ensure that only U.S. citizens vote in elections.

The government expanded the database by adding information from the Social Security Administration, which enabled searches using Social Security numbers and allowed officials to do bulk searches.

After states started putting their voter rolls through the newly expanded system, some local officials noticed mistakes; many of the flagged registrants were newly naturalized citizens, according to reporting from ProPublica and The Texas Tribune.

Texas was one of the first states to put its full voter rolls — more than 18 million registrations — through the SAVE database last year. Just three people have been charged with voting illegally as a noncitizen.

A federal judge blocked the Trump administration plan, with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reaching the same conclusion.

In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said that the district court’s ruling “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections” by preventing the government from responding to state requests to verify the citizenship of potential voters.

Opponents argue the expanded database could force bureaucratic obligations on newly naturalized citizens who are asked to prove their citizenship after being flagged by the system.

Noncitizen voting is extremely rare. All states are required to conduct voter roll list maintenance under federal law, and states already have processes to identify any noncitizens who do accidentally make it onto the voter rolls.

World.title: New Jersey’s governor calls on her lieutenant governor to resign over ethics report
World.content:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Thursday evening that she gave Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell “until tomorrow” to resign after an investigation found he had violated state ethics and harassment policy.

“Today, I’m announcing the conclusion and findings of an independent investigation into allegations regarding Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell,” Sherrill wrote on X. “The investigation found that the Lieutenant Governor engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office. I’m calling for his resignation and giving him until tomorrow to do so.”

The state said this month that it had hired a law firm to investigate allegations against Caldwell, a Democrat who was elected on the ticket with Sherrill last year, claiming that he had behaved inappropriately toward women.

Lt. Governor-elect Dale Caldwell speaks during a press conference discussing the transition of Governor-elect Mikie Sherrill, left, to governor in Trenton on Wednesday, Nov. 5, 2025. Julian Leshay Guadalupe / USA Today Network via Reuters file

Sherrill said Caldwell’s “ethical lapses persisted despite multiple warnings and trainings.”

“The substantiated finding of sexual harassment is extremely troubling. I’ve seen firsthand how a hostile culture can undermine everyone’s ability to succeed. It’s insidious and ruptures the trust within an organization,” she said.

Sherrill said that the investigation “fully examined the evidence, followed the facts, and protected everyone’s privacy” and that Caldwell’s resignation “is necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents.”

Lawyers for Caldwell, who has denied the allegations, said in a statement Thursday night that they “strongly disputed the three findings in the investigation,” as its conclusions “go further than the evidence supports.”

“This unnecessarily protracted and one-sided process lacked the requisite due process that should be afforded every citizen of this state,” said Thomas Calcagni, a lawyer for Caldwell.

Calcagni said Caldwell was “not provided a meaningful opportunity to address each of these anonymous allegations or offer readily identifiable witnesses who possessed more pertinent, first-hand knowledge of the events in question.”

The 61-page report found that Caldwell sexually harassed a young female staffer and her friend. Caldwell was also found to have violated state ethics rules for using his office to try to promote a state employee whom he had a romantic relationship with “on multiple occasions,” without disclosing the relationship.

He also violated ethics rules by making a practice of taking personal guests to ticketed events without providing payment or reimbursement for the tickets, the report said.

State Senate Republican Leader Anthony M. Bucco said in a statement Thursday that the investigation’s findings were “deeply disappointing.”

“This situation has gone on for far too long, and if he doesn’t agree to resign, the Legislature should follow the necessary protocols to resolve this matter once and for all,” Bucco said.

Caldwell is only the fourth lieutenant governor in New Jersey history, as the role was established by referendum in 2005. It includes the responsibility of taking over as governor when the governor is away, which Caldwell has done numerous times since the investigation began.

Caldwell is also New Jersey’s secretary of state, overseeing elections, a critical role as the midterm elections approach in November.

World.title: Should you bring iced coffee to a job interview? Question brews generational debate
World.content:
What started as a conversation about job interview tips online escalated into a generational debate over whether it’s taboo to show up with an iced coffee to talk to a potential employer.

The discourse over the caffeinated beverage gained momentum on TikTok this week after a creator, who goes by @caitlinrecruiter on the platform, shared a video in which she said she believes “when you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte that this interview is just a stop on your list of errands for the day.”

“It looks a little too casual to me,” she said in the video, which she posted Sept. 16.

Caitlin Wehniainen, whose profile states she has 16 years of recruiting experience, has just over 1,000 followers on TikTok. But in the last week, her video has been clipped and recirculated by dozens of creators online, who engaged in a heated back-and-forth about whether she’s right.

Wehniainen did not respond to request for comment.

The divide seemed to primarily be between younger and older users — with the former group suggesting Wehniainen’s tip “makes no sense at all” and that such a perspective is archaic.

Others, many who identified as Gen Xers in comments, agreed with Wehniainen, writing that “arguing against this is insane” and telling applicants that they should “save the iced coffee for when you actually get hired.”

By Monday, even the coffee giant Starbucks had taken a side, alluding to the debate in an Instagram post that featured an image of someone holding an iced coffee in one hand and sunglasses and their handbag in the other. “Pulling up to the interview like,” the caption read. Meanwhile, The Coffee Bean and Tea Leaf, another coffee chain, commented on Wehniainen’s video: “We’d hire them on spot...”

The timing of the conversation coincides with a tough job market: Recent college graduates are facing higher unemployment rates than other age groups as it’s becoming more difficult to obtain entry-level jobs, NBC News reported last month. Employers are not looking to add talent, and employed people are not moving to new positions, as a rise in AI continues to threaten jobs.

For Los Angeles-based TikTok creator Esha, who preferred to be identified by only her first name, citing privacy concerns, Wehniainen’s words couldn’t be further from the truth. She was among the many weighing in online, telling her 81,000-plus TikTok followers that “the iced coffee controversy completely misunderstands interviews.”

“Thinking of a job interview as a stop in your day is very normal,” Esha, 22, added in an interview with NBC News, noting that she’s brought iced coffees to several interviews and hasn’t thought twice about it.

“Gen Z had this shift in recent years, where we can still have a life outside of work,” Esha said. “So, like, why am I changing who I am? Why am I missing my coffee for the day for this interview?”

In her video, she elaborated further on her take, saying that “the most easily relatable thing in corporate America is a coffee addiction.”

“Unless you’re like over the age of 30 and you can relate on having kids, and doing stuff with your kids, coffee is the main thing. Everyone’s like, ‘Gotta get that coffee’ ... and finding something personable about a person is so important,” she said. “Like, who is not starting their workday off with a coffee?”

Catherine Fisher, vice president of communications at LinkedIn, said she’s not surprised by the generational divisions when it comes to job etiquette.

“Gen Z is entering this workforce at such a challenging time, it’s such a competitive job market, and to then get judged by bringing an iced coffee just seems like, ‘Have we lost the plot here?’” she said.

That said, Fisher is among the cohort who believes it’s best to skip the iced coffee when headed to an interview.

“Even though I don’t like the answer, I think because everyone is so divided on it, I would be cautious and not bring one,” she said. “You just don’t know who’s on the other side of the interview, so why risk it over something so silly?”

Etiquette expert Thomas Farley, who is known as Mister Manners to his followers online, agreed with the more traditional point of view.

“I think it sends the wrong message in so many respects,” he said. “I think it shows you to be someone who didn’t plan your time accordingly, and you’re multitasking, and that’s not what you should be doing during the interview.”

Farley also warned of the physical pratfalls a coffee could bring.

“There are real practical considerations when you bring a liquid into someone’s office,” he said. “Where does it go? What happens if you spill it?”

While he doesn’t think it should be the deciding factor for any hiring manager, Farley argued candidates should be doing everything in their power to leave a positive impression.

“If it’s between you and three other people, and everyone’s qualifications are more or less equal, and that’s the one thing that potentially sinks your chance to get the job, I think that would be really unfortunate,” he said. “That would be a very expensive $7 cup of iced coffee.”

Still, Gen Zers like Esha are not convinced that bringing the beverage would make or break their job opportunity.

As another TikTok creator put it in their video: “It’s really, really not that serious most of the time.”

World.title: Facebook found liable of deceiving users in Cambridge Analytica case
World.content:
A New Mexico jury on Friday found Facebook liable for deceiving users about privacy protections on the social media platform.

It is now up to the judge to determine how much the company would pay, with attorneys representing the state asking for the maximum $5,000 penalty per violation.

The two-week trial in Santa Fe centered on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads. The now-defunct firm's clients included the 2016 campaign for Donald Trump.

Jurors sided with prosecutors, finding Facebook's failure to protect users' data impacted New Mexico's entire population of more than 2 million people. The New Mexico Attorney General's office is expected to hold a press conference at 2 p.m. local time Friday to discuss the case.

Jurors also found Facebook misled the public about investigations into data brokers following the Cambridge Analytica scandal, finding the company liable for over 2 million violations.

In this photo illustration, the Facebook logo is seen displayed on a smartphone screen. Photo Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

During closing arguments, lawyers for Facebook claimed the state's evidence was outdated and that despite having five years to gather material, New Mexico failed to find more than one other instance of a data breach.

A Meta spokesperson told CBS News the company disagreed with the jury's verdict and will continue to defend "against efforts to distort our records." The company also noted that free speech issues "featured very prominently" in the case.

"We have a First Amendment right to manage those platforms in a way we believe best serves the interests of our community," the spokesperson said. "This means prioritizing free speech, protecting our users' information and giving them control over their data."

Meta agreed in August to pay up to $18 billion to settle the multistate lawsuit surrounding child safety issues. Buried in the 130-page settlement was an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach, making New Mexico the only state to pursue a case. Florida was the only other state that did not sign the settlement, saying it was not tough enough on Meta.

Also this year, New Mexico won judgments totaling $942 million from Meta in a two-phase trial about the company's safety protections for minors. Furthermore, the court ordered Meta to implement new safeguards, including age-verification technology and time limits on its platforms.

World.title: Abraham Accords countries hold first official meeting since Oct. 7 attacks
World.content:
Ten blocks away from the United Nations General Assembly, U.S. diplomats quietly kickstarted the expansion of the Abraham Accords from the 43rd floor of a midtown Manhattan office tower.

On Thursday morning, State Department officials participated in the first official meeting of the Abraham Accords countries — the United States, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Morocco — since Oct. 7, 2023, when the Hamas attacks on Israel derailed the expansion of the Accords to more countries in the Middle East, Africa and Asia.

A meeting of nations who are part of the Abraham Accords in New York City on Sept. 24, 2026. N7 Foundation handout to CBS News

The Abraham Accords countries were joined Thursday for the first time by officials from Kazakhstan, which expressed an interest in joining the Accords last year.

"We see the Accords as a platform to reinforce political dialogue across the Middle East and neighboring regions by expanding trade and investment, strengthening connectivity, promoting technological cooperation and creating tangible economic opportunities," Kazakhstan Ambassador Kazykhan told CBS News Friday in a statement.

The U.S. delegation was led by a senior State Department official, Under Secretary of Political Affairs Allison Hooker.

"Nearly three years after October 7, the Abraham Accords countries are back together," Hooker said, adding that President Trump brokered the historic agreements during his first term, and Thursday was an important signifier that the accords are "moving forward again."

The meeting was hosted by the N7 Foundation, a U.S.-based organization that has convened multilateral meetings of the Abraham Accords countries since 2021.

"The next phase is about deepening the relationships that already exist and identifying practical opportunities for countries to work together," said Jeffrey Talpins, founder of the N7 Foundation, who chaired the meeting.

Another senior administration official who was not authorized to speak publicly told CBS News that Secretary of State Marco Rubio's team and Steve Witkoff, the White House Special Envoy for Peace Missions, "are clearly prioritizing this effort."

Also present at the meeting were Aryeh Lightstone, special adviser to the Board of Peace, an international coalition dedicated to peace and reconstruction in Gaza, Ryan Arant, chief of staff to Under Secretary Hooker at the State Department, and Oren Eisner, president of the N7 Foundation.

The Abraham Accords are a set of agreements that normalized diplomatic relations between Israel and several Muslim countries. The first of a series of agreements was signed in 2020, toward the end of Mr. Trump's first term.

The UAE and Bahrain became the first two Gulf Arab countries to formally recognize Israel. Morocco soon followed.

Before the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks, momentum was building for Saudi Arabia and other Muslim countries to join the accords, but the attack and the wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran that ensued stalled further expansion.

President Trump announced Kazakhstan's intention to join the Abraham Accords during an Oval Office meeting with Kazakhstan President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in November 2025.

"We will soon announce a Signing Ceremony to make it official, and there are many more Countries trying to join this club of STRENGTH," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.

Participants discussed next steps to formalize cooperation among Abraham Accords countries, according to a person familiar with the meeting.

"The Abraham Accords have demonstrated what is possible when countries come together around shared interests with a common vision for a more integrated and prosperous region," Talpins said.

World.title: Soaring U.S. diesel prices slam local communities as fuel costs surge
World.content:
Soaring diesel prices are rippling through the U.S. economy, putting a financial squeeze on schools, farmers and small businesses as their fuel costs spike.

Average diesel prices hovered around $6.50 a gallon on Friday, just below their record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22 and up from $3.69 a year ago, according to AAA. That jump is raising the cost of operating school buses and forcing some institutions to scramble for ways to cut costs.

Farmers, who rely on diesel to run agricultural machinery, also face sharply higher costs, while enterprises ranging from construction firms to food banks report sharply higher expenses to fuel their vehicles and delivery trucks.

One Georgia food bank said it will spend an extra $100,000 this year on diesel, money that otherwise would have gone to feed families.

"That would actually translate to about 122,000 meals that we would be able to provide if we didn't have to spend that on unexpected diesel fuel prices," Kenneth Hill, the supply chain officer for the Atlanta Community Food Bank, told CBS News Atlanta.

Georgia diesel prices averaged $6.32 a gallon on Friday, up from $3.54 a year ago, according to AAA.

Ranchers are feeling the pinch due to their reliance on diesel-powered trucks to check on herds and water pumps, said Andrew Coppin, CEO of Ranchbot, which sells remote monitoring technology for water pumps and other equipment.

"Outside of labor, diesel is the single biggest input into a lot of farming operations, so it's a very material increase in the cost of operations," he told CBS News, noting that his company has seen a major increase in inquiries from ranchers due to surging diesel prices. "If it's an F-250, a Ram 2500 or a Silverado, we're talking 1-ton diesel trucks, and on a good day they are getting 12 miles to a gallon."

Diesel's impact on inflation

Diesel is widely used in commercial trucking, agriculture, and construction, and rising prices can increase the cost of transporting goods across the country.

Gasoline prices have also soared, although not as much as diesel, which is facing a global shortage due to shipping and refining disruptions stemming from the Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars.

As a result, economists warn that the spike in diesel costs could fan inflation, which rose in August at an annual rate of 3.4%, up from 2.4% at the beginning of 2026.

Inflation could jump to 3.6% by year-end due to the rise in fuel prices, according to EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco.

"Higher domestic fuel prices feed directly into passenger and goods transportation costs, which will eventually be passed on to consumers," he said in a Sept. 23 analysis.

Those higher costs are also being felt more broadly across local communities.

"Certainly, when I wake up in the morning, I'm thinking about diesel," Marty Gray, owner of Gray Farms in Watseka, Illinois, told CBS News Chicago. "I'm thinking about the trucks running, the [grain] elevator and stuff like that."

Gray also said his family-owned farm is facing tight margins as harvest season gets underway. "So, we're just trying to decide do we fill up the tanks now, or do we need to wait a little bit? Will it get better, or will it get worse?"

Raptor Roll Offs, a Colorado waste management and dumpster rental business that uses diesel trucks to deliver dumpsters to and from homes and industrial sites in the Denver area, may need to pass higher fuel costs on to customers, owner George Dempsey told CBS News Denver.

"We're holding on as long as we can," Dempsey said. "We can't absorb it all ourselves, and so you have this trickle effect."

Colorado diesel prices now average $6.16 per gallon, compared with $3.51 a year ago, AAA data shows.

Colorado's Cherry Creek Schools relies on diesel to power its more than 300 buses, which transport roughly 24,000 students across the district. It's facing an additional $500,000 in diesel costs this year, pushing its total fuel budget to about $2 million — far higher than the $1.5 million it had originally budgeted, Mark Ingram, the district's director of transportation, told CBS News Denver.

Ingram said the school district is weighing consolidating some routes and scaling back certain activity trips to save fuel costs.

Would a diesel export ban help?

Some Republican lawmakers are calling for the U.S. to ban diesel exports to lower costs. The U.S. refines more diesel than it can use domestically, with energy companies selling the remainder abroad.

Although an export ban might initially lower diesel costs in some U.S. regions, it could eventually backfire by worsening global shortages, according to energy experts and economists. That would likely send diesel prices even higher, they say.

"A ban would temporarily lower prices, but short-term relief would be uneven geographically," Oxford Economics said in a report. "Price declines would be concentrated in the Gulf Coast and Midwest, where most refining capacity is located. Distillate shortages are concentrated in the Northeast and West Coast, and these regions would see little benefit from an export ban."
