World.title: Netanyahu rages against critics, including Mamdani, at the U.N. General Assembly
World.content:
Netanyahu rages against critics, including Mamdani, at the U.N. General Assembly

toggle caption Seth Wenig/AP

Protesters rallied outside the United Nations building in New York and many delegates inside walked out of the room as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave a fiery address to the General Assembly, denying allegations of genocide and slamming his critics, including the city's mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

He called allegations of Israeli genocide in Gaza "the biggest lie of the century" and defended attacking Iran alongside the U.S., calling it "one of the easiest decisions I've ever had to make." He added: "if we hadn't done it, we'd all be dead."

Sponsor Message

In his Thursday speech, he lashed out against the protesters outside — who included Hollywood stars Susan Sarandon and Hacks actress Hannah Einbinder, both detained during the anti-Netanyahu protest — calling them "phony" and asking why they hadn't all protested when Iranian security forces killed thousands of demonstrators in January.

He also berated the dozens of U.N. delegates who walked out when he started his speech, calling them "moral cowards."

Netanyahu then attacked Mayor Mamdani, who has called him a war criminal and pushed for federal authorities to act on the International Criminal Court-issued arrest warrant for him.

The Israeli leader called Mamdani, New York's first Muslim mayor, "antisemitic."

"Mr. Mamdani, you tried to stop me from coming here. You tried to silence me. Well, you can't silence me, and you can't silence the truth," Netanyahu said in his speech.

In a statement responding to Netanyahu's criticism, Mamdani dismissed the Israeli leader's speech as "baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide against Palestinians."

Palestinian leader's address

The Israeli leader's comments came after Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas delivered his address via a recorded video. The Trump administration had denied a visa to Abbas, on the grounds that the Palestinian leadership is undermining the prospects for peace, even though Abbas has been consistent in his call for a settlement with Israel. It's the second year in a row the U.S. has denied Abbas a visa for the assembly.

toggle caption Seth Wenig/AP

In his address, Abbas condemned Israeli actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank and again called for a two-state solution. "We seek a democratic Palestinian state that respects the rule of law and human rights, a non-militarized state that lives in security and peace alongside the state of Israel," he said.

Sponsor Message

He also called Israel's war in Gaza a "genocidal war that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe."

Netanyahu's defensive address responds to criticism

Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza has been a major topic of the week, as several world leaders have used their speeches to bluntly criticize Israel's conduct. A U.S.-mediated truce between Israel and Hamas has been in place since last October, but Israel has continued its attacks. More than 1,300 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire agreement, according to the Hamas-run Gaza health authorities.

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the Hamas-led attack on Israel in 2023 but said what followed by Israel was an "onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza." Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan described Gaza as "the most inhumane, most shameful concentration camp of our time." Jordan's King Abdullah II, whose country has maintained a peace treaty with Israel since 1994, called Israel a "regional threat" that operates with "terrifying levels" of impunity.

Netanyahu called the world leaders who criticized him "tyrants" and pushed back on much of what was said.

toggle caption Heather Khalifa/AP

He rejected claims of genocide by Israel and downplayed settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, saying it was the work of 150 "juvenile delinquents." But NPR has found that violence is widespread and destructive. The United Kingdom recently said such settler attacks and land grabs amount to "ethnic cleansing."

He also accused the media of not telling the truth about the war in Gaza. Israel has not allowed outside journalists to enter Gaza to independently report in almost three years.

Increasingly isolated, Netanyahu's combative address comes as he faces an election next month that will decide if he remains prime minister.

Yemen crisis

Under scrutiny will be his handling of the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel by Hamas that killed about 1,200 people and prompted Israel's ground offensive in the Gaza Strip. Almost 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since that 2023 attack, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.

Sponsor Message

Another key issue is the war in Iran, launched by Israel and the U.S. in February, that has affected key waterways through which Gulf countries export their oil. The seven-month war has shaken global markets as numerous attempts at diplomacy to end it have failed.

Yemen Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer, part of the country's internationally recognized government, also addressed the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday. He warned that recent advances by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait pose an "international economic risk." Some 12% of the world's trade passes through the strait.

The Houthis, who have controlled the capital, Sanaa, and part of Yemen's north since 2014, seized the important port city of Mokha earlier this month from the country's government forces, which are backed by Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have declared a blockade on Saudi shipping and have attacked its oil tankers.

Since the surge in fighting in Yemen, tens of thousands of people have been displaced, and a humanitarian crisis is deepening.

World.title: Danielle Smith’s popularity dips as her party now tied with NDP in support: poll
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

New polling suggests both impressions of Premier Danielle Smith personally and support for her party are slipping in Alberta, with the UCP now essentially neck-and-neck with the opposition NDP.

The Janet Brown Opinion Research Poll for CBC News suggests 41 per cent of respondents would vote for the UCP if an election were held today, while 41 per cent would vote for the NDP.

In a similar poll conducted this spring, pollster Janet Brown said Smith’s government was enjoying the longest honeymoon period since the Ralph Klein-era.

But now?

“I think the UCP is having a struggle navigating this difficult situation that we're in right now,” said Brown. “Having a controversial referendum, the premier taking one position on the referendum [and] also trying to advocate for the nine other questions.”

Brown says it appears the party is shedding support on both sides of the independence debate: from separatists who wish Smith had taken a stance of support, and federalists frustrated by the question in the first place.

“She’s trying to walk the middle of the road, between the moderate, business conservatives and the far-right populist base that’s still angry over COVID restrictions,” said John Santos, data scientist with Janet Brown Opinion Research.

“And she’s getting hit by traffic on both sides of the road.”

The random survey of 1,200 Albertans was conducted between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21, with a margin of error of +/-2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Breaking down the numbers

The poll suggests the UCP has dropped eight points since April, while the NDP has seen its share of voter intention rise five points over that same time, putting the two parties at a tie.

“Obviously the NDP would take a lot of pleasure in seeing these numbers,” said Lisa Young, political science professor at the University of Calgary. “It suggests that they're on a trajectory that might make them competitive in the election.”

There’s also an increase in the number of respondents who say they would vote for another party, up six points since April, and the number of political “orphans” in the province: those who wouldn’t vote UCP or NDP, but also could not name which party they’d support instead.

Regionally since the April poll, the UCP saw a drop of 14 points in areas outside Calgary and Edmonton, and a drop of 10 points in Calgary.

“That would have surprised me, were it not for the Calgary-Shaw byelection,” said Brown. The NDP pulled out a victory in that byelection, claiming what had been a UCP riding.

Brown says the drop in UCP voter intention in Calgary is likely among those supporting the remain side, while rurally it reflects a drop in voter support from those who would vote to separate.

Young says the numbers mean Calgary should be a key battleground in coming months.

“But we're a year away from the election. If the referendum is in fact what's driving support away from the UCP, the government will have an opportunity to try to win that support back,” Young said.

And with the price of oil still high and the province’s finances looking to be in better shape, Young says that could give the government more money in the coffers to spend big and woo voters.

Albertans’ impressions of Danielle Smith have also soured slightly in recent months, with the poll suggesting a drop of six percentage points in those very or somewhat impressed with her, and a seven point increase in those not at all impressed with her.

Twenty-five per cent of respondents are very impressed with NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi, the poll suggests.

“What Albertans are saying is they're not feeling highly impressed with either of these leaders right now,” Brown said.

Carney’s popularity keeps rising

But the honeymoon period seems to be still going strong for Prime Minister Mark Carney in Alberta. Fifty-two per cent of respondents said they are very impressed with him, up six points since the last poll.

“We're in this strange universe where a Liberal Prime Minister is doing better than either the premier, or the leader of the Opposition here, and doing much better than the leader of the federal Conservative Party in terms of popularity,” Young said.

Young credits approval largely to Carney’s handling of trade tensions with the United States. He’s also likely benefitting from Albertans happy with his commitment to get a pipeline to the B.C. Coast, she says.

It’s a project Smith is, of course, also pushing for.

“I think there's a bit of an irony here that the MOU is working well for Mark Carney and his popularity, but Danielle Smith doesn't seem to be benefitting from her part in creating the MOU,” said Brown.

Brown notes favourability does not equal voter intention, and some Albertans might appreciate Carney’s style but still be unlikely to cast a ballot for the Liberals.

But Carney does boast a higher score than Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, with just 26 per cent of those polled saying they are very impressed with him.

"Which has got to be a concern for the Conservative Party, because this is the Conservative heartland,” Brown said.

The CBC News random survey of 1,200 Albertans was conducted using a hybrid method between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21, 2026, by Edmonton-based Trend Research under the direction of Janet Brown Opinion Research. The sample is representative of regional, age and gender factors. The margin of error is +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.

The survey used a hybrid methodology that involved contacting survey respondents by telephone and giving them the option of completing the survey at that time, at another more convenient time, or receiving an email link and completing the survey online. Trend Research contacted people using a random list of numbers, consisting of 30 per cent landlines and 70 per cent cellphone numbers.

Telephone numbers were dialed up to five times at five different times of day before another telephone number was added to the sample. The response rate among valid numbers (i.e., residential and personal) was 11.3 per cent.

World.title: Police investigating threatening email sent to Muslim schools across Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A number of regional police forces in Ontario have launched an investigation into an email sent to Islamic schools across Canada over the course of this week, which threatened to kill Muslims unless they are deported.

The Muslim Association of Canada, which runs the eight private schools that received the email, said they alerted municipal police in Ontario, Vancouver and Montreal, as well as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, on Thursday morning.

The MAC schools follow standard provincial educational curricula, on top of Islamic, Quranic and Arabic-language education.

The email — which CBC News has seen — was fired off from a party identifying themselves as "Jehu, Citizen Vigilante" and came from an account titled "exposingNWO@protonmail.com." It was time-stamped last Sunday, Sept. 20.

Using dehumanizing language against Muslims, it says "millions on top of millions of people in the nation of Canada are ready to take up arms."

The email alludes to the upcoming Alberta referendum, which includes a question asking voters there to decide if the province should remain a part of Canada or eventually hold a vote on secession, and states Muslims will be "deported or slaughtered" once "Alberta becomes its own nation."

It then says this will happen "regardless of the election results," and "you won't be warned again."

Investigations underway

CBC News reached out to the RCMP and the six local forces where the eight schools are located.

In a statement, the London Police Service said it is investigating a threat to a local school and "collaborating with partner law enforcement agencies to gather information and assess any potential connections." Potential criminal code offences may include uttering threats, criminal harassment, or inciting willful hatred, the service said.

In the Greater Toronto Area, Peel Regional Police also posted a statement on the social media platform X, saying its hate crime unit is actively investigating. It said it beefed up officer presence overnight near local mosques and schools, and patrols will continue over the weekend.

Waterloo Regional Police said its officers visited a school after receiving notification of an emailed threat and conducted safety planning. The Ontario service's hate crime unit has launched an investigation, and are aware of emails sent to other jurisdictions as well.

The Ottawa Police Service confirmed it received a complaint and said it is working with law enforcement partners as part of an ongoing investigation.

"As a precaution, police visibility remains increased around religious institutions and the educational facility that received the complaint," the OPS said in a statement. "At this time, we have no information indicating a specific or imminent threat to religious or educational institutions in Ottawa."

Scope of threat unprecedented: MAC

Nabil Sultan, a spokesperson for the Muslim Association of Canada, said while the organization has received "hate comments and emails on social media" in the past, a single note targeting many of its schools is something it has never experienced before.

"Such a disturbing email to be received by teachers and administrators, and families and children, really makes it difficult for us to live as a community feeling good about ourselves, feeling that we are welcomed in this society," he said in an interview with CBC News from London, Ont., where two of the schools that received the email are located.

Sultan said it was hard not to think of the Afzaal family, which lost four of five members after a man deliberately drove his truck into the group while they were out on an evening stroll in June 2021. London police called it a hate-motivated crime and a sentencing judge said it was a terrorist attack.

"A part of you wants to move on, and a part of you wants to believe that it was a lone wolf incident, and that something like this should not happen again," he said. "And this is a reminder that that is not the case, and we're still under threat."

CBC News visited one of the two Ottawa schools that received the emailed threat, Abraar Elementary, on both Thursday afternoon and Friday morning, around the times parents were picking up or dropping off their children.

An Ottawa Police Service vehicle was parked outside the school on Thursday.

Mohammed Saleem, the principal of Abraar Elementary School in Ottawa, said the level of violence in the email was a shock. (Pierre-Paul Couture/CBC)

Sara Omar, who had just dropped her five-year-old daughter, spoke to CBC News outside the school on Friday.

"Definitely me and my husband, and other moms in group chats, we were worried and anxious. But at the same time, honestly, we won't be intimidated," she said.

"We have confidence in our schools, in our community. So we won't stop living and bringing our children to school because of these threats."

Omar said she and her husband are still trying to figure out how to have a conversation with their daughter about the threat.

"If there is a lockdown, what does that look like? How to listen to her teachers in that moment — in such an intense moment. How do you even have these conversations with a five-year-old?"

The school's principal, Mohammed Saleem, said getting the note in his inbox was a "total shock," given the "explicitly violent language" and clear threats to children in the email.

Parents at the school were notified by email and teachers were preparing to have classroom talks with students on Friday, he said.

Saleem said he is unsure how long heightened security measures, including police stationed in front of the school and patrolling the neighbourhood, might last.

"Usually, we will work with the police, consult with them to see, because they will let us know from time to time what they are hearing on their radar, what they're seeing," he said.

The school recently temporarily hired security guards, he said, after gunmen killed three people during a mosque shooting in San Diego last May in what police have called a hate-motivated crime .

Push for more government action

Statistics Canada reported in March that police-reported hate crimes in Canada more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, jumping from 1,817 to 4,882. Incidents involving Islamophobia in Canada nearly tripled, growing from 84 reported crimes to 229 over the same period.

The agency also noted a tripling of reported hate crimes targeting Jews from 2020 to 2024, rising from 331 incidents in 2020 to 920 in 2024.

Concerns over the email come on the heels of a shooting near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., which police have said was a deliberate, hate-motivated attack aimed at the Jewish community.

Saleem said the incident highlights a hole left behind when the federal government scrapped two offices — focusing on combating Islamophobia and antisemitism respectively — earlier this year . They were replaced with an advisory council that is meant to combat all forms of hate .

"It was the wrong move," Saleem said. "It's important that we kept that office to make sure that proper interventions, policies are being enacted to combat Islamophobia."

Amira Elghawaby, in her former capacity as Canada's special representative on combating Islamophobia, speaks during a news conference in Ottawa on Dec. 10, 2024. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

In an interview, Amira Elghawaby, the former special representative on combating Islamophobia, did not go as far as saying her office should be restored, but said that the federal government needs to continue to "meet and uphold its commitments on human rights, which includes making sure that Canadians of all backgrounds, including faith minorities like Canadian Muslims, have the protections and supports and the solutions they need to live lives of dignity in Canada."

She spoke to CBC News from New York City, attending meetings on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly, where she said it was clear to her that both Islamophobia and antisemitism continue to be dangerous at the global level.

World.title: Trump's top trade envoy says U.S. 'comfortable' with state of relationship with Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump is "comfortable" with where things stand with Canada — his country's once closest ally — and is in no rush to reach a new trade deal, according to his top trade envoy.

"The reality is President Trump is comfortable where we are on Canada," United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a Friday morning interview with the American network CNBC.

"They call us now and then and we have good conversations about potential deals. But there's no urgency on our side."

The two countries have been embroiled in a trade dispute since Trump was re-elected, but the relationship further soured after talks to reach a deal collapsed at the 11th hour last month.

The U.S. side maintains Canada walked away from a good deal. The Canadian side has accused the Americans of not negotiating in good faith and encroaching on Canada's sovereignty.

Greer, who mainly spoke to CNBC about new trade negotiations with Chinese President Xi Jinping, was asked about the state of the trade relationship with Canada.

"We're still getting what we need from them in terms of oil, gas, potash, all of these things. We're shipping [agricultural products] back and forth across the border, so there's still a lot of strong trade between the two countries," he said.

The U.S. slapped 50 per cent duties on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods on Aug. 22. Canada started collecting retaliatory tariffs Sept. 8. The summer measures are on top of existing levies on Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and lumber.

Starting next week, the Trump administration plans to ban the import of certain products including Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and molasses.

Trump has also ratcheted up his jabs at Canada since trade talks fell apart, including posting to social media a map of North America with the U.S. flag covering Canada and another post showing a cartoon version of himself standing over a sprawled out Prime Minister Mark Carney during a hockey game saying, "Get up, governor."

He has also signed an order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

LeBlanc says he talks to Greer a few times a week

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Greer's comments are consistent with his conversations with the U.S. trade representative — adding he talks to his counterpart a few times a week including later Friday afternoon.

"We'll continue to do the good faith work to try and get the agreement, but I'm not waiting by my phone to see if I have a text from [U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard] Lutnick on Mr. Greer," said LeBlanc from Moncton, N.B.

"We're continuing to do the work, but we are always ready to talk to the Americans about trying to find the right agreement."

Former Canadian ambassador to the U.S. Frank McKenna said he'd be careful with the rhetoric coming from the south that there's no sense of urgency for a deal.

WATCH | LeBlanc on his conversations with Greer: Canada not 'desperate' to get a U.S. trade deal 'at any cost,' says minister | Duration closed caption 1:27 Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says comments from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer that the Trump administration is not in a rush to make a deal with Canada are 'consistent with the conversations' he's had with his U.S. counterpart. LeBlanc says the government will keep working to reach an agreement, but 'we're not waiting by the phone.'

"I would think in terms of some of the states in play in this midterm election — which is starting to swing pretty sharply blue — there would be some urgency because the affordability issue is the big issue, and trade is associated with affordability," he told CBC's Rosemary Barton Live.

The former diplomat said that with the two parties still in contact, "at some point, this will become ripe and some kind of a trade deal will be done."

McKenna, who is also a former premier of New Brunswick, said it's "a logical imperative" that two countries bound as closely as Canada and the U.S. "would end up eventually having a trade deal."

World.title: Taylor Swift dropped 4 new songs. Here's what fans are sleuthing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If there’s one thing guaranteed to turn the internet into a room full of amateur detectives, it’s a new Taylor Swift track. Make that four and they go full-blown CSI.

The pop star dropped The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, the extended version of her 2025 album that includes four new tracks.

It's part of a broader trend of pop artists releasing an extension of their album as a deluxe, with experts speculating it is done to boost streaming revenue, or sell more units as physical media makes a comeback. Artists like Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo, Zara Larsson and Charli XCX have all done the same.

Swift says the new tracks came together after she went to Sweden to celebrate the success of The Life of a Showgirl with collaborators Max Martin and Shellback.

All four songs have since charted in the Top 10 on Apple Music but have been receiving mixed reviews, with some Swifties expressing letdown over the star's output.

"As a Swift fan, I find the four new songs quite disappointing," one fan wrote on X.

"I guess this era isn’t really just for me ," another wrote on Instagram. " NO ITS SO SO GOOD," a third commented.

We scrubbed through the internet to find out what fans are thinking. Shall we dive into the rumour mill? Let's go track by track.

Patient Zero

This is the lead single, she announced the other day on Instagram.

On first listen, fans think this one puts Swift in the role of "patient zero," and that she seems to be talking to an ex's new partner, singing: "I've been there. Felt the reeling, done the healing," and, "If he’s killing you, I see you. I was patient zero.”

Some speculate it could be Sofie Turner and Joe Jonas, who Taylor Swift also dated way back when. But fear not: Swift herself confirmed the meaning to Capital FM radio Friday.

“I was hanging out with a bunch of friends, and one of my friends told us that she had been reached out to by the new girlfriend of an ex of hers, asking for guidance on if she had had the same experiences with this guy that this new girlfriend was having,” Swift told the station.

“And everyone in our group just immediately started saying like, 'Oh, I've been through that too,' and telling the stories of when this kind of reach-out had happened for them.”

A music video for the song will air at this weekend's MTV VMAs, starring Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell.

Cleveland!

It doesn't require much decoding to decipher the subject of this song as Swift's husband Travis Kelce. The two got married at Madison Square Garden earlier this year. Fans think she's speaking to her critics in this one.

"He already took me to Cleveland and showed me The Heights," she pens. "And now I'm wearing white, so hate all you like this is the love of my life."

Its simplistic lyrics have Swifties spinning, some upset with her output.

"Cleveland … we need to talk," one user wrote on X. Others are coming to her defence. "Cleveland is corny and THANK GOD IT IS!!!!!!" wrote another .

Pink Clouding

This song seems to be a lyrical apology for being a "liar" in a previous relationship.

“Years later, I still wonder how to tell you sorry,” Swift sings.

Many fans are theorizing it's a message to Tom Hiddleston because of its apparent callbacks to songs from her catalogue like Getaway Car, which fans also think is about Hiddleston. The two were briefly coupled up in 2016.

“Having a Taylor Swift song about Tom Hiddleston in the big 2026 feels like sleeping with a cold pillow,” one user wrote. “Didn’t expect a hiddleswift apology in the year of 2026 i love her bad,” wrote another .

Babylon

Thing is, even Swifties can't pin down exactly what this one is about.

"Am I stupid what is she trying to say in Babylon," one fan wrote on X. "I have no idea what Taylor Swift is singing about in Babylon, but it’s my favourite movie of the year," wrote another.

A look at the lyrics tells you it's about a person who left their small town in Virginia, having regrets at a casino and on a train.

"You never knew that it was Babylon 'til it was gone," Swift writes, leading some to believe it's a message about nostalgia.

World.title: CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette warns of risk of U.S. interference in Quebec election
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebec's incumbent premier says she is "very concerned" about possible interference in the provincial election by the United States.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette told journalists she reached out to Prime Minister Mark Carney and requested a meeting with him to discuss the matter.

She was reacting to a news report published by Québecor media outlets that said American officials had attempted to negotiate directly with Quebec government officials regarding tariffs.

"I want to ensure that the full truth about this issue comes to light," Fréchette said on the campaign trail. "[The election] must remain in the hands of and be decided by the people of Quebec."

Canada's foreign affairs minister, Anita Anand, said at a news conference in Ottawa that the federal government is taking the issue very seriously.

"Protecting our democracy is of the utmost importance to our country," she said.

She added that she will speak with her American counterpart, Marco Rubio, after reviewing evidence of the allegations.

"Right now I have not seen the evidence," Anand said.

World.title: B.C. attorney general shocked by news report that ChatGPT told Tumbler Ridge shooter how to avoid safeguards
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

British Columbia's attorney general says she's shocked by an article describing alleged interactions between the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter and ChatGPT, in which the AI chatbot vividly describes the effectiveness of a shotgun in a classroom.

The news report, in U.S.-based magazine Mother Jones, also says ChatGPT advised shooter 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar how to get around its own safeguards to obtain information about violent scenarios by framing the content as fictional.

In a social media post, Attorney General Niki Sharma said the details in the article, which does not describe its sources, are "shocking and, as a parent, they are worse" than she ever imagined.

"It should make everybody angry," she said at an unrelated news conference Friday, adding, "If this is not impetus for change, I don't know what is."

On Feb. 10, Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother and half-brother at their family home. She then went to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School, where she shot and killed five students aged 12 to 13 and a 39-year-old education assistant, before killing herself.

The small community in the foothills of the Canadian Rockies near the Alberta border has been devastated by the tragedy.

After the shooting, OpenAI, the American company behind ChatGPT, said it had previously banned Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT account, but that it didn't meet the "higher threshold required" to report it to law enforcement.

The B.C. government, survivors and witnesses of the shootings at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School are suing OpenAI, alleging negligence.

The article published on Thursday says Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT account was banned for discussing committing an attack with a "famous real-world mall as the target."

But it says she then used a second account, which advised her about how to "never get flagged again” by describing situations as fictional or hypothetical.

"Don’t use real-world locations," the article quotes ChatGPT as saying, before adding: "You can still be twisted. Just be clever about it."

OpenAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the article about the chatbot's interactions with the shooter.

WATCH | Mother Jones journalist describes investigation into chat logs: Tumbler Ridge shooter's use of AI 'far more disturbing' than previously known, says Mother Jones journalist | Duration closed caption 10:56



The article says Van Rootselaar asked ChatGPT for a scenario about attacking a college campus with a shotgun for maximum effect.

It says that the chatbot initially declined to help, but after Van Rootselaar added "hypothetically" to her prompt it responded.

"In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 (Remington shotgun) is brutal," it quotes ChatGPT as saying. "Close quarters is its playground."

The article says ChatGPT went on to say: "Assuming each shell results in one hit, you might down 10 to 20 people max, depending on spacing, density, reaction times, and chaos."

OpenAI did not immediately respond to an email sent to their general press address and to an individual spokesperson. General counsel for the company, Che Chang, did not immediately respond to a message sent to his LinkedIn profile.

Federal AI Minister Evan Solomon said in a statement Friday morning that he was not previously aware of the specific conversations outlined in the Mother Jones report.

"What has been reported raises serious questions about how OpenAI identified and responded to warning signs," he said.

He added that Ottawa has demanded clearer pathways for escalating credible threats and noted OpenAI has since established direct contact with the RCMP's cybercrime centre.

"Those actions matter, but it would be premature to say they are sufficient," Solomon said.

RCMP Staff Sgt. Kris Clark said the investigation into the shootings had "utilized all available legal processes to obtain all information available from various social media and digital platforms" relevant to the attack.

"To date, all companies that have received requests have complied," Clark said.

World.title: Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? A visual investigation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Satellite imagery shows Israel compacting and removing rubble and debris from Gaza, with possible human remains and potential evidence of war crimes still trapped under it, a CBC News visual investigation of several sites has found.

Multiple destroyed areas in formerly populated areas of Gaza are being cleared, according to CBC's analysis, to make way for new military outposts for Israeli Defence Forces (IDF).

Families in Gaza say this prevents them from retrieving the bodies of loved ones trapped under the ruins.

"Where are the bodies? Where are the houses? Where's the rubble?" said Dalal Faraj, a Palestinian whose home in Gaza City was bombed, after CBC freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife showed her satellite footage of the now-cleared site.

UN officials have raised concerns in recent weeks that Israel is not properly handling rubble — and bodies that may still be under it — left by strikes in the almost three-year conflict sparked by the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.

WATCH | Investigating the clearing of rubble in Gaza: Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? | Duration 4:10 CBC�’s visual investigations team uncovers new satellite imagery that shows the IDF removing rubble from sites in Gaza that it bombed, which experts and human rights advocates warn risks destroying evidence of alleged war crimes. Families in Gaza interviewed by CBC say this activity prevents them from retrieving the bodies of loved ones trapped under the rubble.

In 2024, the International Court of Justice ordered Israel to take measures to preserve evidence of alleged violations of the UN Genocide Convention in Gaza.

"It is Israel's obligation under international law to do everything possible to ensure these remains are found, identified and buried with dignity," said Ajith Sunghay, head of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

In a statement to CBC News, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it clears structures and dismantles infrastructure in Gaza "based on tactical necessity" and to "reduce the level of risk posed" to its troops. It says this activity is "carried out in accordance with operational necessity, the provisions of international law, and IDF directives."

The IDF denies any accusations it isn't preserving evidence and recovering remains, saying it "treats every body found in the area with respect and seriousness."

Families that CBC News spoke to say no one contacted them about the retrieval of the bodies before or after the IDF removed the rubble from their homes.

IDF military base built over neighbourhood

"Impossible … This is our area?" Dalal Faraj told CBC News, looking at satellite imagery of her former neighbourhood. "Where did the houses go? Where are my husband and son?"

Dalal Faraj, who lives with her children in a displacement camp in Gaza City, looks at satellite imagery of her former neighbourhood. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

In October 2023, as the war picked up pace, Faraj left her home in Shuja'iya, a neighbourhood in Gaza City. Her husband, Taha, 48, and son Nasr, 16, told her to take the five younger children and head to a safer location. Taha and Nasr told her they would catch up when they could.

On Oct. 8, 2023, a day after the war started, an Israeli strike hit her home. She hasn't heard from her husband or son since.

Nasr Faraj, left, and his father, Taha. (Submitted by Dalal Faraj)

The satellite images that CBC's visual investigations team was able to gather show the buildings that once stood in Faraj's neighbourhood are all gone.

As the area was cleared of rubble, a new Israeli military base was built on top of it.

This composite image shows satellite footage of the Faraj family neighbourhood and the location of their home in August 2023, left, two months before the start of the war, and in August 2026, with the Israeli military base at the centre. (Google Earth, Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

On March 10, 2026, a satellite captured a rubble-clearing operation in the Faraj family neighbourhood. CBC News identified 11 diggers and one truck in the area just north of their home.

A composite image of heavy land-clearing machinery the CBC News visual investigations team identified in a March 10, 2026, satellite image. The image shows a clearing operation near the Shuja’iya military base. The colour of the machinery suggests it’s not military, but probably civilian subcontractors. (Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

A month later, satellite imagery shows four diggers clearing terrain west of the Faraj family house.

In April 2026, excavators moved west of the military base, clearing rubble, as shown in this composite image. (Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

Faraj, who now lives with her children in a displacement camp in Gaza, said she's been waiting for years to be able to return to her home to retrieve Taha and Nasr's remains and rebuild. Seeing the pictures broke the last of her hope, she said.

"This area used to be my home. We used to live in a safe place. We would go to school, go out and have fun. Suddenly, this happened," Faraj said.

CBC asked the IDF how many bodies found under the rubble in Gaza since last year's ceasefire have been returned to Palestinians. It did not answer the question.

Destruction of the 'Swedish Village'

Shaher Mohamed Abu Ouda, 36, says 14 members of his family are still missing after the family home in southern Gaza was destroyed.

Abu Ouda lived in a settlement in the Rafah Governorate known as the "Swedish Village." Abu Ouda left the area in 2024, and Rafah was occupied by Israel in 2025.

Shaher Mohamed Abu Ouda, left, speaks with family members about their neighbourhood in Rafah Governorate, which has been destroyed and cleared. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

"Warplanes started shooting at us, then came the F-16s, it shot at the house which we were in," Abu Ouda told CBC. "I left by a miracle."

Eight of the 14 members of the Abu Ouda family whose whereabouts are unknown after the IDF cleared rubble that may have contained their remains. (Submitted by Shaher Mohamed Abu Ouda)

"Until today, I think about what happened that day," he said. "I thought I would go back and see them, but after all these years, I won't even find a blouse."

Comparison shots of the location of Abu Ouda's home show the rubble was there until at least May 2026. By August, the rubble was gone, with heavy machinery tracks visible.

The three satellite images in this composite show the location of the Abu Ouda family home in Swedish Village in October 2023, May 2026 and August 2026. (Google Earth/Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

Footage from May 2026 shows a clearing operation, with six vehicles removing the rubble where the Swedish Village once stood.

CBC News identified vehicles clearing rubble in the satellite image taken on May 7, 2026, at the centre of what was Swedish Village, preparing the location for the military base. (Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

The latest satellite imagery from August 2026 shows the neighbourhood completely flattened, with a military base on top of it.

This composite image shows how the Swedish Village area looked in June 2024, left, and August 2026. (Google Earth/Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

Abu Ouda is not surprised by the satellite images of his neighbourhood, because Rafah has been under Israeli control for years. But the images provided confirmation that he is unlikely to be able to retrieve his family's remains, he said.

"Fourteen people lost their lives and we still know nothing about them," he said. "Even the rubble is not there."

'A new type of destruction'

Júlia Nueno Guitart, a researcher at Forensic Architecture, an independent research group tracking developments in Gaza, confirmed CBC's findings. She said her group has collected more than 2,000 similar incidents and managed to confirm 43 cases "where people have remained under the rubble."

"We have been able to do so either by visual evidence, graffiti on the walls of some of the buildings where people remain or by reports from [Gaza's] Civil Defence, where they inform us of the impossibility of retrieving bodies under the rubble," Nueno Guitart told CBC News.

A graphic shows instances Forensic Architecture has identified in which civilians are reportedly under rubble. (Forensic Architecture)

According to Forensic Architecture's findings, the Israeli military is compacting and clearing rubble around newly established military bases even in areas where bodies are still under the rubble.

"What we are seeing after the ceasefire in Gaza is a new type of destruction, different to the one we have been documenting before the ceasefire," Nueno Guitart said.

According to Janina Dill, a professor at Oxford University in the U.K. and an expert on international law, removing rubble and flattening the bombed area is only compatible with international law if the war dead are collected, identified and buried, and if evidence required to prosecute potential war crimes or suppress violations of international law is preserved.

"If [the rubble removal] is done without taking care of these two considerations, then it is absolutely prohibited and incompatible with Israel's obligations under the Geneva Convention," Dill said.

World.title: AI 'slop' is dominating menus, as some restaurant owners turn to it to save time and money
World.content: The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. From cartoonish-looking sandwiches to doughnut-shaped shrimp , AI might be on the menu at your local fast-food restaurant. Diners have taken to the internet to share photos of sandwich boards and window displays bearing food they say looks rubbery, surreal and seems to be created with artificial intelligence tools — which have made it increasingly easy to generate visuals on the cheap. "This looks like what aliens would put in a presentation about what Earth food is," a Reddit user captioned in a post accompanied by a picture of a sandwich board with breaded shrimp and gyros with suspiciously geometric textures. Others described a CNE sandwich they assumed to be AI-generated as " uncanny and nauseating " and "slop." And for some Toronto customers, these kinds of images aren't just stomach-turning — they take them as a signal of the restaurant's values. "I feel like it's really inauthentic and it doesn't make me wanna go eat at your restaurant," said Cynthia Lem. For her, AI-generated imagery raises questions about what the actual food would look like once it arrives, making her wary of any establishments using the technology. The death of folk graphic design in favor of AI slop across our country's delis is leading to some incredibly Lovecraftian food horrors pic.twitter.com/snDyC675Ei —samfbiddle While some consumers say these images are ruining their appetites and raising worries about possible misrepresentations of menu items, those in the restaurant business say it's helped them reduce costs in a notoriously difficult industry. And marketing experts say use of the tech isn't necessarily bad if it's done thoughtfully. Not all AI use created equally Before taking a single bite, restaurant-goers rely heavily on imagery to dictate what they order, according to business consultant and Schulich School of Business marketing professor David Pullara. And that means businesses relying on heavy-handed AI imagery are taking a big risk. "Great food photography sells," said Pullara. "So if you're using AI to generate an image that's terrible, it's going to hurt your sales, it's going to hurt your brand." But while some consumers might object to the use of AI on principle, he thinks the risk of using it to enhance food photography is low if done well — especially if it can help small- and medium-sized businesses manage their costs. Restaurant businesses face thin margins, often making it difficult to turn a profit . According to Restaurants Canada's most recent survey of some of its members , 41 per cent said they were operating at a loss or just breaking even, with rising fuel costs only exacerbating issues. Pullara says hiring a professional photographer is expensive, and might be out of budget for a small restaurant business. For that reason, taking a high-resolution photo of food and using an AI application to make small tweaks could create an image worthy of putting on a menu, Pullara says. "I don't think it's the AI that makes the image unappealing. I think the problem is asking AI for a photo and just not using a common-sense filter about [whether] this actually looks good," Pullara said. That tweaking of real photos is how the marketing team at The Fancy Induced Burger uses AI. Fez Mian is a marketing manager manager for Canadian burger franchise The Fancy Induced Burger. He says staff at the company take pictures of food with their phones and enhance them using AI tools before using them on menu boards, in-store advertising and online. (Tina Mackenzie/CBC) A marketing manager for the Canadian franchise, Fez Mian, says he'll snap a picture of a burger as it comes out of the kitchen and run it through an AI application like ChatGPT, prompting it to enhance the texture and freshness of menu items. Those images are used across the business — on menus, in-store posters and online. The company doesn't rely on professional photographers or graphic designers as much these days as a result. That's saved them money and time, as Mian no longer needs to book a photographer, wait for the shoot date and then wait to receive the images before using them in marketing. "We're not, like, spending endless time planning and scheduling and whatnot," Mian said. "Within … five minutes, 10 minutes it's out the door." That speed is especially important on social media, Mian says, enabling them to create and post new content more frequently. Does AI cross the line into false advertising? For some consumers, the worry is about how the food item that shows up on their plate will compare to the enhanced image on the menu. WATCH | Some customers find AI food ads unappetizing : AI food pics on menus leave some customers with a bad taste | Duration closed caption 1:58 More small restaurants are turning to AI instead of professional photographers to generate food pictures for their menus, but the often unrealistic images are starting to turn some customers off. If AI imagery is vastly different from the actual product, Rotman School of Management marketing professor David Soberman says that could be a problem. "You wanna make your products look good, but you don't want your products to be misleading," Soberman said. If an AI-enhancement makes a steak look like it's an inch thick but the actual product is half the size, for example, that would be a problem. Burgers, fries and 'cheesy nuggets' enhanced with AI are pictured on the menu board at The Fancy Induced Burger. The marketing manager for the company says staff at the franchise take pictures of real food on their phones before tweaking them with AI and using them on menus boards, in marketing imagery and online. (Tina Mackenzie/CBC) But the same is true for food imagery enhanced using run-of-the-mill staging and image editing, Soberman says. Both Soberman and Pullara say they don't think AI imagery generally raises the likelihood of misleading consumers, especially since most have come to accept that images on menu boards will look better than the real deal. "I think people just kind of know that there's going to be some variance between what you're seeing on these professionally shot, produced photos and what you actually can have prepared in the back of the kitchen in two minutes," Pullara said. At The Fancy Induced Burger, Mian says there's always a human involved in checking the company's AI-enhanced images to make sure no extra ingredients were added in the process that might mislead customers. Still, Toronto-based food stylist Zoe Rousseau says they think the work they do is more authentic than AI-generated food imagery. Despite some common misconceptions based on industry standards from decades ago, Rousseau says food staging doesn't involve fake food most of the time. Instead, they take their time to pick the best-looking ingredients, make sure they're perfectly placed, and work with a team of photographers and prop stylists who help achieve a beautiful end product. Zoe Rousseau is a Toronto-based food stylist who has worked with major brands like Shake Shack and Boston Pizza as well as smaller companies. They say their work doesn't often involve inedible items; instead they take a lot of time to make the real ingredients look their absolute best. (Mark Bochsler/CBC) Rousseau says they understand why small businesses trying to cut down costs would try AI, but if the generated imagery simply "doesn't look like the food," it won't work to pull customers in. "I think that restaurateurs are better off taking pictures with their iPhone," Rousseau said. For that reason, they're not too worried about AI coming for their job. They hope that the backlash to AI menu items might even compel more businesses to invest in stylists and photographers, boosting their industry. "I can play with texture and I can play with angles," Rousseau said. "Just the freshness of it … the AI can't do that."

World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.

We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issued to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: “The UN has more reason to exist every day”, Uruguay's president said two days after Milei
World.content:
“The UN has more reason to exist every day”, Uruguay's president said two days after Milei

25th Friday, September 2026 - 10:41 UTC Full article

“The UN has more reason to exist every day,” Orsi said, while calling for multilateral institutions that are “more effective, more representative” and closer to people's needs

Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi defended the United Nations' relevance and condemned the economic embargo on Cuba before the General Assembly on Thursday, in an address of just under twenty minutes that contrasted with that of his Argentine counterpart, Javier Milei, two days earlier from the same podium.

“The UN has more reason to exist every day,” Orsi said, while calling for multilateral institutions that are “more effective, more representative” and closer to people's needs. “We cannot go on being hostages to the will of a handful of countries that can be counted on the fingers of one hand,” he said, referring to the workings of the Security Council. Milei, on Tuesday, had described the organisation as a fossilised institution and questioned the point of resolutions that go unenforced.

Orsi speaks from a dual regional position: he holds the pro tempore presidency of Mercosur since July 1 and that of the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States since March 21. It was his second address to the assembly since taking office on March 1, 2025.

The passage with the greatest domestic political impact concerned Cuba. “We cannot be indifferent to the pain of an endless state of war, the fear and pain generated by organised crime, the permanent threat of terrorism, the repression that arises from tyranny, or the suffering caused by a tight economic blockade such as the one the Cuban people endure,” he said. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had already denounced the embargo on Tuesday.

The speech opened with a greeting to the American people on the 250th anniversary of their independence, marked in July, and a reference to that country's founding values: that people hold rights, that life, liberty and happiness should guide every government, and that the governed decide who governs them, principles he said were inherited in South America half a century later.

AHORA | HABLA EL PRESIDENTE ORSI EN LA ONU



“Ninguna nación tiene el monopolio de las soluciones; ningún pueblo debería ser condenado a elegir entre modelos impuestos desde afuera”



“Hoy vivimos un tiempo particularmente difícil” con “desigualdad extrema”, “pobreza” y ”las… pic.twitter.com/MZ7Z5cEK0Z — Telemundo (@TelemundoUY) September 24, 2026

Orsi described Uruguay as a country “of great convictions” rather than “great stridency”, championed humility in international relations — “nobody is more than anybody”, “no country owns the absolute truth” — and said no people should be forced to choose between models imposed from outside. He reaffirmed Uruguay's participation in UN peacekeeping missions and argued that peace is not “simply the absence of war”. He closed with the phrase “we are and we transform ourselves together”.

The president avoided taking sides in ongoing conflicts and did not mention Gaza or the Middle East. “We do not believe that taking one side or the other in a war, a confrontation or a dispute necessarily helps resolve it. Often, on the contrary, it deepens those divisions,” he said. In another passage, without naming any country, he said: “We know well that this is not about good guys and bad guys. Often the good become bad very quickly, or those we condemned harshly yesterday magically become reference points in our alliance for good.” Executive sources cited by the Uruguayan daily El País read that passage as distancing from US policy towards Venezuela; the president made no reference to that country.

Figures from the National Party, unnamed in that same coverage, called the speech “vague” and said the president had acted as “a spokesman for the Cuban regime”. Reception within the governing coalition was favourable, including among sectors that have voiced differences with the government's foreign policy: Socialist senator Gustavo González highlighted the reference to the embargo as “a humanitarian situation that must be addressed”.

World.title: Poverty in Argentina rises to 32.3%, ending two years of decline
World.content:
Poverty in Argentina rises to 32.3%, ending two years of decline

25th Friday, September 2026 - 10:26 UTC Full article

The measurement covers the 31 urban agglomerations surveyed by the Permanent Household Survey, where 9,729,000 people fell below the poverty line and 2,249,000 below the extreme poverty line

Poverty in Argentina reached 32.3% of people in the first half of 2026, an increase of 4.1 percentage points on the second half of 2025, the National Institute of Statistics and Census reported on Thursday. The figure interrupts the downward path the indicator had followed since mid-2024. Extreme poverty rose 1.2 points, from 6.3% to 7.5%.

The measurement covers the 31 urban agglomerations surveyed by the Permanent Household Survey, where 9,729,000 people fell below the poverty line and 2,249,000 below the extreme poverty line. Projected to the country as a whole, estimates published by Argentine media place the figure at between 15.4 and 15.5 million people in poverty and around 3.6 million in extreme poverty. In household terms, 24.4% fell below the poverty line and 5.6% below the extreme poverty line.

The year-on-year comparison gives a different result. Against the first half of 2025, when poverty stood at 31.6% and extreme poverty at 6.9%, the increases are 0.7 and 0.6 points respectively. The second-half 2025 reading of 28.2% had been the lowest since 2018, when it closed at 27.3%.

In Argentina poverty is measured by income: the cost of a basic basket is compared with each household's available resources, making the indicator sensitive to inflation. In June, a family of four needed 1,531,473 pesos to stay above the poverty line and 689,853 to avoid extreme poverty.

Figures by age show a higher incidence among children: 44.5% of those under 14 live in households below the poverty line, against 36.9% among those aged 15 to 29 and 28.8% among those aged 30 to 64. Geographical differences are also pronounced. Concordia recorded the highest level, at 56.2%, followed by Gran Resistencia at 48.6% and Posadas at 42.2%. In the Buenos Aires metropolitan area, the surrounding districts reached 36.9% against 11.1% in the City of Buenos Aires. Agglomerations of fewer than 500,000 inhabitants recorded a 4.9-point rise, greater than the 3.9 points in larger centres.

Leopoldo Tornarolli, a researcher at the Centre for Distributive, Labour and Social Studies at the National University of La Plata, said the result “is not a surprise” and confirms a trend already visible between the third and fourth quarters of last year, though the scale of the rise was larger than expected. He attributed it to two factors: the increase in inflation between May 2025 and March 2026, and weak dynamism in the formal labour market. He said the slowdown in prices in recent months has probably already halted the rise, but warned that returning to a sustained path of reduction requires “a more dynamic labour market”.

The agency simultaneously released economic activity data showing a 2.9% fall in July compared with June. Economy Minister Luis Caputo attributed it to “transitory shocks”: lower gas availability for industry, exceptional rain and snowfall, and fewer hours worked in some sectors because of the football World Cup. On poverty, he said on X that both rates “recorded a sharp fall relative to the first half of 2024”.

In that half, the first of Javier Milei's administration, poverty had reached 52.9% and extreme poverty 18.1%, following the devaluation of more than 110% and the price corrections implemented in December 2023. Hours before the report was released, Milei had told business figures at Citi's headquarters in New York that his administration had lifted “14 million people out of poverty” and that “we are the ones who have done the most for the most vulnerable sectors”.

World.title: Trump and Xi end the state visit with the trade truce extended and no substantive deals
World.content:
Trump and Xi end the state visit with the trade truce extended and no substantive deals

25th Friday, September 2026 - 09:37 UTC Full article

Artificial intelligence was the clearest point of declared agreement

Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to Washington ended on Thursday with a two-month extension of the bilateral trade truce, agreed before the meeting itself, and no progress on the central issues dividing the two powers: tariffs, rare earths, agricultural purchases, Taiwan and export restrictions on advanced chips.

The extension was settled on Wednesday night, after an unscheduled meeting between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng. It runs to January 10 an agreement that was due to expire on November 10 and which had lowered US tariffs and suspended Chinese export controls on rare earths and critical minerals. Those same talks produced a commitment to explore a communication mechanism for artificial intelligence incidents affecting national security.

Each side arrived with a request that went unanswered. Washington wants Beijing to use its influence over Tehran to end a war approaching its seventh month. Xi is seeking a permanent halt to arms sales to Taiwan and an easing of restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports. According to Chinese state agency Xinhua, he urged the United States to “adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence and handle the Taiwan issue with prudence”, one of his most explicit statements on the matter. After May's summit in Beijing, the US administration postponed a US$14 billion arms sale to Taipei; Trump has described such sales as “a very good negotiating tool” in dealing with China.

Artificial intelligence was the clearest point of declared agreement. Xi said both countries “have the capacity and the responsibility to develop and manage AI effectively, ensuring its development remains under human control”. Trump had written before the meeting that he wanted to leave it “exactly as it is”, attributing the same position to China.

It is the first state visit by a Chinese leader to the United States since 2015, though Xi was in the country in 2023 for the APEC summit in San Francisco. The three-day visit began with his arrival on Wednesday evening at Joint Base Andrews, where Trump met him at the foot of the aircraft steps, and continued with a Thursday ceremony featuring a military review, gift exchange and flyover. Trump spoke of a “truly great friendship” built on “mutual respect and the vital interests of our people”.

The day closed with a state banquet for 134 guests in the White House East Room, decorated in red and gold. Neither the speeches nor the toast referred to bilateral tensions. Trump said he and Xi had “never” got on “better” and presented a carving of a bald eagle as a gift. Xi called on both countries to act “as responsible major powers” and to “explore a new path” for cooperation. The menu combined American ingredients with Chinese influence and opened with the same wine shared by Richard Nixon and Zhou Enlai during the visit that restored relations between the two countries.

Guests included Elon Musk, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, AMD's Lisa Su, Alphabet co-founder Sergey Brin and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman. The Chinese delegation included no business figures, an early sign the summit would not produce concrete results.
