The two will meet twice more before the end of the year: in November in Shenzhen, at the APEC summit, and in December in Miami, at the G-20, both after the US midterm elections.

World.title: Nine days from the vote, neither Brazilian front-runner comes close to 50%
World.content:
Nine days from the vote, neither Brazilian front-runner comes close to 50%

25th Friday, September 2026 - 00:10 UTC Full article

The survey was conducted on Tuesday 22 and Wednesday 23 among 2,002 voters in 125 municipalities, with a margin of error of two percentage points

Neither of Brazil's two leading presidential candidates is approaching the threshold needed to win outright on October 4, according to the latest Datafolha poll, which puts President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on 40% of voting intentions and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro on 36%.

The survey was conducted on Tuesday 22 and Wednesday 23 among 2,002 voters in 125 municipalities, with a margin of error of two percentage points. It was commissioned by the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo and TV Globo, and is registered with the electoral authorities under code BR-00304/2026. The field is completed by Augusto Cury on 5%, Ronaldo Caiado on 4%, Renan Santos on 3%, and Romeu Zema and Samara on 1% each. Blank or spoiled ballots account for 5% and undecided voters for 2%.

In a prospective October 25 runoff, Lula takes 47% and Bolsonaro 45%, a statistical tie. The previous week's readings were 39% and 36% in the first round, and 46% to 44% in the second, placing the shift within the margin. Folha stresses that this is a snapshot rather than a prediction.

The most significant finding is that Bolsonaro has interrupted a run that over four months had narrowed the gap from ten points to three; it is now back to four. In the unprompted question, without names presented, Lula records 36% and Bolsonaro 27%. Some 80% of voters say their choice is settled, and among those who identify with neither camp, 35% say they could still change their minds. Against the other candidates, Lula is also tied with Cury, 46% to 43%, and beats Caiado 46% to 42%, and both Zema and Renan Santos 48% to 39%.

By segment, Lula leads Bolsonaro among the poorest 50%, 46% to 32%, among the least educated 29%, 49% to 29%, and in the Northeast, the country's second largest electorate with 28% of voters, where he records 55% to 25%. Bolsonaro leads among evangelicals, 47% to 27%; among those earning two to five minimum wages, 40% to 34%; and in the South, 47% to 27%. In the Southeast, the most populous region with 42% of the sample, he holds a numerical advantage within a statistical tie, 37% to 35%. According to Folha, Lula's challenge is mobilising an electorate that tends to show higher abstention.

The poll also captured the week's political developments. The 15% increase in the Bolsa Família benefit, announced by Lula less than three weeks before the vote, did not shift the vote among recipients: the president moved from 52% to 53% and his rival from 28% to 27%. Bolsonaro accused him of trying to “buy the poor” with the measure.

The external factor returned to the centre of the campaign. The United States and fourteen countries announced in New York on Wednesday, after a meeting of the Americas Shield, their intention to take coordinated measures against 24 transnational criminal organisations, including the Brazilian factions First Capital Command and Comando Vermelho, involving asset freezes and immigration restrictions. Brazil is outside the mechanism. Washington designated both as terrorist organisations in May, a classification Lula's government rejects on the grounds that it could open the door to US military intervention on Brazilian territory, while Bolsonaro backed it after meeting Trump that same month. The senator accused the president of leniency towards organised crime; Lula had criticised foreign interference in electoral processes before the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, without naming Trump.

World.title: Netanyahu rejects genocide allegations before an assembly emptied by dozens of delegations
World.content:
Netanyahu rejects genocide allegations before an assembly emptied by dozens of delegations

25th Friday, September 2026 - 00:08 UTC Full article

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday called genocide allegations against his country over the war in Gaza “the biggest lie of the century”, in an address to the United Nations General Assembly that dozens of delegations left before he began speaking.

“If there are any other moral cowards who haven't yet left this hall, please do so now,” he said as he opened his remarks. The walkout was led by representatives of Arab, Muslim and African countries. Figures differ by source: Foreign Policy counted more than a hundred delegates; Fox News, 77 delegations. The US delegation remained seated, and members of the Israeli party shouted “Am Yisrael Chai”.

Netanyahu argued that Israel acted to avoid becoming the victim of a genocide rather than to commit one, and linked the accusations to growing persecution of Jews. He described the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023 as “the darkest day in Israel's history” and “the largest massacre of Jews since the Holocaust”, comparing the roughly 1,200 victims to “40,000 innocent Americans slaughtered in less than 24 hours”, sixteen times the toll of the September 11, 2001 attacks.

On the legal position: the International Criminal Court is investigating Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity, not genocide. There is also a genocide case against Israel before the International Court of Justice, brought by South Africa and joined by other states, with no ruling on the merits. A growing number of specialists and the International Association of Genocide Scholars hold that Israel has committed that crime; Israel rejects this.

The prime minister defended the campaign against Iran, launched alongside the United States in February. Attacking that country “was one of the easiest decisions I've ever had to make”, he said, arguing that in defending itself Israel “is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall”, whose leaders, he said, thank him privately. He thanked Donald Trump for what he described as an act “to save civilisation”, and repeated: “We will continue to win because we have no other choice.” He noted that a country the size of New Jersey was fighting a war on seven fronts.

On settler violence in the West Bank, which has prompted sanctions from several Western countries led by the United Kingdom, he described those responsible as “a handful of juvenile delinquents”, around 150, accountable for “maybe two or three deaths” so far this year. These are his figures, disputed by UN monitoring bodies. He also attacked New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York”.

Hours earlier, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas had addressed the assembly by video from Ramallah, after the United States denied him a visa for a second consecutive year. The assembly had voted 152 to 3 to allow him to speak remotely; the United States, Israel and Paraguay voted against. Abbas described Israel's campaign as a “genocidal war that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe” and denounced a policy of “racial discrimination, ethnic cleansing and terrorism” aimed at forcing Palestinians off their land. “Do not allow a new Nakba, do not allow more massacres,” he said, asking “how much longer some states will remain silent about Israel or continue supplying it with weapons”.

Netanyahu spoke a month before Israeli elections in which his continuity in government is at stake.

World.title: Punta Arenas/Falklands maritime links are based on history, economics and geography
World.content:
Punta Arenas/Falklands maritime links are based on history, economics and geography

24th Thursday, September 2026 - 23:47 UTC Full article

El Tratado de Límites de 1881 estableció un régimen excepcional para el paso marítimo bioceánico, que el Tratado de Paz y Amistad de 1984 reafirmó de manera específica

The announced maritime and trade link between Punta Arenas in Chile and the Falkland Islands has been strongly argued and supported by the main newspaper from the Chilean austral city on the Magellan Strait and capital of the Magallanes Region.

In its editorial La Prensa Austral argues that the recent transversal support from Chilean Senators during their trip to Punta Arenas transcends Argentine warnings in the event of the establishment of a trade link of the Chilean city with the Falklands/Malvinas.

“For Magallanes it is essential, given the freedom to develop its economic links from Chilean territory in accordance with Chilean and international law, no matter what third countries pretend or wish to condition activities of companies and/or individuals from the region”.

In the event of a resumption of a maritime exchange with the Islands, this must not be scrambled with the sovereignty dispute between Argentina and the UK over that territory.

“They are different issues, one is the position of a State regarding a conflict and the other very different, pretending that such a controversy should limit the capacity of established operators in Chile to develop licit commercial activities”.

The daily adds that Punta Arenas is not planning an artificial relation or lacking background. During most of its history Punta Arenas has had close trade and maritime contacts with the Islands, and as it has been repeatedly pointed out by businesses involved it is precisely to recover that relation which existed for over a century.

But the debate acquires a larger dimension when it is linked to the Magellan Strait.

The Boundaries treaty of 1881 established an exceptional ruling for the maritime bi-ocean passage and which the 1984 Treaty of Peace and Friendship reaffirmed specifically, ‘the Strait has been neutralized to perpetuity and its navigation ensured for the flags of all nations”. The 1984 treaty adds that Argentina must maintain “at any time and circumstances” the right for all ships to navigate expeditiously and without obstacles through its jurisdictional waters, from and towards the Strait.

This is a historic ruling that can’t be made relative in light of current controversies. It was conceived precisely to avoid that one of the strategic maritime corridors in the extreme continental austral could be subject to restrictions as a result of conflicts between States. Its fortress resides in the fact that the rules have been established before circumstantial differences.

That is why we also need to separate concepts. Strait treaties guarantee freedom of navigation and do not constitute a commercial authorization for each operation done from Punta Arenas. But this distinction does not weaken the fundamental argument. Chile exercises jurisdiction over its territory and ports, and companies operating legally from them develop their activities subject to Chilean legal system. The free crossing of the Strait also impedes converting the maritime passage in an indirect pressure mechanism on routes or destinations that may result politically uncomfortable for third parties.

This is why the Senators’ declaration is so relevant, precisely because it transfers discussions from rhetoric to the Treaties and permanent rules.

In a region whose history and development are indissolubly linked to the sea, these facts are particularly significant. Punta Arenas emerged and grew as an open port to the world, connected with diverse routes, markets and territories, this condition does not constitute any provocation at all, but simply are part of its own economic and geographic nature.

World.title: UK replies to Milei: “not the behaviour we expect of a democracy”
World.content:
UK replies to Milei: “not the behaviour we expect of a democracy”

24th Thursday, September 2026 - 10:59 UTC Full article

Photo: REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

The United Kingdom has asked for a written statement to be placed in the official record of the UN General Assembly in response to Argentine President Javier Milei's address, saying Buenos Aires' conduct over the Falklands “is wholly incompatible with the principles established in the United Nations Charter and is not the behaviour we expect of a democracy”.

The text, released by the British mission to the organisation, was submitted under agenda item eight of the 81st session, after Milei referred on Wednesday to sovereignty over the archipelago and over South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. It is the same procedure London used in 2012 to reply to then president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.

The document states that the United Kingdom “has no doubt” about its sovereignty over both territories and their surrounding maritime areas, and that it remains steadfast in supporting the islanders' right of self-determination, set out in the UN Charter and Article 1 of the two international human rights covenants. It says Argentina “continues to deny that this fundamental human right applies” to those inhabitants and actively seeks opportunities in international fora to assert its sovereignty claim.

The United Kingdom has no doubt about its sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.



Our statement in response to the Argentine General Assembly Statement regarding the Falklands: pic.twitter.com/eWw8aS2MDI — UK at the UN (@UKUN_NewYork) September 23, 2026

The statement rebuts point by point the legal argument Milei set out. It says General Assembly Resolution 2065 “does not prohibit economic development or displace the Islanders' right of self-determination”, and that Resolution 31/49 “likewise does not limit or remove the rights of the Islanders to freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development”. It adds that calls for negotiations “do not modify or dilute the obligation of nations to respect the legally binding right of self-determination”. These are UK government positions, contested by Argentina.

On the ongoing dispute over oil companies, the text says efforts to obstruct and harass international companies involved in the archipelago's hydrocarbons, and other local industries, “are a wholly unacceptable attempt to exercise extra-territorial jurisdiction, and have no justification whatsoever in international law”, describing them as obstructive to global business and inconsistent with free trade. It further states that hydrocarbon development is a legitimate commercial venture regulated by the legislation of the archipelago's government in strict accordance with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, and that Argentine domestic law does not apply there.

The document includes a detail about the 2013 referendum that London does not usually highlight: alongside the 99.8% vote to maintain the current status, on a 92% turnout, the vote was supervised by independent observers from Canada, the United States, New Zealand and three South American countries: Uruguay, Chile and Brazil.

The statement closes a forty-eight-hour sequence. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham included the archipelago among the challenges to the rule of law in his address; that same night, Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno exercised the right of reply before the plenary and said “the illegal British occupation of the islands dates back to January 1833”, when the authorities and the established Argentine population were expelled. Milei spoke on Wednesday, and the British text followed hours later.

Argentina has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors. None of the allegations has been proven.

World.title: Delcy Rodríguez tells the UN there will be elections in Venezuela, without setting a date
World.content:
Delcy Rodríguez tells the UN there will be elections in Venezuela, without setting a date

24th Thursday, September 2026 - 10:47 UTC Full article

It was the first address by a Venezuelan head of state to the body's plenary since 2018, when Nicolás Maduro spoke

Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, announced on Wednesday before the United Nations General Assembly that her country will hold elections, without specifying when, and thanked US President Donald Trump for “his willingness to return to the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation”.

“Democracy is not measured by the existence of elections. Democracy is measured by the quality of the competition that precedes those elections. An election should be a solution, not a generator of irreconcilable conflicts,” she said before the announcement. She added: “I want to say it very clearly in this General Assembly: in Venezuela there will be elections and, in that direction, we have begun a political dialogue with sectors of the opposition,” under “equal conditions for all”. On timing, she said “the Venezuelan people, with their ancestral wisdom, will determine the right moment”.

Rodríguez said Venezuela has begun an “orderly, institutional and verifiable” transition to democracy, citing among its pillars a reform of the justice system and the “responsible exercise” of politics. She said the country had endured “two great and painful trials” this year: the “strangulation of its internal political life and the sharpened confrontation with the United States”, and the double earthquake of June 24, which left more than 6,500 dead. “Venezuela is being reborn,” she concluded, in a speech lasting under twenty minutes.

It was the first address by a Venezuelan head of state to the body's plenary since 2018, when Nicolás Maduro spoke. The tone contrasted with Rodríguez's own remarks in the same forum in 2019, when as vice president she said she came “in the name of the Venezuela that does not kneel before any imperial power”, conveyed Maduro's greetings and denounced Trump's “supremacist hatred” and “imperial claws”.

She did not mention Maduro at any point. Her predecessor remains in US custody alongside his wife Cilia Flores, awaiting trial on drug trafficking and related charges, which he rejects. Before her address, videos circulated in which Rodríguez declined to say whether she would visit Maduro at the Brooklyn detention centre where he is held.

The acting president also praised the agreement granting the United States access to more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, a share the US government puts at around a quarter of the country's total. Trump had referred to the deal the previous day, from the same podium, with the phrase “to the victor belong the spoils”.

According to Axios, citing White House sources, Trump pressed Rodríguez during Tuesday's meeting to call elections: “In the end, you're going to have to call elections,” he reportedly said. Neither participant confirmed that account. Secretary of State Marco Rubio framed it differently on Wednesday, saying the ultimate goal is “free and fair elections” but that an economic collapse must first be avoided. “If there is a social collapse or an economic crisis in Venezuela, not only are the elections in jeopardy, but also the survival of democracy in the country,” he said.

Rodríguez took office in an acting capacity on January 5, two days after Maduro's capture in a US military operation in Caracas, and faces questions over her legitimacy for not having been elected. Separately, the circle around opposition leader María Corina Machado said this week that three attempts to return to the country from Panama had been thwarted, bringing the total to seven in recent weeks.

World.title: Tabasco homicides dropped over 50% since 2024, officials report: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📍 Sheinbaum on tour: As is often the case on Fridays, President Sheinbaum held her press conference outside Mexico City. Her mañanera today was held in Villahermosa, the capital of the Gulf coast state of Tabasco.

As is often the case on Fridays, President Sheinbaum held her press conference outside Mexico City. Her mañanera today was held in Villahermosa, the capital of the Gulf coast state of Tabasco. 📉 Homicides down 54% in Tabasco : National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported Tabasco’s daily homicide rate hit 1.6 in August, a 54% drop from the November 2024 peak of 3.5 per day.

: National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported Tabasco’s daily homicide rate hit 1.6 in August, a 54% drop from the November 2024 peak of 3.5 per day. 🚔 Over 6,500 arrests since October 2024 : Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 6,527 people were arrested in Tabasco between October 2024 and September 15, 2026. He said that 2,053 firearms and nearly 13 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period.

: Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 6,527 people were arrested in Tabasco between October 2024 and September 15, 2026. He said that 2,053 firearms and nearly 13 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period. 🔻 La Barredora “greatly diminished” : Asked about the criminal group once allegedly led by Tabasco’s ex-Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena, García Harfuch said the organization has been “greatly diminished” and “practically split in two.”

: Asked about the criminal group once allegedly led by Tabasco’s ex-Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena, García Harfuch said the organization has been “greatly diminished” and “practically split in two.” 🗨️ Sheinbaum weighs in on Trump-Xi meeting: The president called Thursday’s meeting in Washington between Trump and Xi “very interesting.” She warned that rivalry between the two powers creates global uncertainty and reaffirmed Mexico’s preference for “peace and cooperation for development.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Villahermosa, capital of the Gulf Coast state of Tabasco.

Security officials presented data showing that the federal government has made significant progress in combating violence in the state, including through the arrest of alleged criminals accused of fueling it. Officials reasserted that the government’s security strategy is yielding results in Tabasco and across the country.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s comments on the meeting in Washington, D.C., on Thursday between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Sheinbaum will join both leaders, and various others, at the APEC Summit in China in November.

Government reports 54% reduction in homicides compared to 2024 peak

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that the daily homicide rate in Tabasco in August was 1.6, a reduction of 54% compared to November 2024, the month with the highest murder rate —3.5 per day — since the current federal government took office in October 2024.

“Thanks to the strengthening of the national public security strategy and coordination with the state government, a reduction in this crime has been achieved,” she said.

According to the data Figueroa presented, the year-over-year decline in homicides in August was 16%.

Figueroa also reported that Tabasco has recorded an average of 10.3 high-impact crimes per day so far in 2026.

That figure represents a decline of 12% compared to 2025 and a reduction of 18% compared to 2024. Among the offenses classified as high-impact crimes are homicides, kidnappings, acts of extortion, violent robberies and rape.

More than 6,000 people arrested in Tabasco since October 2024

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported that more than 6,500 people — 6,527 to be exact — were arrested in Tabasco between Oct. 1, 2024 and Sept. 15, 2026.

Data he presented showed that 2,053 firearms and 12.97 tonnes of drugs were seized in the state in the same period.

García Harfuch said that the arrest of “important targets” in Tabasco has had a “direct impact on the reduction of violence.”

He mentioned a number of the most significant arrests that have been made in the state, including that of a man accused of nine homicides.

García Harfuch: La Barredora has been weakened

A reporter asked García Harfuch about the current strength in Tabasco of La Barredora, a criminal group that was formerly allegedly led by ex-Tabasco Security Minister Hernán Bermúdez Requena.

Bermúdez, who served as security minister in the state government led by former Governor Adán Augusto López Hernández, was arrested in Paraguay in September 2024 and subsequently extradited to Mexico, where he is in prison awaiting trial. López, a Morena party senator and former federal interior minister, has faced claims from opposition parties that he was also involved in La Barredora when the group was allegedly led by Bermúdez.

García Harfuch said there have been “a lot of arrests” of people linked to the criminal group. He subsequently praised the Tabasco state police for their efforts to combat organized crime.

“This organization is greatly diminished,” he said, referring to La Barredora.

“It’s practically split in two,” García Harfuch said.

Sheinbaum comments on Trump-Xi meeting

A reporter asked the president about the meeting on Thursday between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, noting that the latter stated that China and the United States must maintain a peaceful relationship and engage in “healthy” competition.

Sheinbaum described the meeting between the U.S. and Chinese presidents as “very interesting.”

“… The idea of rivalry between two important nations such as China and the United States creates uncertainty in the world,” she said.

“And what Mexico has always sought is peace and cooperation for development,” Sheinbaum added.

She said that her government’s view is that economic competition shouldn’t create “rivalries between countries.”

Mexico has important economic relationships with both the United States and China. Mexico and the United States are each other’s largest trading partner, while China is a large exporter of goods to Mexico.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Cano’s ‘Malinche’: A musical that’s not all song and dance
World.content:
Just about every evening for the past year and a half, more than 1,000 people have made their way to El Frontón, a century-old Art Deco theatre in Mexico City’s small but historic enclave, Tabacalera.

There, the musical, “Malinche,” has been in full swing, having recently kicked off its second run on Aug. 15, with more than 80 cast members singing and dancing flamenco, urban, hip-hop and contemporary to the vision of Jesús Carmona, donning face paint, leather crop tops and fringed two-pieces in an auditorium seating 1,299.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MALINCHE EL MUSICAL (@malinchethemusical)

Created, written and directed by Nacho Cano, the show entered the Mexican theatre scene in March 2025 after a two-and-a-half-year run in Madrid, where it was housed in the IFEMA complex.

It wasn’t exactly Cano’s vision, who unsuccessfully pitched for a 30-meter Aztec-inspired pyramid in Hortaleza, but the venue was still kitted out with a small pyramid, cenotes, pyrotechnics and live bands, making a sizeable impression in Spain’s commercial theatre market.

Since its opening night, though, “Malinche” has faced backlash for what some consider historically insensitive depictions of the 1519 Spanish Conquest, including its retelling of Aztec emperor Moctezuma’s Christian awakening.

The controversy surrounding “Malinche” requires a discussion that centers not only its account of the titular Nahua woman, but also the political background of those who paved the way for its success.

Navigating the history and identity of Malinche

Much of popular art cannot be separated from its contemporary political milieu, both socially and geographically, and Nacho Cano’s work is no exception.

It was just seven years ago that then-President Andrés Manuel López Obrador sought an apology from Spain’s King Felipe VI over the colonial treatment of Indigenous Mexicans. After he failed to deliver such an apology, the king was subsequently excluded from President Claudia Sheinbaum’s inauguration, though he has since acknowledged that “there were significant abuses.”

Often described to those who don’t know her as the “Mexican Pocahontas,” it is widely understood that Malintzin, Doña Marina (her Christian name), or Malinche was an Indigenous woman who became Hernán Cortés’ interpreter and thus played a critical role during Spain’s conquest. Around 14 years old when she met Cortés, Malinche would eventually give birth to their son.

In no uncertain terms, Malinche’s history has been written for her. There is no surviving account from her own voice, only skewed and holey Spanish and Nahuatl accounts of the conquest. As an interpreter pushed into slavery, a potential informant of the Cholula massacre, or a willful lover — depending on who you ask — Malinche’s story becomes warped and warbled on the tongues of many.

A contested icon across modern political agendas

Like any cultural paradigm, scholars have attempted to categorize her perception and presentation both temporally and by groups supporting varying ideologies.

A traditional nationalist slant views Malinche as a traitor, “La Chingada,” taking on an Eve-like persona in her betrayal of the nation for the conquistadors, ultimately facilitating the tragic end of the Mexica. Others stress her victimhood not only at the hands of her oppressors but also in her literary portrayal as a traitor.

Here we see, through the abstraction of Malinche, the reduction of the female to a single narrative. Her portrayal even inspired the neologism “malinchista,” which refers to those favoring foreign cultures and ideals.

Meanwhile, feminist and Chicanx discourse have outlined Malinche’s dynamic representation in alignment with varying political agendas and strived to empower her agency. Many view her as a victim of colonial patriarchy who, as scholar Gloria Anzaldúa described it, exists beyond the “traditional/treacherous binary,” and chose to “be a survivor” who “cast her lot with the Spaniards to ensure survival of a race.”

Other postcolonial scholars take on such subaltern perspectives but question Malinche’s true autonomy, often highlighting the backdrop of religious colonial values of benevolence that Malinche was constructed and demonized against.

Acutely relevant, a pro-Hispanic and contemporary transformation of the narrative sees Malinche much like Disney portrays Pocahontas — a young woman whose love for the heroic Western explorer enabled the birth of the mestizaje, making her the “mother” of Mexico.

And so enters Nacho Cano, creator of “Malinche.”

Nacho Cano’s path from pop star to controversy

Ignacio “Nacho” Cano is a former member of the popular band Mecano, a luminary of Spain’s ’80s music scene and one of the biggest Spanish pop stars of the time. The band’s debut album sold 1 million copies in Spain alone, and they have since sold more than 30 million records worldwide.

Cano went on to develop the wildly influential “Hoy No Me Puedo Levantar,” a musical exploring Madrid’s post-Franco countercultural movement, La Movida, and one of the most financially successful Spanish musicals to date.

Despite his status as a 20th-century pop idol, Cano also established himself as a controversial political figure. He’s an avowed ally of the right-wing president of the Community of Madrid and People’s Party, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, who presented him in 2021 with the Order of the Second of May.

Ayuso herself was described by Politico as being in a “nationalistic showdown with Mexico.”

Such political dissension stems from her admiration of Cortés and defense of the Spanish Conquest as a civilizing mission, perhaps most notably at this year’s “Celebration of Evangelization and Mestizaje in Mexico.”

Sheinbaum has rebuked Ayuso’s characterization of the “conquest as salvation,” while Ayuso has been dubbed by Morena party members “the heir to the Spanish Falange,” a far-right fascist political movement founded in Spain in the 1930s.

Cano has similarly argued that “without Cortés there would be no Mexico,” a sentiment reflected in the feathers and flashlights of his extravagant musical production.

Divided perspectives and powerful corporate backing

In July 2024, Cano was arrested for alleged improprieties and poor working conditions for the performers in Madrid’s “Malinche,” including undocumented immigrants. The charges were dropped the following year, with Cano insisting that left-wing leaders led an alleged coordinated attack.

Beyond the show itself, Cano offers viewers a more detailed insight into the 10-year process behind his play in the 2021 Netflix documentary, “Making Malinche,” a name whose very essence speaks volumes. Malinche is once again a woman methodically remade and reduced, this time to an unwavering, consensual lover.

In an interview with El Mundo, Cano argued that Mexico’s history has been told “deliberately poorly,” and claimed in the documentary that his work is more historically accurate.

The overarching narrative he perpetuates is that Malinche was not a betrayer, but a woman whose passionate love for a Spaniard gifted humanity the New World.

We have seen a correlation between Malinche’s shifting portrayal and shifting Mexican cultural identity, as critics argue Cano has both sanitized and romanticized the violent reality of Spanish conquest.

Left-wing critics have argued the musical erases Indigenous trauma and experience in its “perpetuat[ion] of a Eurocentric narrative,” describing it as a “spectacle of postmodern Falangism.”

On the other end of the spectrum, conservative critics have chided Cano for doing a disservice to Catholicism, accusing him of not pushing far enough “an authentic ode to the history of Spain, against ideological revisionism and the Black Legend,” a reference to a school of thought that suggests “anti-Catholic” and “anti-Spanish” narratives deliberately position the Spanish Empire as singularly motivated by cruelty and greed.

However, these are not the only reasons many people in the left-wing community have boycotted “Malinche.”

The champions of ‘Malinche’

Ricardo Salinas Pliego, a Mexican television magnate and chairman of Grupo Salinas whose net worth is estimated to be US $5 billion, is responsible for bringing “Malinche” to Mexico and promoting it on his network, TV Azteca. His wife, María Laura Medina de Salinas, served as an executive producer during its opening in Mexico last year, after falling “in love” with it in Madrid and “form[ing] a synergy” with Cano, according to José Manuel Azpiroz, the director of communications at Salinas’ Grupo Elektra.

What’s more, the show is officially “presented” by Banco Azteca, part of Salinas’ conglomerate.

Much like Cano, Salinas is no stranger to controversy, having been accused of tax evasion to the tune of US $3 billion while also flirting with a presidential run.

Once labeled “the newest face of the Mexican new right,” he is an outspoken critic of Sheinbaum and supporter of the National Action Party (PAN), with a political temperament that follows in the footsteps of Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Salinas and Cano also have close ties to Juan Miguel Zunzunegui, a Mexican historian and avid rejector of the Black Legend. He defends the Spanish empire and upholds a history that dismisses Indigenous suffering and denies the mass violation of women.

In an interview with El Mundo, he said, “[t]he Spaniard who thinks they did horrible things in America does so out of ignorance.”

Cano recently wrote the prologue to Zunzunegui’s book, “Hernán Cortés,” and Zunzunegui is involved in the current run of “Malinche,” making a special appearance as Spanish friar and translator Jerónimo de Aguilar.

Turning historical violence into a love story

Malinche’s representation has been utilized as a vehicle to express specific sociopolitical ideologies within Mexican society, both at home and abroad. The question now is why proponents of “Malinche” feel a desire to promote a history of colonial violence as a love story that’s couched in consent and results in creation?

Some have asked a similar question of Disney’s romanticization of colonial relationships in its 1995 adaptation of “Pocahontas,” with the understanding that depicting a “mutually satisfying encounter” legitimizes what they describe as the violence of Western history.

“Malinche” too warrants consideration as part of a broader ideological posture seeking to sublimate Spain’s imperial legacy. However, with its second season running through January 2027, its popularity, devoid of nuanced conversations about who gets to write and rewrite history, speaks for itself.

Millie Deere is a freelance journalist.

World.title: The Mexico City neighborhoods where earthquakes are barely felt
World.content:
Mexico City was built over five ancient lakes. Although those bodies of water dried up during the invasion of Tenochtitlán — the ancient imperial capital of the Mexica — 500 years later, we still grapple with the consequences of that lacustrine past.

The soil in the Mexican capital is remarkably uneven — so much so that the local government classified the city into “zones,” distinguishing the soil types found in each borough.

Zone II, for example, is characterized by sandy soils, meaning earthquakes are felt with greater intensity at the surface. What’s more, this type of soil makes buildings prone to collapse if civil protection measures are not followed.

According to a UNAM Global report, the Roma, Condesa and Juárez neighborhoods fall within this zoning area. As such, they are among the neighborhoods that sustained the most structural damage during the 2017 and 2019 earthquakes.

Unfortunately, the Cuauhtémoc borough is among those that have been most ravaged by Mexico City’s earthquakes. Despite being one of the city’s major tourist draws — home to the Historic Center and the iconic Roma and Condesa neighborhoods — it has historically been devastated by these natural disasters, followed by the Benito Juárez, Coyoacán and Xochimilco boroughs.

Which neighborhoods, then, have suffered the least damage from earthquakes? Read on to find out if you live in one of them.

Safest neighborhoods during earthquakes in Mexico City

If you are looking to escape earthquakes in Mexico City, I have bad news for you: it isn’t possible. However, there are neighborhoods, many of which are located in the city’s southern reaches, where the movement is barely perceptible.

This is because, around 1,770 years ago, the Xitle volcano erupted in what is now the city’s south. Even today, the area retains this natural advantage, resulting in stable ground, as documented by the Mexico City government.

Having established that areas in Mexico City’s south, with its preserved volcanic soils, tend to be safer during earthquakes, which neighborhoods experience the least seismic activity?

Colonia Jardines del Pedregal

One of the most famous neighborhoods for being “safe during earthquakes” is Jardines del Pedregal. Designed by Diego Rivera and architect Luis Barragán in the 1940s, this area is recognized as one of the city’s wealthiest neighborhoods.

Characterized by huge houses and spacious pavilions and gardens, it sits on volcanic rock terrain that absorbs much of the seismic shock.

As mentioned, the neighborhood features natural volcanic stone details integrated into its urban architecture — and sometimes even into the houses themselves. So, in addition to being one of the city’s most exclusive areas, it also has the wonderful advantage of being barely affected by earthquakes.

Ciudad Universitaria at UNAM

In addition to being home to one of the most beautiful ecological reserves in the south, UNAM’s Ciudad Universitaria (CU) is one of the places in Mexico City where earthquakes are least perceptible.

As seen in El Pedregal, it is common to find large chunks of volcanic rock embedded in the ground, forming part of the area’s natural beauty.

Often, because these materials are so ancient, age-old trees have grown atop the volcanic rocks, providing shade to the university’s community. So yes, you can stroll through its vast green spaces and enjoy its UNESCO World Heritage-listed views in complete tranquility.

Colonia Guadalupe Inn

Known as the “little queen of the south,” the Guadalupe Inn neighborhood is one of the most traditional in the southern part of the city. Like its neighbors Chimalistac and San Ángel, it retains a colonial charm in its homes and businesses — a quality few places in the capital have preserved so gracefully.

Established in the mid-20th century on the grounds of the former Hacienda de Guadalupe, its streets bear the names of famous Mexican composers and are often lined with beautiful jacaranda trees, as well as other species found only in southern Mexico City.

Beyond its remarkable architectural and natural beauty, the neighborhood also tends to be spared during earthquakes.

Colonia San Ángel

If Guadalupe Inn is the “little queen of the south,” San Ángel is the empress. Classy, ​​upscale and undeniably stylish, it is another neighborhood where Mexico City’s tremors are barely felt.

Like the other southern colonias mentioned in this article, it is situated on volcanic soil, which absorbs much of the seismic impact.

During the colonial era, San Ángel was a small village in its own right, and it shows. The neighborhood boasts a Baroque church at the heart of a stone-paved plaza, a magnificent flower market, and fantastic cobblestone streets. What more could you ask for?

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: More than 7,000 ignore clouds to gather at Chichén Itzá for the equinox
World.content:
Thousands of people gathered in the esplanade in front of the great pyramid of Kukulcán in the Chichén Itzá archaeological site in the state of Yucatán on Monday and Tuesday to witness the famous descent of the serpent.

The spectacular light and shadow phenomenon takes place during the spring and autumn equinoxes each year when afternoon sunlight hits the pyramid at a particular angle. As a result, the silhouette of a serpent is projected on the wall of the north balustrade of the structure known as El Castillo.

The intricate design of El Castillo, also called the Temple of Kukulcán, allows for the projection of seven isosceles triangles of light which appear to the observer as a luminous and magical serpent moving down the pyramid toward the carved serpent head near its base.

This fascinating interplay of light and shadow — known as the hierophanies of the equinoxes — typically lasts from 10 to 30 minutes.

This year, the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) implemented a special operation to receive tourists beginning on Sunday as the interplay of light and shadow was visible from Sunday through Tuesday.

El Castillo was built in a geometric pyramid shape with nine truncated levels, superimposed and progressively smaller with a small temple at the top.

Central staircases on each of the four sides, each with 91 steps. allowed access to the temple. In total, there are 364 steps, but including the platform on which the pyramid rests, the result is 365, precisely the length of the Maya civil year.

“It reminds us of the admirable precision with which the ancient Maya observed the movement of the sun and the cycles of the seasons,” the INAH said in a statement, adding that the calculations were fundamental to Maya agriculture.

INAH said the instant of the equinox this year occurred at 3:51 p.m. on Monday. In all, INAH recorded more than 7,000 visitors at Chichen Itza from Sunday through Tuesday.

Because autumn starts before the rainy season ends, there are often clouds at the equinox hiding the effect. This year was no exception, but there were enough breaks in the cloud cover for the visitors to get good looks at the phenomenon.

Last year, Chichen Itza surpassed Teotihuacán and Tulum as the most popular cultural tourism site in Mexico, according to the Tourism Ministry.

With reports from La Jornada Maya, National Geographic and Yucatán Magazine

World.title: Mayor of Juchitán, Oaxaca, arrested over alleged CJNG ties, triggering blockades and protests
World.content:
Federal and state security forces on Wednesday arrested the mayor of Juchitán, Oaxaca, and another man on charges of aggravated extortion and crimes against state security. The arrests triggered road blockades and protests in Juchitán, located on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec.

The federal Security Ministry (SSPC), Security Minister Omar García Harfuch and the Oaxaca Attorney General’s Office (FGEO) all announced the arrests of Miguel Sánchez Altamirano, a Morena party mayor, and Alberto de la Paz López, a man known as “La Parca” (or “La Parka).

En el marco de la política de Cero Impunidad instruida por la Presidenta @Claudiashein, durante un despliegue operativo en Oaxaca, elementos de @SEMAR_mx, @SSPCMexico, @Defensamx1, @FGRMexico y @GN_MEXICO_, en coordinación con la @FISCALIA_GobOax y @SSPC_GobOax, detuvieron a… pic.twitter.com/6xlOskXAh7 — Omar H Garcia Harfuch (@OHarfuch) September 23, 2026

The SSPC said in a statement that the arrests were carried out “within the framework of Operativo Enjambre” (Operation Swarm), a federal security strategy aimed at combating collusion between organized crime and municipal government officials.

“As part of an investigation into a criminal network linked to extortion, … small-scale drug dealing, human trafficking … and homicides — as well as protection schemes that allegedly facilitated the operations of members of criminal groups — agents pursued various lines of inquiry,” the Security Ministry said.

“As a result of these efforts, Miguel ‘N,’ the mayor of Juchitán de Zaragoza, and another person were identified. Both had active arrest warrants for … aggravated extortion and crimes against state security. Consequently, an inter-institutional operation was launched, during which both men were arrested,” the SSPC said.

The FGEO described the arrests as a “head-on strike against criminality.”

In a statement, the state Attorney General’s Office said that Sánchez, mayor of Juchitán since late 2022, is linked to a criminal group called Los Cromos. It said that the group — of which de la Paz is an alleged member — “functions as an operational arm” of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

The FGEO said that “intelligence work” determined that the mayor “participated in, promoted, and covered up criminal activities in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, due to his close relationship and strategic ties with” Los Cromos.

Juchitán, a city of around 115,000 people, is located near the southern coast of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Mexico’s narrowest stretch of land between the Pacific Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico.

From Ciudad Ixtepec, also located on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, both Sánchez and de la Paz were transferred to Mexico City on a Mexican Navy plane. They are currently in prison pending initial court appearances.

UIF blocks accounts of people linked to Juchitán investigation

García Harfuch said in an X post that the Finance Ministry’s Financial Intelligence Unit froze assets and blocked bank accounts of people linked to the investigation that led to the arrest of Sánchez and de la Paz.

He subsequently thanked the government of Oaxaca and Governor Salomón Jara for their “ongoing collaboration and coordination” with federal authorities.

“Investigations and operational actions to completely break up this criminal structure and detain all those involved are continuing,” García Harfuch wrote, referring to Los Cromos.

“As new arrests are made, we will continue to report,” he wrote.

An angry response in Juchitán

The arrest of Sánchez and de la Paz on Wednesday morning sparked a hostile reaction in Juchitán.

The Reforma newspaper reported that main roads were blocked and protests were held in Juchitán. The newspaper wrote that moto-taxi drivers, Juchitán residents and even municipal police officers joined the protests.

At one point on Federal Highway 185, moto-taxi drivers and residents laid tires across the road and set them on fire to block traffic and “demand the release of Sánchez Altamirano,” Reforma reported.

La Jornada reported that Juchitán moto-taxi drivers were involved in a drug-dealing and extortion scheme allegedly led by de la Paz and allegedly protected by the city’s mayor.

🚨 Bloquean accesos a Juchitán de Zaragoza, Oaxaca, tras la detención del alcalde Miguel ‘Quetú’ Su detención forma parte de una investigación contra una estructura criminal a la que las autoridades relacionan con distintos delitos, entre ellos extorsión y cobro de piso a… pic.twitter.com/oRmJwl2RB0 — Milenio (@Milenio) September 23, 2026

Citing “sources close to the operation” and local media reports, Reforma reported that police officers “closed off the city’s entry and exit points following the arrest of their own mayor.”

If their goal was to prevent the transfer of Sánchez and de la Paz to Ciudad Ixtepec, where a military airport is located, they failed.

The Juchitán mayor is among more than 100 municipal officials who have been detained since Operación Enjambre began in late 2024. Among the other mayors who have been arrested are the mayor of Tequila, Jalisco, who was detained on extortion charges in February, and the mayor of Atlatlahucan, Morelos, who was taken into custody in May.

García Harfuch said earlier this year that the arrest of officials is part of the government’s commitment to “zero impunity.”

When there is proof that a current or former official has committed a crime, he or she will be “investigated and arrested” no matter what political party he or she belongs to, he said May 27. García Harfuch also said that officials detained during the current administration are from “all” of Mexico’s political parties.

With reports from La Jornada and Reforma

World.title: Senate bill would force Mexican pro soccer to bring back promotion and relegation
World.content:
The fight over the elimination of promotion and relegation in Mexican soccer has moved deeper into the Senate, where lawmakers this week published a bill that would require Liga MX to restore a path for second-division clubs to reach the top flight.

The proposal, introduced by Senator Clemente Castañeda, a member of the opposition Citizens’ Movement party from Jalisco, would amend Article 50 of the General Law of Physical Culture and Sport. It reportedly has support from 10 senators from several parties.

The bill would require promotion and relegation when two or more professional divisions operate within the same national competitive structure.

While its language could extend to other sports, the immediate target is Liga MX and the closed system separating the top division from the Liga de Expansión MX. Before 2020, that second-tier professional league was named Ascenso MX — “ascenso” meaning promotion.

“When they closed off the possibility of promotion, they didn’t just change a sporting rule,” Castañeda said. “They also restricted a path for players, staff and sports projects to grow in a country that needs to open up opportunities.”

The bill presented Wednesday must clear Senate committees and pass both houses of Congress before it can become law.

Liga MX owners suspended promotion and relegation in 2020 as part of a Mexican Football Federation (FMF) restructuring during the COVID-19 shutdown. Officials said a six-season promotion pause was needed to stabilize financially troubled lower-division clubs.

The system was expected to return after the 2025-26 season — with one second-division club getting promoted and one Liga MX club relegated each year.

Instead, Mexico’s soccer authorities removed it from league regulations, prompting protests by clubs, players and fans.

Still, the FMF insists that second-division teams are “eligible” for promotion if they meet certification standards, such as financial solvency and a formal organizational structure. One of the requirements is stadium capacity of 30,000 — a threshold that even some Liga MX clubs do not meet, critics say.

Five Liga de Expansión teams — Cancún FC, Atlético La Paz, Atlético Morelia, Leones Negros de la Universidad de Guadalajara and Mineros de Zacatecas — appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport after the policy change.

A 2025 ruling by the Lausanne, Switzerland-based body found that the FMF’s six-season suspension ran only through the 2025-26 season, clearing the way for promotion and relegation to return.

But the FMF and Liga MX instead removed the system from the regulations for the current 2026-27 season.

At Liga de Expansión opening matches last month, players from several teams spent the first minute standing still or passing without attacking to protest the policy. The disciplinary commission warned clubs that additional disruptions could result in fines.

The dispute has broadened beyond the Senate. Mexico’s National Antitrust Commission this month opened an investigation into possible monopolistic practices in pro soccer. The FMF could face fines of up to 10% of annual revenue if authorities find violations of competition law.

This week’s Senate proposal could also raise questions under FIFA statutes, which require member federations to manage their affairs independently and without undue third-party influence. FIFA’s council may temporarily suspend an association that seriously violates its obligations.

Mexico’s closed Liga MX structure contrasts with the major European leagues. The English Premier League, Spain’s La Liga, Italy’s Serie A, Germany’s Bundesliga and France’s Ligue 1 all promote clubs from and relegate clubs to their second divisions based on results.

But Liga MX is not alone. Major League Soccer in the U.S. and Canada and the A-League Men in Australia also operate without promotion and relegation.

With reports from ESPN, Associated Press and TUDN

World.title: Is internet satire under threat in Mexico? Why the ‘Anti-Meme Bill’ is controversial
World.content:
A Senate bill meant to strengthen intellectual property protection has sparked controversy over possible digital censorship in Mexico, particularly as it could apply to parodies or satires aimed at the government.

The bill, sent to the Senate by President Sheinbaum in May and due to be voted on soon, entails amendments to the Federal Penal Code and the Federal Law for the Protection of Industrial Property (LFPPI).

The initiative is part of a broader set of reforms that, according to the federal government, aim to strengthen the criminal framework regarding intellectual property and align it with international treaties such as the United States-Mexico and Canada Agreement (USMCA).

Critics, such as PAN Senator Ricardo Anaya (in the video), have dubbed the bill the “Anti-Meme Law,” arguing that its wording could affect journalists, cartoonists, and content creators who use official elements in satirical works.

That same “Anti-Meme Law” moniker has also been applied to a separate but similar reform — an amendment to the Federal Copyright Law regarding the liability of internet service providers — currently under debate in the Chamber of Deputies.

Regarding the LFPPI, the opposition parties say they are concerned about the addition of Article 403 Bis, which establishes an offense related to the misuse of government identity.

The original wording penalized the commercial use of logos, domain names, graphic identities, or official symbols of governments and public bodies — including via digital means — to deceive people, with sentences ranging from three to seven years in prison and fines of up to 1.17 million pesos (US $65,000).

Following public criticism, voting committees amended the proposal by reportedly reducing the prison time to one to five years. More importantly, it was clarified that the offense would only apply to those who use the government’s image for commercial, deceptive, or fraudulent purposes.

Under the amended terms, content that uses an official logo or colors for satire, parody, criticism, or memes — and is easily recognizable as unofficial — would not constitute an infringement.

In a statement, Morena Senator Javier Corral said that the interpretation of the bill had been blown out of proportion.

“I want to reject the idea that jail time is being proposed for memes or parodies, and to clarify that this provision has nothing to do with regulating freedom of expression. That is not the case,” he said.

“The wording we are now proposing not only eliminates any ambiguity but specifically seeks to establish that the act of misleading or deceiving one or more persons [through the use of government logos] must have the commission of an unlawful act as its purpose.”

It is anticipated the bill would be approved under the new terms.

With reports from El Universal, Eje Central, and El Financiero

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Floating billboards, restaurant closures and a key resignation
World.content:
Puerto Vallarta is navigating a series of challenges as the city balances tourism, economic pressures and environmental concerns. A floating advertising screen has sparked debate over the bay’s visual and environmental impact, while a difficult low season has forced restaurants to cut staff and temporarily close. Meanwhile, the resignation of the city’s Environmental Guard director has added another layer to ongoing questions about how the municipality will manage growth and preservation.

Floating screen sparks controversy in Puerto Vallarta

A vessel featuring a large-format LED screen has begun sailing off the coast of Puerto Vallarta, displaying commercial s visible from various points along the tourist strip.

Residents, visitors and local representatives have warned that the screen could not only damage the natural landscape through light pollution but also the bay’s image as a tourist destination.

The screen has been linked to Oceanic Marketing, a company that offers maritime advertising via vessels displaying ads visible from the shore.

In response to the criticism, Municipal President Luis Ernesto Munguía González asked environmental federal authorities, as well as the navy ministry and port authority, to review the vessel’s operating conditions. The request includes verifying maritime and environmental permits, as well as safety standards regarding navigation and the use of maritime space.

The municipal government said that local regulations restrict large-scale billboards on land. However, authorities added there are currently no regulations pertaining to advertising installed at sea.

As such, authorities are now working to clarify which rules would apply



Puerto Vallarta restaurateurs affected by tourism decline

The sharp drop in visitor numbers during the low season has led Puerto Vallarta restaurants to implement staffing and operational adjustments to curb losses.

In the city center — particularly along the Malecón and its surrounding areas — some establishments have introduced staggered shifts, unpaid leave and early vacation scheduling, as a strategy to cut costs in the face of declining sales.

These measures primarily affect workers who rely on tips and commission, as lower foot traffic reduces both available working hours and daily earnings.

The situation has also led to temporary closures.

Martha Parra, head of the National Chamber of the Restaurant and Seasoned Food Industry (CANIRAC) in Puerto Vallarta, told news outlet Jafrico that at least 15 businesses have temporarily ceased operations and two have permanently closed.

Parra acknowledged that the combination of fewer tourists, high rent and overall economic downturn has made it hard for businesses with slim margins to stay afloat.

She noted that although the current off-season has been more challenging than previous years, it is not an isolated problem, as restaurants in other destinations have also reported declines between 20% and 30% compared to 2025.

Head of Puerto Vallarta’s Environmental Guard resigns

The restructuring of Puerto Vallarta’s city council saw a high-level departure this week, after Diego López Coronado resigned as director of the Environmental Guard.

The former official announced his departure on Wednesday via his official social media channels, describing his decision as “well-thought, deliberate and made with a strong sense of responsibility.”

In his letter to Municipal President Luis Ernesto Munguía González, López Coronado said his decision was based on personal and professional interests, adding that he had different views on certain municipal matters.

“Over time, however, I have found myself at odds with several of the decisions that have been made, and I reached a conclusion I cannot avoid; there are things that can no longer be defended,” López Coronado wrote.

López Coronado had previously served as director of social development before taking on the newly created environmental division, established through an administrative restructure approved by the city council a year ago.

López Coronado’s departure comes amidst an ongoing review of the organizational structure and assessment of the performance and tenure of municipal officials.

So far, the municipal government has not announced who will replace López Coronado, nor has it detailed whether further cabinet changes are forthcoming.
