Africa Intelligence Dossier — Friday, 25 September 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web. Read the web dossier → · The dossier archive →

Madagascar — Betrayed, and told to celebrate the revolt anyway. South Sudan — Cleared of everyone but its president, three months before a vote. Zimbabwe — Asking its own parliament to call the country an emergency. Liberia — Quarrelling about what a citizen may lawfully type.

Africa’s temper this Friday is impatience with its own institutions rather than with anyone abroad. Four governments spent the week arguing with their own citizens about who is owed what.

The register is tired book-keeping rather than rage. Malagasy activists are auditing what their revolt bought them, Zimbabwean members of parliament are auditing sewage works, and South Sudan’s president has audited his cabinet away.

Antananarivo is the sharpest case, because both sides are marking the same anniversary. Streets around Anosy and Ambohidahy were closed to traffic from 7 a.m. local time on Friday for the unveiling of a memorial stone.

Juba emptied itself on purpose. President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government and removed every vice-president and minister by decree on Tuesday evening, three months before an election set for 22 December.

Southern Africa’s story this week is plumbing, and it is being counted rather than shouted. A parliamentary committee’s report told Zimbabwe that only 20 of the country’s 63 sewage treatment plants still work.

What steadies the week is being built rather than announced. Uganda has begun a power line into South Sudan, and Madagascar’s footballers were in Nigeria on Friday for a match the whole island could watch.

Key Facts — Madagascar’s contested holiday. Antananarivo marked the first anniversary of its 2025 revolt on Friday, a day the labour minister confirmed as paid and non-working after his ministry’s page had denied it. — South Sudan’s emptied government. Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government by decree on 22 September, removing the first vice-president, all ministers and every state assembly before a vote on 22 December. — Zimbabwe’s broken sewage works. Only 20 of Zimbabwe’s 63 sewage treatment plants still function, a parliamentary committee’s report found, asking for a state of emergency by 31 December 2026. — Liberia’s detained cybercrime suspect. Jerry Nyantee Wrato was still in the dock on 24 September, when a judge postponed his habeas corpus hearing to Friday because no police officer appeared. — Mali’s escorted fuel convoys. More than 900 fuel tankers reached Bamako under military escort on 14 September, a year into the blockade of the roads that supply Mali’s capital. — Uganda’s new power line. Uganda has begun a 299-kilometre high-voltage line to South Sudan with about US$121 million from the African Development Fund, to be built between 2026 and 2029. — Lake Tanganyika’s night sinking. At least 41 people died and 49 were rescued when a boat from Kigoma capsized near Mapera in Congo early on Thursday 24 September. — Ethiopia’s competing battle claims. Ethiopia’s army said it killed 272 Tigrayan fighters and wounded 260 in Amhara, while the Tigray front’s vice-president called the fighting full-blown war.

Madagascar Marks A Revolt It No Longer Trusts

Madagascar spent Friday marking an uprising whose authors say it was taken from them. The first protest, over chronic water and power cuts, was held on 25 September 2025.

The officers who ended up governing are now the people the protesters complain about. Felana Andriatahina, 32, who runs an eco-construction business and belongs to the activists’ collective, told Agence France-Presse “It’s a betrayal”.

Her reasoning is about who benefited. She told the agency that it was the movement’s street protests that put the present rulers in office.

The state’s own answer this week was a public holiday, and then a row about it. Midi Madagasikara, a Malagasy daily, reported on 23 September that a decree numbered 2026-2212 made Friday a paid non-working day nationwide.

Its stated purpose was to honour those killed or hurt in 2025. The labour ministry’s own Facebook page then said that the declaration was untrue.

The minister blamed intruders rather than his own department. Denis Franconio Mac said the ministry had lost access to that page and pointed at people out to sow disorder, the Malagasy news site 2424.mg reported on 24 September.

His own account is that the holiday stood after all. Mr Mac said the day was paid and non-working under a decree signed by the prime minister in the Conseil de gouvernement, the cabinet meeting the prime minister chairs.

The other body is the one that did not sign it. A Conseil des ministres is chaired by the head of state, and it is that distinction the row turned on.

The head of state had said something different from New York. The site 2424.mg reported that Colonel Michael Randrianirina denied the announcement on 23 September, saying no such decision had been taken.

The arrangements went ahead regardless of the payroll. Antananarivo’s city authority closed Rue Jean Ralaimongo, Rue Mohamed V and Rue Titsy to traffic from 7 a.m. local time until the ceremony ended, the site reported on Friday.

The memorial itself is at Anosy. L’Express de Madagascar, a Malagasy daily, reported that a commemorative stele had been erected at the roundabout leading towards the Ambohidahy tunnel, to be unveiled at the ceremony.

The theme was set by the organisers. L’Express reported that the day ran under the words “Engagement et unité pour la patrie”, or engagement and unity for the homeland.

The head of state was expected there with four High Counsellors of the Refoundation. He had addressed the United Nations General Assembly the day before.

What he said in New York was a year. The site 2424.mg reported that Colonel Randrianirina reaffirmed the Refoundation authorities’ intention to hold elections before the end of 2027.

Not every part of the movement accepted the official version of its own anniversary. L’Express reported that a hardline faction of the Gen Z movement had distanced itself from the ceremony, saying its struggle had been stolen.

What turned relief into grievance was a set of arrests. Herizo Andriamanantena, 30, an agricultural engineer, is one of the movement’s best-known faces.

His own case is the one most often cited. He was held for 13 days after a march in April 2026 against the pace of reform, and six demonstrators were detained in all, Agence France-Presse reported.

He described the two feelings of the year in one interview. Of the day the old president fell he said “It was really both joy and relief”.

A second account is harder still. Nomena Ratsihorimanana, 36, who had worked for the National Human Rights Observatory, was held for five days.

He described the arrest itself. Mr Ratsihorimanana said “They put guns in our mouths, they threatened to kill us”.

The lawyers’ objection is about which charge is reached for. Maromanana Aliarivelo, a Malagasy lawyer, called the state-security charge “the tool par excellence used for ages by those in power in Madagascar”.

What steadies this is that the movement’s arithmetic has not changed. About 70 per cent of Malagasy are under 30, on United Nations children’s fund figures cited by Agence France-Presse.

The cost of last year is the other half of the ledger. At least 22 people died in the unrest of 2025.

The mood a year on is flat rather than angry. Midi Madagasikara wrote on 17 September that the generation which began it is disappointed to the point of paralysis.

Juba Clears The Room Before It Votes

South Sudan’s president answered his coming election by removing almost everyone else from office. Salva Kiir issued a Republican Order on the evening of Tuesday 22 September dissolving the transitional unity government created by the 2018 peace agreement.

The text was read out on the state broadcaster. Radio Tamazuj, a South Sudanese news service, reported that the order dissolved the national legislature and the Council of States.

The removals went further than the chamber. The order removed the first vice-president, Riek Machar, with the four other vice-presidents, and dissolved all ten state governments and their assemblies.

Somebody had to keep the lights on. Radio Tamazuj reported that 13 caretaker ministers, three deputy ministers and ten caretaker governors were named in the same order.

The ministries were told to carry on without their political heads. The order said all “substantive National Ministers and Deputy Ministers are hereby relieved of their portfolio duties”.

Their instruction was to keep working anyway. They were directed to “continue operating under an interim or caretaker structure” until the election.

The law that permits this was altered days earlier. President Kiir signed amendments to the National Elections Act of 2012 on 22 September, Reuters reported.

Two conditions came out of it. The amendments removed the requirements for a permanent constitution and a national census before any vote.

The same amendments resize the state. Radio Tamazuj reported that the new national assembly has 270 elected members, with 66 appointed to represent veterans, organised forces, minorities and people with special needs.

The states shrink in the same way. Their ten assemblies will hold 580 members between them, 58 each, half from constituencies and half from party lists.

The presidency keeps what the deputies lose. Vice-presidents must leave office three months before polling day, while the incumbent president retains full constitutional powers until the elected president takes office.

The presidency’s account of it is procedural. Africano Mande Gedima, the minister for presidential affairs, said the amendments brought the election law into line with the transitional constitution, Reuters reported.

Mr Machar’s party rejects the whole design. Oyet Nathaniel Pierino, acting chairman of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement in Opposition, said in August that the changes stripped out the census and the constitution as conditions.

He put it as a legal charge. Mr Pierino accused the president of trying to “legalize” violations of the 2018 agreement, Radio Tamazuj reported.

Not every opponent takes that view. A rival faction of the same movement, led by the peacebuilding minister Stephen Par Kuol, supports the December vote.

A candidate outside both camps objects to the appointments rather than the election. Kornelio Kon Ngu leads the National United Democratic Front and was once third deputy speaker.

His complaint is about a broken understanding. Mr Kon Ngu said the parties had agreed that appointments would be made through consultation, and added “But this has not happened”.

Constitutional lawyers put the consequence bluntly. Michael Wani, who sat on the constitution drafting committee, said “Kiir will be the only person in power, without vice-presidents, without the executive, without the parliament”.

An analyst reads the same law as an escape route. Machot Amuom, an independent analyst, told Al Jazeera, the Qatari state-funded broadcaster, that it could let the president put the vote off for another year or two.

One civic voice made it a warning instead of a legal argument. Edmund Yakani, who directs the Community Empowerment for Progress Organisation, told Reuters “Don’t return us to war”.

The reason a reader far away should care is what a failed vote could restart. About 400,000 people died in the civil war that the 2018 agreement ended.

The man who signed that agreement is not free to contest this one. Mr Machar has been held since March 2025 on treason and murder charges that he denies.

Something is also being built across the same border. Uganda has begun a 299-kilometre high-voltage line joining its grid to South Sudan’s, the Nile Post, a Kampala news site, reported on Friday.

Uganda’s share of the money is one figure counted two ways. Its part is 91.7 million units of account, which the Nile Post put at about US$121 million.

The Fund’s own arithmetic is a little lower. The African Development Fund valued Uganda’s loan at US$119.21 million when it approved the financing, a difference of conversion date rather than of substance.

The whole link costs more than either country’s share. The Fund approved US$153.66 million towards a project costing US$260 million, with a US$32.50 million grant for South Sudan beside it.

The point of the line is diesel. Baba Fataja of the African Development Bank said “South Sudan is really struggling to have a reliable supply of electricity, which is very expensive because they depend on diesel”.

The Fund puts a number on who gains. It expects the link to reach 286,710 people in South Sudan and to carry 624 gigawatt hours between the two countries each year.

Uganda’s stretch is half the distance. It runs about 150 kilometres from Olwiyo to the border by way of Bibia, and the work runs from 2026 to 2029.

Downtown Harare. A parliamentary committee has asked the president to declare a state of emergency over the capital’s sewage, with twenty of the country’s sixty-three treatment plants still working.

Harare Asks To Be Declared An Emergency

Zimbabwe’s parliament has put a number on its own sanitation and asked the president to act. Only 20 of the country’s 63 sewage treatment plants still function, NewZimbabwe.com, a London-based Zimbabwean site critical of the government, reported on Friday.

The report is older than the week it was read in. The portfolio committee on environment, climate and wildlife tabled it in July 2025, and it was released this week.

The figures explain the request. The plants still working discharge an estimated 570 megalitres of raw sewage every day.

One place is worse than all the others. At Amalinda Crossing, trunk mains that have given way have been discharging about 80 megalitres of raw sewage a day into the Mukuvisi River for 15 years.

Harare’s own works run below what they were built for. The Firle plant was designed for 144 megalitres a day and treats about 54, while the Crowborough plant does not work at all.

The river’s chemistry is in the report as well. Dissolved oxygen measured 51.2 per cent against a safe level of 60, and biological oxygen demand was 9.48 milligrams a litre.

The committee’s request carries a date. It asked the president to declare a state of emergency over the water and sanitation crisis by 31 December 2026.

A town next door is served worse than the capital. Chitungwiza receives about 12 megalitres of water a day against a demand of 112.5, NewZimbabwe.com reported.

Its own treatment works stopped long ago. The Zengeza wastewater plant has not functioned since 2007, and about 40,000 unlawful structures stand on protected wetland.

The remedy proposed for that town has a price and a deadline. The committee wants water authority status for Chitungwiza by December 2026 and a cholera alleviation programme costing about US$426.3 million.

Cholera is the word the committee reaches for because it is in living memory. The outbreak of 2008 and 2009 killed about 4,200 people and infected about 98,000, NewZimbabwe.com reported.

The city has not yet put its own account beside the committee’s. Harare’s council had published nothing about the report in its own newsroom by 16.35 UTC on Friday.

What was there instead was routine. The most recent item in that newsroom was dated 23 September and concerned a women’s leadership forum.

The national government’s position on councils is already on the record, and it is not sympathetic. Daniel Garwe, the minister of local government, addressed all 92 local authorities in June.

He drew the comparison himself. Mr Garwe said he would not tolerate one town with clean water beside another facing “a cholera outbreak due to broken-down sewer systems”, NewsDay, a privately owned Harare daily, reported.

He put the money problem in one figure. Mr Garwe said internal audits found councils spending up to 80 per cent of revenue on salaries and administration, leaving under 20 per cent for services.

He also told them the rules had changed. Mr Garwe called the new minimum service standards “no longer suggestions”.

In the same week the country began preparing for too little water rather than too much. Anxious Masuka, the minister of agriculture, said “Government has already approved a drought mitigation plan with six pillars”.

The new part of it is aircraft. Mr Masuka said a contingency plan agreed this time would use conventional aeroplanes and drones, 263Chat, an independent Harare online outlet, reported on 24 September.

Three aircraft are involved and the forecast is the reason. They will work from Harare, Bulawayo and Masvingo alongside drones.

The forecast is put as a possibility rather than a certainty. The Meteorological Services Department has said rainfall could be “erratic, poorly distributed and separated by prolonged dry spells”.

One official emphasis matters for a foreign reader. Obert Jiri, the permanent secretary for agriculture, said the next season was “expected to be drier than normal” and that “We are looking at irrigation development”.

The coming harvest is what those words are about. It decides how much maize Zimbabwe has to buy in.

Monrovia Quarrels Over What A Citizen May Type

Liberia is testing a new law against a doctored picture of its own vice-president. Police charged Jerry Nyantee Wrato with four offences under the Cybercrime Act of 2025.

The pictures were made by machine. The images and video of Vice-President Jeremiah Kpan Koung were produced with artificial intelligence, The Liberian Investigator, a Monrovia news site, reported on 21 September.

The charges are named in the police account. They are misuse of devices, cyberstalking, distribution of data messages inciting damage to property or violence, and distribution of harmful data messages.

The unusual part is who asked for the man’s release. Mr Koung said he had “no desire to press charges against this young man, or anyone else, merely for creating or sharing such content” about him.

He went further than that. Mr Koung said “I have therefore requested his immediate release”, The New Dawn, a Monrovia daily, reported on 21 September.

He added a line about how office should behave. Mr Koung said “Our laws must protect citizens, but leadership must also exercise tolerance, restraint and compassion”.

The police refused him. Gregory Coleman, the inspector-general, said that once such conduct comes to the attention of law enforcement, “the matter is no longer determined solely by the personal wishes of the individual affected”.

He was careful about what the charge meant. Mr Coleman said the action was not a determination of guilt.

The case has since stalled in a courtroom rather than moved. Judge Pape Suah of Criminal Court B postponed a habeas corpus hearing on Thursday 24 September, FrontPage Africa, a Monrovia paper known for investigations, reported on Friday.

Nobody came from the police for a second time. The arresting officer, the inspector-general and officers from three units all failed to appear, and the judge called their absence “a disrespect”.

The judge gave them one more chance and a clock. He moved the hearing to Friday 25 September at 11 a.m. local time and called it the respondents’ “last opportunity”.

The man himself has not been released. Mr Wrato sat in the dock during Thursday’s proceedings and remains in police custody.

His counsel says the detention is already unlawful. Garrison Yealue said the police had “illegally arrested the Petitioner and illegally kept him for more than 120 hours”.

He objected to the delay itself as well. Mr Yealue called the request to postpone “made in bad faith” and “a complete disrespect” to the court.

The law’s sponsor says none of this is about opinion. Francis Saidy Dopoh II is the senator for River Gee County and chairs the Senate committee on posts and telecommunications.

His own words were categorical. Senator Dopoh said “On free speech, let me be clear: this law has no intent to silence free speech”, the Liberian Observer, another Monrovia daily, reported on Friday.

He listed what the law is for. The Liberian Observer reported that the act covers threats of violence, harassment, incitement to violence, fraud and child exploitation, alongside cyberstalking and identity theft.

He also asked for machinery before enforcement. Senator Dopoh called for a national cybersecurity centre, published regulations, police training and a public awareness campaign before the law is pressed hard.

He addressed the public directly as well. Senator Dopoh said “To every citizen: learn the law, use the internet responsibly, and report abuse”.

The attack on the law comes from more than one direction. Samuel Tweah Jr., a former finance minister, called the cyberbullying provision “draconian”.

His argument is about where the man should be. Mr Tweah said “He should not be behind bars for free speech in the first place”.

The journalists’ objection is constitutional rather than political. Peter Quaqua, president of the West African Journalists Association, wrote that “The fact that speech is delivered electronically does not automatically remove its constitutional protection”.

One senator tried to set a threshold rather than repeal anything. Nya Twayen Jr., the senator for Nimba County, said “Offensive or unpopular opinions alone should not constitute sufficient grounds for prosecution”.

He wants the justice ministry to publish how it will act. Mr Twayen said the law “should not be used to criminalize criticism, comedy or the expression of an opinion”, The New Dawn reported on 24 September.

The constitutional balance he invokes is written down. Article 15 of Liberia’s 1986 constitution guarantees freedom of expression while making each person responsible for its abuse.

Even the day the law took effect is reported two ways. The Liberian Observer said President Joseph Nyuma Boakai approved it on 3 July 2026, while The New Dawn said he signed it on 19 August 2026.

The principle that will decide the case is older than the internet. Garpue Wonlue, the city solicitor, said “Criminal cases are prosecuted in the name of the Republic, not the complainant”, FrontPage Africa reported on 21 September.

Bamako Buys Its Fuel With A Military Escort

Mali marked 66 years of independence on 22 September with its capital supplied by convoy. More than 900 fuel tankers reached Bamako under military escort on 14 September, Al Jazeera reported.

The blockade behind that arithmetic is a year old. Hassane Koné of the Institute for Security Studies, a Pretoria research body, wrote that the group began obstructing traffic on 3 September 2025.

The roads it chose were the import roads. Mr Koné wrote that the routes linking Mali to Senegal and Mauritania were targeted around Kayes and Nioro, along with the corridor in from Côte d’Ivoire.

The escorts are not new either. Mr Koné wrote that the army began escorting tankers into Bamako from 10 September 2025, and that the prime minister announced protective measures on 16 September that year.

The group doing this has a name a foreign reader will not know. Fighters of Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, the al-Qaeda-linked alliance usually called JNIM, have kept the pressure on since.

The effect inside the city is measured in schools and lights. The shortages have closed schools and cut electricity in Bamako, the broadcaster reported.

The mood in the capital is scepticism rather than panic. One resident told the broadcaster that the government says the army is operating and the situation is under control.

The same resident set the doubt out plainly. He said “people are asking themselves what ‘under control’ really means”.

The war has already reached the government itself. JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front attacked military sites in Bamako, Kati, Mopti, Gao and Kidal in April 2026.

One of those attacks killed a minister. The defence minister, Sadio Camara, died in the April attacks, the same broadcaster reported.

Analysts read the alliance rather than the roadblocks as the strategic problem. Beverly Ochieng, a senior analyst at the consultancy Control Risks, said it “poses a threat to the government’s consolidation of national territory”.

She named what that consolidation is worth to Bamako. Ms Ochieng said it is a key goal of the military government.

The human figure here is displacement rather than deaths. The United Nations refugee agency counted more than 400,000 people displaced inside Mali as of June 2026, concentrated in Gao, Mopti, Menaka and Timbuktu.

The price of the commodity being blockaded moved sharply this week. Brent crude’s November contract, the front month for that grade, settled at US$106.60 a barrel on Thursday 24 September.

It gave part of that back on Friday. The same contract was reading US$105.35 at 13.58 UTC.

That is why roadblocks work as a weapon. A capital fuelled only by escorted convoy pays the world price and the cost of the escort.

The shape of the price is also against Bamako. The gap between the November and December Brent contracts widened to US$6.38 on Thursday’s settlements from US$4.96 on Wednesday’s.

Magadi Wants More Than A Lifeline

Kenya has told a company that has been at Lake Magadi for two decades to leave. President William Ruto ordered Tata Chemicals Magadi to stop work and go on 3 September.

The order followed a suspension two months earlier. The mining ministry suspended operations on 28 July, and the High Court declined to lift that suspension, Pulse Kenya, a Nairobi news site, reported.

The president’s complaint was about what the country got back. Mr Ruto said the company had run its contract for more than 100 years without enough benefit reaching Kajiado, The Kenya Times, a Nairobi news site, reported.

The lake itself is the reason anyone cares. Lake Magadi holds trona, which is processed into soda ash, the raw material for glass and detergent.

The scale is national rather than local. Kenya produced 264,921 tonnes of natural soda ash in 2024 and exported nearly 249,000 tonnes of it, the world’s fourth-largest output of the natural kind.

Almost none of it is used at home. Tata Chemicals reports that more than 95 per cent of its soda ash output is exported, Pulse Kenya reported.

That is the government’s whole objection. Hassan Joho, the cabinet secretary for mining, listed unresolved royalties, weak export reporting and the absence of a plan to process the mineral in Kenya.

His legal position is narrower than the president’s speech. Mr Joho said “Past oversights do not grant immunity from existing laws”, Al Jazeera reported.

The company denies the premise. Tata Chemicals told stock exchanges that it was “fully compliant with the regulatory requirements”, ETV Bharat, an Indian broadcaster’s news site, reported.

It also said it had handed over what was asked for. The company said it had submitted the information and documentation requested and had demonstrated compliance, Pulse Kenya reported.

There is a bigger bill behind the argument. Kajiado County has pursued claims of about 17.45 billion shillings (about US$135 million at a market rate of 129.52 shillings to the dollar) over land rates and royalties.

The courts have not settled it either way. The Court of Appeal sided with Tata on key points in October 2025, and the Supreme Court gave the county more time in 2026.

The community around the lake is not of one mind. Esther Nganoni said “Tata Chemicals Company has been our lifeline”, citing school bursaries, water and health care.

The complaint from the other side is about dependence. Nkanoi Matipei said the company’s help had been “trickling, sustaining us but denying us economic freedom”, the broadcaster reported.

What follows is a tender rather than a nationalisation. Mr Ruto said “We will advertise the contract afresh and open the opportunities to greater participation”, The Kenya Times reported.

The condition attached is a factory. Mr Ruto said winners must build processing and manufacturing inside Kenya, and no tender date has been announced.

The works have been there longer than the country. Soda ash has been dug at Magadi since 1911, and Tata Chemicals inherited the operation when it bought Brunner Mond in December 2005.

Tigray Goes Dark And Its Young Men Go South

Ethiopia’s northern war produced a blackout on Friday and two incompatible accounts of the week. Telephone and internet networks stopped working across Tigray, Al Jazeera reported.

The order to cut them is said to have come from inside. The broadcaster reported that the Tigray People’s Liberation Front had told operators to shut the networks down.

The army’s claim is precise. The Ethiopian National Defence Force said it killed 272 Tigrayan fighters and wounded 260 in a counter-attack in the Amhara region.

The place it names is a district border. The attempt it says it repelled was on North Wollo, and Xinhua, the Chinese state news agency, carried the statement.

The front answered with a description rather than a number. Amanuel Assefa, its vice-president, told Agence France-Presse “We are in the situation of full-blown war now”, in remarks the broadcaster carried.

He put Tigrayan forces outside Tigray. Mr Assefa said they were fighting alongside local groups in the Afar and Amhara regions.

The people leaving are the story underneath both claims. Young men are going south to Addis Ababa to avoid recruitment, the same broadcaster reported.

One of them put a price on getting out. A 27-year-old called Gebru said his parents paid 20,000 birr, which the broadcaster put at about US$123, to have him released before he fled.

A second man’s reason was shorter. Shewit, 24, had been studying at Mekelle University, and said “I had already survived one war” before leaving for the capital.

Human Rights Watch has documented the practice. Laetitia Bader, its Horn of Africa director, said “We found that both former fighters but also civilians – young men, sometimes boys – were being abducted, detained”.

The organisation put an age on it. It reported the recruitment of boys as young as 15 in July.

The front rejects that reading and added nothing to it this week. Michael Asgedom, its spokesman, has previously called the allegations a mistaken narrative, and did not respond to the broadcaster’s requests for comment.

One academic set the limit of the 2022 settlement. Muauz Gidey Alemu of the Tigray Institute of Policy Studies said “Pretoria produced an effective cessation of large-scale warfare but an incomplete peace settlement”.

His standing is worth stating. Mr Muauz is an assistant professor of political science and lead researcher there.

The outside pressure is the one steadying thing here. The African Union called for restraint and de-escalation on Wednesday, Xinhua reported, and it is the only request this week addressed to both sides at once.

Congo’s Lake Boats Keep Their Old Habits

A boat crossing Lake Tanganyika in the dark took at least 41 people with it. Al Jazeera reported on Friday that the vessel was travelling from Kigoma in Tanzania to Kalemie in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

It was carrying more people than a small boat should. About 100 people and cargo were aboard when it capsized near the village of Mapera early on Thursday 24 September.

Forty-nine people were pulled out of the water. Norris Mulongoyi, the transport minister for Tanganyika province, told the Associated Press that the search for the missing was under way.

The minister would not name a cause. Mr Mulongoyi said the cause of Thursday’s sinking was not immediately clear.

A survivor described the moment plainly. Annie Moyoni told Radio Okapi, the United Nations-backed Congolese station, that passengers were woken at about one in the morning local time and found the boat tilting to one side.

What makes this ordinary rather than exceptional is the pattern around it. The broadcaster reported that boats on these routes commonly carry no life jackets and are often overloaded.

The same crossing lost a vessel a month ago. The MV Pacifique caught fire and exploded at Kigoma’s port on 28 August, killing six crew members with one reported missing.

The toll is the same from two directions. Sky News, a British broadcaster, also put the dead at at least 41 and those rescued at 49.

What This Means From Latin America

Latin America heard this week’s African argument about money in a familiar voice. Ghana’s president, John Dramani Mahama, told the United Nations General Assembly on 24 September “Africa does not seek charity”.

He said what he wanted instead. Mr Mahama said Africa sought “equal partnership anchored in mutual respect”, Citi News, a private Accra broadcaster, reported.

The demand behind that sentence is one Brasília and Bogotá have made in the same building. Mr Mahama asked for “long-term, affordable, and accessible concessionary financing” for human capital, industry and climate adaptation.

He also had a domestic figure to show. Mr Mahama told the assembly that Ghana had achieved a “dramatic turnaround” in its economy, the Ghana Broadcasting Corporation, the state broadcaster, reported.

A transitional government promising a vote is familiar ground here too. The region has watched officers take power with a timetable and then argue about the timetable.

Madagascar has now named a year. Its head of state told the General Assembly that the Refoundation authorities intend to hold elections before the end of 2027.

The comparison is set out at greater length elsewhere. The dossier carries the leader, the country health check and the outcome table with its Latin America column — open the Africa Intelligence Dossier.

One more parallel is about plumbing rather than politics. São Paulo and Lima have both argued for years about who pays to treat a city’s sewage.

Harare has now put one figure on that answer. Its parliamentary committee wants about US$426.3 million for a single cholera programme.

What We Are Watching

Friday 25 September: Antananarivo commemorates — Streets around Anosy and Ambohidahy closed to traffic from 7 a.m. local time for the unveiling of a stele. The head of state was expected with four High Counsellors of the Refoundation, L’Express de Madagascar reported.

— Streets around Anosy and Ambohidahy closed to traffic from 7 a.m. local time for the unveiling of a stele. The head of state was expected with four High Counsellors of the Refoundation, L’Express de Madagascar reported. Friday 25 September: Liberia’s habeas corpus hearing — Judge Pape Suah moved the hearing to 11 a.m. local time and called it the respondents’ “last opportunity”. Jerry Nyantee Wrato remained in police custody after Thursday’s sitting, FrontPage Africa reported.

— Judge Pape Suah moved the hearing to 11 a.m. local time and called it the respondents’ “last opportunity”. Jerry Nyantee Wrato remained in police custody after Thursday’s sitting, FrontPage Africa reported. Friday 25 September: South Africa’s higher rate begins — Thursday’s brief reported that the Reserve Bank had published no effective date. The position is that the Bank’s own September statement says the increase to 7.25 per cent applies from today, and that the decision was unanimous.

— Thursday’s brief reported that the Reserve Bank had published no effective date. The position is that the Bank’s own September statement says the increase to 7.25 per cent applies from today, and that the decision was unanimous. Friday 25 September: Nigeria plays Madagascar in Uyo — The two open Group L of qualifying for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium at 16.00 UTC. Only one place is available, because the co-hosts Tanzania are already through, Vanguard, a Lagos daily, reported.

— The two open Group L of qualifying for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium at 16.00 UTC. Only one place is available, because the co-hosts Tanzania are already through, Vanguard, a Lagos daily, reported. About Monday 28 September: Malawi’s election body answers its staff — The Malawi Electoral Commission’s staff union wrote on 21 September demanding a meeting within seven days. Its chairperson, Justice Annabel Mtalimanja, is also resisting a relocation to Blantyre ordered in October 2025, Nyasa Times, a Malawian news site, reported.

— The Malawi Electoral Commission’s staff union wrote on 21 September demanding a meeting within seven days. Its chairperson, Justice Annabel Mtalimanja, is also resisting a relocation to Blantyre ordered in October 2025, Nyasa Times, a Malawian news site, reported. Monday 28 September: the General Assembly debate closes — The annual United Nations general debate ends on this date. The African speeches of this week, Ghana’s and Madagascar’s among them, can then be read as one set rather than as separate appeals.

— The annual United Nations general debate ends on this date. The African speeches of this week, Ghana’s and Madagascar’s among them, can then be read as one set rather than as separate appeals. Tuesday 22 December 2026: South Sudan votes — The first national election since independence in 2011 is scheduled. A caretaker administration appointed on 22 September is to run it, under an elections act amended the same day.

— The first national election since independence in 2011 is scheduled. A caretaker administration appointed on 22 September is to run it, under an elections act amended the same day. Thursday 31 December 2026: Zimbabwe’s emergency deadline — This is the date by which the committee has asked the president to declare a state of emergency over sewage. It is also the date by which it wants water authority status granted to Chitungwiza.

— This is the date by which the committee has asked the president to declare a state of emergency over sewage. It is also the date by which it wants water authority status granted to Chitungwiza. Undated: Kenya re-advertises the Magadi contract — President William Ruto has said the soda ash concession is to be offered afresh to as many as ten bidders. Each is to be limited to part of the Kajiado parcel, and no date has been announced.

The Bigger Picture Three of Friday’s stories ask the same question in different currencies. Madagascar’s young ask what their revolt actually purchased, and South Sudan’s opposition asks what a vote without a census proves. The third is being asked in a courtroom. Liberia’s judges are deciding what a rude picture of a vice-president should cost the man who made it. Two others are about plumbing and weather, which is where consent is quietly won or lost. Zimbabwe’s parliament counted 20 working sewage plants out of 63 and asked for emergency powers. One thing was going the other way. Uganda and South Sudan spent the same week beginning a power line instead. The price of oil sits underneath most of it. Brent’s November contract settled at US$106.60 a barrel on Thursday and read US$105.35 at 13.58 UTC on Friday. That number reaches a long way. It is behind Bamako’s escorted convoys, and behind the fuel shock South Africa’s Reserve Bank named when it raised its main rate to 7.25 per cent. What steadies the day is real and partial, as it usually is. A power line has its money, and Antananarivo closed three streets for a commemoration rather than for a confrontation. One market number is worth holding beside that. The last Nigerian session with a published figure, on Thursday, left the All-Share Index up 0.38 per cent at 252,150.01 points.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Madagascar a year ago?

Protests over chronic water and power cuts began on 25 September 2025, and President Andry Rajoelina left the country in October. Colonel Michael Randrianirina was sworn in as interim leader on 17 October 2025, and at least 22 people died in the unrest.

Why did South Sudan’s president dissolve the government?

Salva Kiir issued a Republican Order on 22 September ending the transitional unity government created by the 2018 peace agreement, three months before an election set for 22 December. He had signed amendments to the elections act the same day removing the requirements for a permanent constitution and a census.

What did Zimbabwe’s parliament actually ask for?

A parliamentary committee’s report, tabled in July 2025 and released this week, asked the president to declare a state of emergency over the water and sanitation crisis by 31 December 2026. It found only 20 of 63 treatment plants working, and Harare’s council had published no answer in its own newsroom by 16.35 UTC on Friday.

Is Liberia’s cybercrime law being used against critics?

The first prominent case is a prosecution over images of Vice-President Jeremiah Kpan Koung made with artificial intelligence, and the vice-president himself asked for the suspect’s release. The police refused, Jerry Nyantee Wrato was still in custody after Thursday’s court sitting, and a judge moved his habeas corpus hearing to Friday.

World.title: Brazil: Forgotten PIS/Pasep Money — New Payout Batch Lands Today
World.content:
Money: Brazil

Key Facts —Payday. A new batch of “forgotten money” from the old PIS/Pasep quota fund is being paid out on 25 September 2026. —Who. People who worked formally between 1971 and 1988 — private-sector staff (PIS) or public servants (Pasep) — and never withdrew their quotas; heirs of deceased holders can also claim. —This batch. The 25 September payment covers workers who requested reimbursement by 31 August, according to the official calendar reported by Terra. —How much. Amounts vary with work history and are corrected for inflation; estimates put the average near R$2,800 per person. —How to check. Via the REPIS Cidadão portal with a gov.br login, the FGTS app, or a Caixa Econômica Federal branch.

Brazil is paying out a fresh batch of forgotten PIS/Pasep money on 25 September — funds owed to people who worked formally between 1971 and 1988, and to the heirs of those who have died.

Caixa Econômica Federal handles the PIS reimbursements. (Photo: The Rio Times archive)

What Is Being Paid Today

The payment landing on 25 September is the latest batch in Brazil’s long-running reimbursement of the old PIS/Pasep quota fund — money earned by formal workers between 1971 and 1988 that, for millions of people, was simply never claimed.

This round goes to workers — or their heirs — who filed a reimbursement request by 31 August and had it approved. Payment is made by Caixa Econômica Federal for PIS beneficiaries, credited to an existing account or to a no-fee digital social savings account opened automatically where the beneficiary has none.

The programme has been running in batches through 2026, each tied to a request deadline. Earlier rounds this year covered requests filed by March, April and July; the calendar continues for later filers.

The money itself is historic. The PIS/Pasep fund channelled part of employers’ contributions to workers from 1971 onwards; when Brazil’s 1988 constitution redirected those contributions into the FGTS, existing balances were converted into individual quotas — which is why the entitlement window closes in 1988.

Who Is Entitled

The entitlement is historical, not current. You may have money waiting if you worked with a signed employment card (carteira assinada) in the private sector between 1971 and 1988 — the PIS years — or served as a public servant in the same period, which falls under Pasep.

Crucially, the money does not die with the holder. Heirs of deceased workers can claim the amounts, provided they present the required documentation, such as proof of dependants or a court authorisation. Given that the entitlement window closed almost four decades ago, heirs now make up a large share of claimants.

Amounts depend on how long the person worked and what they earned at the time, and the values are corrected for inflation. Estimates circulating in Brazilian consumer coverage put the average payout near R$2,800 per person.

How to Check and Claim

The consultation is free and runs through official channels only. The main route is the REPIS Cidadão portal, run by the Ministry of Finance, which requires a gov.br account at silver or gold level. Entering the NIS number — the same as the PIS number — shows whether balances exist.

Two alternatives exist: the FGTS app, under “Ressarcimento PIS/Pasep”, which lets the holder submit documents digitally, or any Caixa branch, where staff can check balances and take the request in person with an official photo ID.

Requests are reviewed by the Ministry of Finance before Caixa releases payment — which is why each batch pays out those who filed by a specific cut-off date. Anyone who has never checked should assume the process takes weeks, not days.

One caution: the consultation is always free. Consumer coverage in Brazil warns of intermediaries charging to “recover” the money — no third party can speed up an entitlement, and official channels never request fees.

Do Not Confuse It With the Salary Bonus

PIS/Pasep is also the name of Brazil’s annual salary bonus (abono salarial), which pays up to one minimum wage — R$1,621 in 2026 — to lower-income formal workers for the 2024 base year. That programme is separate: it is paid on a birth-month calendar that ran from February to August, with withdrawal available until 29 December 2026.

The forgotten-quotas reimbursement being paid on 25 September is a one-off settlement of historical entitlements, not an annual benefit. Confusing the two leads people to check the wrong system — the quotas are consulted via REPIS Cidadão or the FGTS app, not the salary-bonus calendar.

What We Could Not Confirm

Neither Caixa nor the Ministry of Finance figures we could access state the total value or the number of beneficiaries in the 25 September batch specifically. The roughly R$2,800 average is an estimate from consumer-finance coverage, not an official figure.

We also could not confirm the precise cut-off dates and payment dates for batches after this one; workers filing now should verify the current calendar on official gov.br channels. We will update this report when official batch-level data is published.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who can receive the forgotten PIS/Pasep money in Brazil?

Anyone who worked formally between 1971 and 1988 — private-sector employees under PIS or public servants under Pasep — and never withdrew their quota balances. Heirs of deceased holders can also claim with the proper documentation.

How do I check if I have forgotten PIS/Pasep money?

Use the REPIS Cidadão portal with a gov.br login, the FGTS app under “Ressarcimento PIS/Pasep”, or visit a Caixa Econômica Federal branch with a photo ID. The consultation is free.

Is this payment the same as the 2026 PIS/Pasep salary bonus?

No. The salary bonus (abono salarial) is an annual benefit of up to R$1,621 for the 2024 base year. The 25 September payment is a one-off reimbursement of historical quotas from 1971–1988 — a separate programme with its own consultation channels.

World.title: South Africa: Petrol Price Nears R30 a Litre as Record October Hike Looms
World.content:
Economy: South Africa

Key Facts —October outlook. Late-September Central Energy Fund data points to an under-recovery of about R2.71 per litre for petrol 93 and R2.88 for petrol 95 — putting October on track for another steep increase. —Record risk. Petrol 95 is tracking within roughly 20 cents of R30 per litre, beyond the all-time high of R28.06 set in June 2026 during the Iran war shock. —Driver. Oil has climbed past US$99 a barrel as the US–Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz tensions tighten supply; the Ukraine war adds further pressure. —No cushion. The temporary fuel-levy relief ended on 1 July 2026; full levies (R4.10 petrol, R3.93 diesel) are back in the price. —Timing. Final figures depend on month-end data and the rand; the official adjustment is due in the first week of October.

South African motorists face a potential record petrol price in October, with late-September recovery data pointing to an increase of close to R3 per litre as oil approaches US$100 a barrel.

Fuel prices in South Africa are heading towards record territory in October. (Photo: The Rio Times archive)

The Numbers Behind the October Warning

South Africa’s fuel prices are set monthly, driven by the Central Energy Fund’s daily “over- or under-recovery” calculation — the gap between what the regulated pump price brings in and what importing refined fuel actually costs. A persistent under-recovery translates almost mechanically into a price increase.

The late-September snapshot is grim. BusinessTech’s tracking of CEF data shows petrol 93 running at an under-recovery of about R2.71 per litre and petrol 95 at R2.88. Earlier in the month the figures were already deeply negative — R1.81 and R1.93 for the two petrol grades, with diesel between R1.73 and R2.03 — and the trend has worsened since.

On current data, petrol 95 is tracking within roughly 20 cents of R30 per litre — a level no South African motorist has ever paid. Diesel, which hit a record R31.88 per litre (wholesale, 0.005% sulphur) in May, is also pointed back towards record ground.

A Year of Relentless Escalation

The October threat caps a brutal year at the pumps. Petrol 95 stood at R20.30 in March, jumped through the autumn as the Iran war shock hit global energy markets, and set an all-time record of R28.06 in June. September brought yet another rise — R1.34 per litre for petrol and up to R3.15 for diesel — which we covered when it took effect on 2 September.

Cumulatively, the post-war adjustments have added more than R6.80 per litre to petrol since March, and over R11.60 to diesel. If the current under-recoveries hold to month-end, October would push those totals to roughly R8.75 and R13.63 respectively.

To avoid a new record, the petrol under-recovery would need to fall back to around R1.13 per litre by month-end — an improvement of about 80 cents in the final days of September. Nothing in the market currently points that way.

Why Oil Is Doing the Damage

The driving force is geopolitical. The US–Iran conflict has kept Middle Eastern supply risk elevated for months, and oil has pushed past US$99 a barrel, closing on the psychological US$100 mark. Saudi Arabia has halted some energy operations near its border with Yemen after attacks, adding to supply fears, while the war in Ukraine continues to tighten global markets.

Hopes in July that the Iran war was winding down — which briefly pulled oil back towards US$70 — collapsed with the peace talks. Since then, prices have climbed steadily, and South Africa’s position as a fuel importer means every dollar on the oil price lands directly in the local calculation.

The rand is the second lever. A weaker exchange rate against the US dollar amplifies the oil shock in rand terms; a strengthening rand is the only realistic near-term offset, and so far it has not delivered one.

No Levy Cushion Left

Earlier this year, government softened the blow with a temporary cut of up to R3.00 per litre in the general fuel levy — relief that was phased down in June and ended entirely on 1 July. Since then, motorists have paid the full budget levies of R4.10 per litre on petrol and R3.93 on diesel, plus the Road Accident Fund and carbon levies.

Treasury has signalled there is little fiscal room for fresh relief. The April-to-June levy holiday alone cost an estimated R17.2 billion in foregone revenue, and repeating it into a record-price environment would be significantly more expensive. For now, no new intervention has been announced.

What Happens Next

The Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources sets the official adjustment after month-end, using the full month’s average recovery data. New pump prices then take effect on the first Wednesday of the month — for October, that is 7 October.

Until the final data lands, the projections can still move in either direction — but with oil near US$100 and no levy cushion left, the risk is firmly to the upside. We will publish the confirmed figures as soon as the department announces them.

What We Could Not Confirm

The October figures cited here are projections from Central Energy Fund recovery data, not official announcements. The final adjustment can differ — sometimes materially — depending on the last days of September and the rand’s path.

We could not confirm late-month under-recovery figures for diesel and illuminating paraffin matching the petrol data above, nor whether government is considering any renewed levy intervention. No such measure has been announced as of 25 September.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much could petrol go up in South Africa in October 2026?

Late-September Central Energy Fund data shows an under-recovery of about R2.71 per litre for petrol 93 and R2.88 for petrol 95, pointing to an increase close to R3 per litre if the trend holds to month-end. Final figures are set after the month closes.

When do South Africa’s October 2026 fuel prices take effect?

The Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources announces the adjustment after month-end, and new pump prices take effect on the first Wednesday of the month — 7 October 2026.

Why are South African fuel prices rising so fast in 2026?

Oil has climbed past US$99 a barrel on the US–Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz supply risks, compounded by the war in Ukraine. A soft rand amplifies the shock, and since 1 July motorists have again paid full fuel levies after temporary relief ended.

World.title: Cuban Minister Brands Venezuela’s Turn to Trump ‘Betrayal’ in Facebook Post
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

CUBA · VENEZUELA

Key Facts — The country Cuba is a Communist-run Caribbean island of about 9 million people, roughly the population of New Jersey. Its state-run economy depends on imported fuel, and officials plan growth of just 1% this year.

— Why it matters For years Venezuela was Havana’s closest ally and main oil supplier. In 2025 it still sent about 26,500 barrels a day, roughly a third of Cuba’s needs, Reuters reported.

— Why now US forces seized Venezuela’s leader, Nicolás Maduro, on 3 January. His deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, took over, oil to Cuba stopped, and this week she thanked Donald Trump at the United Nations.

— What happened On Wednesday 23 September, Cuba’s economy minister shared a Facebook post attacking Rodríguez and added: “Betrayal has only one name: betrayal.” It is known only from screenshots on Cuban news sites critical of Havana.

— Who is involved Joaquín Alonso Vázquez, Cuba’s economy and planning minister; Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s acting president; and pro-government Cuban commentators who also attacked her.

— What it means for you No quick end to Cuba’s blackouts. Anyone living in or visiting Cuba should still plan for long daily power cuts, with no sign of Venezuelan oil returning.

— Still open The minister has not confirmed the post, which one outlet says later vanished. Neither Havana nor Caracas had responded by Friday, and it is unclear whether he spoke for anyone else.

A senior Cuban minister appears to have used Facebook to brand Venezuela’s turn toward Washington a betrayal. The post is known only from screenshots published by Cuban news sites critical of Havana, and he has not confirmed it.

Joaquín Alonso Vázquez, Cuba’s Minister of Economy and Planning, shared a post on Wednesday 23 September attacking Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez. With it he wrote: “La traición solo tiene un nombre: Traición” — “Betrayal has only one name: betrayal.”

The flags of Venezuela and Cuba flying side by side. Venezuela was Cuba’s largest oil supplier until shipments stopped around the turn of the year. (Photo: The Rio Times archive)

What the minister posted

The post he shared came from a Facebook user identified as Vicente Leal. It criticised Rodríguez for sitting in silence while Trump spoke at the United Nations on Tuesday.

“Delcy Rodríguez watched at the UN as Trump called Maduro a ‘criminal’ and boasted of his kidnapping,” Leal wrote.

“She did not get up. She said nothing,” he added.

Leal’s text also attacked Venezuela’s oil agreement with the United States. The minister added only his one line, which did not name Rodríguez.

ADN Cuba, 14ymedio and CiberCuba, three Cuban news sites run from abroad, all read the line as aimed at her. All three are critical of Havana’s government.

ADN Cuba said the minister had implicitly accused Rodríguez of betrayal. 14ymedio quoted the same line on Thursday in an opinion column.

A post that did not stay up

CiberCuba reported on Friday that the post disappeared from the minister’s profile hours after it went up. A later screenshot showed Facebook’s notice: “This content is not available at this time.”

By then the post had drawn seven reactions and seven shares, the site said. It is not clear whether the Cuban minister deleted it or only restricted who could see it.

According to CiberCuba, the post was documented by Pedro Jorge Velázquez, a pro-government commentator known online as El Necio. ADN Cuba reported the post on Thursday without mentioning any removal.

CiberCuba credited the post to a Facebook profile named “Joaco Alonso.” The minister has made combative Facebook posts before; a 2020 post targeting opposition figures was later taken down.

Only CiberCuba has reported that the post vanished. Neither the minister nor the Cuban government has commented on it.

Why Havana feels abandoned

For years Venezuela sold oil to Cuba on preferential terms, while Cuban doctors and security advisers worked in Venezuela. The alliance dates back to Hugo Chávez and Fidel Castro.

In 2025 Venezuela was still Cuba’s largest supplier, at about 26,500 barrels a day, Reuters reported from shipping data. That was roughly a third of the island’s daily needs.

Cargoes stopped around the turn of the year under a US blockade of Venezuelan oil. On Saturday 3 January, US forces seized Maduro in Caracas and flew him to New York, where he awaits trial.

Rodríguez, his vice-president, took over as acting president. Washington then took control of Venezuela’s oil exports, and none went to Cuba in January, Reuters reported.

By February, Cuban medical staff and security advisers were leaving Venezuela under US pressure, Reuters reported. Venezuelan oil deliveries to Havana have not resumed, according to Cuban news outlets.

A week in New York that stung

On Tuesday Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that Cuba was “an absolutely failed state” and that “it will fall.” Cuba’s delegation walked out of the hall.

Rodríguez stayed in her seat as Trump called Maduro “a criminal, a dictator,” El País reported. Late that evening she met Trump at a Manhattan hotel, their first meeting since the raid.

Related: Trump Venezuela Meeting Ends Without a Deal After Donald Trump and Acting President Delcy Rodríguez Spoke in New York on 22 September 2026. On Wednesday Rodríguez addressed the Assembly herself.

She thanked Trump for his willingness to restore diplomatic relations and cooperation, the Associated Press reported. She promised elections without setting a date and never mentioned Maduro.

Pro-government voices in Havana reacted fast. Henry Omar Pérez, a journalist at the state Cuban News Agency, wrote that “the Bolivarian Revolution has died.”

The Bolivarian Revolution is the name of the movement Chávez founded. El Necio, for his part, pointed out that her speech never mentioned Maduro.

Cuba’s own crisis

Behind the words sits an energy emergency. On Friday 18 September Cuba’s national grid collapsed, cutting power across the island, Reuters reported.

Several total blackouts have hit Cuba this year; see Cuba Grid Failure: Line Trips, Not Gunfire, Caused 8th Blackout of 2026. Even when the grid is up, rolling blackouts leave millions without power.

The state utility has forecast evening shortfalls above 2,000 megawatts this month, against peak demand of about 3,000 megawatts. In other words, about two thirds of the power Cubans need at night is missing.

Havana blames US pressure: since January Trump has threatened tariffs on any country that supplies Cuba with oil. Washington says the outages show the failure of Cuba’s state-run economy.

What comes next

Havana has announced no break with Caracas. In January Cuban leader Miguel Díaz-Canel spoke to Rodríguez by phone and offered Cuba’s “backing and solidarity,” ADN Cuba recalled.

A single Facebook comment by a Cuban minister is not a change of policy. It does not mean Cuba is cutting ties with Venezuela, and neither government had responded by Friday.

What it does show is strain. CiberCuba argued that Havana is trapped between anger at Caracas and hope that its oil might one day return.

The next signals to watch are any official comment and any Venezuelan oil reaching Cuba. In February the US Treasury said it would license resales of Venezuelan oil to Cuba’s private businesses, though not to state bodies.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Joaquín Alonso Vázquez?

He is Cuba’s Minister of Economy and Planning, the official who presents the government’s annual economic plan. In December 2025 he presented a 2026 plan that aims for growth of about 1%.

Did the Cuban minister call Delcy Rodríguez a traitor?

Not by name: he shared a post criticising her conduct at the United Nations and wrote “Betrayal has only one name: betrayal.” Three Cuban news sites critical of Havana read the line as aimed at her, and he has not confirmed the post.

Was the post deleted?

CiberCuba reported that the Cuban minister’s post disappeared hours later and that Facebook showed it as unavailable. It is unclear whether it was deleted or hidden, and no other outlet has confirmed the removal.

Why does Venezuela matter so much to Cuba?

It was Cuba’s largest oil supplier, sending about 26,500 barrels a day in 2025, according to Reuters. Those shipments stopped around the start of 2026, deepening Cuba’s blackouts.

Sources: ADN Cuba, 24 September 2026; 14ymedio, 24 September 2026; CiberCuba, 25 September 2026; Diario de Cuba, 16 February 2024; Associated Press, 23 September 2026; El País, 23 and 24 September 2026; BBC and WLRN, 22 September 2026; Reuters, 8 and 13 January, 2 and 25 February and 18 September 2026; Associated Press and DW on Cuba’s blackouts, September 2026; Ministry of Economy and Planning of Cuba, December 2025.

World.title: Honduras Remittances Hit US$9.3 Billion, Up 11% as US Deportations Rise
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

HONDURAS · REMITTANCES

Key Facts — The country Honduras, Central America’s second-largest country, has about 11 million people, close to the US state of Georgia. Output per person is about US$3,600 a year, less than a twentieth of the US level.

— Why it matters Money sent home by migrants, almost all of it from the United States, equals about 30 percent of the economy. More than 3.1 million Hondurans receive it.

— Why now US deportations of Hondurans are rising, Washington has cancelled their temporary protected status, and a 1 percent US tax on transfers paid in cash took effect on 1 January.

— What happened Honduras remittances reached US$9.33 billion between 1 January and Thursday 10 September, up 11.4 percent on a year earlier, the Banco Central de Honduras reported.

— The numbers About 98 of every 100 dollars come from the US. The bank forecasts US$13.16 billion for 2026, after about US$12.2 billion in 2025.

— What it means for you The flood of dollars keeps the lempira predictable. It has lost under 2 percent against the dollar this year, useful for visitors budgeting a trip or investors pricing costs.

— Still open Whether lost protected status and more deportations cut the flow in 2027. Analysts’ estimates of the loss range from about US$310 million to US$700 million a year.

Honduras remittances, the money migrants send home, reached US$9.33 billion between 1 January and Thursday 10 September, the central bank reported. That is 11.4 percent more than in the same period of 2025.

The money now equals about 30 percent of the Honduran economy, one of the highest shares in the world. It keeps rising even as the United States deports more Hondurans and taxes some transfers.

What the central bank’s numbers show

The Banco Central de Honduras (BCH), the country’s central bank, tracks the foreign currency that banks and exchange agents buy and sell. Its weekly bulletin counts remittances from 1 January to each reporting date.

In that series, Honduras remittances were US$8.76 billion on 27 August, US$9.05 billion on 3 September and US$9.33 billion on 10 September. A year earlier, the 10 September figure was US$8.38 billion.

By the end of August the total was US$8.92 billion, the Tegucigalpa daily El Heraldo reported, citing the bank. Official monthly totals run slightly above the weekly series, which counts only currency traded through the financial system.

Month by month, the bank’s figures show more than US$1.1 billion arriving in every month from March to July. June was the largest, at US$1.22 billion, and July brought US$1.18 billion.

About 98 of every 100 dollars come from the United States. Honduran estimates put the number of Hondurans living there, with and without legal status, at 1.8 million to 2 million.

Why the money keeps coming despite deportations

Between 1 January and 20 August, the US, Mexico and Guatemala deported 30,965 Hondurans, the National Migration Institute says. Of those, 27,828 were flown home from the United States.

The International Organization for Migration, a UN agency, counted a 40 percent rise in returns in the first half of the year. Washington has also cancelled Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Hondurans, a decision US courts have so far let stand.

That permit let tens of thousands of Hondurans live and work legally in the US. Some Honduran analysts see fear as part of the reason the money keeps rising.

César Castillo, who coordinates a migration observatory at the National Autonomous University of Honduras, expected a short-term boom. His reasoning: migrants fearing removal would try to build up savings or property back home.

A new US tax has not stopped the flow either. Since 1 January, senders who pay with cash, money orders or cashier’s checks owe a 1 percent federal excise tax.

Transfers paid from a US bank account or with a US-issued debit or credit card are exempt, the Internal Revenue Service says. On the average monthly remittance of about US$500, the tax comes to about US$5 when it applies.

What the money means for a Honduran household

More than 3.1 million Hondurans receive money from relatives abroad, El Heraldo reports. That is close to three in every ten people in the country.

The central bank’s January 2026 survey of migrants found they send an average of US$506 a month. That is more than the country’s output per person, which the IMF puts at about US$300 a month.

Men send more than women, US$614 against US$362 a month on average. More than eight in ten migrants send money at least once a month.

Most of it is spent at once. In the survey, household upkeep came first, at 55.4 percent, and medical treatment second, at 23.8 percent.

Business investment drew just 0.8 percent. For many families the transfer is the grocery budget, the pharmacy bill and the school costs, not a savings plan.

What the dollars do for the lempira and the economy

Honduras remittances are the country’s largest single source of dollars. From January to July they brought in more than twice as much as exports of goods, central-bank data show.

That supply keeps the lempira steady, at a central-bank reference rate of 26.88 per dollar on 10 September. Market quotes on 25 September were about 26.86 lempiras per dollar.

The currency has lost 1.93 percent against the dollar since the end of 2025, the bank says. Net international reserves rose by US$1.35 billion over the same period, covering 6.7 months of imports.

For foreigners, a currency that has moved less than 2 percent this year makes local costs easier to plan. The wider rules are set out in Investing in Honduras as a Foreigner 2026: Property, Energy and the Rules After ICSID.

The World Bank credits record remittances and strong coffee for growth of 3.8 percent in 2025. It expected slower growth this year, with remittances dropping; so far they have kept rising.

The pace stands out in the region. Neighbouring El Salvador’s remittances rose 3.8 percent from January to August, and 4.66 percent in August alone, to US$863.4 million.

Mexico has had a bumpier year, as told in Mexico Remittance Rebound Reaches 3.8% as Latin America Braces for US Tax Vote.

A new government between Washington and the families

President Nasry Asfura won the November 2025 election and took office in January, succeeding Xiomara Castro. His government asked Washington for an orderly transition for Hondurans losing protection.

Asfura asked the US for more time and for work permits to stay valid for now. In early September, Foreign Minister Mireya Agüero said Washington had refused any further extension. She has ruled out an immediate mass return or a severe blow to remittances.

At home, the government plans to give each returning migrant 2,500 lempiras (about US$93) on a card usable at cash machines. No start date has been announced.

What comes next

The bank’s coming weekly bulletins will show whether growth holds near 11 percent into the autumn. Its official forecast, raised in July, is US$13.16 billion for 2026, about 7 percent above 2025.

If the trend holds, Honduras remittances would end the year above that forecast. El Heraldo estimates a close between US$13.38 billion and US$14 billion.

The larger risk lies in 2027, when the bank expects growth of just 2 percent. Jorge Henríquez of Fosdeh, a Honduran economic think tank, puts the cost of losing TPS at about US$310 million a year.

Migration specialist Ilis Cornejo estimates up to US$700 million a year once further deportations are added. Neither figure is an official forecast.

What the numbers do not show is a collapse, or proof that deportations are harmless. A record year says little about the next one, and the 1 percent tax’s effect cannot be read from the totals.

Families still depend on relatives abroad whose legal footing is weaker than a year ago. For now, the money is arriving faster than either the central bank or the World Bank expected.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much money do Hondurans abroad send home?

Honduras received US$9.33 billion between 1 January and 10 September 2026, 11.4 percent more than a year earlier. The full-year total for 2025 was about US$12.2 billion, according to the Banco Central de Honduras.

Why are Honduras remittances still growing despite deportations?

Deportations so far touch a small share of the roughly two million Hondurans in the US. Analysts expect the loss of TPS permits to cut flows mainly from 2027.

What is the US remittance tax?

Since 1 January 2026, transfers abroad paid for with cash, money orders or cashier’s checks carry a 1 percent federal excise tax. Transfers funded from a US bank account or a US-issued debit or credit card are exempt.

How important are remittances to Honduras?

They equal about 30 percent of the economy and are the largest source of dollars. More than 3.1 million Hondurans receive them, and most of the money pays for food, health care and schooling.

Sources: Banco Central de Honduras, weekly executive reports on financial-system indicators of 27 August, 3 September and 10 September 2026; Banco Central de Honduras monthly remittance figures via EFE, 27 August 2026; El Heraldo, 11 September 2026; La Tribuna, 9 August 2026; La Prensa (Honduras), 19 and 22 August 2026, including the central bank’s January 2026 migrant survey; Infobae, 3 and 12 September 2026; Hondudiario, 23 September 2026; US Internal Revenue Service and Federal Register notice on the remittance transfer tax, April 2026; World Bank Honduras overview and data; IMF World Economic Outlook; La Prensa Gráfica, 24 September 2026, on El Salvador and the International Fund for Agricultural Development.

World.title: Chile Credit Rating Stays at A as S&P Warns Budget Repair Will Take Longer
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

CHILE · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Chile is a South American country of about 20 million people and the world’s largest copper producer. Its economy, about US$357 billion in 2025, is roughly a tenth the size of Britain’s.

— Why it matters A credit rating is a grade on whether a government will repay its debts. Chile holds the highest S&P grade in Latin America, which keeps its borrowing cheaper than its neighbours’.

— Why now Chile missed its own deficit targets in 2023, 2024 and 2025. President José Antonio Kast took office in March promising cuts, and the agencies are now checking the results.

— What happened S&P Global Ratings kept Chile at A, with a stable outlook, the Finance Ministry said on Friday 25 September. S&P now sees net debt reaching 41% of output by 2029.

— The numbers S&P rates Chile A, Moody’s the equivalent A2, Fitch one step lower at A-. S&P rates the United States AA+, Britain AA and Uruguay, the next-best in the region, BBB+.

— What it means for you For investors, Chile’s government bonds stay four steps above junk. For residents and visitors nothing changes directly; the grade mainly affects what the state pays to borrow.

— Still open Whether the 2027 budget, due in Congress by Wednesday 30 September, restrains spending enough, and when Moody’s publishes its next review of Chile.

S&P Global Ratings has kept the Chile credit rating at A, Chile’s Finance Ministry said on Friday 25 September. It is the highest grade the agency gives any Latin American country, but it came with a warning about the budget.

S&P, one of three big agencies that grade government debt, now expects Chile’s budget repair to take longer. Net public debt reaches 41% of annual economic output (GDP) by 2029 in its forecast, not the 37% plateau expected last year.

Central Santiago at dusk, with apartment blocks, a church bell tower and the Andes foothills behind. Chile’s capital is home to the Finance Ministry, which announced the S&P decision. (Photo: Álvaro Orozco, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)
