What S&P decided

S&P affirmed Chile’s long-term foreign-currency rating at A and its local-currency rating at A+. The outlook on both stays stable, meaning the agency does not expect to change them soon.

The foreign-currency grade covers debt Chile owes in dollars and other currencies. Agencies often rate local-currency debt higher, because a government repays it in a currency it issues itself.

The Finance Ministry, led by Jorge Quiroz under President José Antonio Kast since March, announced the decision on Friday morning. Its statement stressed S&P’s view that the authorities have shown commitment to fiscal restraint.

S&P also cited the National Reconstruction Law, which the government passed without a majority in Congress, the ministry said. The law speeds up environmental approvals for large projects and cuts corporate tax gradually from 27% to 23%.

Quiroz had signalled good news was coming. On Monday he told coalition lawmakers that positive news from the agencies could arrive within weeks, the business daily Diario Financiero reported.

Why the repair is taking longer

S&P’s central point is that commitment has outrun results. Authorities have shown commitment to restraint, it said, but revenue has fallen short of forecasts and weak consolidation has added to debt.

The shift is clearest in S&P’s own forecasts. In October 2025 it expected net government debt to stabilise at about 37% of GDP between 2025 and 2028.

Now it sees net debt rising from 36% of GDP in 2025 to 41% in 2029, the Santiago daily La Tercera reported. Before the pandemic the figure was 15%.

Net debt is what the government owes minus the cash and financial assets it holds. It also rises when a government spends down savings, and Moody’s has said rebuilding Chile’s once-large reserves could support its rating.

S&P expects the general government deficit to narrow from 2.6% of GDP in 2025 to 1.4% in 2029. Interest payments will take about 5.5% of government revenue on average from 2026 to 2029, La Tercera reported.

The agency named two drags on that path: interest costs and the gradual cut in corporate tax. It expects growth, copper and spending adjustments to soften them, and called rebuilding buffers against future shocks important.

The government’s own June decree already accepted a slower path, as reported in Chile Drops Its Balanced-Budget Pledge in New Fiscal Decree.

It targets a structural deficit of 2.6% of GDP this year, falling to 1.5% in 2030. That measure strips out swings in the economy and in copper prices.

Copper and growth carry the case

Copper is Chile’s largest export, and S&P leans on it heavily. The agency expects favourable prices, citing demand from renewable energy, electric vehicles and the data centres behind artificial intelligence.

S&P expects only a gradual rise in copper output, limited by falling ore grades and recent disruptions. It said permit delays have also held back projects in recent years.

For growth, S&P forecasts just 0.7% this year and 2.9% in 2027, as this year’s disruptions fade. It sees unemployment at 9% this year and 8.7% next year.

Record copper prices have already shaped the government’s spending plans, as covered in Record Copper Prices Reshape Chile’s 2027 Budget. S&P’s forecast relies on prices staying favourable.

How the three agencies line up

S&P’s decision came a week after Fitch Ratings affirmed Chile at A-, also stable, on Friday 18 September. Details are in Chile Keeps Its A- Rating From Fitch as Growth Forecast Falls to 0.7%.

Fitch cut its 2026 growth forecast to 0.7% from 1.6%. It also measures debt differently, counting gross general government debt.

Fitch sees that figure rising to 42.8% of GDP in 2026 and settling near 43%. The median for A-rated countries is 59%.

Chile’s own fiscal rule uses a third measure, gross central government debt, with a prudent ceiling of 45% of GDP. The three numbers are not interchangeable, but all point the same way: debt still edging up.

Moody’s Ratings rates Chile A2 with a stable outlook, the same level as S&P’s A. Its most recent periodic review, completed in October 2025, left the rating unchanged.

In April, Moody’s lead analyst for Chile, Kathrin Muehlbronner, said she saw no immediate change in the rating. She also said the corporate tax cut would need other savings or revenue to pay for it.

What an A grade means for a foreign reader

A sovereign rating is an opinion on how likely a government is to repay its debts in full and on time. Investors use it to decide how much interest to demand.

S&P’s scale runs from AAA at the top down to D for default. A is the sixth-highest grade, four steps above BBB-, the last grade before debt is classed as speculative, or junk.

Many pension funds and insurers may only hold investment-grade bonds. Staying well above that line keeps Chile’s pool of buyers wide and its borrowing costs lower than its neighbours’.

For scale, S&P rates the United States AA+ and Britain AA, four and three steps above the Chile credit rating. Lithuania and Latvia share Chile’s A grade.

In Latin America, Uruguay is next at BBB+, two steps lower. Mexico is BBB, Peru BBB-, and Brazil and Colombia sit in junk territory.

Chile has been higher. S&P rated it AA- from 2013 to 2017, S&P director Constanza Pérez Aquino has said, before rising debt contributed to downgrades.

What comes next

The next test for the Chile credit rating is the 2027 budget bill, due in Congress by Wednesday 30 September. Pérez Aquino said this month S&P would watch where it sets the bar on spending.

That is a live tension. Quiroz said this month that public finances were more under control and the government may use spending to revive a stalled economy.

The decision does not mean Chile’s finances are fixed, and it is not an upgrade. S&P’s own forecast has debt rising for four more years, and growth this year below 1%.

Nor is it a warning of a downgrade. A stable outlook means S&P sees a rating change as unlikely over the next year or two.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Chile credit rating now?

S&P Global Ratings rates Chile A for foreign-currency debt and A+ for local-currency debt, both with a stable outlook. Moody’s rates it A2, the equivalent of A, and Fitch rates it one step lower at A-, also stable.

Why does S&P say Chile’s budget repair will take longer?

Tax revenue has come in below forecast for several years and deficits have added to debt. S&P now expects net government debt to reach 41% of GDP by 2029, against about 37% in last year’s forecast.

Does the decision change what Chile pays to borrow?

Not immediately, because an unchanged rating mostly confirms what bond investors already expected. It keeps Chile four steps above junk, supporting demand for its bonds and lower borrowing costs than most of the region.

How does Chile’s rating compare with the US and UK?

S&P rates the United States AA+ and Britain AA, four and three steps above Chile’s A. Within Latin America, Chile has S&P’s highest grade, two steps above Uruguay at BBB+.

Sources: S&P Global Ratings, research update on Chile, as published by Chile’s Finance Ministry and reported by La Tercera and Emol, 25 September 2026; S&P and Moody’s reviews of Chile, Finance Ministry, October 2025; Fitch Ratings, affirmation of Chile, 18 September 2026; Moody’s Ratings, remarks by Kathrin Muehlbronner, Diario Financiero, April 2026; Diario Financiero, 15 and 23 September 2026; Chile Decree of Fiscal Policy, June 2026; Central Bank of Chile and S&P sovereign rating tables.

World.title: Unemployment in Mexico Edges Up to 3%, With 55% of Workers Off the Books
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

MEXICO · JOBS

Key Facts — The country Mexico has roughly 130 million people and an economy of about US$2.1 trillion, close to Australia’s in size. More than four-fifths of its exports go to the United States.

— Why it matters Mexico has no national unemployment insurance, so few people can afford to stay jobless for long. Most take whatever work they find, often without a contract or social security.

— Why now US tariffs and a year-by-year review of the North American trade pact have stalled new foreign investment. On Thursday the central bank, Banxico, held its key rate at 6.5 percent.

— What happened INEGI, the statistics institute, said on Friday 25 September that unemployment in Mexico reached 3.0 percent in August. It was 2.9 percent in July and a year earlier.

— The numbers 1.88 million people out of work, 87,000 more than a year before. 55.0 percent of workers informal. Factory employment down 263,000 in a year. Seasonally adjusted, the rate held at 2.7 percent.

— What it means for you Daily life in Mexico will not change. For investors, weak factory hiring says more about US-linked demand than the headline rate does.

— Still open Whether the rise lasts. September figures are due on Thursday 22 October, and Banxico’s next rate decision on 5 November.

Unemployment in Mexico rose to 3.0 percent of the labour force in August, the national statistics institute INEGI reported on Friday. That was up from 2.9 percent in July and in August 2025.

By most countries’ standards, 3 percent looks like a job market with nothing to spare. In Mexico it mainly shows that people cannot afford to be without work, and more than half of them work informally.

Office towers along Avenida de la República in central Mexico City. The grey building at centre carries the sign of ISSSTE, the social-security institute for public-sector workers. (Photo: Carlos Valenzuela, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What the August survey shows

INEGI stands for the Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía. It measures jobs through ENOE, the National Survey of Occupation and Employment, which visits a little over 150,000 homes each quarter.

Someone counts as unemployed only if they did not work even one hour in the survey week. They must also have actively looked for a job.

On that measure, 1.88 million people were unemployed in August, about 87,000 more than a year earlier. Over the same period the labour force grew by 1.3 million, to 62.6 million people.

Employment rose by 1.2 million over the year, to 60.7 million. The share of people aged 15 and over who work or seek work rose to 59.3 percent, from 58.8 percent.

The 3.0 percent figure is not adjusted for the seasons. On INEGI’s seasonally adjusted series, unemployment stayed at 2.7 percent, unchanged from July and 0.1 point above August 2025.

So the rise from July largely reflects the usual August pattern rather than a sudden turn. One detail points the other way.

People jobless for six months to a year numbered 158,755, against 87,128 a year earlier. The group is still small, but it nearly doubled.

Why 3 percent does not mean full employment

Mexico has no national unemployment-insurance scheme, a gap the OECD, the club of mostly rich economies, has flagged for years. A worker who loses a job gets no regular benefit while searching.

So most people who lose a job take whatever work they can find, often self-employed or in small unregistered firms. That is why unemployment in Mexico looks so low.

INEGI therefore publishes wider measures. In August, 55.0 percent of workers, or 33.4 million people, were in informal employment, up from 54.8 percent a year earlier.

Informal means working without social-security protection, or for a business that is not registered. The OECD finds that only about one in ten informal employees has a written contract.

Informal work absorbed most new jobs earlier this year, as Mexico Informality Drove 82% of Job Growth in Second Quarter showed.

Another 7.0 percent of workers, some 4.3 million people, were underemployed, meaning they wanted and were available to work more hours. Seasonally adjusted, that rate rose to 6.8 percent from 6.4 percent in July.

INEGI also counts 5.0 million people outside the labour force who say they could work but are not looking. They do not appear in the unemployment rate at all.

INEGI’s broadest gauge, called critical working conditions, covers people on too few hours against their will or on very low pay. It reached 37.8 percent of workers, up from 37.3 percent a year earlier.

Factories shed jobs while services hire

The sector breakdown shows where the pressure sits. Manufacturing employed 9.7 million people in August, 263,000 fewer than a year earlier.

Farming lost 290,000 workers and retail and wholesale trade 161,000. Construction added 146,000.

The gains came in services. Restaurants and hotels added 538,000 jobs, a catch-all group of other services 790,000, and government 242,000.

Manufacturing matters because it is the part of Mexico most tied to US demand. Transport equipment, such as cars and parts, makes up about 21 percent of factory output, INEGI data show.

The shift has not made work more formal: the informality rate rose 0.2 point over the year. The share working in unregistered household businesses rose 0.7 point, to 30.3 percent.

The formal payroll count tells a similar story

A second source counts formal jobs: registrations with IMSS, the Mexican Social Security Institute, which covers private-sector employees. In August it recorded a net gain of 38,319 jobs, after a loss of 19,550 in July.

Traditional jobs rose by 86,765, while registrations of app-based platform workers fell by 48,446. Even so, platform registrations are up 49.8 percent over twelve months, IMSS said.

Adjusted for the seasons, the picture is weaker. The Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas calculates that formal employment fell by about 9,100 jobs in August, a second straight monthly decline.

Over twelve months, IMSS-registered jobs rose by 343,556, or 1.5 percent, to 22.8 million. In August 2023 the monthly gain was 111,736, according to the newspaper El Economista.

For scale, 22.8 million is fewer than four in ten of the 60.7 million people the survey counts as working. IMSS leaves out government staff, who have their own institute.

Tariffs, a trade review and a central bank on hold

The United States buys about 83 percent of Mexico’s exports, according to the consultancy Deloitte. Most goods still enter duty-free, but US tariffs fall on cars, auto parts, machinery and steel.

The bigger drag is uncertainty. In July Washington declined to renew the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the regional trade pact, opting for annual reviews instead, Reuters reported.

New foreign investment in Mexico fell 13 percent in the first half of 2026, Reuters found. Fixed investment fell year on year for 19 straight months through May, according to IMEF, Mexico’s finance executives’ institute.

The central bank, Banco de México or Banxico, held its overnight rate at 6.50 percent on Thursday 24 September. It was the third meeting in a row without a change.

Banxico said it need not track the US Federal Reserve mechanically (see Banxico Holds Rates at 6.5% and Splits From the Fed). Private forecasters polled by Banxico in August expected growth of 1.3 percent this year.

What comes next

INEGI publishes the September figures on Thursday 22 October. Banxico releases the minutes of its September meeting on 8 October and decides rates again on 5 November.

The August reading does not signal a recession or mass lay-offs. The seasonally adjusted rate has not moved, and total employment is 1.2 million higher than a year ago.

Nor does one month settle whether weaker hiring will push Banxico to cut again. The bank has named no date for its next move.

What August does show is a job market absorbing people mainly outside factories and, often, outside the formal system. That is the part to watch while the trade review drags on.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is unemployment in Mexico so low?

Mexico has no national unemployment insurance, so few people can afford to go without work while they search. Many take informal jobs instead, and the survey counts anyone who worked even one hour as employed.

What does informal work mean in Mexico?

INEGI counts as informal anyone working without social-security protection, or in a business that is not registered. In August that was 55.0 percent of workers, or 33.4 million people.

Did Mexico lose formal jobs in August?

Not on the raw count: IMSS registered a net gain of 38,319 jobs. A seasonally adjusted estimate by the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas shows a small decline, of about 9,100.

When is the next jobs report?

INEGI publishes the September survey results on Thursday 22 October 2026. Banxico’s next interest-rate decision follows on 5 November.

Sources: INEGI, Encuesta Nacional de Ocupación y Empleo, monthly indicators for August 2026 (bulletin 606/26, 25 September 2026) and July 2026; IMSS formal-employment report for August 2026, as reported by EFE, El Economista, Luces del Siglo and LJA.mx; Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, Mexico economic update, 23 September 2026; Banco de México decision of 24 September 2026, as reported by El Economista, El Financiero and Proceso, and Banxico’s 2026 monetary-policy calendar; Reuters, 1 September 2026; Deloitte Insights, Mexico economic outlook 2026; Mexico Business News on INEGI GDP data and IMEF; OECD labour-market and informality reports; IMF World Economic Outlook database.

World.title: International News: Saint Lucia PM calls for Climate Finance that matches scale of crisis
World.content:
International News: Saint Lucia PM calls for Climate Finance that matches scale of crisis

By Zoila Palma: Saint Lucia Prime Minister Philip J. Pierre has called for greater international support for countries facing the impacts of climate change, stressing that climate finance is a matter of justice, responsibility and survival. He made the remarks this week during the General Debate of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Pierre said Small Island Developing States, including Saint Lucia, are experiencing the consequences of a climate crisis they have contributed little to causing. He described climate change as a direct threat to national security, economic stability, food and water security, and human survival, pointing to unusual droughts during the rainy season, severe flooding during the dry season, and the impact of sargassum on beaches and coastlines.

The Prime Minister called for climate finance that matches the scale of the crisis, including expanded grants and concessional funding, faster and simpler access to financial resources, meaningful debt relief, and full support for loss and damage.

He stressed that vulnerable countries should not be forced to take on additional debt to repair damage caused by a crisis they did not create.

“A United Nations that delivers for all must deliver for those on the front lines of climate change through accessible finance, concrete support and measurable results, not merely through declarations,” Pierre stated.

World.title: Man allegedly kicks GI3 officer in chest after stepson calls police on him
World.content:
Man allegedly kicks GI3 officer in chest after stepson calls police on him

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an alleged aggravated assault against a GI3 officer after a man reportedly kicked the officer in the chest while resisting detention on Police Street Thursday morning.

According to a police situation report, officers were called to a residence on Police Street at around 8:45 a.m. on September 24 after receiving a request for assistance from an officer already at the scene.

Police say a minor alleged that he had been physically assaulted by his stepfather.

Officers informed the parties that they would be escorted to the Raccoon Street Police Station for the matter to be investigated.

Police allege that the stepfather refused to cooperate and began physically struggling with officers as they attempted to handcuff him.

While officers were escorting the man from the residence, a detective constable was positioned near the steps recording the encounter with a police-issued body camera when the man allegedly kicked him on the left side of the chest, causing pain.

The matter is being investigated as aggravated assault.

World.title: PM Briceño discusses Tourism and Garifuna culture with Saint Vincent PM
World.content:
PM Briceño discusses Tourism and Garifuna culture with Saint Vincent PM

By Zoila Palma: Prime Minister John Briceño met with Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Prime Minister Dr. Godwin Friday during the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York to discuss tourism and opportunities to strengthen cooperation between the two countries.

The discussions included support for the enrichment and promotion of Garifuna culture, highlighting the importance of cultural heritage in strengthening ties between Belize and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

As part of the meeting, Briceño presented Prime Minister Friday with handcrafted bowls made by a Garifuna artist and purchased from the Garifuna Museum in Belize.

The gift represents Belize’s rich cultural heritage and formed part of the cultural exchange between the two leaders.

World.title: Shyne to politicians “Put your political arms down in your Independence Day address”
World.content:
Shyne to politicians “Put your political arms down in your Independence Day address”

By Zoila Palma: Former Leader of the Opposition Shyne Barrow is urging politicians to keep their Independence Day addresses focused on the celebrations.

“I confess in my first addresses as Leader of the Opposition I followed the precedent set by former Opposition Leaders John Briceno and Dean Barrow who engaged in straight up partisan assault in their Independence Day speeches!

I think I was the two of them multiplied in my offensive. Honestly, I never felt comfortable doing it deep down inside, so when Prime Minister Briceno called me in 2024 a few weeks before Independence Day and proposed that we battle it out in the State of the Nation address and reserve celebratory reverence for Independence Day with no political attacks, I did not hesitate to agree,” Barrow explained.

Barrow further urged all elected officials and aspirants to follow the precedent set by him and PM Briceno.

“ Put your political arms down in your Independence Day addresses. Let’s offer Belizeans congratulations, reflection, introspection and your vision for where Belizean should be in the next 45 years,” Barrow said.

World.title: Woman detained after allegedly presenting fake driver’s license at Cemetery Road checkpoint
World.content:
Woman detained after allegedly presenting fake driver’s license at Cemetery Road checkpoint

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a 35-year-old woman after an enforcement officer allegedly discovered that the driver’s licence she presented at a Belize City checkpoint was not in official records.

According to police information, an enforcement officer was conducting a vehicular checkpoint on Cemetery Road in front of Constitution Park at around 9:45 a.m. on Thursday, September 24, when she stopped a gold Chrysler Aspen SUV.

The driver was identified as a Nicaraguan national residing in Belize City.

The officer reportedly noticed several inconsistencies while inspecting the license and contacted both her records department and the Transport Department to verify it.

According to the report, neither agency found a record of a driver’s licence issued to the woman.

She was subsequently escorted to the Precinct One Police Station, where a formal report was made in relation to suspected uttering upon a false document.

World.title: Camera allegedly catches thief stealing nearly $1,000 in power tools from unlocked SUV in Benque
World.content:
Camera allegedly catches thief stealing nearly $1,000 in power tools from unlocked SUV in Benque

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Benque Viejo taxi driver is seeking police action after surveillance footage allegedly captured a man entering his unlocked vehicle and stealing almost $1,000 worth of tools.

A 31-year-old Benque resident reported that he parked his 1999 Toyota 4Runner outside his residence on Wednesday evening, September 23, leaving the vehicle unsecured.

Inside were three INGCO impact drivers, two batteries and a backpack with a combined reported value of BZ$996.

When he checked the following morning, the items were missing.

According to police, the homeowner’s surveillance camera allegedly captured a man entering the vehicle and taking the items.

Police subsequently prepared a search warrant for that man’s premises, but the search reportedly did not turn up the stolen property.

World.title: Benque woman reports common-law husband after allegedly throwing object at her that left her head bloody
World.content:
Benque woman reports common-law husband after allegedly throwing object at her that left her head bloody

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police in Benque Viejo del Carmen are investigating a reported domestic assault after a 34-year-old woman alleged that her common-law husband struck her with an object and punched her in the face Thursday night.

According to a police situation report, the woman told officers that her 47-year-old common-law husband returned to their home at around 8:00 p.m. on September 24 and appeared to have been drinking.

The woman alleged that later that night her husband became verbally abusive and threatened her before the couple went into their bedroom.

She told police that while she was lying on a bed, her husband allegedly grabbed her foot and swung his hand as though throwing an object at her. Fernandez said she then felt blood running down her forehead.

She further alleged that Torres punched her on the left side of her face, causing pain.

Fernandez requested court action, and police recorded a statement in relation to a report of wounding.

World.title: $8.9 million secured to boost Economic activity in Southern Belize
World.content:
$8.9 million secured to boost Economic activity in Southern Belize

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize has secured BZ$8.9 million to support economic activity and resilience in Southern Belize through the PROSPER Project.

During a partnership signing ceremony at the Punta Gorda Sporting Complex, representatives from 12 Toledo communities signed letters of intent to partner with the Government and the International Labour Organization (ILO) on the initiative.

The PROSPER (Participation, Ownership, and Sustainable Progress for Economic Resilience) Project is a joint effort involving the Government of Belize, the European Union and the ILO, targeting communities in the Stann Creek and Toledo districts.

Through the project, Maya and Garifuna communities will establish local action groups to develop and implement economic plans focused on local industries, including cacao agroforestry and sustainable tourism, with the aim of creating opportunities and strengthening local economies.

World.title: KC principal responds to viral video of student being held over railing
World.content:
Kingston College Principal Dave Myrie speaking at morning devotion on Monday, March 31, 2025 as the school celebrated its 36th Boys’ Champs title. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Kingston College (KC) has launched an investigation after a video surfaced online showing a student being held by colleagues over a railing before falling.

In an official statement dated September 23, Principal Dave Myrie said the school’s administration and Board of Management are aware of the matter and are conducting a “thorough investigation” into the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Myrie said, however, that no student was injured.

“The School Administration and the Board of Management are aware of the matter and are currently conducting a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident,” Myrie said in the statement.

He assured parents, guardians, students and members of the wider KC community that the matter was being taken seriously and would be addressed in accordance with the school’s established policies and procedures.

The principal also reiterated the school’s commitment to maintaining what he described as a safe, disciplined and supportive environment for its students.

KC has also appealed to members of the school community to refrain from sharing or reposting the video.

According to Myrie, further circulation could unnecessarily compromise the privacy, dignity and welfare of the young students involved.

“Any further information considered appropriate will be communicated through the School’s official channels,” the statement said.

Myrie has served as principal of Kingston College since 2012.

– Howard Walker

World.title: Court walkout looms
World.content:
Defence attorneys staging a ‘silent protest’ outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston on Wednesday demanding that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Defence attorneys have been placed on alert to pull their services from the island’s courts for an entire week, starting next Monday, a move that will deal a significant blow to the Michaelmas term which began just over a week ago.

The lawyers arrived at the decision after a meeting on Thursday with Justice Minister Delroy Chuck which they say failed to produce any meaningful plans to reform the 2022 Firearms Act.

The emergency meeting was called following Wednesday’s ‘silent protest’ outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston, where members of the Jamaican Bar Association, the Advocates Association in collaboration with Bar associations across the island, armed with placards, demanded that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform.

Some hours later, Chuck indicated that he would be meeting with representatives of the bodies to hear their concerns.

However, following those discussions, defence attorney Tamika Harris, a member of the Bar Council of the Jamaican Bar Association and chair of its Criminal Practice and Procedure Subcommittee, who was a key figure behind the protest, told the Jamaica Observer that the meeting amounted to little less than an exercise in futility.

“The minister could not give a timeline as to when anything would be taken to the legislature, and he has asked for the discussion to be placed in writing but before [the Act was passed] the Bar Association… made a submission to Parliament. We are not asking for anything different, so it’s not like our argument is new,” Harris stated.

“The meeting, in my mind, was an opportunity for us to say the same things we have already said, but we have not gotten any response from the minister to, for example, say when he will go to Parliament [with proposed amendments]. I know everything takes time, but I did not get any idea of a plan to put in action. So the minister didn’t confirm that he was going to put a plan in action, so there is no resolution,” Harris declared.

As such, she said attorneys will be moving to action the next stage of their protest.

“He was very courteous and he listened. He expressed that he understood our concerns, but he did not go any further to say exactly if they were going to be dealt with and when, so there is nothing. I am aware he has already been presented with similar arguments by the director of public prosecutions and even the chief justice. I am going to ask my members to withdraw our services,” Harris told the Observer.

“We are going to use the opportunity, perhaps, to do quick education. The public needs to be aware that we are not saying legislation must be weak on persons who use firearms to terrorise our Jamaican citizens, we are not saying the legislation needs to be weak; we are saying that the legislation is to be fair and cognisant that not every case is the same,” Harris said.

The protests come just over a week after the justice minister’s comments at the Annual Assize Service of the judiciary. Chuck said, while the mandatory minimum sentences contained in the provision were being reviewed because of widespread concerns, “The security forces and a number of my colleagues feel that the Act is working and it is bringing down murders and shootings.

“It is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country, and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms. But it is under consideration,” Chuck said.

The comments triggered furious commentary from several quarters.

A week later members of Jamaica’s legal profession met on Saturday, September 19 to consider what they described as “the operation and impact of the Act, particularly its mandatory sentencing provisions and the restrictions placed on judicial discretion”.

In a statement issued following that meeting, the attorneys said, “The legal profession supports strong and effective laws to combat gun violence and punish those who use illegal firearms to murder, rob, terrorise and intimidate our citizens. Our concern is not with strong penalties. Our concern is with a sentencing regime that does not adequately allow judges to distinguish between offenders, offences, and individual circumstances.”

The Act, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for specified violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons. It establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities, and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

According to the advocates, their September 19 meeting “identified several areas of serious concern, including the restriction of judicial discretion; the proportionality of mandatory minimum sentences in individual cases; the diminished incentive for early guilty pleas; the resulting increase in matters proceeding to trial and pressure on an already burdened criminal justice system; the treatment of imitation firearms; and the consequences of certain provisions for licensed firearm holders”.

“The legal profession is calling for urgent amendments to the Act, including consideration of an ‘exceptional circumstances’ provision allowing judges appropriate discretion in deserving cases, meaningful sentencing incentives for early guilty pleas, reform of the certificate regime, and a review of the provisions governing imitation firearms and licensed firearm holders. The profession also calls for urgent, structured consultation with the Government, Opposition, Parliament, the judiciary and other relevant stakeholders on the proposed amendments”, the attorneys said in that statement.

World.title: Christiana clampdown
World.content:
Vendors on Wildman Street in Christiana on Thursday (Photos: Kasey Williams)

CHRISTIANA, Manchester — Mandeville Mayor Donovan Mitchell says, effective today, there will be a clampdown on unapproved buildings and illegal vending, as part of enforcement activities in the south-central town of Christiana.

“Yesterday (Wednesday) I came into Christiana and as the chairman of the local Board of Health I spent about five hours walking the streets of Christiana. I visited the abattoir. I visited the market. I visited the transportation centre. I looked at some businesses [and] buildings going up. I know at the council meeting early this month I made a statement and some people are up in arms and all of that… What is happening in the parish will not continue,” he said on Thursday while addressing the launch of Sam Fo Meats mobile application on Wildman Street in Christiana.

“I said it yesterday (Wednesday) to my team that Wildman Street, please be prepared, because I am going to be changing the entire look of Wildman Street. There will absolutely be no selling on the street. I am warning the businesses that are putting their sewage and grey water into our water channels to stop and stop before tomorrow [Friday] morning, because a team from the public health service will be coming out and we are going to make sure it cannot continue,” added Mitchell.

He pointed to the public safety concerns and hazards of waste water flowing on the busy commercial street.

“You cannot be walking on the street and all you are seeing is grey water. Businesses can’t build their buildings and put their grey water on the street. What about our children, the elderly? You are walking and miss your step in soap water and you break your leg and the first thing is they call the parish council,” said Mitchell, who chairs the Manchester Municipal Corporation.

“I am warning people who are building houses without plans from the Manchester Municipal Corporation. I am not holding bar; you have to do better. When a building collapses because you have not done the correct thing, who is the first person you blame? Government. Where was the Government when you were building? Not around, because you put zinc all around your place and you do what you have to do and when you are finished you open up the zinc and you see a building there that has not gone through the proper channel,” added Mitchell.

Pertaining to the Christiana abattoir, Mitchell said he is contemplating closing it for renovations.

“We are having some problems and I will tell you that maybe, based on the letters I am getting from the health services, I may have to close it even temporarily to make sure that things go right. I am warning, since I am in Christiana, that things are not going to be the same in Christiana. There has to be some changes,” declared Mitchell.

World.title: Skippa in int’l spotlight
World.content:
Dancehall artiste Skippa was named as one to watch by Jamaica Observer at the start of 2026 .

When the Jamaica Observer named Skippa one of its artistes to watch at the start of 2026, the prediction came with the expectation that the young dancehall artiste’s momentum was worth keeping an eye on. What has followed, however, stretches well beyond even his own expectations.

There was the touring, the growing audiences, the songs steadily finding new listeners, and, perhaps most significantly, recognition from one of the music industry’s most established brands — Billboard.

Still, as the artiste himself revealed, 2026 has so far surpassed his wildest imagination.

“We had goals around touring and growing the music, but everything kind of surpassed what we had in mind. The amount of shows, the places we’ve been received, the people connecting with the music in places we didn’t necessarily expect, and then Billboard on top of that — it’s been crazy,” he shared. “We’re grateful for all of it, because you can set goals, but sometimes the reality goes way beyond what you planned for.”

Speaking to the Splash, the entertainer said that, although he has been putting in the work, he was taken aback when he was named by Billboard as a Caribbean Rising Star. He admitted that the honour caught him completely off guard and that he had to resist getting swept up in the whirlwind that the moment ushered in.

“Honestly, I was taken aback. I’m not really the type to overreact, so I was just there trying to take in the moment,” he said. “Billboard recognising me as a Caribbean Rising Star, in a room with so many people who have been doing this at the highest level, that’s crazy. I’m grateful, for real, and it’s something I’ll always remember.”

For an artiste whose career has accelerated considerably in recent years, the recognition represents another marker in a journey that appears to be moving faster than he anticipated. Billboard may have just caught up to Skippa’s burgeoning career, but the proverbial writing was on the wall since the latter part of last year.

By December 2025, YouTube year-end statistics showed that the entertainer had already emerged as Jamaica’s third-most-viewed artiste on the platform, behind Chronic Law and Vybz Kartel, with approximately 79.9 million views. His numbers remained consistent in 2026, with the artiste repeatedly placing multiple songs among Jamaica’s most-streamed records.

Still, he remains humble, crediting his chart success to his loyal fan base rather than to a secret creative formula.

“I wouldn’t say I figured out some formula, because I think what really sets my work apart is that people just relate to me. I’m being myself and making music from my own experience and perspective, and people see themselves in that,” he said.

That connection, he believes, matters more than the numbers themselves — or any ‘trending list’ he may or may not find himself on.

“I don’t chase whatever trend is happening just because it’s working for somebody else. I just try to make good music and stay authentic, and the people decide what they want to run with,” he said.

It is a philosophy that has become increasingly important as the numbers have grown.

For Skippa, there is a difference between having a hit song and building something that can last.

“Consistency, for sure. I think that’s one of the biggest things,” he said. “You can have one song that catches fire, but building a career is different. You have to keep showing up, keep making music, keep performing, keep connecting with the people, and keep growing.”

With that mindset, the entertainer shared that he is looking at his recent success as motivation to go even further, rather than being tricked into believing he has somehow arrived.

“To come into this space and, in such a short time, see my name alongside artistes who have been doing this for years, that’s a big thing. It’s definitely something I’m grateful for and amazed by,” he said. “But I don’t look at it like I’ve arrived and that’s it. It just makes me appreciate the journey even more and motivates me to keep working.”

The entertainer sought to acknowledge the machinery working for his good behind the scenes. Naming his manager, Cristina; engineer, producer and DJ Travis; Chargie Records; Solitary Muzic; and Bankroller, among others, as people who have contributed to his progress, Skippa expressed that, “Everybody played their part, so when I’m on that stage accepting something like Billboard Rising Star, I know it’s not just about me.”

The prediction made by the Observer at the beginning of the year has taken on a life of its own. Having lived up to the ‘one to watch’ status, Skippa is now ready to take things to the next level as he cements his place among dancehall’s best.

World.title: GOV’T QUERIES WINDALCO SALE
World.content:
The entrance to Windalco’s Ewarton Works plant in Clarendon

THE Government says it has received no notice that UC Rusal plans to sell Windalco and is seeking answers from the Russian company’s parent after a report that it has begun looking for buyers.

Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Mining Floyd Green told the Jamaica Observer that checks with Rusal’s local team had produced no information about a possible sale.

“Government has no record or notification any such plans and checks with the local UC Rusal team have indicated that they have no information or correspondence on that matter. We will be reaching out to the parent company regarding the unsubstantiated reports,” Green said.

Bloomberg reported Tuesday that Rusal had begun sounding out potential buyers for Windalco in Jamaica and its bauxite operation in Guyana. It cited people familiar with the matter, but said the plans were at an early stage and a sale might not happen. Rusal declined to comment to Bloomberg.

The report comes as producer prices in Jamaica’s bauxite and alumina industry remain below last year’s levels. The latest figures from the Statistical Institute of Jamaica show that the producer price index for bauxite mining and alumina processing was down 8.4 per cent in August compared with a year earlier. It rose 0.4 per cent from July, after falling 2.2 per cent that month.

Those figures cover the industry as a whole rather than Windalco’s sales. They do, however, show why any question about the future of a major alumina producer will draw attention from workers, suppliers, and the communities around its operations.

Meanwhile, Green pointed to Windalco’s recent spending as evidence that work on the ground is continuing.

“Windalco just completed a major haul road investment and are mining a new area,” he told the

Business Week.

The haul road in St Ann cost about US$29 million and opened access to more high-quality ore, Green told Parliament in May. However, the investment does not settle whether Rusal might consider selling the business.

Windalco’s operations include the Ewarton alumina refinery in St Catherine, bauxite mines and shipping facilities at Port Esquivel. Its assets also include the Kirkvine Works in Manchester. Rusal has owned the company outright since acquiring the Government’s remaining seven per cent stake in 2014.

— Karena Bennet

World.title: SMART PLAY
World.content:
SPEID... we’ll do what we have to do in the right moments (Photo: AFP)

JAMAICA’S Reggae Boyz will be in action at the National Stadium tonight, hosting Guatemala in their Concacaf Nations League A opener at 7:00 pm. Interim head coach Rudolph Speid says the main goal for his team is to play smart, adapt, and do the basics well.

“It’s a performance where we do everything correctly as the needs arise,” Speid said during a pre-match press conference on Thursday morning. “What we have tried to do is to talk about adaptability. So, whatever needs to be done, we’ll be doing it. We’re going to try to play properly — we’ll do what we have to do in the right moments.”

Speid, who was in charge on an interim basis for the World Cup play-offs in Mexico last March, and the Unity Cup in London in May, returned on an interim basis last month but he has had only three days of training with the squad in this international window. He dismissed concerns about the short preparation window and questions about his own coaching future.

“It is what it is; we have three days in training so we just made the best use of it,” Speid said. “That [my future] is not important at the moment. What is important is that we try and win these four games.”

While Speid focuses on tactical execution, tonight carries deep personal significance for midfielder Courtney Clarke.

The Walsall midfielder grew up in the community of Hazard in May Pen. After showing his capabilities to overseas fans during the Unity Cup, tonight marks his first opportunity to play a senior international match on home soil in front of his family.

“I’d say I’m more than ready now; I’ve been waiting for a while,” Clarke said. “The Unity Cup gave me the confidence to show the Jamaican fans in England [what I can do]. Now I’m going to be on home soil and show everybody. Everybody’s been working harder, pushing everybody and the goal is to get it done.”

For Clarke, lining up at “The Office” is a milestone moment in his career, and one he hopes to mark with a win.

Addressing the team’s recent lack of goals is another primary focus for Speid. Instead of changing the entire tactical system, he wants his players to move better off the ball.

“Usually, when you’re not scoring goals, it’s usually the movements that are the problem,” Speid said. “So we have been working on that and we hope that with better movements from the attackers, we’ll be able to score goals.”

Jamaica will be without winger Leon Bailey due to an ankle injury. He has been replaced by Jahmarie Nolan. Speid sees Bailey’s absence as an opportunity for younger wide players like Renaldo Cephas, Kaheim Dixon, and Tyreece Campbell to step up.

“Jamaica has a lot of talented players so once Leon is not available, it gives another player an opportunity to come into the team,” Speid said. “There are a lot of players champing at the bit. So, while it’s bad in one sense, it’s still good for us to expose other players.”

Jamaica has extra motivation tonight after losing 1-0 to Guatemala in their last official meeting at the Concacaf Gold Cup last year under previous head coach Steve McClaren. Óscar Santis scored the winner in that match.

Speid respects Guatemala’s playing style but says his team is ready for the challenge.

“We recognise that they’re a tough team, they like to play with the ball at their feet,” Speid said. “So they have some strengths, but we’re aware of what those strengths are.”

Speid says the squad is focused on getting the right result tonight.

“They’re very motivated,” he said. “It’s a new-look squad, but I think we have the right players here to go forward.”
