World.title: Parliamentary immunity: a loophole for politicians, or a shield against arbitrary power?
World.content:
The debate has flared up after prosecutors requested the lifting of the immunity of Péter Magyar and two Fidesz MPs. But is parliamentary immunity still necessary at all?

The timing of the request from the Office of the Prosecutor General was enough to set Hungarian public life buzzing. The immunity of three MPs was requested on the very same day, even though one case concerns a missing mobile phone, while the other two involve alleged financial damage worth billions of forints.

So what exactly are these three cases about?

Three cases, three very different allegations

The differences between the three cases are obvious at first glance.

According to prosecutors, in Péter Magyar’s case, proceedings should continue over a suspected theft. The prosecution alleges that in June 2024, at the Ötkert nightclub in Budapest, Magyar took a man’s mobile phone and subsequently threw the device into the Danube.

The allegations involving Miklós Seszták and Balázs Hankó are of an entirely different scale.

Seszták is facing suspicions of accepting a bribe in connection with his official duties, while Hankó is suspected of breach of fiduciary duty causing particularly significant financial damage. According to the prosecution, the case linked to Seszták involves more than HUF 11 billion in unlawful advantage.

Is a crime only a crime when it involves billions?

Magyar’s case therefore pales in comparison with the other two in purely financial terms.

But that does not make it legally irrelevant. Theft is a criminal offence under Hungary’s Criminal Code, and one that can be prosecuted by the state.

The real question, then, is not whether we consider one case more serious than another. It is whether smaller offences should effectively be overlooked simply because someone else is accused of committing a much larger one.

And, of course, the mobile-phone case did not begin yesterday.

Proceedings over the incident were already being considered when Magyar was still a Member of the European Parliament. Hungarian authorities asked the European Parliament to waive his immunity, but in a decision adopted in October 2025, the EP declined to grant the request.

Magyar moves to seize the initiative

Magyar has once again sought to take control of the political narrative. Alongside his unusually sharp attack on the Office of the Prosecutor General, he quickly put forward his own proposal: parliamentary immunity should be abolished in cases involving offences prosecuted by the state.

At first sight, the proposal may look like a major political move. Political analyst Gábor Török has pointed out, however, that its practical impact might be considerably smaller than it appears, since Parliament has generally lifted MPs’ immunity in cases involving publicly prosecuted offences.

But there is an important detail that can easily get lost in the political argument.

Parliamentary immunity is not only about whether Parliament ultimately allows an MP to be prosecuted.

It is also about what happens before that decision is made.

For an ordinary citizen, certain immediate investigative measures and coercive measures may be available to the authorities. In the case of an MP, however, parliamentary authorisation may be required.

This means that immunity can provide more than a symbolic shield. It can give a politician time, information and a degree of procedural protection. An MP may have an opportunity to prepare for proceedings rather than being caught completely off guard by a search of their home or another coercive measure.

What happens to MPs without immunity?

The arguments on the other side, however, are not without merit either.

The original purpose of parliamentary immunity was precisely to protect MPs from politically motivated prosecution and to safeguard the independence of the legislature. That is why modern democracies do not generally treat immunity simply as a personal privilege for politicians.

The real question, therefore, is not whether the issue is about Péter Magyar or Fidesz.

Nor is it a question of HUF 11 billion versus a mobile phone.

The fundamental issue is where to draw the line between protecting elected representatives from political abuse of state power and giving politicians special protection during criminal proceedings.

That line matters regardless of who happens to be in government, who sits in opposition and whose name appears in a prosecutor’s request.

After all, parliamentary immunity was not created to put politicians above the law. Its purpose was to ensure that the law could not simply be turned into a political weapon against them.

The difficult part is deciding where one protection ends and the other begins.

As we wrote on Wednesday, PM Péter Magyar accuses prosecutors of ‘protecting mobsters’ in escalating immunity row.

World.title: Revolut Hungary set to enter ATM market – what will change for customers?
World.content:
Revolut Hungary could soon become a much more visible part of the country’s banking infrastructure, as the fintech company is expected to join Hungary’s ATM deployment programme. The change could eventually bring hundreds of new cash machines, although customers should not expect an immediate transformation in cash withdrawals.

Hungary’s ATM network shrank slightly in the second quarter of 2026 despite regulations designed to expand access to cash. According to Bankmonitor, however, the decline is likely to be temporary, with Revolut expected to become involved in the nationwide expansion of cash machines.

The number of ATMs in Hungary stood at 5,688 at the end of the first quarter of 2026, before falling by 29 to 5,659 at the end of the second quarter. The decrease was particularly noticeable in and around Budapest.

Further expansion is nevertheless expected. By the end of 2026, settlements with more than 500 inhabitants are required to have at least one ATM.

Why Revolut Hungary may have to install ATMs

A customer is using the ATM at Revolut Hungary. Source: despositphotos.com

Hungarian rules require payment service providers whose issued bank cards account for at least 1% of the market to operate a minimum number of ATMs. The machines must also be distributed geographically, meaning providers cannot simply concentrate them in Budapest and other major cities.

Revolut has around two million customers in Hungary, according to Bankmonitor, putting it comfortably above the relevant threshold. Until recently, however, the company was not considered a domestic payment service provider for the purposes of the requirement.

That changed after Revolut established a Hungarian branch and began migrating existing Hungarian customers to it in May 2026.

Bankmonitor reports that the National Bank of Hungary (MNB) has confirmed that Revolut will have to participate in the ATM installation programme in the future. As a result, the central bank could require the company to install several hundred machines from next year.

For foreign residents, this is significant because Revolut is widely used as an alternative to traditional Hungarian banks, particularly by customers who frequently make international payments or hold several currencies.

If you missed it: You can run to Revolut, but you can’t hide: Debt collectors can now freeze Hungarian accounts

What changes for Revolut customers?

For now, very little.

Determining Revolut’s precise ATM quota and installing the machines will take time, meaning the current cash withdrawal options available to customers are not expected to change in the short term.

According to Bankmonitor, Revolut cards are still treated as foreign-issued cards for ATM withdrawals. This is important because some Hungarian banks charge an additional fee when customers use Revolut cards.

At present, Erste ATMs charge HUF 1,200 (approximately EUR 3.30) and OTP ATMs HUF 1,999 (around EUR 5.50) for withdrawals made with Revolut cards, Bankmonitor reports. Other Hungarian banks do not currently impose this particular additional fee. Euro conversions are approximate and based on an exchange rate of roughly HUF 366 to EUR 1 on 25 September 2026.

The arrival of Revolut’s own ATMs could therefore give customers another option for accessing cash. It remains unclear, however, exactly how the machines will operate or what fee structure Revolut will apply.

Bankmonitor also notes that, over the longer term, the costs of installing and operating a sizeable ATM network could potentially be reflected in Revolut’s pricing in some form.

Revolut Hungary enters a changing cash market

The expansion comes at an unusual time for Hungary’s payment market. The government and central bank have introduced several measures intended to preserve access to cash, including mandatory ATM coverage in smaller settlements.

At the same time, Hungarians are increasingly turning to electronic payments.

According to MNB data cited by Bankmonitor, electronic transactions reached a record share in 2025, accounting for 50% of payments compared with cash transactions. Bank transfers are also becoming cheaper: 48% of retail transfers were free in 2025, compared with 37% in 2023.

Hungary has also doubled the monthly limit for certain free cash withdrawals to HUF 300,000 (approximately EUR 820).

The expected arrival of Revolut ATMs therefore comes as two trends develop simultaneously: authorities are working to guarantee nationwide access to physical cash, while consumers continue moving towards cards and digital payments.

For Revolut Hungary customers, the immediate impact will be limited. In the longer term, however, the company’s entry into the Hungarian ATM market could expand withdrawal options and make Revolut an increasingly physical presence in a market where it has so far operated primarily as a digital banking service.

As we wrote earlier, Revolut launches Hungarian bank accounts.

World.title: Where Japan fits in Hungary’s changing ties with Asia
World.content:
While much of Hungary’s recent foreign-policy attention has focused closer to home, its relationships across Asia have continued to develop in parallel. China and South Korea have become increasingly visible through major investment projects, particularly in electric vehicles, batteries and manufacturing. Meanwhile, Japan, one of Hungary’s longest-standing Asian partners, has remained a quieter presence.

Written by Kate Berbano

Earlier this month, Japan and the Visegrád Four held their first foreign ministers’ meeting in five years near Bratislava, Slovakia. Hungarian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán joined her Czech, Polish and Slovak counterparts in talks with Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi. Their discussions centered on science and technology, artificial intelligence, economic security and connectivity.

Japan and the Visegrád Four held their first foreign ministers’ meeting in five years near Bratislava, Slovakia. Source: Facebook

Still, Japan’s role in Hungary has continued to evolve. The Japan External Trade Organization’s Budapest office, or JETRO Budapest, and historian Dr. Umemura Yuko provide different perspectives on what has changed, and where the relationship may be heading next.

A relationship built before the boom

Hungary’s relationship with Japan reaches much further back than the current expansion of Asian investment in Central Europe. According to Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, their formal ties stretch back to 1869, while diplomatic relations were restored in 1959 after the disruption caused by the Second World War and the Cold War. Japan later supported Hungary during its transition towards democracy and a market economy, while Japanese companies were among the early foreign investors to establish operations in the country.

For historian Dr. Umemura Yuko, that longer history still matters. “Among Asian countries, Hungary has the longest history of exchanges with Japan, so that tradition already exists,” she said in written responses translated from Japanese.

Umemura also pointed to periods of close cultural ties before the Second World War, saying that this background still contributes to a sense of familiarity between the two countries.

Daily News Hungary has followed that relationship before. In a 2024 interview with Japanese Ambassador Hikariko Ono, the ambassador highlighted Japan’s long-standing economic presence in Hungary and emphasised areas such as digital transformation, green technologies and start-ups as possible directions for deeper cooperation.

Two years later, Japan’s presence is already well established. The question now is what that presence looks like in its next phase.

Japanese investment is changing in character

According to JETRO Budapest, around 195 Japanese-affiliated companies currently operate in Hungary, employing approximately 30,000 people. Around 53 are manufacturers, while others are active in trading, logistics, IT and business services. Many long-established firms, including Suzuki, Denso and Ibiden, have become closely integrated into Hungarian and European supply chains.

JETRO sees the bigger change in the way Japanese companies are investing today. “The most significant change is not necessarily the sectors in which Japanese companies operate, but the way they invest.”

During the 1990s and 2000s, Japanese investment in Hungary was often associated with large greenfield manufacturing projects aimed at supplying European markets. More recent investment, according to JETRO, has increasingly centred on expanding existing operations and strengthening companies’ positions within European value chains.

One recent example is Hodogaya Chemical’s acquisition of Framochem in Kazincbarcika, which JETRO points to as part of a bigger move towards building on existing operations rather than starting from scratch. That type of investment attracts less attention than a newly announced multibillion-euro factory, but it reflects a relationship that has moved beyond its first stage.

China and South Korea move to the forefront

Japan’s lower profile also reflects the growing weight of China and South Korea in Hungary. Daily News Hungary’s recent interview with China’s ambassador explored its expanding ambitions in areas including robotics and artificial intelligence, while South Korean Ambassador Chul-min Park told DNH in June that Hungary was developing from an investment destination into a partner in innovation and research.

Umemura sees Japan’s quieter profile partly through that economic change. “Japan is gradually becoming unable to compete with China’s growth and economic strength, so I think it is only natural that Chinese expansion into Hungary is now much greater than Japan’s,” she said. She added that “Japanese manufacturing is no longer as active in expanding overseas as it was in the past.”

At the same time, she does not see the broader relationship as weakening. She pointed to the continued popularity of Japanese studies, manga, anime and Japanese food in Hungary, noting that the university department where she taught remained highly popular.

Less about volume, more about quality

Looking ahead, JETRO Budapest expects Japan-Hungary economic relations to be shaped “less by volume and more by quality.”

“In addition to traditional investment projects, we see growing opportunities for collaboration between companies, universities, research institutes, startups and business support organizations in both countries.”

Umemura also sees an imbalance in how well the two countries know each other. “When it comes to Hungary in Japan, there is still far too little information and knowledge,” she said. For JETRO, the next stage is similarly about widening those connections: “Ultimately, the greatest potential lies not only in new investment projects, but also in creating more connections between Japanese and Hungarian companies, institutions and entrepreneurs.”

China and South Korea may command more of the newest investment headlines, but Japan’s place in Hungary now rests on something harder to build quickly: depth.

World.title: Bosnia Court Blocks Republika Srpska From Funding Secessionist Lobbying
World.content:
Bosnian lawmaker Denis Zvizdic, who initiated teh legal challenge. Photo: EPA/FELIPE TRUEBA.

Bosnia’s Constitutional Court on Friday declared that budgetary funds used by Bosnia’s Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity to pay foreign consulting firms to lobby for independence violate the state’s constitutional architecture.

The ruling targets a consulting agreement signed between the Republika Srpska Representative Office in Vienna and a Montreal-based firm, Dickens & Madson Canada Inc., which listed “the independence of Republika Srpska” as a core political objective.

The legal challenge was initiated in April by a state-level lawmaker, Denis Zvizdic, who argued that using taxpayers’ funds to lobby against Bosnia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity was unconstitutional.

A 2008 ruling allowed the entity to engage foreign firms for general economic promotion. However, the court has now established that funding campaigns explicitly promoting secession represents an assault on the constitutional order.

“The Constitutional Court hereby prohibits all payments from the budget of Republika Srpska regarding the consulting services contract concluded with Dickens & Madson Canada Inc.,” the court said. “Financing lobbying services for goals that run counter to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina is strictly incompatible with the constitutional order.”

The applicant, Zvizdic, welcomed the announcement, saying the entity had weaponised massive public funds for anti-state campaigns.

“Public money cannot be used to finance lobbying aimed against the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its territorial integrity, sovereignty and its institutions,” Zvizdic stated.

“This binding decision establishes a clear legal standard: citizens’ money must serve development and investment, not the undermining of the state,” he added.

Under Bosnia’s state-level laws, entities possess no constitutional right to unilateral secession. Furthermore, ignoring or violating a binding order of the Constitutional Court carries severe penalties.

The court said the full text of the judicial decision will be delivered to all parties and published on its official website within the month.

World.title: Serbia Sees First TV Debate Between Ruling Party and Student List
World.content:
Serbia’s first election debate ahead of October 25 polls aired on TV on Thursday night, pitting former prime minister and current speaker Ana Brnabic – third on the government’s “Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia” list – against Mirjana Nikolic, Rector of the University of Arts in Belgrade and a candidate on the rival “Student List – Students Win”.

The debate on the N1 TV channel was supposed to focus on education but quickly expanded into a wider confrontation over the anti-government student movement, the media, universities and the overall political situation.

Nikolic said she was initially apprehensive about debating a senior ruling-party official but welcomed the chance to present the Student List’s programme.

She said her previous meetings with Brnabic at parliament’s Education Committee had been marked by confrontation, adding that the televised debate offered a chance for both sides to present their programmes.

The appearance was notable because ruling SNS officials have largely avoided N1 during previous election campaigns and Brnabic last appeared in 2017.

“To be honest, I was not particularly happy to come to N1 this time either, given the way your television station has, over the past ten years, engaged in what I see as the dehumanisation of my President and my friend,” Brnabic said.

She accused N1 of having spread false information but said she had agreed to appear after Vucic encouraged her to give the television station “a chance”, following its change of management.

The debate quickly became heated, including an exchange over Nikolic’s alleged refusal to shake Brnabic’s hand.

The candidates also clashed over the student-led university blockades. Brnabic said students had been discriminated against “thanks to the Student List and the blockades”, while Nikolic accused her of promoting a misleading narrative about the protests and about how universities functioned.

On education, Brnabic defended the SNS record in government, pointing to higher teachers’ salaries, increased education spending and investment in science and technology infrastructure.

Nikolic challenged the figures, arguing that nominal salary increases did not necessarily mean education workers were better off, and questioned delays to university infrastructure projects.

She also criticised Brnabic’s understanding of Serbia’s education system, telling her: “As a professor, I have to tell you – Ana, you failed, you failed the exam.”

Nikolic said the Student List advocated free education, equal opportunities for students and teachers and the modernisation of the education system.

The debate was the first in a series of thematic election debates announced by N1 ahead of the October 25 parliamentary election.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czechia Restricts Rules for Russian Diplomats Travelling
World.content:
Sikorski confronts Lavrov as tensions rise; Russian helicopter enters Polish airspace

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski used a UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday to deliver a direct message to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov: that after more than four years of full-scale war, Russia had failed to achieve its central objectives in Ukraine, and lacked the economic weight to outlast the countries supporting Kyiv. “You have been trying to conquer Donbas for over 12 years and Kyiv for over four,” Sikorski said. Ukraine, he noted, has only one-tenth of Russia’s GDP. But Poland alone has almost half Russia’s GDP, while Europe has roughly 10 times as much and NATO 25 times as much. “You can still kill a lot of people, but you cannot win,” Sikorski said. “You can stop this imperial war of choice at any time.” He ended by addressing Lavrov personally: “Sergey, I know you’re listening. Tell your boss: enough is enough.”

Hours before Sikorski spoke in New York, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter flying from the Kaliningrad region crossed into Polish airspace north of Braniewo at 11:08 on Wednesday. According to Poland’s Operational Command, it penetrated about 300 metres into Polish territory and remained there for 42 seconds. Warsaw scrambled fighter jets and raised the readiness of its ground-based defences. The Operational Command said the flight pattern suggested Moscow was again probing Poland’s ability to respond. The pressure continued on Thursday morning, this time from attacks inside Ukraine. PM Donald Tusk said Russian strikes close to the Polish border forced authorities to evacuate the border crossings at Hrubieszow and Dorohusk. “Just as we were talking, Ukraine was attacked again near the Polish border,” Tusk said during a meeting with Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev. He warned that “autumn and winter may be critical”.

The incidents come as Warsaw is seeking stronger security guarantees from Washington and dealing with an unexpected hitch in talks over a permanent US military presence. Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz had been due to meet his US counterpart Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Wednesday, with a permanent US Army base in Poland among the expected topics. The visit was cancelled at Washington’s urgent request, officially because of a scheduling conflict connected with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US. No replacement date has been announced. The timing caused unease in Warsaw. Onet reported, citing unnamed government sources, that some Polish officials suspect Hegseth may be seeking to slow discussions on the permanent base. Subsequent reporting, however, indicated that the Pentagon initially tried merely to change the meeting’s time before cancelling it, suggesting the explanation may be less straightforward. The uncertainty comes days after Donald Trump said “significant progress” had been made towards establishing a US Army base in Poland and suggested its location could soon be announced.

World.title: Fading Away: Sicily’s Ancient Albanian Community Fears its Identity Risks Erasure
World.content:
Piana degli Albanesi sits among the fertile mountains of western Sicily, overlooking farmland and a lake whose waters have receded dramatically.

Its Arbereshe name is “Hora e Arbereshevet”, or, “Town of the Arbereshe”, the only one among the several other Italian towns to maintain a distinct name connected to the ethnic group that inhabits it.

The word “Hora”, explains Mayor Rosario Petta, as he walks through the town’s cobbled streets, is an old Albanian word for a town or homeland that is no longer commonly used in modern Albanian.

In Piana, however, the name is everywhere. It appears on street signs, public buildings and local businesses, a reminder that this is not simply a Sicilian town with an unusual history. It is the centre of one of Italy’s most important ethnolinguistic communities.

Petta says that in Albania, the Arbereshe are almost mythical figures –reminders of a version of Albania that disappeared centuries ago but still exists in these communities.

There is a strange historical relationship between the two sides.

The people of Piana look towards Albania as the ancestral land from which their communities emerged. Meanwhile, in Albania, the Arbereshe represent a living connection to an older version of Albanian language and culture that they can no longer experience in their homeland.

But the community in Piana is shrinking.

Over the past five years, according to Petta, the town has lost more than 20 per cent of its population. Its official population is now below 6,000, although the actual number of people living there is believed to be lower.

“The more people we lose, the more our ancient heritage is threatened,” Petta said.

The reasons are familiar across rural southern Italy: limited employment, young people leaving for larger cities or abroad, and the decline of traditional agriculture.

In Piana, climate change is adding another layer to the crisis.

The olive groves around Piana are increasingly exposed to drought, extreme temperatures and wildfires.

In 2023, wildfires destroyed several hectares of land around the town. The water crisis is also affecting farmers directly.

“We have felt the water crisis a lot and it is reflected in the quantity, quality and timing of our produce,” Claudio said.

Harvests have been brought forward as summers become longer and hotter. Trees are showing signs of stress that were previously unusual.

“The summer season is longer,” he added. “This year the grape harvesting season came earlier because of weather changes.”

The climate crisis, therefore, threatens more than individual farms. Agriculture has historically been one of the ways Arbereshe communities have remained rooted in their villages and integrated within Italian and Sicilian society. If farming becomes economically unsustainable, one of the remaining reasons for younger people to stay also disappears.

The Scalia siblings are trying to make agriculture part of the solution.

Their company was established in 2022, building on an olive grove planted in 1998. Their aim is to combine modern agricultural practices with the cultural heritage of Piana.

Their products are organic, with the longer-term ambition of securing territorial recognition such as the IGP designation. Alongside olive oil, they produce honey and other agricultural products, including plums.

The names of their products pay homage to their Arbereshe heritage. One of them, “Filari”, refers to the rows of olive trees while evoking “fili d’oro”, the golden threads used in traditional Arbereshe clothing.

The point is to make the connection between agriculture and culture more visible.

“Few people invest in agriculture and innovation in these historical times,” Claudio Scalia said. “Those who do struggle to live exclusively from it these days. To keep our farming culture alive, we are also taking on other jobs to financially sustain ourselves in a more stable way.”

Children no longer speak the language

World.title: Bringing the Balkans into Schengen: a Win-Win Scenario for Europe
World.content:
How would all this work? The member states would ask the Commission to prepare a roadmap of criteria: the Schengen acquis.

That means external border control, visa policy, the Schengen Information System, police cooperation and data protection – reinforced by rule-of-law conditions.

The Commission would report on progress every six months, and once a country met all the criteria, the member states would have to give their consent in the Council.

Reforms and the closer cooperation they bring can strengthen security rather than weaken it. When the Schengen area grew from 15 to 24 members in 2007, Germany’s then Interior Minister, Wolfgang Schauble, said: “We will have a gain in security, not a loss.”

The main argument against admitting Western Balkan countries has recently evaporated. For over a decade, several EU interior ministers saw the Western Balkan borders as a brake on irregular migrants and asylum seekers heading from Turkey and Greece into central Europe.

The admission of Bulgaria and Romania to the Schengen area in 2025 overturned that. Why would anyone on that route cross several tightly controlled borders when they could travel from Greece through Bulgaria and Romania to Hungary and Austria without ever leaving the Schengen area?

Reforms and eventual membership would meanwhile help to stabilise the region’s most fragile states – Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Kosovo, where Bosniaks, Serbs and Albanians live on both sides of the borders. As EU membership has receded into the distant future, the dangerous narratives of the late 1980s, that led to the wars of the 1990s, are returning, and with them ideas of redrawing borders along ethnic lines (floated by the presidents of Serbia and Kosovo in 2018).

The recent state funeral in Belgrade for Bosnian Serb wartime military commander Ratko Mladic, convicted of committing genocide in Srebrenica, is only the latest reminder of that.

It is precisely because these forces are gaining ground that the EU needs a stronger counter-offer. Schengen could be one. It does not move borders but makes them invisible, as they are between France and Germany, or Lithuania and Poland.

But you cannot make a border invisible before its status is settled, and the line between Serbia and Kosovo is the very thing being fought over. Settling it would become the price of a prize that’s within reach. It is a far stronger incentive than EU membership, which is at least a decade away.

Several countries already belong to Schengen but not the EU: Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein. Unlike with earlier Schengen enlargements, this time no new external borders would be required. Surrounded by Schengen members, the borders of the Western Balkan countries could simply be collapsed inwards.

Offering such a roadmap would cost the EU little, and only serious reformers would ever join. Yet the process alone would hand the EU influence and win back some of its lost credibility. More importantly still, it would offer the Balkans something better than more quarrels over where lines should run. Borders would no longer matter.

Kristof Bender is Deputy Chairman of the European Stability Initiative (ESI).

A German version of this article first appeared in the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ).

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Mr Who? Professor in Race Against Time to Convince Serbia’s Undecided Voters
World.content:
On one hand, Ilija Srdanovic’s greatest asset might be his lack of political baggage. On the other, his obscurity may prove a hindrance.

With the 56-year-old medical professor from Novi Sad, northern Serbia, now the figurehead of a grassroots movement to unseat Serbia’s ruling party and president, voters will give their verdict on October 25.

Largely unknown to the wider Serbian public until this month, Srdanovic has been thrust into the spotlight, his every move and utterance picked over by tabloids and pro-government broadcasters.

Srdanovic hails from the city where 16 people were crushed to death in November 2024 when a concrete canopy at a newly renovated railway station collapsed, triggering an outpouring of anger and frustration at what many Serbs say is the mismanagement, corner-cutting and corruption that has flourished during 14 years of rule by the Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, and President Aleksandar Vucic.

Chosen by the students who took up the call for change, Srdanovic finds himself effectively going head-to-head with Vucic, a seasoned politician and, his critics say, an autocrat in the mould of Viktor Orban.

World.title: Here’s How the New Zagreb Pedestrian Zone Will Look
World.content:
September the 25th, 2026 – The brand new Zagreb pedestrian zone has been presented as part of European Mobility Week.

Zagreb’s city administration has emphasised that the presented solution retains hospitality terraces as an important part of the social life of the Lower Town, but provides for their uniform design and better integration into the public space. Poslovni reports that three years after the temporary arrangement of the pedestrian zone in Masarykova Street, the City of Zagreb has presented the project for its permanent and comprehensive arrangement that covers Masarykova and Teslina streets as well as parts of Preradovićeva and Gajeva up to Berislavićeva Street.

The project envisages uniform paving of the entire space, divided into a pedestrian zone and a calmed traffic zone between Republic of Croatia Square and Gundulićeva Street, as well as the formation of new public focal points at key intersections and points within the zone. Special emphasis has been placed on the greening of the space. The planting of around 50 new trees connected into a continuous tree line between the two arms of the Green Horseshoe is planned, along with additional green surfaces, urban furniture, drinking water fountains and spaces for rest. The project also includes new bicycle parking, zones for short-term stopping and delivery, as well as a series of measures that improve accessibility for persons with disabilities and the safety of all users of the space.

a unique and well connected pedestrian zone in the heart of zagreb

The conceptual design was prepared by the Institute for Spatial Planning of the City of Zagreb, and an extensive participatory process included citizens, residents, business users and experts of various profiles, it was announced on Thursday from the Office of Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević.

Zagreb Deputy Mayor Luka Korlaet said that by arranging the pedestrian zone they are creating a complete public space intended for safer and higher-quality pedestrian movement, staying, socialising and public events. It is especially important, he says, that they are connecting the existing pedestrian spaces and expanding the pedestrian zone on the northern arms of the Green Horseshoe, from Republic of Croatia Square to Zrinjevac. In this way they are creating a unique, connected and passable pedestrian whole in the very centre of Zagreb, Korlaet emphasised.

Director of the Institute for Spatial Planning Nikša Božić said that an interdisciplinary team of the Institute worked on the project, which brought together architects, landscape architects, traffic experts and other collaborators.

“It is particularly important to us that through the preparation of the conceptual design we built on the tradition of arranging public spaces that the Institute developed in previous decades, participating in projects such as the arrangement of Jurišićeva and Draškovićeva streets, the Stock Exchange Square and other important city locations,” Božić said.

what are the top priorities?

He noted that in preparing the solution the Institute took into account the collected views, proposals and needs of citizens as well as the results of expert analyses of the space and its development potentials.

The results of a survey fully completed by around 3,400 citizens showed that 88.4 percent of participants support the comprehensive arrangement of the space. The temporary arrangement was rated as positive or extremely positive by 76 percent of respondents, while 72 percent of them supported the expansion of the pedestrian zone to Teslina and Gajeva streets. As the most important priorities citizens highlighted more greenery, benches and spaces for staying, as well as better organisation of traffic and delivery.

World.title: Zagreb City Break, Remote-Worker Style – Why 90 Days Could Be All You Need
World.content:
September the 25th, 2026 – Zagreb is an up and coming city break, but it could be more than that thanks to the remote worker boom. Many talk about Croatia’s famed “digital nomad visa”, but 90 days and zero admin could be all you need.

Not every remote worker wants (or needs) a full digital nomad visa. For many professionals, the classic Croatian “temporary stay of digital nomads” route – with its income thresholds, documentation piles and multi-month planning – is overkill. If your passport already allows visa-free entry to the Schengen area, you can simply turn up and stay for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. That window is long enough to settle into a real routine, yet short enough to feel like an extended city break rather than a bureaucratic relocation. Zagreb is perfectly suited to this lighter approach.

the 90 day limit could be all you need

Unlike the coastline and the islands, which swing between peak-season summer intensity and winter quiet, Zagreb functions as a proper European capital all year. Trams run, cafes stay open, co-working spaces keep their regular hours, and the cultural calendar never really stops. You get the infrastructure of a serious city without the summer price spikes that hit Split or Dubrovnik.

Reliable high-speed internet is the baseline, not a luxury. The co-working scene is mature and varied – from community-focused hubs to quieter central spots – so you can choose between focused workdays and networking as the mood takes you. Plenty of remote workers simply rotate between a well-chosen apartment and a handful of cafes with strong Wi-Fi and power sockets; the cafe culture here is built for lingering.

a big-little city with plenty to offer

Outside working hours, the city rewards curiosity. Upper Town’s cobbled streets and the instantly recognisable St Mark’s Church, the Museum of Broken Relationships, Maksimir Park, Lake Jarun (Zagreb’s unofficial “sea”), and the open-air Dolac Market are all within very easy reach. In the evenings, the bar and restaurant scene is lively without being overwhelming. Weekends open the door to day trips – Plitvice Lakes, the hills around Samobor, or a quick train to Ljubljana – without the stress of long-haul logistics.

Cost of living remains noticeably lower than in most Western European capitals, so a three-month stay feels financially sustainable rather than extravagant.

you don’t need to be a digital nomad to… be a digital nomad

Croatia’s official digital nomad temporary stay is designed for longer periods (up to 18 months) and requires proof of remote work for a non-Croatian entity, health insurance, a clean criminal record, and a minimum income currently set at 2.5 times the average net salary – currently over €3,600 per month, or the equivalent in savings. Processing takes time and the paperwork is real.

The 90-day Schengen short stay, by contrast, asks far less of you if your nationality qualifies for visa-free entry. You arrive, register your accommodation as required, work remotely for your existing foreign employer or clients, and leave before the 90 days are up (or before you hit the 183-day tax-residency threshold if that matters to you). No special permit, no income threshold tied to Croatian averages, no multi-week application process. It is simply a long, productive city break with a laptop. Of course the usual rules apply: you cannot take local employment, and the days count toward your overall Schengen allowance. But for many remote professionals testing life in Croatia, or simply wanting a change of scenery without administrative drama and a baptism of fire from the Croatian bureaucratic machine, that is precisely the point.

who could this work best for?

This approach suits a whole cohort of people; those who already work remotely for a company or clients outside Croatia and hold a passport that allows 90 days visa-free in the Schengen zone, those who want a proper base rather than a series of hotel stays and those prefer a walkable, cafe-packed European city with four seasons and good transport links, and those who are curious about Croatia but not yet ready to commit to the full digital nomad process. It also works well as a trial run. Spend 60–90 days in Zagreb, get a feel for the rhythm, the food, the community and the climate, then decide whether a longer digital nomad stay or a return trip next year makes sense for you.

no visas, no paperwork, and full freedom

Book a furnished apartment or serviced flat with reliable internet rather than a short-term tourist rental if you can. Join a coworking space for at least a few days a week to meet people. Use the city’s excellent public transport and the green spaces to keep the work–life balance healthy. And treat the weekends as genuine exploration time – Zagreb rewards slow discovery more than checklist tourism.

In short, you do not need a special visa to work remotely from Croatia for three months. You just need a laptop, a passport that opens the Schengen door, and a city that actually works for everyday life. Zagreb quietly delivers on all three. For practical information on accommodation, events and getting around, the Zagreb Tourist Board is a good starting point. The rest is simply showing up and getting to work – and leisure.

World.title: Končar Showcases Croatian Manufacturing to the World in Berlin
World.content:
September the 25th, 2026 – Končar has showcased Croatian manufacturing to the world in Berlin, taking the most prominent positions at this year’s InnoTrans.

Končar’s striking visuals were visible in the most prominent positions right at the entrance to the space of the prestigious fair, and the scene at the very entrance to the exhibition area was spectacular, where Končar’s train, a top product of Croatian industry, was positioned in a more prominent place than giants such as Alstom and Stadler. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that after it was put into regular service on the Zagreb – Split route a week earlier in cooperation with the customer HŽ Passenger Transport, the second train from this series has now also been presented to the international public. With the global premiere of its latest solution for more modern, more comfortable and more sustainable passenger transport, Končar has once again confirmed that the knowledge, competences and technological solutions developed in Croatia compete on equal terms with the biggest names in the European railway industry.

croatia impresses visitors from around the world

The InnoTrans fair in Berlin once again brought together the world’s leading manufacturers, carriers, operators and experts from the fields of transport technology, railways, public transport and sustainable mobility. Among the most visited parts of the fair was the outdoor exhibition area with 3,500 metres of track, on which 130 exhibitors from 17 countries of the world exhibited a total of 113 vehicles, including the latest generations of trains, locomotives and vehicles with alternative propulsion systems. Precisely in such an international environment Končar is presenting technological solutions developed and produced in Croatia for the jubilee 10th time, confirming its position among the relevant European manufacturers of modern rail vehicles and advanced solutions for sustainable urban mobility.

berlin breaks records

All 42 exhibition halls in the Berlin Messe complex, with a total exhibition area of around 200 thousand square metres, are completely full. After two years ago it was the only one at InnoTrans to present a battery train, which then also became the first such product in commercial use in Europe and one of the first such products in the whole world, Končar has also displayed its new bimodal electro-diesel train at one of the most attractive positions on the outdoor exhibition area of the fair – on 75-metre-long tracks.

At the same time, the latest solutions for railway infrastructure, electrification, urban mobility and traffic digitalisation were presented on the spacious indoor area, further emphasising the ability of the domestic company to independently develop and deliver integrated technological solutions for the transport systems of the future.

“The presentation of our latest bimodal train at InnoTrans is confirmation that Končar today stands side by side with the leading European manufacturers of railway vehicles. It is a product of a new generation that confirms the strength of domestic knowledge, innovation and industrial competences and Končar’s ability to respond to the requirements of modern and sustainable railway transport. We believe that precisely with such projects we contribute to strengthening the competitiveness of the Croatian economy and positioning Croatia among the countries that actively participate in shaping the future of sustainable mobility in Europe,” emphasised Končar Management Board President Gordan Kolak.

One train, two sources of propulsion and no compromises – precisely this idea guided the development of the new Končar bimodal electro-diesel train that combines the advantages of electric and diesel traction and enables uninterrupted traffic on electrified and non-electrified sections of the railway network. Additional operational adaptability is provided by the possibility of controlling up to three coupled units from one driver’s cab, whereby the capacity of the train can be adapted to the actual transport needs. Accordingly, it is an innovation that represents a direct response to the need for more sustainable and more efficient railway transport on long routes that encompass both types of infrastructure, and is the result of many years of experience and independent development at Končar – Electric Vehicles.

With its presentation Končar rounds off a unique development portfolio of trains and, after electric, diesel-electric and battery trains, is introducing the fourth propulsion platform developed and produced in Croatia to the market. The new train is also one of the best references of the long and successful application of Croatian products in domestic railway transport. Namely, the model from the new generation that was put into service last week represents a total of the 70th train that Končar has delivered to HŽ Passenger Transport, which further confirms the joint orientation towards the modernisation of the domestic railway system.

a new era

“The new train for long-distance transport combines the development, design and production competences of the Končar Group. Thanks to the bimodal propulsion system it ensures a high level of reliability and quality of service on the entire network, while bringing passengers a higher standard of comfort through first class, a catering zone and full accessibility for persons with reduced mobility. It is a technologically advanced and operationally flexible solution that meets the requirements of modern railway transport and the long-term needs of sustainable mobility,” emphasised Josip Ninić, President of the Management Board of Končar – Electric Vehicles.

By developing advanced rail vehicles, digital platforms and integrated solutions for critical infrastructure, including railway and transport systems, Končar is increasingly entering a new era of electroenergetics and urban mobility and occupying the position of a serious European partner for the implementation of complex projects. In this way it not only confirms the technological strength of Croatian industry, but also actively contributes to positioning Croatia as a relevant participant in the European green and digital transition and one of the centres of development of the technologically most complex solutions in this part of Europe.

This year InnoTrans is celebrating its 30th anniversary – and, quite fittingly, the fair is recording new record figures. For the first time more than 3,170 exhibitors will participate, which is around 200 more than in 2024, which was also a record year. All 42 exhibition halls in the Berlin Messe complex, with a total exhibition area of around 200 thousand square metres, are completely full. The same applies to the outdoor exhibition area of InnoTrans of 20 thousand square metres, where this year 113 vehicles from 17 countries will be exhibited.

Of the approximately 130 exhibitors presenting themselves on the outdoor area, around 30 of them are participating in that segment for the first time. Therefore the event has great prospects of surpassing the record attendance of around 170 thousand visitors from 2024. That is a huge advance compared to the modest beginnings of what is today the world’s leading railway transport fair.

World.title: Exotic Indian Bananas Successfully Being Grown in Međimurje
World.content:
September the 25th, 2026 – Exotic Indian bananas are successfully being grown in Međimurje, seeing seeds turn into three thousand seedlings.

In the municipality of Štrigova, an area in the north of Međimurje known primarily for its vineyards, one of the largest plantations of Indian bananas in this part of Europe was planted a few years ago. Index reports that behind the project is the family of Ivan Žižek, who decided to grow this unusual fruit after learning that it tolerates low temperatures well and is not attacked by diseases, HRT reports.

3,000 seedlings

The Žižek family planted a plantation of Indian banana, also known as pawpaw (asimina), in the village of Banfi three years ago. Since the seedlings are expensive and they needed more than three thousand of them, they opted for a cheaper but slower route. “We obtained a larger quantity of fruit from Italy, manually extracted the seeds, processed them and put them to germinate. Luckily, everything germinated excellently so we grew the first rootstocks of asimina that way. After that I personally started grafting them,” Ivan explains.

The trees are not yet in full yield so for now the family is selling only fresh fruit. In a year or two they plan to start production of food and cosmetic products from that fruit. “A tree in full yield can give around 20 kilograms. We plan to place 20 to 30 percent on the market through retail chains, and the rest would go into the food industry – for craft breweries, jams, liqueurs and aromatic wines,” says Roman Mraz.

hail reduced the yield

This year’s plantation was also quite damaged by strong hail that hit the area in June. “Still, with some earlier varieties we noticed that the first fruit we tasted was of good quality and tasty inside,” Ivan emphasises.

The Indian banana plantation is not the only example of growing exotic crops in that area. Namely, next to the edge of the plantation of fruit that originates from North America, the Žižek family is also growing 16 pistachio trees, whose original homeland is the Middle East, and 65 feijoa bushes, a fruit species from South America.

World.title: Croatia Needs to Keep Investing in Nautical Tourism
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – Croatia must keep investing in its nautical tourism sector as 2.7 million overnight stays are recorded so far in 2026.

In the first eight months of this year, over 431,000 charter guests visited Croatia, who recorded more than 2.7 million overnight stays. Ana Blaskovic reports for Poslovni that Croatia must continue investing in nautical tourism in order to maintain competitiveness, while also resolving the issue of concessions that are expiring for individual marinas, it was said at the conference Nautical Tourism of Croatia 2030.

The country currently has 216 nautical tourism ports and other facilities for berthing and accommodating vessels, with almost 19 thousand berths. Minister of Maritime Affairs Oleg Butković emphasised that the key challenge remains seasonality, since the highest traffic and revenues are realised in July and August. The goal is to develop a year-round business model and additional content that would attract nautical tourists outside the main season as well.

According to his words, the Croatian Government should soon adopt decisions on the extension of concessions for individual existing concessionaires who have the documentation ready. The process, he said, is being prepared in cooperation with the ministries of tourism and finance and the European Commission. At the Croatian Chamber of Economy they emphasise that for further investments it is necessary to ensure legal certainty and a competitive business framework.

Concessionaires say they are ready to continue investing in marinas and charter, while the sector is at the same time being pressed by rising operating costs and a shortage of quality labour. The Ministry of Tourism and Sport highlights the green and digital transition as important directions of development.

World.title: Zoran Milanović Harshly Criticises “Out of Control” Croatian Prices
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – President Zoran Milanović has harshly criticised “out of control” Croatian prices, saying that time flies and things are getting “worse and worse”.

President Zoran Milanović is participating in the Lider conference Day of Big Plans, which is being held at the Westin hotel in Zagreb. Index reports that the conference discusses the macroeconomic and economic challenges and circumstances coming in 2027. “Time flies, and things are getting worse and worse. Not only in Croatia, but everywhere around us, things are slowly slipping out of control. The UN and the international system of collective security are being mocked by their biggest financiers,” Milanović said at the beginning, reports N1.

“the international order has ceased to exist”

“The international order has ceased to exist. Every sanction – a bilateral sanction – anyone’s, without UN verification is illegal. On the surface, the numbers have all advanced, GDP per capita, often a very deceptive piece of data about prosperity behind which great inequality is often hidden. Purchasing power parity is such that the differences aren’t too great in relation to some countries that we once looked at with envy,” the president stated.

“Average salaries aren’t small… However, what can be bought with that money? Croatian prices have completely spun out of control, we can only hope that things will start to eventually calm down,” he said. The worst thing, the president says, is that no one specific can be blamed for that situation, neither the governor, nor the finance minister, nor the prime minister, but one has to look at the surrounding countries, much larger than Croatia.

on the topic of europe

“The European Union and Europe as a continent have been in regression for the last hundred years, with flashes of progress that occurred after the great wars into which Europe dragged the whole world. Europe is in a cycle of shrinking into itself. Nothing that comes from Berlin or some other European metropolis should be taken either too seriously or not seriously,” Milanović said.

“Europe has some very serious problems with energy that it hasn’t managed to solve for decades already, but the moment that is said out loud, you are immediately labelled extreme left, extreme right, pro this, pro that, but that is not the way we can talk and plan, that is not a conversation at all,” the Croatian president clearly states. We have to build a nuclear power plant, Milanović said, adding that when one country attacks another, the whole world gets a bill to pay.

on america and iran

The president also commented on the situation between the USA and Iran. “It’s a symptom of the disease of large systems and large empires when people no longer want to sacrifice themselves for that system,” he stated.

“The European Union is not democratic and when I say that, I don’t necessarily mean that that makes it bad in itself, on;y that it is not democratic – people are appointed to the highest and most important positions by processes that are not democratic, and more and more people see and feel that and that is why more and more of them vote the way they vote,” Milanović warned.

World.title: “Revolutionary” New Croatian Road Toll System is, Of Course, Delayed
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – The so-called “revolutionary” new Croatian road toll system is delayed, which comes as a surprise to absolutely nobody.

Croatian Motorways still haven’t selected who will create the application and everything else needed for the upcoming Croatian road toll system. Poslovni reports that the project is worth around €160 million and we’re yet to have any idea when it will finally start functioning. All drivers on Croatian motorways should be able to drive without stopping and messing around with tolls and ENC’s as of March, but this “revolutionary” move has, of course, stalled. An unexpected problem has appeared in the development of the application into which every driver would have to enter their data and card details, reports klikni.hr.

Because of an appeal lodged by a company among whose owners is also a firm registered at the Commercial Court in Bjelovar, with its seat in Zdenci, Croatian Motorways have hit a roadblock (no pun intended). Portals with cameras are already being installed on the motorways, but the web portal, mobile app and integration data buses – that is, the part of the system with which drivers will directly interact – is still far from realisation. To make the irony greater, that part of the work is estimated at “only” €330,000 excluding VAT.

appeals, delays and issues – a true croatian saga

Let us recall, at the end of May Croatian Motorways awarded that job to a consortium of bidders consisting of the Zagreb companies Bos Projekt and Infinum and the British AMR CyberSecurity. The Zagreb company Abysalto appealed against the decision, and the State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures back at the end of July partially accepted its claims and annulled the selection decision.

HAC now has to re-evaluate the bids. According to data from the court register, Abysalto has three members of the company: the firm King ICT, Stipo Matić and the firm Novčić više. Matić is, at the same time, the president of the supervisory board of Abysalto. Novčić više is registered in the register of the Commercial Court in Bjelovar, and its seat is in Zdenci, a municipality in the east of Virovitica-Podravina County that had a mere 1,453 inhabitants when the last census was carried out. In the list of activities of that company, IT is not mentioned. It is registered, among other things, for the production of pellets, biomass and biogas, forest management, energy distribution and waste transport.

The sole founder of the company from Zdenci is King ICT, and the director is Stipo Matić, which means that the same owner appears in Abysalto both directly and through the company registered in Bjelovar. The share capital of Abysalto was increased in the middle of last year from €7,000 to €5.3 million, and in the same period part of the assets of the company Omega software was also transferred to the company.

the clock is ticking and time is running out

Time for the new Croatian road toll system of toll collection is rapidly running out. The development of the software and application takes six months, and the company responsible for implementation would like to start testing as early as January. The situation is all the more complex because even after HAC reselects the contractor a new appeal is possible, and with it further delays in the realisation of this job.

Transport Minister Oleg Butković despite the standstill claims that the system will start on time. “We’re sticking to that deadline, everything is proceeding at its own pace,” Butković said rather vaguely. From Croatian Motorways they state that all activities are being carried out according to the legal deadline, but they do not deny that it is a complex project in which the appeal deadlines in public procurement procedures must also be respected.

World.title: As Many as 40% of Croatian Retirees at Risk of Poverty
World.content:
September the 24th, 2026 – Another horrendous statistic for the country as as many as 40% of Croatian retirees are formally at risk of falling into poverty.

Just over the border in neighbouring Slovenia, 27 percent of retirees over the age of 65 are at risk of poverty, and in Norway, just nine percent are in the same category, the report states. Poslovni reports the shameful statistic that around 40 percent of Croatian retirees over the age of 65 live at risk of poverty, according to recent Eurostat data. Only Latvia and Lithuania have a higher share, while the European Union average is 19 percent.

Melita Čičak, acting director of the Pension System Directorate, warned in an interview for Dnevnik Nova TV about the difference in the length of working service between Croatia and other countries.

“All of these countries that are ahead on this list have significantly longer service; for example, in Slovenia the average service is 38.9 years, while in Croatia it’s 32 years,” she said. According to the data presented, the average pension in Croatia has risen by 113 percent since 2016 and now amounts to €764. That is laughable given that the staggering rise in the cost of living is burdening everyone, particularly retirees, who allocate a large part of their income to their most basic needs.

“Inflation always hits retirees first. We know that they’re unfortunately a social category and that they spend the largest part on healthcare, utilities, on medicines,” said economist Petar Vušković. The report also warns about the rise in heating and fuel prices, which further pressures retirees. Speaking about people remaining for a longer time in the world of work, Čičak concluded: “We haven’t yet decided to raise the age for acquiring the right to a pension like other countries, but through other mechanisms we encourage longer remaining in the world of work.”

World.title: Tartu wants to buy 1,000 new rental bikes
World.content:
To ensure the long-term success of its bike-share system, Tartu wants to acquire 1,000 new electric bikes compatible with the existing system.

For more than seven years, the city of Tartu has operated its bike-share system with a fleet that now needs renewing to ensure the service can continue over the longer term. The latest procurement for new bikes failed this spring. The city government is now trying again. A tender could be announced later this month under which the city would purchase 1,000 new electric bikes over four years through a framework agreement, Tartu Deputy Mayor Priit Humal said.

"We want to use a single procurement to buy a larger number of bikes so that the quantity the city needs is clear to all potential bidders and gives them confidence to plan their operations and development accordingly. On the other hand, we also want to get a lower price for the city. Until now, bikes have been purchased in smaller quantities and, as a result, the price per bike has been too high," Humal explained.

The city hopes the tender will attract bids for bikes costing less than €2,000 each. The estimated value of the procurement is €1.6 million, Humal added.

"The exact price and decisions will come once we receive the bids in the public procurement."

If the procurement is successful, the first batch of at least 250 new electric bikes could arrive on Tartu's streets as early as next season, said Roman Meeksa, head of Tartu's city transport company.

"The most important thing for us is that the bikes fit into our existing system, both in terms of infrastructure, so they can dock at and charge in our docking stations and, of course, that they are compatible with our software," Meeksa said.

Compatibility with the existing infrastructure has also been one of the main concerns in the past, Humal said.

"Since the current docking system provider ceased operations several years ago, there aren't too many companies on the market offering bikes compatible with this docking system. We see that for suppliers to enter the tender, they have to make additional efforts and incur additional costs to make their bikes compatible with our docking system," the deputy mayor said.

Meeksa added that a market survey was conducted in preparation for the procurement. The survey confirmed that there are enough suppliers on the market capable of producing suitable bikes.

"The main purpose of the market survey was to see whether, in addition to the current suppliers capable of producing bikes for our system — a manufacturer in Tallinn and one in Portugal — there are others that could offer their bikes for our system, increase competition and also bring down the price. There is interest. Whether they actually submit bids is another matter and if they do, what price they offer remains to be seen, but interest has been shown," Meeksa said.

Last year, more than 13,000 people took at least one trip using the bike-share system, which currently has around 6,000 regular users.

World.title: Months later, Estonian Navy patrol vessel still out of service
World.content:
The Estonian Navy patrol vessel Raju has been out of service since spring and may remain so for another six months after repairs in dry dock failed to go as planned.

The EML Raju (P6732) has been in dry dock for repairs at Pärnu's ARC Repair after a stabilizer came loose last winter. The repair work, however, has not gone as planned.

"There was an incident in the dock where the ship's propellers were damaged," said Marek Mardo, strategic naval category manager at the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (ECDI).

The propellers have since been repaired, he added, but the vessel is still experiencing vibration and remains at the dock awaiting further repairs.

The Raju was built by Saaremaa-based Baltic Workboats (BWB) in 2017, and the possibility of sending it back to its original shipyard has been discussed. Mardo said this would require first thoroughly documenting the ship's current condition before it could be handed over.

The Navy declined to comment on camera, but acknowledged in a written statement to "Aktuaalne kaamera" that being down one patrol ship is affecting its operations.

The EML Raju (P6732), an Estonian Navy patrol vessel. Source: Estonian Navy

"The absence of a patrol ship affects the Navy's operations and its ability to carry out assigned duties," the statement read. "The resulting capability gap is being addressed by rearranging the activities of other vessels to the extent possible."

Another up to six months

ARC Repair also declined to comment, saying the ECDI had advised the company not to discuss the matter.

"If I had the right to, I'd be happy to talk," said ARC Repair board member Martin Kuusik, confirming the situation has been discussed. "But I looked into it a bit and they'll be commenting on it themselves."

At the ECDI, Mardo said the Raju's repair timeline depends on the nature and extent of the damage found, adding that there are likely several significant areas of damage involved.

"That will take time," he said. "If the propeller shafts are bent, they'll have to be repaired, and we don't know how long that will actually take. It'll be worse if we have to order entirely new ones — that could take up to six months."

World.title: Expert: Drop in Center Party support tied to shrinking backing among Russian‑speaking voters
World.content:
The decline in the Center Party's rating in surveys is connected to the decrease in their support among Russian‑speaking respondents, while the rise in the Reform Party's rating may be associated with their remaining at the center of media attention, says Emor research expert Aivar Voog.

"I think the most important changes concerned the Center Party and, on the other hand, also the Reform Party and the Social Democrats," Voog said while commenting on Emor's latest party popularity survey results on ERR's web program.

According to the survey, the Reform Party's support has risen to its highest level in the past 14 months, while the Center Party's support has fallen for four consecutive months. Voog also pointed out the Social Democratic Party's (SDE) rating, which usually drops again in the next survey after rising in one month, but this time has remained stable for several months.

Speaking about the Center Party's decline in support, Voog noted that in this survey the number of people without a preference had increased compared with previous surveys specifically among voters of other nationalities, which may be a sign of confusion among them.

"Perhaps with an active campaign they can again make themselves more understandable, but this may also be one reason why the Center Party has had a declining trend for four months among people of other nationalities," he reasoned.

If in June the Center Party's decline among other nationalities was compensated by a rise among Estonians, then since July the Center Party's support has had a negative trend in both national groups, with the decline larger in Tallinn and more stable in Ida‑Virumaa, Voog described.

"In Tallinn, the Center Party's lead over the Social Democrats has become extremely small. That is where the Center Party's decline has taken place. So perhaps the reasons can also be found in Tallinn — maybe they have not been as visible as the Reform Party, which has dominated media coverage," he said.

Jevgeni Ossinovski (SDE). Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Voog suggested that in Tallinn the Center Party may also have been affected by the fact that during the previous city government and the tenure of Social Democrat mayor Jevgeni Ossinovski, the city media was abolished, which had provided the Center Party with greater media coverage and visibility in Tallinn.

The decline in the Center Party's support among Russian‑speakers in Tallinn may also have been one reason why support for the Social Democrats has risen in the capital, Voog noted.

"Among Tallinn residents, nearly half of citizens — around 40 percent — are of other nationalities, so the Social Democrats' small rise in Tallinn may also have been due to that, because their support among people of other nationalities in Tallinn has also increased," he said.

Martin Herem Autor/allikas: Priit Mürk/ERR

Media exposure helped the Reform Party

Commenting on the significant rise in the Reform Party's support, Voog pointed out that the party's media coverage increased sharply.

"It wasn't only criticism — there were other events too: the departure of the former leader (Siim Kallas — ed.) and other emotional events. There were a lot of such events," he said. "For people, perhaps the most important was the artillery procurement, but in that case a compensatory move was offered by highlighting Martin Herem, who is trustworthy. He apparently offset some of the impact of the criticism. But the fact that the Reform Party dominates media coverage also means that others were more overshadowed," Voog explained.

The Emor research expert also noted that Herem, who became defense minister, is already included in the new popularity survey of government members, the results of which will be published next week, and he is there by far the minister with the strongest support.

"And perhaps also the fact that although they are a minority government, they have still managed to give the impression that they can function and make decisions. It is visible that among older people, aged 50+, their positive trend has recovered. Among young people, no — because among young people they have one major competitor, the Social Democrats, who are very strong among those under 35," Voog added.

In addition, the rise in the Reform Party's support may have been helped by the increase in consumer confidence during the summer months, and also by the fact that the fuel‑price rise associated with the Hormuz crisis had not yet reached people by the time of the survey, Voog noted.

The Emor expert also recalled that while the Reform Party, similarly to the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE), has a very determined supporter base, the Social Democrats and Isamaa have a much less stable one, which can more easily shift behind other parties.

In addition, the supporter bases of Isamaa and EKRE are relatively similar — according to Voog, like connected vessels: "If Isamaa were to fail or seem unstable, then part of that shift could occur."

Rainer Saks Autor/allikas: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Parempoolsed sit between two camps

Speaking about Parempoolsed, which have reached roughly 10 percent support, Voog pointed out that if Estonian parties can be conditionally divided into two clusters — one consisting of Isamaa, the Center Party and EKRE, and the other of Eesti 200, the Social Democrats and the Reform Party — then Parempoolsed are somewhere in between. "They have overlap with both the Reform Party and Isamaa, and to some extent also with the Social Democrats. They are not really on either side, which allows them to draw support from both," he noted.

In connection with this, the program also discussed the decision of one Parempoolsed member, security expert Rainer Saks, to become the next president's security adviser, which means the party loses one of its few well‑known faces.

"If you imagine a person in a specific election situation — they look at one list and another, one has a better reputation, the other a worse one, but the one with the worse reputation has more well‑known individuals," Voog described a possible election scenario.

Touching on the possibility that by the time of the Riigikogu elections on 7 March, the support of three or four parties may be quite equal, Voog said this would give reason to expect higher voter turnout. "In recent times turnout has always increased — perhaps also this time," he noted.

Voog also pointed out an interesting development where young Russian‑speaking respondents define themselves as Estonians, which makes presenting survey results based on nationality less accurate than before.
