World.title: Nepal's flood survivors still waiting to find out what comes next
World.content:
A month after catastrophic floods swept through Nepal's Nuwakot district, the town of Devighat still smells of death.

Excavators continue to claw through vast layers of grey mud that swallowed homes, businesses and roads. As the earth is turned over, the smell of decay rises again.

From above, entire sections of the town appear to have been erased.

Nepal rescue efforts head to the skies A desperate Australian family charters a helicopter to fly over the Nepal-Tibet disaster zone to search for missing loved ones.

The Trishuli River runs beside a landscape of sludge, broken concrete and twisted metal. Some homes remain standing but are buried through their lower floors. Others have disappeared altogether.

The August disaster began when a massive collapse of ice and rock in the Himalayas sent a torrent through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems, devastating communities on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border.

More than 1,400 people have been killed and more than 5,700 remain missing, including 34 Australians.

A town still buried

The streets of Devighat have been turned into a wasteland. Restoring the town will likely take years. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Maina Pariyar keeps returning to the patch of mud where her house once stood.

She lived there for more than 35 years and raised eight children. Now there is little to show that those decades of family life took place.

"I spent so much time, energy and money building my house … all our lifelong hard work is gone," Ms Pariyar said.

"We could not even find a spoon from our house."

Ms Pariyar walks slowly through what remains of the neighbourhood, pointing towards places that are no longer recognisable.

The flood stripped families of almost everything they owned. But for many, leaving permanently feels almost as difficult.

Despite the loss of her house, Maina Pariyar cannot bear leaving the place she has called home for 35 years. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Ms Pariyar now sleeps in a small tent in a relief camp about 10 minutes from her old home. Her few remaining possessions fit inside.

Days are structured around basic needs — collecting water, keeping the tent clean, lining up for meals and clearing grass around the shelters.

Ms Pariyar's children have asked her to move to Kathmandu. She has refused.

"This is the place where I was born. I don't want to leave my roots," she said.

"If I am nearby, at least I would be able to come and see my place."

Even the temporary camp brings little sense of security. Ms Pariyar worries about further rain and what would happen if the river rose again at night.

"If the flood comes during the day, I can still manage to run and save my life. But if it comes at night, how do we even run?" she said.

"There is no safety anywhere, and our lives are safe nowhere."

Relief is not recovery

For many survivors of the flood, these tents are the only home they have left. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Aid poured into the region the immediate aftermath of the disaster.

A Nepal Scout official working in the Bidur and Devighat area said teams had distributed supplies, recovered bodies, helped children return to school and travelled by road and helicopter to communities that were difficult to reach.

But a month later the surge is slowing.

"There were too many efforts then, but right now, it's slowing down," he said.

Food, clothes and basic supplies are still being delivered, but Nepal's finance minister has said the country would need $US4-5 billion to properly rebuild.

Aid workers help allocate donated supplies for those living in the disaster relief camp. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

The government is seeking $US20 million from the United Nation's loss and damage fund, which was created to provide financial assistance to developing countries impacted by climate change.

But what survivors increasingly want is an answer to a much bigger question: where are they supposed to live?

Parbat Sharma regularly returns to his family's damaged home.

Six ground-floor rooms were destroyed and thick debris remains inside the first floor. The area has since been declared a red zone, leaving him unsure whether repairing the property would be safe, or even permitted.

"If I spend money rebuilding my house here and the government does not allow me to stay, then who will bear that cost again?" Mr Sharma said.

"I think what we need right now is a decision from the Nepal government to tell us whether we can live here in the future or not."

Some localities have been so badly damaged by the disaster that residents question whether they can or should rebuild at all. (ABC News: Prabin Ranabhat )

He has spent weeks living between damaged buildings and temporary accommodation.

"Sometimes, I sleep on the floor, sometimes I'm just around," Mr Sharma said.

" At night, I wait for the morning. I hope nobody goes through this. "

Survivors in Devighat have spent a month without knowing what is coming next. Thousands of kilometres away, others are also living in uncertainty.

A different kind of waiting

Shylaja, Aarush, Ashwin and Chandrasekaran Muralitharan were part of a tour group before they went missing in the Nepal-Tibet flood. (Supplied)

At her parents' home in Sydney, Vaishnavi Kowshikan opens a laptop and zooms in on a map of the Nepal-Tibet border.

She points to the area where her sister Shylaja Muralitharan, her brother-in-law and their two sons were last believed to have been. All four remain missing.

The photographs from the days before the flood show a family on a mission: taking part in religious prayers, climbing through spectacular mountain landscapes and making their way along the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage.

Now those images are part of a painstaking effort to reconstruct where they went and what may have happened next.

"The fact it's been four weeks is something I can't myself come to terms with," Ms Kowshikan said.

"It's stagnant because nothing's changed. We're living in that same space that they're missing and there is no further information."

Ms Kowshikan regularly checks WhatsApp groups and Facebook posts, scans survivor lists and tries different combinations of her relatives' names in databases.

Sometimes she types only part of a surname, hoping a spelling difference might uncover something missed before. The result is always the same: "no rescue records found."

Some neighbourhoods were almost entirely washed away by the flood, leaving little apart from memories and a thick, muddy scar. (ABC News: Prabin Ranabhat )

Ms Koshikan is constantly worrying about whether the Nepali authorities have missed a spot her family could be in. She is especially concerned about her two nephews, 14-year-old Ashwin and 11-year-old Aarush.

"If there's some people who are there that are unconscious or unidentified or unable to speak up for themselves to say, 'This is who I am', has that been checked?" she said.

As the weeks have worn on the stream of information has become thinner while the family's need for certainty has grown.

In Devighat, survivors can at least return to the places where their homes once stood.

For Ms Kowshikan, the landscape exists largely through satellite images, maps, photographs and fragments of information.

Her parents are too distressed to speak publicly.

Despite incredible hardship, those left in Devighat still find time to talk, smile and plan for their future. (ABC News: Bhat Burhan)

Ms Kowshikan has been doing much of the searching and led the effort to keep her missing family visible.

"With not having [Shylaja] here, it's like one third of me is missing," she said.

"How do I navigate now until I can find her again?"

A month after the floods, it is a question thousands of families across the world are still trying to answer.

If you want to help support the thousands affected by the crisis, the ABC is supporting the Emergency Action Alliance member charities and their local partners. You can find more information here.

World.title: 'Ethical' hacker doubts Open AI will face charges over Medicare hack
World.content:
When Nik Cubrilovic saw the news of the OpenAI Medicare hack this week, he knew the tech giant was unlikely to suffer any legal consequences.

Not like the ones he faced.

Almost a decade earlier, Mr Cubrilovic was slapped with more than 50 charges — some carrying a possible jail time of up to a decade — related to computer crimes.

Not for hacking into the federal government's system storing health care data, but for unauthorised access to computer systems belonging to a company — car booking platform GoGet — that he claims he accessed as an "ethical hacker" and gave forewarning about.

An ethical hacker is someone who legally breaks into a computer system to find security flaws before nefarious hackers can exploit them.

While some experts and politicians have called for OpenAI to face legal consequences for its agent's hacking into the Medicare statistics portal, other experts and the government worry Australian computer hacking laws may not capture the conduct of OpenAI and its AI agents.

OpenAI hacked Medicare portal, Anthony Albanese says Anthony Albanese says he has spoken to the Open AI chief executive to express his concern about the incident and the length of time it took the tech company to inform the government of the breach.

OpenAI has acknowledged its models "took actions we did not intend", the company would review what happened, and was working with the affected organisations to address security vulnerabilities.

But the incident highlights novel questions about who is legally responsible for the conduct of an AI agent: is it the user or the company that trained it?

Is it some combination of the two, or even neither?

'All it takes is one executive to feel offended'

There was no ambiguity about who was responsible for Mr Cubrilovic's conduct.

Even still, he told the ABC, he was not initially sure which hacking attempt he was being arrested for.

"It was so funny when I got arrested. I had a knee in my back from a SWAT team member when I asked what this was for? They said, 'GoGet'," Mr Cubrilovic recalled.

After 18 months on bail, he pleaded guilty to some charges in exchange for the majority of them being dropped.

He avoided jail and instead was sentenced to a two-year good behaviour bond, 400 hours of community service, and ordered to pay about $1,600 in compensation.

'Self-confessed' hacker faces court over alleged theft of 33 GoGet rides A man accused of hacking car-sharing business GoGet more than 30 times last year is refused bail.

Mr Cubrilovic also had his laptops and phones incinerated by police, who claimed they could still have had user data on them.

His legal fees approached $100,000, he said, and he was not allowed to use the internet for the 18 months while on bail.

Mr Cubrilovic, who continues to work as a software engineer today, maintains that all the charges related to activity he undertook as an ethical hacker were to point out flaws in GoGet's system.

"I had a 15 to 20-year history of showing well-intentioned cybersecurity flaws that I had reported to 300 companies. But all it takes is one executive to feel offended and to direct the power of the state against you," he said.

Prior to the GoGet incident, he had discovered and disclosed major exploits in Facebook and MyGov.

The court heard Mr Cubrilovic had previously disclosed a number of vulnerabilities in GoGet's systems.

Police alleged, separate to those disclosures, that Mr Cubrilovic used his skills to access GoGet's customer database when his girlfriend's account was suspended and made dozens of bookings that he charged to other people's accounts.

Ultimately, charges relating to unauthorised access of customer data were dropped, and he pleaded guilty to charges relating to driving a car without permission and dishonestly obtaining financial advantage by deception.

GoGet did not respond to requests for comment by email or phone.

'They need to sort their s*** out'

Mr Cubrilovic cited international legal examples of people being "overcharged" for computer hacking incidents, like the case of American computer programmer Aaron Schwartz, who died by suicide while facing up to 50 years in prison for downloading a large number of academic papers illegally.

"There's a long history of prosecution against individuals but large companies like OpenAI have the resources to make sure that this doesn't happen," he said.

The prime minister says he voiced Australia's concern about the hack to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (pictured). (Reuters: Kim Kyung-Hoon)

Mr Cubrilovic said he was not frustrated that OpenAI would not face legal ramifications like he did.

"I don't think they should, but at the same time, they definitely need to sort their shit out," he said.

While a lot is not yet known about the details of the OpenAI Medicare incident, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the AI agent went beyond just visiting web pages by "writing" to a government server.

This distinction takes the AI agent's conduct from typical passive usage into what is often considered hacking, even though the government has repeatedly stressed that it was a "minor" incident.

Mr Albanese said there would "obviously be legal consequences", but senior ministers have subsequently said the government was considering legal frameworks and questioned whether "if that is possible to happen".

Other politicians such as Greens senators David Shoebridge and Sarah Hanson Young, ACT independent senator David Pocock, as well as experts like UNSW professor Toby Walsh have called for legal consequences, including criminal prosecution.

University of Sydney AI evaluation and governance expert Rebecca Johnson said she believed any human who did what OpenAI's agent did would face legal consequences.

"Any person who broke through to Medicare would be in trouble. A company that does that needs to be held responsible and accountable," she said.

Dr Johnson said one of the challenges now was ensuring that AI acts in accordance — or "aligned", in AI parlance — with our national rules and values.

OpenAI acknowledged its agent "took actions we did not intend". (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

As an AI user himself, Mr Cubrilovic said he was concerned about more people having access to its cyber-offensive capabilities, comparing it to nuclear proliferation.

He questioned whether it would be possible to prove OpenAI had the intent behind the AI agent's Medicare hack.

"I'm sure there was some high-fiving when they found out it happened, but I don't think that OpenAI or Anthropic want this to happen," he said.

Mr Cubrilovic said he still hunts for weaknesses to expose, like he always has. He always uses his real name, and he contacts the company.

But since the GoGet incident, he has changed some things.

"Now, I send them a nice note first," he said.

World.title: From The Beatles to psychedelia, discover how 1966 changed music forever
World.content:
When you think about the biggest albums of 1966, two records stand head and shoulders above the rest.

The Beatles' Revolver and The Beach Boys' Pet Sounds have tended to overshadow everything else released that year.

But the mythology surrounding the albums has also overshadowed the actual music on the records themselves.

So, let's dive into the sounds of 66 to get a better understanding for where music was at 60 years ago.

Oh, I almost forgot the obligatory historical context of 1966: Harold Holt was sworn in as prime minister in January (almost two years before his fateful swim), Australian currency went decimal, The Sound Of Music and Doctor Zhivago dominated the Oscars, England clinched its only FIFA World Cup, and St Kilda won its lone AFL/VFL grand final.

The big two of 1966

While there was much more to the music of 66 than just Revolver and Pet Sounds, you can't ignore these records. They literally changed music.

Revolver The Beatles Read more Read more In his detailed day-by-day breakdown titled The Complete Beatles Chronicle, Mark Lewisohn wrote: "In 1965 the Beatles' recordings had been progressing quite nicely, but here was a quantum jump into not merely tomorrow but sometime next week." He was writing about Revolver, but specifically Tomorrow Never Knows, the album's insanely adventurous closing track which, Lewisohn wrote, displayed "an unrivalled musical progression [and] The Beatles' willingness first to observe the boundaries and then smash right through them". Revolver was a pioneering example of using the recording studio as a musical instrument itself, and nowhere better exemplified this than Tomorrow Never Knows, a whirling hallucinogenic groove unlike anything ever heard before. The Beatles weren't always the first to use particular recording techniques attributed to them, but they typically popularised them by combining little-known studio tricks with the canny songwriting skills of Lennon, McCartney and Harrison. On Revolver they used such unheard-of or rarely used ideas as tape loops, artificial double tracking, backwards tracking, sampling, varispeed recording, plugging the bass directly into the mixing desk to record it, and the bold move of putting microphones as close as possible to the instruments and amplifiers (something that caused conniptions among the lab-coated technicians at Abbey Road Studios). All this made Revolver sound unlike any other record, but it meant nothing without the tunes to back it up. Taxman, Eleanor Rigby, Yellow Submarine, I'm Only Sleeping, Here, There & Everywhere, She Said She Said, Got To Get You Into My Life and Tomorrow Never Knows are all among the best songs The Beatles ever recorded (and that's not to mention Paperback Writer and Rain, which were recorded during the Revolver sessions but carved off for a standalone single). Revolver pointed the way towards so many new musical styles by incorporating psychedelia, Indian music, and sampling, and pushed the recording studio to new extremes. It also just so happens to be a collection of damn fine songs from a band that was quite rightfully the biggest on the planet 60 years ago. Pet Sounds The Beach Boys Read more Read more The story goes that The Beach Boys' Brian Wilson heard The Beatles' late 1965 record Rubber Soul and decided to top it with Pet Sounds. A work of unrivalled beauty in pop music at the time, Pet Sounds saw the band ditch their surf rock roots and beach party vibes for something deeply introspective and hymnal. Wilson worked closely with lyricist Tony Asher (and, occasionally, bandmate Mike Love) to compose a suite of songs that hinted at Wilson's increasingly fragile, questioning and insecure state of mind; That's Not Me, I Know There's An Answer, and I Just Wasn't Made For These Times are two key examples. Elsewhere the album is an ode to love. Wouldn't It Be Nice, You Still Believe In Me, Don't Talk (Put Your Head On My Shoulder), and Let's Go Away For A While are all paeans to devotion, affection and connection, illuminated by the beautiful melodies, harmonies and accompaniments that go with them. But perhaps best of all is God Only Knows, generally (and rightly) regarded as one of the greatest songs of all time. Like other songs on the record it combines typical rock and orchestra instrumentation, plus some unusual ones such as harpsichord, accordion and sleigh bells, all working in service of Carl Wilson's angelic vocal performance, and Brian Wilson and Asher's tender heartfelt lyrical ode to eternal undying love. Wilson would later use the term "teenage symphony to God" when describing his unsuccessful and unfinished follow-up Smile, but the words fit just as beautifully as a descriptor for Pet Sounds. Painstakingly crafted, the songs remain among the most harmonically and melodically rich of not just the 60s, but any era in music. While Pet Sounds sounds decidedly square compared to the likes of The Beatles, Dylan and The Rolling Stones, it set a benchmark for beautiful pop music and was an important step in its evolution. As Paul McCartney put it, "no-one is educated musically till they've heard that album".

Rockin' in the USA

The mid-60s were a strange time in music, particularly in America.

Jazz was still big, the crooners (Frank, Tony, Dean and co) still held some sway, and one of the biggest bands in America was Herb Alpert & The Tijuana Brass.

Meanwhile rock music was 10 years old, the invasion of British bands had started to peter out, folk music was still popular though morphing in new and strange ways, and everyone still wanted to be The Beatles three years on from their worldwide explosion.

Seriously, it's crazy how many albums from 1966 featured a Beatles cover.

But the end result in the US was a wild melting pot of sounds, perhaps best exemplified by these six albums.

Parsley, Sage, Rosemary & Thyme Simon & Garfunkel Read more Read more The folk duo of Paul Simon and Art Garfunkel had effectively broken up in mid-1965. But then a forgotten song on their 1964 debut album Wednesday Morning, 3AM became a belated surprise hit. The Sound Of Silence, with new added rock'n'roll overdubs, went to number one and became the title track of a thrown-together follow-up album released by the hastily reunited Simon & Garfunkel in January 1966 to capitalise on their new-found success. But it was the follow-up album Parsley, Sage, Rosemary & Thyme, released in October 1966, that really showed the breadth of the duo's talent and fittingly catapulted them to fame. From the haunting medieval beauty of Scarborough Fair/Canticle to the jazzy The 59th Street Bridge Song, from the pretty For Emily, Whenever I May Find Her to the sad longing of Homeward Bound, it's an album that packs a lot into its 29 minutes. If You Can Believe Your Eyes & Ears The Mamas & The Papas Read more Read more Just about every rock'n'roll trope can be found in the short but influential career of The Mamas & The Papas. Drugs, affairs, dodgy record deals, infighting, studio obsessing and sackings are all part of the folk-pop group's story. But more importantly, their first album helped shape the California sound and the following year's Summer of Love with its sunshine harmonies, jangly folk guitars, beat rhythms and teen-targeted lyrics about "somebody groovy" and hanging with the "in" crowd. The big singles are Summer of Love anthem California Dreamin' and the Grammy-winning Monday, Monday, both of which helped propel If You Can Believe… to number one in the US and top five on the NME and Melody Maker charts in the UK, but in between are decent Beatles homage Straight Shooter and the freewheeling Go Where You Gonna Go. Blonde On Blonde Bob Dylan Read more Read more By his seventh album, Dylan had well and truly gone electric. He'd also dispensed with his spokesman-for-a-generation mantle and was deep into building his own mythology. Blonde On Blonde is stacked with material that's kept Dylanologists busy for 60 years, as he paints incredible lyrical images and dips in and out of his own relationships from one song to the next. Featuring the much-acclaimed Visions Of Johanna, the aching Just Like A Woman, the high-as-a-kite Rainy Day Women #12 & 35, and the epic romance of Sad Eyed Lady Of The Lowlands, this hefty double album is one of Dylan's best, capping off an incredible trilogy of rock records after Bringing It All Back Home and Highway 61 Revisited. Buffalo Springfield Buffalo Springfield Read more Read more Buffalo Springfield's rise was rapid and fascinating. Within five days of meeting they were playing at a top Hollywood club. Within a few weeks they were the house band at Whisky A Go Go. Within a few months they had a record deal. Within six months they had released their first album. And within a couple of years they were no more. Neil Young and Stephen Stills would go on to even greater success, but their self-titled debut is a solid and influential effort featuring groovy rocker Sit Down I Think I Love You, the jangly Burned, and Young's early psychedelic gem Out Of My Mind. But the best track was recorded on the day the album came out and only added to the track listing months later when it became a hit single: For What It's Worth (aka Stop, Hey What's That Sound) became not only Buffalo Springfield's defining song, but a defining song of the 60s. The Monkees The Monkees Read more Read more Of all the bands trying to ape The Beatles, none did it as successfully as manufactured TV show band The Monkees. Its self-titled debut was the first of four consecutive US number-one albums released in just 13 months. While The Monkees had no creative control over their first two records and were largely forbidden from playing instruments, Mickey, Davy, Mike and Peter nonetheless became the biggest thing since John, Paul, George and Ringo. The only single off their self-titled debut is the iconic Last Train To Clarksville (easily among their greatest tracks), but there's also the similarly Beatlesy Saturday's Child, Let's Dance On, and Tomorrow's Gonna Be Another Day. However tracks like This Just Doesn't Seem To Be My Day and Sweet Young Thing are among the more interesting numbers here. Freak Out! The Mothers Of Invention Read more Read more Frank Zappa released 62 albums in his lifetime (and another 70 and counting since his death). But Freak Out! is the first and one of his most important, kicking off a career that was one of the most fascinating and vital in American music. Considered one of the first double albums and concept albums by a rock band, Freak Out! was a biting satire on American society and unlike anything else released at the time. A lot of the songs are spot-on parodies of the inane presentation of teen culture in pop music (Go Cry On Somebody Else's Shoulder, How Could I Be Such A Fool, and You Didn't Try To Call Me), while much of the rest of the album is an excoriating take-down of the United States. Check out songs such as Who Are The Brain Police?, Hungry Freaks, Daddy, and the blistering attack on America's systemic racism Trouble Every Day (key line: "I'm not black, but there's a whole lotta times I wish I could say I'm not white").

After the invasion

The Beatles had kicked open the door to the US for English acts, and every Tom, Mick and Eric was clambering to follow suit.

But the so-called British Invasion, which saw the US Billboard charts successfully infiltrated by UK bands, had started to wane by 1966.

Regardless, some fascinating sounds were continuing to emerge from the British Isles.

Some of the soon-to-be-biggest bands in the world were taking interesting steps in some intriguing directions.

Aftermath The Rolling Stones Read more Read more It's not the greatest Stones record, but Aftermath is an important step forward for the band nonetheless. It hasn't aged well. Some of the album's more misogynistic lyrics were bad enough in 1966, let alone 60 years later. But The Rolling Stones' fourth album was the first to feature nothing but Jagger-Richards compositions, and sees some musical experimentation yielding two of their best early tracks — Under My Thumb (sadly, one of the worst lyrical offenders) and Out Of Time — as well as the intriguing tale of suburban drug use Mother's Little Helper and the medieval Lady Jane. Aftermath is the sound of The Rolling Stones stretching out and occasionally finding gold, but is ultimately a stepping stone towards bigger and better things. Fresh Cream Cream Read more Read more The blues came back in a big way in the UK in the 60s, led by the new wave of rock'n'roll bands like The Rolling Stones and The Yardbirds, who tapped into their love of everyone from Muddy Waters to Robert Johnson. Eric Clapton had experience with the new blues-rock sound via The Yardbirds and a short stint with John Mayall's Blue Breakers, but took the idea to new levels by teaming with Jack Bruce and Ginger Baker to create Cream. Fresh Cream, the first of four albums in four years for the short-lived, volatile band, is as good an example of what they did: loud, rocking, jammy blues that's a cornerstone for fans of the genre. Small Faces Small Faces Read more Read more Outside their gorgeous 67 single Itchycoo Park, Small Faces' impact in the US was minimal. But to those in the know, their debut record is a fantastic album that provides a bridge between the Beatlesy rock'n'roll of the British Invasion bands and the harder/heavier rock sound that would follow in the UK in the late 60s and 70s. Led Zeppelin certainly owe a debt; Whole Lotta Love steals outright from You Need Loving, which was a Willy Dixon song Small Faces nicked via a Muddy Waters cover. But right from the opening chord of Shake, Small Faces brought distortion, pace, attitude and the powerful wail of Steve Marriott to the masses. Face To Face The Kinks Read more Read more The Kinks used their fourth album to change gears. One of the great UK bands of the 60s, Face To Face saw them go from being an awesome beat band to a songwriting powerhouse. Led by the immense songwriting talents of Ray Davies, the band turned out an incredible group of songs on Face To Face; character-driven pieces, sometimes satirical, that showcased British life, warts and all, and didn't just ape American musical trends and styles. Sunny Afternoon was the big hit on an album of great songs. The whole thing preceded such "Kinks klassics" as Dead End Street and Waterloo Sunset by mere months, kicking off a new golden era for a band already known for killer rock singles like You Really Got Me, All Day And All Of The Night, and Tired Of Waiting For You. Roger The Engineer The Yardbirds Read more Read more There are differing opinions on which line-up of The Yardbirds was the greatest. The blues rockers featured three of the greatest English guitarists of all time (Eric Clapton, Jeff Beck and Jimmy Page) at various points in their existence, and Roger The Engineer is considered the peak of Beck's time with the band. It was the band's third proper studio album, and many would argue it remains The Yardbirds' greatest non-live record. Amid the R&B rave-ups, there are basic bar-room boogies (The Nazz Are Blue), hypnotic exotic riffs (Over Under Sideways Down), and fun experiments (Hot House Of Omagararshid, Turn Into Earth), but the greatest moment has to be Jeff's Boogie, in which Beck pulls out every guitar trick in the book inside two and a half minutes. A Quick One The Who Read more Read more In 66, The Who were on their way to becoming one of the biggest bands in the world. Much like The Rolling Stones' Aftermath, The Who's A Quick One was a stepping stone. While it lacked a hit single to match the heights of My Generation or Substitute, it contained hints of things to come. The closing six-part suite — A Quick One, While He's Away — is a taste of the rock operas to come (such as Tommy and Quadrophenia). Album opener Run, Run, Run is a hard rocker before such things really existed, Boris The Spider and Cobwebs & Strange showed their diversity and kookiness, while So Sad About Us is a ripping piece of power pop that should've been a hit.

Soul music

Pop, rock, gospel, and rhythm and blues were shifting and swirling together in black communities in America to make something new in the 50s.

By the 60s, it had become soul music and was a juggernaut that dominated black music charts (euphemistically called the R&B charts) and seeped into the white music charts (the "pop" charts), such was its popularity.

Here are three of the big non-Motown soul records of 66 (we'll get to Motown in a minute).

Complete & Unbelievable: The Otis Redding Dictionary Of Soul Otis Redding Read more Read more Otis Redding crammed a lot of incredible music into a short but magical life. He released six studio albums before his untimely death in a plane crash, aged 26, including this collection, which was his fifth studio album. His signature song (Sittin' On) The Dock Of The Bay wouldn't be released until after his death, but Complete & Unbelievable boasts a handful of great Redding moments, including Try A Little Tenderness, Fa-Fa-Fa-Fa-Fa (Sad Song), and his wild cover of The Beatles' Day Tripper. Not only is the album a highlight of Redding's too-short career, but the arrangements and playing are top-shelf, provided by Stax house band Booker T & The MGs, as well as the famed Memphis Horns, and a young piano player by the name of Isaac Hayes. River Deep, Mountain High Ike & Tina Turner Read more Read more Tina Turner was an icon with a voice like no other. While Ike Turner's horrific treatment of Tina casts a sad shadow over their musical output together, nothing can take the shine off the title track of this soul classic (not even the participation of convicted killer Phil Spector). Turner's vocal performance on the opening track is one for the ages, as her voice goes from impassioned scream to beautiful sweetness and back again in a heartbeat. It's so incredible it overshadows the rest of the album. But don't sleep on the rest of River Deep, Mountain High like American labels and audiences did in 66. Tracks like I Idolize You and A Fool In Love are stone-cold soul groovers, while a gender-flipped Save The Last Dance For Me is also a highlight. The Exciting Wilson Pickett Wilson Pickett Read more Read more Wilson Pickett was a prodigiously voiced and gifted performer. This helped make him one of the biggest stars of 1966, which would end up being the peak of his career before a sad decline. Capitalising on the success of his previous record, Pickett's third album saw him re-team with some of the classic Stax house band players (who would become Booker T & The MGs) as well as the equally awesome players from Fame Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama. There are the obvious soul classics here — Pickett's renditions of Land Of 1,000 Dances and In The Midnight Hour are among the greatest songs of all time — but don't sleep on tracks like Something You Got, Ninety-Nine & One-Half, Danger Zone, and Mercy, Mercy.

Psychedelia

As the late great comedian Bill Hicks pointed out, "the musicians that made all that great music that's enhanced your lives throughout the years [were] real … high on drugs".

That's most evident in the emergence of psychedelic rock, strongly influenced by the use of LSD, which was banned in California and Nevada in mid-66, but already had a foothold in the arts, music and "counter-culture" communities.

Some historians point to The Beatles' album Rubber Soul (December 1965) and B side Rain (May 66) as precursors to psychedelic rock, and they were certainly among the musicians letting LSD ooze into their music.

While key Californian acid-soaked bands like The Grateful Dead and Jefferson Aeroplane weren't quite there in 1966, plenty of others were already turning on, tuning in and dropping out to make a groovy new sound.

Sunshine Superman Donovan Read more Read more Pinpointing the sound of psychedelic music can be hard (it's all about the vibe, man). But Scottish singer-songwriter Donovan was definitely an early proponent with his third album, which came out in August 66 in the US (and later, for legal reasons, in the UK). The album's mesmerising title track (sampled extensively for Imani Coppola's Legend Of A Cowgirl) referenced LSD and combined sounds new and old, making it one of the first truly psychedelic pop songs. Having a B side called The Trip certainly helped. The album melds folk, jazz and blues with sitar, bouzouki and bongos, with Donovan's lyrical eye and melodic ear making something truly new on tracks such as Three King Fishers, Ferris Wheel and the two-chord apocalyptic pop of Season Of The Witch. Psychedelic Lollipop Blues Magoos Read more Read more The debut album from this New York five-piece was at the cutting edge of psychedelia. A true forgotten gem, it was among the first records to use the P word in its title. The band broke up four years after Psychedelic Lollipop, which was their only record to crack the top 25 in the US. While the lyrics leave something to be desired, the musicality and harmonies are strong, and the record boasts some incredible moments: a startling cover of Tobacco Road, a trippy tape effect that sends Love Seems Doomed into another dimension, the Animals-esque Sometimes I Think About, and their garage rock hit single (We Ain't Got) Nothin' Yet. The Psychedelic Sounds Of … The 13th Floor Elevators Read more Read more The first truly psychedelic band, these madcap Texans took LSD and sure as hell sounded like it. Easily recognisable for the fluttering staccato electric jug playing of Tommy Hall, the Elevators peppered their songs with trippy lyrics, dark atmospheres and Roky Erickson's howling vocals. To call their debut album ahead of its time is an understatement. Hypnotically dreamy tracks like Rollercoaster and The Kingdom Of Heaven are the very definition of psychedelic, but killer tunes like You're Gonna Miss Me and Splash 1 were dark-horse hits dressed in tie-dyed shirts, hippy beads and rose-coloured glasses. Fifth Dimension The Byrds Read more Read more Few albums are more obvious stepping stones into psychedelic rock than this. The third album from Los Angeles folk-rockers The Byrds followed the departure of chief songwriter Gene Clark, which pushed the band in new directions. This included adding Indian influences ("raga rock") and psychedelic guitar solos (inspired by John Coltrane) to their jangly guitar sound and beautiful harmonies. Eight Miles High is the obvious psych highlight, but 5D (Fifth Dimension), What's Happening?, and I See You are equally LSD-tinged. The album's influence extends beyond the psychedelic. For example, I Come & Stand At Every Door sounds almost exactly like REM, just 20 years earlier, while their cover of Hey Joe hints at punk and garage rock. Psychedelic Moods The Deep Read more Read more Another of the first records to adopt the word "psychedelic" to describe their sound (some accounts say the first). However this one-off studio experiment is one of the albums that lives up to that adjective the most. The brainchild of New York musician Rusty Evans, Psychedelic Moods was recorded by a throw-together band in the space of a couple of days, with the musicians sleeping in the studio in between LSD-fuelled recording sessions. At least, that's what the legend says. How much of that is true is up for debate, as is whether or not the album was recorded as a joke or as a serious tribute to its subtitle of "A Mind-Expanding Phenomena". Either way, its heady tunes "actually capture the fuzzy off-balanced mind-bending experience", as one reviewer put it, blending wiry guitars and woozy rhythms with trippy lyrics and out-there sound effects.

Garage rock

Rock'n'roll, or beat music as it was sometimes called, began to diversify and evolve even before anyone coined the term rock'n'roll.

Blues-rock, country-rock, rockabilly, swamp rock — all of these subgenres were getting thrown around long before 66.

But it was only in hindsight that the term garage rock came about, as people tried to find a name for the dirtier rock sound of the mid-60s that would become a bridge to punk, metal, grunge, hardcore, post-punk and a bunch of other alt-rock subgenres.

1966 is littered with great singles and bands that were overlooked in their day. Indeed, without Lenny Kaye's compilation series Nuggets (1972 onwards), many would have been forgotten.

But here are some of the key acts that helped give rock'n'roll music a grittier sound and a tougher attitude.

Midnight Ride Paul Revere & The Raiders Read more Read more Little known outside the US, this Boise, Idaho band were a big deal. So big, in fact, that their fifth album, Midnight Ride, was one of just three US top-10 records the group released in 1966 alone. Best remembered for the pop hit Kicks and the killer tune I'm Not Your Stepping Stone (a later hit for The Monkees), this record is also important for its reputation as a seed of garage rock. Up-tempo tracks like There's Always Tomorrow and Ballad Of A Useless Man boast the slightly grittier sound of the subgenre, though it's I'm Not Your Stepping Stone that is the true signpost; the Sex Pistols cover released over a decade later shows where the band was pointing. Boom The Sonics Read more Read more The loudest of the garage rock bands, Seattle's The Sonics released just three albums with their original line-up before temporarily combusting, however they're the best examples of what garage rock was all about. While their 1965 debut Here Are The Sonics contains their best-known track (a cover of Richard Berry's Have Love Will Travel), the follow-up Boom has plenty of fast-paced fuzzed-out rockers that lay the groundwork for punk, such as Cinderella, He's Waitin', a fantastic cover of Louie Louie, and the killer closer Shot Down. They never sold many records, but The Sonics inspired everyone from The Stooges and The Hives to Nirvana and The White Stripes. The Seeds The Seeds Read more Read more Californian band The Seeds were led by Sky Saxon, the self-proclaimed "King of Garage Rock". Saxon's band put out two rock albums in 1966: their self-titled debut and follow-up A Web Of Sound, which not only paved the garage rock road but also pointed towards psychedelia. The former contains their two biggest hits, Can't Seem To Make You Mine and Pushin' Too Hard, and both feature Saxon's strangled vocals, which were surely a precursor to the punk howls of singers like Iggy Pop. The scuzzy riffs of Evil Hoodoo, the agonised howls of Girl I Want You and Try To Understand, and the anti-authority sentiments of Pushin' Too Hard make this a true garage rock touchstone and go some way towards backing up Saxon's claim to the garage rock throne. Black Monk Time The Monks Read more Read more Nailing down the "first" punk record is impossible, but a lot of people like to point to this album as a kind of birth of punk, and it's a compelling choice. The Monks were five US soldiers stationed in Germany who got monk tonsure haircuts and inadvertently invented a new genre on tracks like Monk Time, Shut Up, Higgle-Dy-Piggle-Dy, and I Hate You, accidentally influencing countless musicians who liked the idea of music being a ferocious, wild and weird parent repellent. The one and only album by The Monks combines fuzz bass, driving rhythms, bursts of noise, and an anti-establishment attitude (oh, and banjo!) to get closer to punk than any other garage rock band of the day. From Nowhere The Troggs Read more Read more "Wild thing, you make my heart sing…" It's the speak-sung, three-chord jam that sparked a thousand backyard bands, and if you're looking for a garage rock song to tag as the genesis of punk rock then this is as good as any. UK band The Troggs are still (sort of) touring to this day and released albums into the 90s, but their halcyon days lasted just 18 months, starting with their cover of Wild Thing in April 66 and ending with the sublime Love Is All Around in October 67. Their debut album From Nowhere opens with Wild Thing, also includes the under-rated With A Girl Like You, and reissues also excellent garage rock hits From Home, I Can't Control Myself, and their version of Louie Louie, the latter containing the dirtiest guitar sound of the era. Love Love Read more Read more Love was a band like no other. Led by the melodic magic of multi-instrumentalist Arthur Lee, the Los Angeles group released three incredible albums between March 66 and November 67 that touched on garage rock, psychedelic rock, jazz, folk-rock and symphonic pop. Their self-titled debut is their most garagey and it rocks hard; Lee's voice cracks and shreds on My Flash On You, their version of Hey Joe moves at breakneck speed, while Can't Explain is one of the great rock songs of the era. This line-up of Love would never be this proto-punk again. Follow-up album Da Capo is more psychedelic and the cult classic Forever Changes is a pop masterpiece that sounds like nothing else, but across all three albums they would leave a huge influence on bands across a wide range of genres.

The sound of Australia

Pop music in Australia in the 50s and 60s was largely content to copy the sounds of the UK and US.

As a result, the albums, songs and acts that endured in the cultural memory are the ones that had something truly special.

Here are three Aussie bands with big albums in 66 that we still talk about today.

It's 2 Easy The Easybeats Read more Read more Pitching the sound of the British Invasion back to Britain may have seemed a bit like selling sand at the beach, but that's what The Easybeats did, becoming Australia's first successful original rock band in the process. 1966 was a prolific year in which the band released two albums (It's 2 Easy and Volume 3) and two EPs (Easy As Can Be and Easyfever), relocated to England, and put out one of the greatest Aussie songs of all time, Friday On My Mind. While they were always more of a singles band than an album band (the book The 100 Best Australian Albums features the compilation The Best Of The Easybeats at number six rather than a studio album), It's 2 Easy is a fascinating document. It precedes Friday On My Mind, but the best tracks on it hint at the driving rhythms and attitude of that incredible single: Women, I Can See and Wedding Ring are great songs, though the album lacks a real killer hit. Spicks & Specks Bee Gees Read more Read more Born in the UK, the brothers Gibb spent eight and a half formative years in Australia, but it was the lack of success for Spicks & Specks, their second album, that sent them back to the UK. While the record didn't set the charts alight, it's filled with charm and the Gibb boys' tight three-part harmonies with highlights including How Many Birds, and the Beatlesy tracks Big Chance, I Don't Know Why I Bother With Myself, and Where Are You. And then there's the title track, one of the greatest Australian pop songs of all time, containing a stomping piano rhythm, two key changes, a beautiful trumpet outro, and the sadness of nostalgia in three powerful minutes. Come The Day The Seekers Read more Read more The Seekers' career arguably peaked about six months after the release of this album. That was when the Aussie quartet played to an unfathomably huge world-record crowd of 200,000 people at Melbourne's Sidney Myer Music Bowl. Come The Day took the band to heights no Australian band had ever reached. The Seekers had hit singles around the world prior, but this album (their fifth) was the first to crack the top 10 in Australia, the UK and the US. Capped off by sparkling single Georgy Girl (which leant its name to the US version of the album), Come The Day showcases the band's strengths, particularly on songs such as the title track, where the lush harmonies and folk-pop playing perfectly accompany Judith Durham's flawless vibrato.

Motown

In its early years, Motown Records operated out of a two-storey home in Detroit dubbed Hitsville USA, which was more than fitting; from 1961 to 1971, the label produced 110 Billboard top 10 hits.

Throughout the 60s and 70s, the label pumped out an insane run of world-changing music, and the genres of soul, pop, R&B and funk wouldn't be the same without Motown and its famed backing band, known fittingly as The Funk Brothers.

Here's a taste of just some of the remarkable music that emerged from the Detroit label in 1966.

The Supremes A' Go-Go The Supremes Read more Read more Between August 64 and November 72, The Supremes released an astonishing 25 albums. Amid that incredible run were 12 US number-one singles, most of which were the work of Mary Wilson, Diana Ross and Florence Ballard. While their other 66 album I Hear A Symphony is adventurous and interesting, especially the dazzling title track, A' Go-Go was led by two stellar singles: the top-10 hit Love Is Like An Itching In My Heart, and the Motown classic You Can't Hurry Love, which stands as one of greatest songs of all time. The rest of the record is a calculated collection of dancefloor-ready covers of chart-toppers previously done by the likes of The Four Tops, The Temptations, Martha & The Vandellas and more, helping make this the first Supremes album to hit the top of the US Billboard 200. Down To Earth Stevie Wonder Read more Read more This is 16-year-old Stevie Wonder's sixth album (and second of 1966). Down To Earth saw Wonder trying to establish himself as a serious musician rather than just an angelically voiced child prodigy. Much like its predecessor Up-Tight (the title track of that record is Wonder's first truly killer tune), Down To Earth is an eclectic mix of covers, ranging from Merle Travis's 16 Tons to Bob Dylan's Tambourine Man, and songs penned by Wonder, Henry Cosby and Sylvia Moy. But on tracks such as soulful swinger A Place In The Sun and dancefloor banger Be Cool Be Calm, you can hear a superstar starting to emerge. On Top Four Tops Read more Read more The Four Tops formed in 1953 as part of the vocal group boom, however the band didn't release its first album until 1965, three years after joining Motown. They quickly became hit machines who, along with label-mates The Supremes, took some choice material from the songwriting powerhouse of Holland-Dozier-Holland to the top of the charts. On Top, the third of five albums released in the space of just three years, isn't laden with hits — its biggest song is Shake Me, Wake Me (When It's Over) — but shows the band's sound growing, with its nod to the past (a Cole Porter cover) and to the present (a Beatles cover). Gettin' Ready The Temptations Read more Read more Gettin' Ready is the second of seven consecutive Billboard top-20 albums for The Temptations. The vocal group was one of the core hit-making vocal groups for Motown in the 60s. The two big hits on Gettin' Ready are Ain't Too Proud To Beg and Get Ready, both of which went to number one on the US R&B charts and remain soul classics. Still performing with 84-year-old founding member Otis Williams, The Temptations would develop their sound after this by adding tastes of psychedelia and funk, and continued to have hits even into the 90s. Watchout! Martha & The Vandellas Read more Read more The Supremes were on the rise in 1966, but Martha & The Vandellas were already on top. Watchout! is Martha & The Vandellas' fourth studio record, and while it doesn't contain anything as legendary as previous hits Dancin' In The Street or Nowhere To Run, it does boast two top-10 hits: I'm Ready For Love (which sounds an awful lot like The Supremes' You Can't Hurry Love) and Jimmy Mack. The latter would be their final top-10 hit and the band would start to fracture in the following years, just as the Motown label also began to hit tough times. But Watchout! marks the last great album from one of Motown's definitive acts. Moods Of Marvin Gaye Marvin Gaye Read more Read more Gaye had 10 top-50 singles on the Billboard charts prior to this, his seventh album, but none had cracked the top 100. Moods was his best effort to date but still fell short, peaking at 118. It was an attempt to present Gaye as a serious artist and not just a pop star. Armed with a strong line-up of songs from Motown's in-house songwriters (including Holland-Dozier-Holland), the album didn't achieve its aim, yet still produced another five top-50 singles including Ain't That Peculiar, Take This Heart Of Mine, and I'll Be Doggone.

And three more …

This article wouldn't be complete without these world-changing albums.

World.title: A week of warnings reveals Europe's dangerous new reality
World.content:
One after the other they lined up to speak: national leaders warning of increasing imminent danger to their countries.

World leaders spent this week bemoaning the big challenges facing the world in speeches to the United Nations General Assembly.

But the more extraordinary line up of warnings has been coming from Europe over the past week.

Last weekend, France, the Netherlands, Finland, Lithuania, and Switzerland all individually warned their citizens of increased threats from Russia.

French President Emmanuel Macron warned of Russian threats to European infrastructure. (Reuters/Mike Segar)

'No one is safe'

This followed Polish prime minister Donald Tusk, citing intelligence assessments, telling the Polish parliament last week that Russia could launch "hybrid drone and missile strikes" against Poland and other NATO countries supporting Ukraine, while portraying them as accidental.

Such attacks could form part of a Russian effort to test NATO's resolve, he said, and cast doubt on whether the alliance would invoke Article 5, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

"These possibilities have been discussed for some time, but the information is now highly consistent and, unfortunately, convincing," he added.

"I want to present the public with the most likely scenario for the next few months, because it is one that envisages serious events and requires focus, seriousness and the mental readiness to face difficult tests," he said.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, followed by calling the leaders of France's political parties — and 2027 presidential candidates — to an emergency briefing at the Elysee Palace to discuss Ukraine, Iran and the growing energy crisis.

He called Tusk's warnings "sound and well-documented" as he announced a new critical infrastructure protection plan.

Guillaume Lacroix, leader of the Radical Party of the Left, left the meeting saying: "At the age of 50, I have rarely felt such vertigo".

"No one is safe," Macron said.

The concern is that Russia may be planning to target critical infrastructure, as well as greater cyber interference, and drones over NATO airspace. (AP: Darko Vojinovic)

Then, on Thursday, the Danish government's defence intelligence service released an assessment that concluded that Russia would increase its threats to NATO nations, "with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past" of hybrid war and sabotage.

Underlying all these assessments of changing threats are not just warnings of greater cyber interference, or the occasional drone over NATO airspace.

The concern is that Russia may be planning to target critical infrastructure as it concentrates more on civilian targets in countries supporting Ukraine.

Several railway lines in the Netherlands and France have recently been sabotaged, for example, with at least one causing many injuries. There have been suspicious fires near explosive manufacturing plants.

Le Monde reported this week that ''more and more experts argue that it is time to abandon the term 'hybrid warfare' and simply call it war".

It is not that European leaders are worried about the threat of an imminent land invasion. It's more the spectre of finding themselves in the same situation as the Gulf countries that have been enduring months of Iranian missile and drone attacks on military and civilian targets as the stalemate between Iran and the US continues.

Germany's lame duck

The European warnings came as the far right, pro-Russian Alternative for Deutschland (AfD) party made more gains in state elections in Germany last weekend and the support for the centre right party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz collapsed.

Merz's leadership of the country was left on life support amid agonising over how he could be removed (apparently not as easy as it is in Australia).

German leader Merz clings on after election 'disaster' Chancellor Friedrich Merz vows to stay in power after announcing the centre-left Social Democrats wanted to remain in a coalition with his conservatives.

In the meantime, there is a sense of lame duck around German politics which is just what Europe doesn't need from its biggest economy just now.

The AfD is pushing for Germany to buy more oil and gas from Russia ahead of an expected cold winter — and generally become more friendly.

Given the German industrial base is undergoing its biggest transformations in a century — from car manufacturing to weapons and defence material — it's hardly surprising that some of its neighbours are watching developments with alarm.

However, it turns out that the AfD is not the only group wanting to buy Russian oil.

The Financial Times reported this week that the US government and Gulf power brokers with ties to the Trump family are backing a bid for the international assets of the Russian oil company Lukoil — put up for sale after it was hit with US sanctions last year.

It turns out that the AfD is not the only group wanting to buy Russian oil. (Reuters/Ramil Sitdikov)

Lukoil's international assets were originally due to be sold to the US private equity group Carlyle. But that deal "has stalled in Washington awaiting final US approval".

"Lukoil's overseas assets, valued at $US20 billion ($28 billion) when they were written off in March, include oil and gas fields from central Asia to Mexico, thousands of petrol stations and a large European refining portfolio," the Financial Times reported.

"The sale of the assets presents a rare opportunity to snap up more than 3 billion barrels of proven and probable reserves, as well as some of Bulgaria and Romania's biggest refineries."

The proposal "would put the US government in the unusual position of simultaneously bidding for the assets while another part of the administration decides their fate," the Financial Times noted with some understatement.

"The proposal raises the question of whether Carlyle would be disadvantaged if pitted against a consortium involving the US government and investors with ties to the administration, in a decision made by the White House. One person familiar with the process said: 'Yes, there is that concern'."

Loading

No action on Gaza at UN

The Trump family's business interests continue to plough on apace, it seems, even as President Donald Trump's power base seemed to be diminishing in inverse proportion to his boasts at the UN General Assembly.

"I have a big decision to make,″ Trump had told the UN on Tuesday.

To make a deal with Iran, or "annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again".

If only the threat was unique enough to be truly, truly shocking.

Yet few other world leaders gave it much credence. It was striking that in the addresses of others, the US/Israeli war on Iran seemed to feature relatively little in speeches, except perhaps from the Gulf states, with more (rhetorical) focus notably on Israel and its actions in Gaza and the West Bank.

Trump's speech seemed particularly directed at his ebbing political support in the US, ahead of mid-term elections.

If only Trump's threat during his UN speech to "annihilate" Iran was unique enough to be truly, truly shocking. (Reuters: Mike Segar)

He boasted he was "reasserting American power" and the country's "unmatched military might": boasts that sounded particularly hollow after a weekend in which he had been building up to join the attack on the Houthis in Yemen, only to pull out at the last moment, reportedly among concerns from military advisers about the perilous state of US weapons stocks.

Despite almost criminal overuse of the words "pomp, and pageantry and red carpet", the media coverage of the state visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping was all framed in terms of the Chinese leader's better tactical hand on AI and other issues.

Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was also using the platform of the UN to appeal to a domestic audience back home ahead of an imminent election, attacking the many detractors who had used the same podium this week to accuse Israel of genocide in Gaza.

For the second year in a row, he faced a walkout of delegates from more than 70 countries.

Loading...

"Shame on you," he declared to all those he said were spreading lies about Israel.

Earlier in the week, Macron had used notably similar language about the world's failure to act on Gaza, after a dozen countries — including France and Australia — last year used the same forum to formally recognise Palestine.

"What credibility do we have if we continue to remain inactive in the face of Gaza?" he said

"Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all? Never!"

Netanyahu attended the meeting despite an International Criminal Court warrant calling for his arrest, while the Trump administration denied a visa for Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas.

Despite leader after leader stepping forward to speak about Gaza this week, there was no more action from the UN on the issue.

Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

World.title: How inner-city stargazers navigate light pollution to capture night sky
World.content:
Densely populated and polluted with light, major cities like Brisbane may not be the most obvious places to see the stars.

But amateur astronomers and astrophotographers say there is still plenty to look at, especially with modern telescope technology.

Astrophotography involves taking photos of the night sky and celestial objects.

Sudath Wijeratne began the hobby five years ago, starting with a simple telescope and camera to snap pictures of the Moon.

Sudath Wijeratne began pursuing astrophotography about five years ago. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

He now has a small observatory on the roof of his Brisbane home and a telescope capable of taking award-winning pictures.

While Brisbane's light pollution can make things more challenging, Mr Wijeratne said it was not a barrier to getting into stargazing or astrophotography.

Mr Wijeratne started by taking photos of the Moon. (Supplied: Sudath Wijeratne)

" There are lots of things above our heads in the sky," he said. "The city doesn't discriminate; they are still there. "

"You start with the moon and your planets, they are the brightest things in the sky, then you have the stars.

"The Southern Cross constellation and sometimes meteor showers that we actually can see from the city without specialised equipment."

The Southern Pinwheel Galaxy is located approximately 15 million light-years from Earth. (Supplied: Sudath Wijeratne)

For his deep-sky photography, Mr Wijeratne uses long exposure techniques to capture nebulae and stars light-years away.

"[It shows] how small we are compared to the universe that's out there," Mr Wijeratne said.

" It's actually encouraged me to see we are part of a much bigger picture. "

The Rim Nebula, also known as the Firebird Nebula. (Supplied: Sudath Wijeratne)

Damian Fletcher is the president of the South East Queensland Astronomical Society. (Supplied: Damian Fletcher)

Damian Fletcher is the president of the South East Queensland Astronomical Society (SEQAS), which runs monthly telescope nights for the public.

He said people are often surprised by what is visible even from inner parts of Brisbane.

"One of my favourite things is when people look through [a telescope] for the first time, it doesn't matter if they're adults or kids, it's the gasp when they first look through and realise what they can see," Mr Fletcher said.

"We all see the beautiful photos from NASA and Hubble, but when you're actually seeing it for the first time, everyone goes 'I didn't realise I could see it like that with my own eyes.'"

The South East Queensland Astronomical Society runs monthly telescope nights for the public. (Supplied: Damian Fletcher)

Smart telescopes making astronomy easier

Mr Fletcher said more people were getting into astrophotography thanks to new technology like smart telescopes.

Unlike traditional telescopes, smart telescopes are an all-in-one system controlled by an app on a smartphone or tablet.

Users can tell the app to navigate to specific constellations or celestial bodies, and the telescope will take a series of short-exposure photos, stacking them together until the image displays clearly on the screen.

Smart telescopes can take photos of nebulae and gas clouds in deep space. (Supplied: Sudath Wijeratne )

Mr Fletcher said they are often much cheaper than a full telescope rig.

"People can plonk them out in their backyards or take them away camping and set them up and then capture all these photos on their tablets, not realising what's out there."

Dr Michael Cowley is an astrophysicist and senior lecturer at the Queensland University of Technology. (Supplied: Michael Cowley)

Astrophysicist and senior lecturer at the Queensland University of Technology, Dr Michael Cowley, said students were also testing out smart telescopes for research.

"Even in the cities, they can get some pretty decent imagery," Dr Cowley said.

" We've managed to pick up some very nice features that otherwise we wouldn't be able to see, such as nebulae. "

Stargazing on a budget

High-quality telescopes can cost tens of thousands of dollars, but Mr Wijeratne and Mr Fletcher said beginners do not have to invest much to give astronomy a go.

The Keyhole Nebula. (Supplied: Sudath Wijeratne)

"To start, you don't need any equipment," Mr Wijeratne said.

" You need a comfortable chair, get out and have a look. "

The State of Liberty Nebula is a star-forming region in the Carina arm of the Milky Way. (Supplied: Sudath Wijeratne)

"From there, if you want to go further, you have options now."

Mr Fletcher said going to free community events were a good place to start.

"Don't just go in and buy the first thing you think you're seeing, or read a review on or listen to some influencer who's just trying to flog a product," he said.

"Just come along, you don't need to spend any money, and you can have all the views in the world."
