World.title: Julia Morris on returning to 'school' with fresh ADHD diagnosis
World.content:
Talking about the past few decades of performing arts in Australia without Julia Morris's name coming up would be a challenge.

It was just over 40 years ago that she came to the fore as an energetic 17 year old on talent show New Faces, her rendition of Bonnie Tyler's "Holding Out For a Hero" imbued with an inimitable confidence.

It took another decade before Morris landed her breakout gig on 90s sketch comedy show Full Frontal, alongside the likes of Shaun Micallef, Kitty Flanagan and Eric Bana. But since then, Morris has toured her stand-up routines at every international comedy festival that counts. She's performed across the stage, in television and film, and been nominated for the Gold Logie Award no fewer than five times.

For the past 12 years, however, Morris has predominantly been associated with one thing: hosting the Australian iteration of competition reality series I'm A Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here — first alongside Dr Chris Brown, then Robert Irwin.

Loading Instagram content

Then in May, Channel 10 announced it wouldn't be commissioning a 13th season. And while Channel 7 later picked the show back up, no hosts were attached to the format.

That's how Morris came to face a question she hadn't had to ask herself in a long time: What next?

To start with, she's returning to school — in a way.

Morris leads as the principal in new TV game show Class Clowns, responsible for corralling her six "students" — really, comedians including Nina Oyama, Matt Okine and Becky Lucas — as they try to complete assignments in everything from maths to sex ed for points.

With heapings of innuendo and the sort of schoolyard banter real teenagers wish they were capable of, the series makes for the easy and frequently titillating viewing you'd expect of a comedy competition show, but the softness and vulnerability Morris extends to her pupils adds an unexpected and earnest depth to this series that could have easily stopped at being silly fun.

And yet, the role comes a little over a year after Morris announced she was diagnosed with ADHD. In doing the promo rounds for the show, the 58 year old has repeatedly said school was not "one of her special gifts".

So, we of course had to find out what made her want to go back, how she's handling all these big life changes — and where we can expect to see her next.

Stream Class Clowns on ABC iview Under the watchful eye of principal Julia Morris, six of Australia's favourite comedians go back to school to compete for the Class Clowns Cup.

Where did you go to school?

I went to St Joseph's Catholic College in East Gosford, NSW, and then Santa Sabina College in Strathfield, where I commuted to and from Gosford — it took an hour and a half on the train, where I busked with my flute.

I left at like 6:00am and returned around 6:00pm, so it was a big day for a student, but it's not like I was doing the schoolwork, so… [Laughs]

Did you actually busk on the train?

Yes! You've gotta busk on the train with your flute, right? It's the only way you can get the coins to buy musk sticks.

The children yearn for musk sticks. What's your fondest memory from Santa Sabina?

All the laughter. My focus was on being funny and liked and lightening moments.

I mean … I must have been so neurodiverse; I didn't realise how bad I was at school. [Laughs] I got 198 out of 500 when I did the HSC.

How do you think your teachers would have described you?

The teachers continuously described me as lovely, but disruptive.

I actually have all the physical copies of my reports, and the signs couldn't have been clearer, but unfortunately, we didn't know that's what it added up to then.

A lot's changed for Julia Morris since she was described as that "lovely but disruptive" school student. (Supplied: Julia Morris)

What was it like attending school in the 70s and 80s as a young woman with undiagnosed ADHD?

It was a lifetime of being in trouble for something I had absolutely no control of.

I just assumed there was something wrong with me, and I didn't know what to do about it.

There was no support. There were kind teachers, but not everybody understood the difference between inattentive and naughty. So, I was in trouble a lot at school — and at home — for what I now understand was my brain function.

Because I was likeable and funny, that's the gift that I worked on.

Was there an element of wanting to reclaim that time, returning to the school environment as Class Clowns principal?

I still had a great time at school — I loved it, I loved my friends. I just couldn't do the work.

"Who would have thought that I would be the grown up in charge?" quips Morris (pictured with her "students"). (Supplied: Julia Morris)

Maybe I wanted to show a capability.

Even before the decision with the jungle [I'm A Celebrity …], I was just desperate for Class Clowns to go to air and be seen in an entirely different light … It was fun to show a pared-down version of my output.

A lot of the time, if we're being interviewed, if we're on a television show, you're kind of on your own high-octane output, "must be funny".

I think people forget comedians aren't just one-note.

Loading...

Which comedian did you think would do the best going into the show, and why?

Bron Lewis, because she has such a strong existing relationship with the school system. But each of the comedians had to work in pairs they didn't choose, [which impacted their results].

Some of them excelled. But the other thing that happens when you get back into school uniform is you revert to your childhood self, maybe just with the added confidence of who you've become.

I got to watch how their minds really work and see a different side of them all after having known most of them their whole careers.

There was a gentle vulnerability … [and] a sense of discovery that I think a lot of them haven't had for a long time.

Bron Lewis and Luke McGregor were paired together to battle it out for points to win the Class Clowns Cup in the game show's inaugural series. (ABC/Warner Bros. International)

Did any school principals of note inspire your performance?

I thought I'd be like the principal in Picnic at Hanging Rock — I really thought I was gonna be much more stern. But that isn't the type of principal I was exposed to as a kid.

And once I got face-to-face with the students, I could see their vulnerability and I didn't want to just knife them for the joke. I found being a school principal akin to being a parent; I wanted to encourage them and get the best out of them.

What's the hardest thing about being in the public eye today as a woman working in the arts?

Days like today, I've had interviews since early so then I'm like, "OK, what am I getting in trouble for today? What is someone gonna take offence to that's gonna have a direct effect on whether I'm earning or not?"

As you get older, and as you get more brutally honest, it's not that you're admired for your honesty — you just look difficult. And you then get more scared, because it becomes easier and easier to lose everything.

So then it's like, what do you do? Do you not talk to anybody? I don't know what you do.

Despite having spent decades in the arts industry, and with five Gold Logie noms to her name, Morris (pictured at this year's Logie Awards) still doubts herself at times. (Getty Images: Hanna Lassen/TV WEEK)

Not a lot of people have to think of really big answers to questions they didn't know were coming and edit on the move while trying not to get into trouble, while trying not to release all of their true feelings, while being neurodiverse and trying to work out that new recipe. [Laughs]

And then you have to try not to take things personally when people are like, "You're s**t, you're dumb, you're this, you're that". It is exhausting.

When the jungle went away, I was like, "Would my services be better on a reception?"

The hardest thing today is not the same as what it used to be.

What's one thing that's changed for the better since you first entered the scene in the mid 80s?

Women are allowed to take up more space, so many women are in charge [now].

When I started, it was men saying, "Your t*ts look great in that top". Now it's people talking to me on the level of a human being.

On the one hand I'm glad to hear that, on the other … the bar is low.

The bar is so low … But look, it's very difficult to be angry with men when I've got men in my life like [fellow I'm A Celebrity … host] Robert Irwin.

"My god, if anyone ever says a cross word against him, I could go round their house and take 'em out," says Morris of Robert Irwin. (Getty Images: Don Arnold/WireImage)

He really is an example of someone actively out there being decent, speaking out where he can.

He gives me hope that there are more out there, they just need to show themselves a little bit louder than the other ones.

After it was announced Channel 10 was dropping I'm A Celebrity … you were quoted in an interview with TV Week as saying you plan to "Betty White this" …

Oh god yeah!

… So I'm wondering, what would be your dream career trajectory from here?

Everything.

The jungle remains one of the greatest things I've ever been a part of and I'm going to miss it desperately … [But it] took up a lot of the year where I simply had to say no to so many other projects.

In having the jungle removed from my path, albeit unexpectedly, what that's done is it's completely reignited my original hustle and delivered me to the Betty White phase [of my career].

The one thing we saw with her was she did many, many, many different projects, from movies to television appearances, to being a talking head pundit, to speaking at symposiums.

I love the idea of going back to showing all the talents I have.

I feel like I'm looking my best, mentally I feel like I'm in a pretty great place. So, it's time to have some fun.

Quotes lightly edited for clarity and brevity.

We've got a story for you. Stream Class Clowns on ABC iview or watch on Wednesdays from September 30 at 8:30pm on ABC TV.

World.title: Trump told Xi helping Iran is unacceptable, US ambassador says
World.content:
Amid the tea-drinking and pleasantries in Washington this week, Donald Trump made clear to Xi Jinping that China's support for Tehran was unacceptable, according to the US ambassador to China.

As the US president showed his Chinese counterpart around the National Archives in Washington on Friday, local time, Mr Trump said two leaders "did" discuss Iran during the state visit.

And when asked if he thought there would be progress on reopening the Straight of Hormuz, he replied: "I think we're going to do great."

President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump showed China's President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan the Constitution at the National Archives. (AP: Alex Brandon)

US Ambassador to China David Perdue told CNBC that Mr Trump made it clear during those talks that Chinese help for Iran was unacceptable.

"We made it very clear to them weeks ago that, you know, any help that they would give Iran, whether it be direct or indirect, whether it be intelligence or parts or military equipment, was totally unacceptable," Mr Perdue said during the interview.

" President Trump made that very clear again. "

Beijing has denied US allegations of helping Iran's leaders during the conflict.

Mr Trump said the summit between the leaders of the world's two largest economies had produced great strides, despite a lack of concrete results.

"I think our farmers are going to be happy", Mr Trump said, without providing more information about that.

Xi says leaders must act responsibly Donald Trump says the US and China have "never gotten along better" as China's President Xi Jinping joins him at a lavish White House state dinner.

Details of the limited agreements the two sides struck regarding their tense trade relationship would be released on Monday, local time, according to US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

"We've had progress, and we will release on Monday, I think, a lot more details about what we've accomplished over the past few weeks in negotiating with the Chinese," he told CNBC.

The US has agreed with China on exempting some key goods from arguments over trade, Mr Greer said, including exports to China of agricultural products and medical devices and imports of consumer and non-sensitive goods.

As the two leaders shared tea in the White House Red Room earlier in the day they heaped more praise on each other and the visit.

President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump attended a tea with China's President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan in the Red Room. (AP: Jacquelyn Martin)

"America is very happy about this visit, and I'm sure China is very happy also," Mr Trump said.

Mr Xi said the US-China relationship had developed into a constructive one of "strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity" and that the two leaders would have two more opportunities to meet this year, the APEC summit in China and a G20 summit in Miami.

AI must stay 'under human control', Xi tells Trump The three-day summit is likely to be more about spectacle than substance.

"I do welcome you, Mr President and the First Lady to visit China," Mr Xi also offered.

The three-day summit ended with a visit to the National Archives, where Mr Trump and Mr Xi appeared to review the US Declaration of Independence and the Constitution and the Bill of Rights.

China has not commented on the visit to the archives, but some analysts say Mr Xi may have been keen to see records relating to the US switch of recognition to communist China from Taiwan in 1979.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: ‘My job is just to exist’: The Palestinian reporter on surviving Gaza, media fatigue and starting fresh
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastLunch with ‘My job is just to exist’: The Palestinian reporter on surviving Gaza, media fatigue and starting fresh Maher Mughrabi September 26, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The last time I sat down to eat with Plestia Alaqad, we were interrupted by diners from three different tables in the restaurant asking if they could take selfies with her. This is not how Palestinian refugees are normally received. But then most Palestinian refugees don’t have millions of followers on Instagram. Palestinian author and journalist Plestia Alaqad at Beit Siti in Coburg. Chris Hopkins “I’m super-grateful for people’s love and support,” she tells me, “and I’m glad using my platform I was able to raise awareness about what’s happening in Palestine and show the world Gaza through my eyes. Yet sometimes I feel misunderstood. “I met one person who said something she thought was a compliment: ‘I only followed what’s happening in Gaza when you were there, once you made it out and were safe I stopped following the news’.



“I was there reporting about a real-time genocide happening to my people. I’m not an actress starring in a drama series that when they drop me from season two you stop watching.” Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israeli veterans’ visit attracts controversy as calls grow for investigation into Zomi Frankcom killing The 45 days of reporting to which Alaqad refers began after Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack on Israel in which about 1200 people were killed and 251 hostages taken. Her Gaza reporting ended with her family’s flight to Egypt and ultimately Melbourne in late 2023, and is documented in her book The Eyes of Gaza, published at a time when Gaza was front-page news around the world. How does it feel to know Gazans are still being killed while much of the media caravan has moved on? “We live in a trend-driven world, whether we like it or not,” she says. “Even people getting killed is a trend … I think it’s Israel’s tactic to make the genocide last long enough so people would feel desensitised. But media plays a role by choosing what they want to show.



“Unfortunately, a lot is happening in the world at the same time … something more extreme [than being killed] needs to happen to us for the world to keep their attention on Palestine.” (In September last year a United Nations Commission of Inquiry found Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel called the assessment “scandalous” and “fake”. The International Court of Justice is yet to rule on a case brought by South Africa that alleged Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.) Alaqad cites an incident during Israel’s 2014 bombardment of Gaza in which four children from the Bakr family were killed while playing on the beach. It wouldn’t be news in 2026, she says. It was witnessed by multiple international journalists, many of them staying at the nearby Deira Hotel to cover the conflict, including Pulitzer-winning New York Times photographer Tyler Hicks. (Israeli authorities declared it a “tragic accident” and found no one culpable.) In the current conflict, foreign media have been denied access to Gaza and the burden of bearing witness has fallen on Palestinian journalists like Alaqad, hundreds of whom have paid with their lives to bring the world images and reportage.



A London street art tribute to Plestia Alaqad. Alamy Stock Photo I ask her what she says to people who question whether those slain are really journalists – an issue that resurfaced in July when the international Committee to Protect Journalists revised a number of cases in its Gaza death toll – and when there is debate here about whether Gazan refugees like her family are adequately screened before entering Australia. “People see you as a journalist once your political views are aligned with theirs,” she says. “They’re not judging it based on whether he or she studied journalism.” Alaqad recalls being linked to Hamas without any evidence by the Jerusalem Post newspaper while she was reporting from Gaza, something she dismissed but which alarmed her family when the article circulated in Arabic. Such attempts to link journalists to the Islamist movement are feared by Gazans as a prelude to assassination by Israel’s military. When it comes to screening, travelling on a Palestinian Authority passport has taught Alaqad – as she put it in her book – that “the world is big, yet there’s no space for me in it”.



“The world is afraid of you as a refugee … but at the same time they’re not afraid of the genocide that creates refugees in the first place.” “Whenever I see privileged people on TikTok choosing to go somewhere new to start fresh, everyone online will be praising them … ‘you’re so adventurous girl, good job!’. But when a Palestinian is forcibly displaced and leaves their country for obvious safety reasons, that’s not seen as brave. “Why do we always have to prove to the world that we’re human enough, that I am a journalist enough?” she asks. We are not in danger of being interrupted by Plestia fans today. It is the last set breakfast of the winter for Rahaf Al Khatib, who has closed her café Beit Siti for a couple of months to relaunch with a spring menu and a community space. Though one passing family, seeing us eating inside, try the door and have to be politely let down.



The galayet bandoora, qudsiyeh and brined goat’s cheese and stuffed baby eggplants at Beit Siti. Chris Hopkins Who can blame them? Because my family are from Jerusalem, or al-Quds (“the holy”) in Arabic, I want to say that the qudsiyeh – hummus topped with stewed fava beans – is my favourite, but the galayet bandoora, a simple but luscious dish of sautéed tomatoes, is even better. The brined goat’s cheese and stuffed baby eggplants spark an animated conversation about sourcing and preparation between Plestia and Rahaf, two Palestinians down under. Alaqad has been back in Melbourne visiting family and is set to return to Beirut to resume her studies. She won the scholarship named after slain Palestinian journalist Shireen Abu Akleh to study at the American University of Beirut in 2024. Alaqad arrived in the city just 10 days before Israel began a major offensive on Lebanon. “When I went to schools and saw displaced families in tents, it helped me understand what had happened to the Palestinian people as well … I wasn’t just surviving [any more], I was processing what happened in Gaza while trying to understand what’s happening in Lebanon.” She sought out the displaced in Beirut’s southern suburbs and the country’s south. In one Instagram clip from the southern port of Sidon, Lebanese children show her what they took with them when forced to flee.



But her attitude to such interactions has shifted. “When I went to schools in Beirut, I posted saying that I don’t want to be there as a journalist because I don’t believe that journalism has the power to change the world any more, but I do believe that being kind to children specifically has the power to change the way they see the world.” In one encounter a girl asked if Alaqad could braid her hair. “I’m not the best hairdresser,” she laughs. “But kids were happy and that’s all that matters.” Many members of Alaqad’s family are still living in Gaza after multiple displacements. “Usually when you start a conversation with anyone you ask ‘how are you?’,” she says. “In Gaza, we don’t dare to ask this ... I let them lead the conversation. The other day my uncle joked that at this point [in the northern summer] we’re not afraid of bombs, we’re afraid of flies [carrying disease]. This dark comedy has become normal.”



She points out that in the confinement of Gaza, “having time to label your feelings is a privilege”, recalling a day she left the family home to find a place to “cry in peace”, but even on the roof of her uncle’s house – since destroyed by Israeli bombing – people were to be found cooking due to the lack of gas. “Do I have to throw myself off the roof to find privacy?” she wondered. Talking about return is never an idle matter for Palestinians, so I hesitate before raising it. “I know I will return … my concern is I will go back to a Gaza I don’t know,” Alaqad says. “I lived there my whole life, I walked in its streets endless times, yet when my friends who are still in Gaza post pictures, I don’t recognise the streets any more. Palestinians inspect the damage following an Israeli airstrike in al-Shati refugee camp in Gaza City on August 24. Bloomberg “That’s why I love the sea … it gives me a sense of direction, a sense of reassurance that home will be rebuilt … I lived in Tel al-Hawa, which is in ruins, but you can still see the sea.”



After the Lebanon war in the 1980s, many who called Beirut home went through similar emotions. When Alaqad told journalist Mehdi Hasan last year that she strangely felt a safety in Gaza she did not elsewhere, I was reminded of the Palestinian poet Mahmoud Darwish’s line that “our siege [in Beirut under Israeli bombardment] is an oasis in a perishing world”. “I don’t think about what my life will be like there,” Alaqad says. “I worry about what life is right now in Gaza. Will people be compensated? What about the hundreds of thousands who lost their jobs? “I believe in the power of education, but some universities have resumed online in a place where students don’t have internet or a laptop ... they don’t have food, shelter, water. “My cousin in grade 6 or 7 is going to school in a tent. There are three-year-olds in Gaza who think a tent is a normal home, as they never knew a home.” The university which Alaqad attended as an undergraduate, Eastern Mediterranean in Turkish-occupied Cyprus, is now offering a media scholarship to Gazan students in her name. I do a double take when she tells me she will soon be “launching my brand” with a line of diaries. But then The Eyes of Gaza began its life as her personal journal.



“The brand is called neýa, which means intention,” she says. “I always think of social media, doomscrolling, how we don’t have any original thoughts any more but are always looking at other people’s reviews and commentary. “Journalling is a place where there aren’t editors over your head telling you what you’re allowed to write, if this or that word is acceptable,” she says, rolling her eyes mischievously at the editor she’s eating with. “I hope neýa reminds people to slow down and write things, rather than typing.” I’m always amazed at the ability of Plestia, who has lived through so much loss and destruction, to put me on the spot like this and make me laugh. I also wonder how she can be a student and still have so many other projects. I ask if she knows the poet Maya Angelou, and she tells me Gazans study her work at school. I say she reminds me of And Still I Rise, in which Angelou writes: “Did you want to see me broken?/Bowed head and lowered eyes?/Shoulders falling down like teardrops/Weakened by my soulful cries?”



She is defiant about being active – and happy. But she is equally firm about where she doesn’t want to go. She interviews ordinary people and not political figures: “People try and reduce our cause to Hamas and the [Palestinian] Authority … we’re past that now.” Receipt for lunch with Plestia Alaqad at Beit Siti in Coburg. On the possibility of appearing on a panel with supporters of Israel, she is adamant: “I don’t put myself in a position where I have to debate whether I have the right to exist as a Palestinian or not. “We passed the point of dialogue the minute Israel started … burning people alive and bombing funerals. All of that can’t be happening back home while I’m sitting on a panel in a country where I have to produce all this documentation just to enter. “My job is just to exist, not to prove that I need to exist.”

LifestyleLife & relationshipsAgeing Opinion What do I do now that I’m retired? The question should be what don’t I do Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist September 26, 2026 — 5:30am

September 26, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As soon as you retire from your nine-to-five job, people say: “How do you fill your day?” Actually, it’s easy. Personally, I’m flat out. Let me add up the minutes. Between sleeping, waking, looking for my glasses and perfecting my bolognese, I’m flat out. Getty Images Walking up in the middle of the night and debating with yourself about whether you need to heave yourself out of bed to visit the loo: 20 minutes. Finally, inevitably, making the trip to the loo: 2 minutes.



Getting back to sleep: 50 minutes. Waking up in the morning, slightly exhausted: 1 minute. Putting on your socks: 2 minutes. Putting on your reading glasses: first, I’ve got to find them. Sitting down on a chair: 2 seconds.



Getting up again: 15 seconds. Doing the Friday crossword: 53 minutes. Complaining to your partner about “that bastard David Astle” and his diabolical crossword clues: 63 minutes. Conducting your daily exercise routine: 20 minutes. Having coffee and cake since you deserve a reward for having conducted your daily exercise routine: 90 minutes.



Admiring a flowering plant on your daily walk and realising, miraculously, you suddenly know its name: 5 minutes. Admiring a bird on your daily walk and realising, miraculously, you suddenly know its name: 5 minutes. That crafty bastard David Astle strikes again. Getty Images/iStockphoto Having the time and mental space to take up the $1 introductory offer for the TV streaming service: 10 minutes. Having the time and mental space to cancel the $1 introductory offer from a different streaming service, a moment before they were about to start charging the full rate: 10 minutes.



Laughing maniacally over this triumphant example of sticking it to The Man: 90 minutes. Becoming so obsessed with your family heritage that you do a DNA test, certain that you are probably a quarter Icelandic or Guatemalan or certainly a member of some sort of royal family: 40 minutes. Drowning your sorrows having discovered your genetic heritage involves nothing more exotic than both sides of some UK slum: 60 minutes. Checking the price of your second tranche Telstra shares in the eternal hope that one day they’ll come good: 1 minute. Drowning your sorrows having realised they’ll never come good: 60 minutes.



Having the time, finally, to join a campaign to save the koalas, or better-fund public education, or to support the use of “youse” as a genuinely useful contribution to the language (other passions are available): 16 hours. Dogs, grandchildren, friends, cooking, art or golf (pick one, or several, but preferably not golf): 16 hours. I may need to go back to nine-to-five employment just to free up spare time. Sitting in mute disbelief when viewing a gum tree, its branches reaching into the sky, thirsty and yearning, dark against the early evening sky: 20 minutes. Falling into a reverie about how you won life’s lottery by getting to live in Australia: 40 minutes.



Finding a way to improve the spaghetti bolognese meal you’ve made for 50 years, simply by adding a splash of Worcestershire sauce: 2 minutes. Wondering why you didn’t realise the power of Worcestershire sauce when you first made spaghetti Bolognaise 50 years ago: 2 minutes. Concluding that it’s good that some of life’s treats and revelations are left until later in life: 60 minutes. Calculating your daily savings after using your seniors Opal seniors card for a trip into town, followed by a visit to the supermarket and then a night out: 2 minutes. Laughing maniacally with delight that you are finally getting something from the government: 60 minutes.



Reverse parking your car: 10 minutes. Having a psychological breakdown about why you can no longer reverse park with ease, when you used to be able to do it blindfolded, wearing sunnies, and with one arm around an attractive friend: 2 minutes. Reading the classic book you’ve been meaning to read for the past 40 years: 10 minutes. Deciding to stop reading the classic book on account that it’s a bit boring: 30 seconds. Daydreaming about doing that driving trip around Australia: 40 minutes.

World.title: Three shots, a shopping trip and 14,000 hours of CCTV: The case against Beau Lamarre-Condon
World.content:
This is what the jury has seen and heard in the trial of the former police officer accused of murdering Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was a seemingly unremarkable scene. Shortly after 9am on Monday, February 19, 2024, a man dressed as an Uber Eats rider, motorcycle helmet on and paper bag in hand, appears on a street in Paddington in Sydney’s eastern suburbs. Within an hour, three gunshots will ring out in a terrace house nearby. The apparent delivery rider, captured in CCTV footage of the street, was the then-NSW police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon, a Supreme Court jury has heard. He was also the alleged gunman. The Crown alleges that Lamarre-Condon stood in his disguise on the street for about 20 minutes, “steeling himself for what he was about to do”. Shortly before 10am, it alleged, he used his police-issued Glock pistol to kill Sydney couple Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, in Baird’s share house, before cleaning the scene and disposing of their bodies in surfboard bags. Lamarre-Condon, 31, a former senior constable, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder. His criminal trial started in Sydney on Monday and is expected to run for up to 12 weeks.



The prosecution case is that Lamarre-Condon murdered Baird, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, after developing an “obsessive and jealous infatuation” with him that escalated when Baird ended their casual relationship in November 2023. Davies, a Qantas flight attendant, was Baird’s new boyfriend. The court heard the two men were “smitten”. “It was the real deal,” a friend told the court. The murder of Baird was premeditated, according to the opening address by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC. The accused’s preparatory steps allegedly included buying a surfboard bag two days before the killing to store his body. The prosecution alleged that the murder of Davies was not planned but that Lamarre-Condon shot him to eliminate a witness to his crime.



At 9.49am and 33 seconds, the prosecution said, the first gunshot was heard in CCTV footage from a neighbouring property, followed by another 4 seconds later. At 9.50am and 28 seconds, the third shot was heard. The defence does not dispute that the then-police officer was wearing the Uber Eats disguise, or that he was at the home when the men died from gunshot wounds. The defence case is that he went to Baird’s home to collect some of his belongings after the break-up, but he expected nobody would be home. He “disguised himself … so he could masquerade as a delivery person if anybody unexpectedly opened the door”, his barrister, John Stratton, SC, said in an opening address to the jury.



The Crown alleges that Lamarre-Condon shot Baird twice in the kitchen of the home, including an execution-style shot through the temple, and shot Davies through the door of the bedroom after he called Triple Zero. The defence case is that the then-police officer, still in disguise, was surprised by Baird once he entered the home after nobody answered his knock. The two men struggled, the defence says, and the accused’s gun went off twice, fatally wounding Baird. The gun was flung into the loungeroom. Lamarre-Condon picked up a mobile phone and started calling Triple Zero, the defence says. Davies was holding a knife and also grabbed the gun, according to the defence, and shot himself accidentally in a second struggle. The Crown case is that Lamarre-Condon engaged in a series of obsessive behaviours in the months before killing Baird, including using his position as a police officer to obtain footage of Baird on a date with another man in May 2023. CCTV of Jesse Baird on a date with another man from the Royal Hotel in Paddington on May 19, 2023.



The court has heard that Baird broke up with Lamarre-Condon for the first time in April 2023, and the accused was disappointed that he did not want a serious relationship. The two men resumed seeing each other briefly in late 2023 before Baird ended it permanently in November. Lamarre-Condon is charged with breaking into Baird’s home in August 2023, after the first break-up, and stealing Baird’s wallet and phone. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated break and enter. The defence case is that he used a key Baird had given him to enter the home. Baird reported the alleged break-in at the time and said he had woken shortly before midnight to a man standing over his bed. Investigating police took a photo of a bobby pin in the lock of Baird’s home, tendered in evidence in the trial. During the first week of evidence, the court heard from a series of witnesses about Lamarre-Condon’s posts on social media about Baird. One professional acquaintance testified that Lamarre-Condon told her he would post photos on Instagram that were not visible to Baird but could be seen by a select audience of potential romantic rivals.

World.title: ‘Sydney by the sea’: Inside the housing boom reshaping the NSW coast
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life ‘Sydney by the sea’: Inside the housing boom reshaping the NSW coast David Barwell September 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For decades, towering cranes and large-scale construction sites have been a symbol of Sydney’s housing boom. Now, that same building activity is spreading up and down the NSW coast, as Newcastle, Wollongong and the Central Coast record an unprecedented wave of high-density development driven by population growth, affordability pressures and NSW government planning reforms designed to boost density in areas previously restricted to low- and medium-rise housing. A concept image of the Newcastle Quay development – one of the largest projects planned across the three regions. NSW Department of Planning The scale of the development is increasingly prompting residents, councils and community groups to question whether infrastructure and essential services can keep pace – and whether coastal communities can absorb growth without losing the character that made them attractive in the first place. Across the three regions, the NSW government has set a target of almost 30,000 new homes by 2029 – 11,100 in Newcastle, 9400 on the Central Coast and 9200 in Wollongong – as part of its commitment to deliver 377,000 homes across the state.



But a Herald analysis of projects already moving through the planning system suggests the eventual number could be substantially higher. More than 16,000 apartments are now proposed through state-significant planning projects alone, including 6341 apartments across 24 developments in Newcastle, 6317 across 22 projects in Wollongong and 4233 across 18 developments on the Central Coast. A concept image of the Gosford Alive development. NSW Department of Planning The state’s transport-oriented development program is adding thousands extra, with more than 20,000 homes approved or under assessment around transport hubs and town centres. Some projects are on a scale more commonly associated with Sydney, including the proposed 1110-home Newcastle Quay redevelopment, a 1500-home development on Gipps Street in Wollongong, and the 39-storey Central Coast Quarter project in Gosford.



The transformation is already visible on the skyline, with crane index data by Rider Levett Bucknall showing 139 cranes were operating across Wollongong during the first quarter of this year, up from 83 a year earlier, while Newcastle recorded 125 cranes and the Central Coast had 44. UNSW City Futures professor Chris Pettit said factors contributing to the construction boom included housing demand driven by outward migration from Sydney. “Since COVID, many Sydneysiders have relocated to regional NSW, and that, combined with land being generally cheaper than Sydney, has made larger construction projects viable,” he said. Planning Minister Paul Scully said Newcastle, Wollongong and the Central Coast were “crucial centres for growth” as the government worked towards its housing targets.



“As someone who was born, raised and now represents Wollongong, it is a growing and dynamic city, but one that also faces the same housing challenges as other parts of NSW,” Scully said. NSW government forecasts show the pressure for more housing is unlikely to ease, with Wollongong’s population forecast to increase by 36,915 people to 270,460 by 2036, making it the state’s fastest-growing regional centre. Planning Minister Paul Scully said planning reforms were designed to address rising housing demand in regional NSW. Sam Mooy The Central Coast is forecast to gain 30,800 residents, taking its population to 393,544, while Newcastle’s population is projected to rise by 20,188 to 199,735. Illawarra buyer’s agent Josh Hynes, who assists Sydneysiders relocating to the region, said modern working arrangements and Sydney’s housing prices had accelerated demand.



“Over the last few years, hybrid work has become more common – if you only have to travel into the office two days a week, suddenly living outside Sydney becomes realistic,” Hynes said. “Instead of being stuck commuting for two hours from western Sydney to the CBD each day, people are realising commute times aren’t much different on the coast and that property is significantly cheaper.” A concept image of a five-tower development, ranging up to 21 storeys tall, at Toowoon Bay Road, Long Jetty. NSW Department of Planning But there are signs the demand driving the coastal boom is weakening the affordability advantage that brought people to the regions, as higher-income workers from Sydney place pressure on housing availability and rents. Domain data shows median house values reached $1.15 million in the Illawarra in the June quarter, up 16 per cent over the year; $1.06m on the Central Coast, up 6 per cent; and $1.04 million across Newcastle and Lake Macquarie, up 9.5 per cent. Units are also becoming more expensive, with median values of $730,000 on the Central Coast, $765,000 in the Illawarra and $758,000 in Newcastle and Lake Macquarie.



Chris Ferreira, head of planning at Urban Property Group, which is developing the Central Coast Quarter project in Gosford, argues affordability pressures strengthen the case for increasing supply. But concerns are mounting that growth is outpacing existing infrastructure and services. Wollongong is experiencing a surge of new high-rise apartments. Janie Barrett This month, about 150 members of Wollongong community campaign group Wrong for the Gong rallied in the CBD, calling for a halt to further high-rise approvals until additional government investment is delivered for roads, schools and hospitals. Leigh Forsyth, who attended the demonstration, said residents were concerned about the scale of change. “We have proposals as tall as 40 storeys, which is unprecedented for Wollongong, and over the next six or seven years there’ll be an extra 6500 people living in Wollongong, and already our infrastructure is not keeping pace.”



The pressure is already being felt at local schools. Wollongong resident Mark Johnston, a member of the P&C at Wollongong Public School, which his son attends, said the campus is already struggling, with 579 students against an official enrolment cap of 462. Mark Johnston picks up his son Owen from Wollongong Public School. Janie Barrett “It’s the oldest public school in Wollongong, it’s nearly at capacity in terms of using all the rooms, and has little land to expand any further,” Johnston said. “A lot of parents are concerned about how the school is going to have capacity to accommodate the extra intake when all these extra planned towers go up.” Healthcare has emerged as another pressure point, with the latest quarterly Bureau of Health Information data showing the Central Coast Local Health District recorded the lowest proportion of emergency department patients treated on time in NSW, at 49.8 per cent. The Illawarra and Hunter New England districts also trailed the state average, recording 66.7 per cent and 68.2 per cent respectively.



Earlier this year, Central Coast Local Health District chief executive Jude Constable warned in a submission to the NSW government that it “cannot be assumed” the local health system had capacity to absorb increased demand generated by large-scale development. Wollongong Lord Mayor Tania Brown said the boom has created a difficult balancing act for local councils caught between state housing targets and responding to community concerns about the scale of development. “Most of the larger developments are approved via the state-significant channel, where developers are asking for far more than what was allowed through our long-held planning controls,” Brown said. “That’s where we’re starting to get the pressure, because our community is concerned at too much height and density happening – you can already see it changing the look and feel of the city.” Central Coast Council director of environment and planning Luke Nicholls said greater investment in community infrastructure would be critical as the region’s population grows.



Transport was a particular priority, he said, with NSW Transport figures showing punctuality on the Central Coast and Newcastle rail line at 77.7 per cent last financial year, compared with 90.8 per cent across Sydney’s suburban rail network. Related Article Property prices Housing affordability craters to record low despite fall in prices Scully said investment was already accompanying development, and the government was spending $81 million a day across regional infrastructure, while introducing measures to speed up housing delivery. Business Hunter chief executive Bob Hawes welcomed the growth, saying construction was the Hunter’s third-largest contributor to gross domestic product, and new energy and defence projects were broadening the region’s job market. “It’s allowed more people to live and work here, particularly younger people who might have had to relocate to Sydney in the past,” Hawes said. “We’re a growing city, and that’s why the new housing is so critical.”



Pettit said the debate unfolding across the three regions was becoming increasingly common across NSW as the state continues to work towards meeting its ambitious housing targets. “It’s the challenge for all NSW: how do you accommodate the population growth without losing the qualities that make people want to live there?” The Morning Edition newsletter is our guide to the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. World.title: Australians may but cutting back on spending, but not on luxury cruises
World.content:
InspirationCruises Australians may but cutting back on spending, but not on luxury cruises Brian Johnston September 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Various surveys over the past year all concur on one thing: Australians would rather cut back on anything except travel. Travel Associates, a premium travel brand owned by Flight Centre, recorded a 57 per cent surge in luxury cruise spending in 2025 compared to the previous year. It says demand for upmarket cruise lines such as Explora Journeys, Regent Seven Seas and Scenic has increased significantly. Luxury hotel brands, such as Ritz-Carlton, are launching new ships. Demand for expedition cruises to pricey destinations such as the Arctic and Antarctic is also strong. Cruisers are spending more money in other ways too, with an uptick in world cruises, back-to-back cruises and longer itineraries. The cash is also being splashed on upgraded cabin categories.



The wider opening of wallets was once attributed to revenge spending following the COVID-19 pandemic, but clearly other forces are now at play. It seems we’re willing to pay for I-deserve-it treats, and more intimate and personalised cruise experiences. 



Do the maths though and you’ll see that a couple will have to cough up $334,280 for the whole journey. Related Article Sponsored

Luxury holidays Travel indulgences that are worth the money Yet that seems like an absolute bargain compared to a mere nine-night Mediterranean cruise on Regent Seven Seas’ new ship Seven Seas Prestige departing in June 2027, on which the top suite goes for $159,050. That’s a person, twin share. Luxury cruise lines are banking on passengers paying for add-ons, too. Anthology restaurant on Explora Journeys’ ships has menus starting from €200 ($334) a person including matching wines, although that’s chump change for those availing themselves of a new watch in the only Rolex stores at sea. Even so-called budget ships expect occasional big spenders. A 100-minute couple’s body massage treatment in Royal Caribbean’s Vitality Spa costs $US599 ($870), far more than the entire basic fare on some of its multi-day cruises.



And on Disney Cruise Line, bottles of 1947 Chateau Cheval Blanc wine from the prestigious Bordeaux estate are reputedly priced at $US25,000. EVERYONE ASKS What does a cruise director do? Cruise directors are one of the most senior crew members and the most visible – and audible, since they make most of the announcements on board. You’ll see them buzzing around ships organising all the onboard activities, from the simplest of trivia quizzes to theme parties, deck barbecues and evening Broadway-style shows. They’re in charge of overseeing everything that the hotel director doesn’t: all the activities, entertainments and shore-excursion scheduling.



Cruise directors are the forward face of the cruise line and need big personalities, endless smiles and great interpersonal skills. But they’re more than entertainers. They also have to deal with passengers, take responsibility for guest satisfaction and oversee the ship’s safety and security. They also have to be highly organised and efficient, act as brand ambassadors, manage the entertainment budget and drive shipboard revenue for those activities that involve add-on cost. They’re the emcee, the ringmaster and activities and entertainment manager. They do all that while working ridiculously long hours. Cruise directors may have some assistants but on small ships will be a one-man or one-woman band. Cruise directors can make or break the atmosphere on a cruise ship, especially on smaller ones where they will likely interact with every passenger.
