Luxury holidays Brian Johnston seemed destined to become a travel writer: he is an Irishman born in Nigeria and raised in Switzerland, who has lived in Britain and China and now calls Australia home.

World.title: Life inside the world’s most famous private school
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the September 26 edition of Good Weekend. See all stories .

Coming off the motorway out of Slough, Archie* marvelled at the miles and miles of playing fields whizzing past on the left. “I don’t think I’d ever seen that many pitches in my life,” he said. A sports-mad, nervous 13-year-old, he took in this expanse of emerald green that was to be his making over the next five years: a whirlwind of rugby, football, “field game” and “wall game” (more on which later). As he zoomed over Windsor Bridge, his new world unfurled before him: Chapel, the red brick wall and College. Eton College, to be precise. “I had a lot of adrenaline. My heart was going crazy. I was terrified,” says Archie, a recent Old Etonian (OE), now aged 23, of his first day at the world’s most hallowed private school. The Berkshire campus is, after all, a rarefied bubble of educational privilege, typified by its grown-up-looking boys in tailcoats. Founded in 1440 by King Henry VI, today it hosts 1345 boarding boys aged 13-18, for a fee of £21,891 ($41,200) per term, with three terms per academic year. Around 20 per cent of the pupils are on up to 100 per cent bursaries, and “probably about 40 per cent come from families for whom the word ‘school’ means Eton,” says insider Michael* – a current Eton parent and OE who knows the school inside and out. “But the mix is far wider and more international than ever it was.” When you’re not sixth generation (and maybe even when you are), nerves are par for the course. But first-generation Archie attests, on arrival, that he was thrown instantly into a game of football and came out muddy, tomato-red and buzzing. Prince George, 13, arrives on his first day at Eton with his parents Catherine, Princess of Wales, and Prince William. Getty Images And now, school’s back. Last month, 250 apprehensive first years began their scholastic careers. Among their number are illustrious names from many nations. But one in particular is historic: Prince George, heir to the British throne. He is following in the footsteps of his father, the Prince of Wales, and no fewer than 20 UK prime ministers. Aside from political beasts (Boris Johnson, David Cameron, Harold Macmillan), there have been literary greats such as George Orwell, tech giants, Olympic stars and grand aristocratic names. “The reason I think Prince George’s parents particularly liked Eton,” says Michael, “is that Prince William, when he was there, felt he could be very much himself. [Because of that] he made so many friends that have stayed with him. [For George, like William] there will be no special treatment: he’ll just be a normal boy.”



Indeed, being a well-connected scion or an heir – even to the throne – does not entitle you to popularity at Eton. In order to become a BNOC (big name on campus), you have to have something more than a rich or royal father. No one cares who your parents are, because almost everybody’s parents are someone. One has to earn their place at the top; and that is a question of character. Related Article Good Weekend From corporate high-flyer to Australia’s culinary queen: How Nagi created a multimillion-dollar empire “The BNOCs were never the people with a famous parent,” says Archie. “It would be people who established themselves as such. It’s the people who see themselves as the bigger characters.” Quite often, he explains, the best sportspeople were also incredible academically, which helped their reputation. Regardless, “Prince George will receive not just the finest education in the world, but possibly the broadest,” explains Tori Cadogan, editor of Tatler’s prestigious annual Schools Guide. “Of course, academics are excellent, with 78.2 per cent of A-levels achieving A-A* in 2025 resulting in 52 Oxbridge offers. But it’s the co-curricular, with their outstanding facilities that really sets Eton apart. “For the famously sporty Wales family, Prince George is in the perfect place,” Cadogan continues. After all, the Prince and Princess of Wales are known sports lovers, and as a primary school student George has been said to be just as keen, participating in triathlon, football, rugby and field hockey. “The fabulous new indoor sports centre, known as Coleman’s, has recently opened, featuring a six-court sports hall, eight squash courts, an athletic development suite, a climbing wall, and enhanced training and wellness facilities,” Cadogan adds. “This is along with the new Athens Centre, housing the incredible swimming pool and indoor basketball court.” Not to mention the 38 football and rugby pitches, 19 cricket pitches, 56 tennis courts, a nine-hole golf course and two-kilometre Olympic rowing lake at Dorney. It’s Disneyland for sportsmen. Prince William on his first day at Eton in 1995. Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images



What else awaits George and his peers on campus? First years move into F Block – which is not a singular block, but refers to groups of 10 new pupils spread out in each of the 25 boarding houses across campus – a day before their seniors return. Each house has a historic name (such as Godolphin, Villiers and Walpole), rendered somewhat useless by the fact they are referred to contemporaneously by the initials of their master. One of Eton’s many idiosyncrasies. Each house also has a dame, Eton’s version of a matron, usually the wife of the house master. She is – among many other things, I’m told – often the arbiter for the appropriateness of posters in dorm rooms. Football team or girls in tennis gear are usually OK. Nudity or vulgarity, not. On day one, students move into their rooms (Etonians are afforded the luxury of a single room to themselves from the start), where beds have custom long and skinny mattresses, and are welcomed by a tea party thrown by their housemaster and dame. “It’s the first time where people can eye each other up and see what the other nine are like,” says Michael. “You always get a very interesting mix of parents, some of whom know the place quite well, and some for whom it’s all new.” This has been the birthplace of many future power bromances – and surely where George will find his first tribe away from home. Prince Harry arrives at Eton, 1998. AP Day two begins with guided visits. Eton, like a village, sprawls over half a mile (800 metres), with lessons (“divs”) in buildings as far as 10 minutes apart. “Etonians tend to walk about 15 per cent faster than anyone else you’ll ever go on a walk with again,” says my insider. The youngsters will have to watch out, too: Judy’s Passage, which runs through the centre of the college, becomes an unruly ruckus between divs, as time is spare and the older boys “tend to throw their weight around”, says Archie. The young ones may have to duck and dive out of the way. George will soon become familiar with things like “Burning Bush” – the Victorian street lamp in Eton town where everyone meets up. The high street is “fabulously old-fashioned”, says Archie. Very important are the two tuck shops, Rowlands and Tudor Stores. “Rowlands sells chips, ice-creams, sweets and sandwiches. And Tudor Stores, on the edge of the high street, is considered to have the best ice-cream in the school,” says Michael.



The F-blockers will already be familiar with any one of its tailors (Tom Brown, Welsh & Jefferies, New & Lingwood, Billings & Edmonds), where they will have recently been measured for two sets of tails, waistcoats and trousers. “It’s very untouched, very old-school, but it’s not a Savile Row experience,” says Archie. “It’s like you walking into a dry cleaners, but every single thing on the shelf is tailcoats, because all the tailors also handle the cleaning. There’s no cigar lounge in the corner.” That evening, they will learn how to apply the stiff collars with studs, as taught by the dame. “It normally takes about three attempts to learn how to do it, then after that it becomes second nature, and you can do it in three seconds flat,” says Michael. Pupils at Eton College wearing the school uniform of tailcoats and starched collars. Getty Images By the third day, George and his contemporaries head to College, the oldest part of the school, where the Provost, Nicholas Coleridge (descendant of Samuel Taylor), ultra charming and ultra connected after decades in leadership at Condé Nast, gives a speech. I’m told last year he advised “finding two or three things that you particularly enjoy doing and doing them”. And goodness do they have choice: sports, theatre, painting, drawing, debating, student journalism, theology … There are some early trials, too – including a mandatory singing test for Eton’s three world-class choirs. “Some boys are very keen to get in and some are very un-keen to be chosen, so they sing badly on purpose,” chuckles Michael. And in classes, which start around day three for the youngsters, the masters (or “beaks”) treat pupils in a very adult way: “You feel like they’re talking to an equal even though they have, like, three PhDs,” says Archie. It is perhaps one of the reasons the OEs leave with such applicable confidence. Soon, the rhythm of the day will kick in. An alarm bell rings throughout the house every five minutes from 7.15am to 7.30am, by which time everyone must be at breakfast, which, on a normal day, is cereal, toast, eggs, beans and bacon, and on Sundays is a full-English-style fry-up. Breakfast is followed by Lower Chapel for the first two years, then they move into the famous big Eton Chapel. It’s a 10-minute morning service, with one hymn and a prayer: “Usually 19 out of 20 boys are sitting alert and to some extent listening, then the 20th has his head resting on a hymn book, and clearly half-asleep,” says the insider. But all agree, even for the non-religious, it is the tradition most missed on departure. Five 40-minute-long divs in the morning are split by Chambers (elevenses – “A morning snack of cheese on toast or a sausage roll,” says Archie. “Occasionally, we’d get a slice of square pizza”) and followed in the first two terms by two hours of intense sport. First years in their first term must choose either rugby or football, but as they get older, more choice opens up. There are two more divs before EW (extra work) and then dinner; for some, in house, and for others, in a communal canteen. “Everyone would pile in and suddenly the noise was a million decibels,” says Archie. ”Then it falls dead silent and the housemaster gives grace.”



A hearty meal has been well-earned by this point, which is why, according to one OE, scandal arose one Friday when a new chef decided to do “healthy” fish ‘n’ chips. “There was outrage,” says the OE. “We’re used to having a big battered cod, big chunky chips, mushy peas, just slopping on a plate. And then you come in and it’s this little pale, white, uncouth boiled cod and new potatoes … We started a food committee after that.” George might also find himself pulling into the illicit world of snack trading. As one insider told me: “A healthy supply of tuck equalled trading power. One student had a fake can of Heinz baked beans that the bottom came out of, and kept the keys in there for his tuck box. He’d exchange a bar of chocolate to make his bed; four slices of toast to take his tails to the cleaning rack.” Eton’s “Wall Game” is unique to the school and is played each year on St Andrew’s Day. Alamy And of course, Eton would not be Eton without its unique sports – wall game and field game, early iterations of rugby and football. “Some people think it’s a very good game, but it must be said it never caught on at any other schools,” says the Eton insider. Nevertheless, for those in a sporty house, winning the annual Ties championship in either sport is the pinnacle of success. For others, it will be top grades and others again learning the ability to debate like a great. “It is a very great privilege to attend such a physically beautiful school,” concludes Michael. “It’s got something slightly more sophisticated in the air, and that often rubs off on a number of the boys.” And, indeed, not one but now two future kings. * Names have been changed. This is an edited extract from The Telegraph, UK

World.title: Stop feeling guilty – there are benefits of doing absolutely nothing
World.content:
Each week, Good Weekend’s how-to column shares expert advice on how to navigate some of modern life’s big – and small – challenges. This week: How to be idle.

Photo: Illustration by Drew Aitken

The Oxford English Dictionary defines idleness, in part, as “the state of being unoccupied … inactivity, indolence” – as if these are bad things. If I’m overinterpreting here, I’m likely not alone. The Protestant work ethic, supercharged by capitalism, seems so ennobled in Western culture that to admit your life’s ambition is simply to loaf about with books and cups of tea sounds borderline seditious. So I’ll keep that to myself.

Regrettably, says psychologist Dr Tim Sharp, many of us tend to measure our self-worth by productivity to the point that when we do have time to relax, guilt or anxiety can ruin the moment. Sharp concedes that he has, to some extent, “helped propagate this culture of ‘optimisation’ through the self-help movement”.

Now, as “chief happiness officer” at Sydney-based The Happiness Institute, he’s encouraging us to embrace the benefits of putting our feet up: from lowering our cortisol (stress hormone) levels to allowing headspace for the blooming of new ideas. “We need to redefine idleness, or particularly rest, as a positive thing. We see rest as the opposite of productivity, but the reality is that rest makes productivity possible.”

World.title: My sincere apologies, but I’m one of those idiots who can’t park a car
World.content:
Q: If I park next to someone who’s parked badly and I also need to leave my car a bit crooked, it looks as though I’m the idiot once the offending car has driven off. Should I leave a note on my windscreen explaining it wasn’t my fault? T.J., Battery Point, TAS

Photo: Drew Aitken

A: This is the vehicular equivalent of using a toilet that’s been tainted by a previous user and when you walk out, someone’s waiting to go in – then you have to explain that it wasn’t you who made the mess, it was there when you arrived and you’re happy to provide DNA samples if they want to cross-check.

No one wants to be blamed for someone else’s offensive business, whether it’s a badly parked car or a badly cacked mark. And in the case of the car, I offer my sincerest apologies to you and the wider car-parking community because I’m one of those idiots responsible. I can’t park a car: I just can’t do it. If I reverse-park, I wind up with one wheel on the footpath, and one wheel on the foot of the person sitting at an outdoor cafe. If I park frontward, I wind up with a wheel on the kerb and my arse sticking out – my actual arse because I have to get out of the car to see where my hubcap rolled off to. If I park between lines, I wind up at a 30-degree angle, try to straighten up, try again, then drive home and catch public transport back to where I started.

World.title: Want to put a bounty on the head of a cyber criminal? Now you can
World.content:
A new international programme has put a $40,000 bounty on a group of hackers that attacked the health system in New Zealand last year.

It is the first bounty issued under Crime Stoppers International's scheme to help police crack down.

Glenn Maiden, who helped set it up, says the first target is a prolific group Inc Ransomware - if the criminals in it are prosecuted, the bounty can be paid to the informant.

"In the case of Inc Ransomware, they will get US$22,000 (NZ$37,000)," Maiden told RNZ.

"The bounty isn't limited to that US$22,000. So if you've got more or less than that you want to post a bounty, we'll absolutely look at it."

Inc Ransom has been hacking in Australasia and the Pacific, and last year raided data from a Wellington medical centre. The national cyber watchdog warned against the group.

Immediate warning

Hackers have grabbed worldwide attention this week by going after the FBI and after a break-in on Australian government agencies by an OpenAI swarm on its own volition.

The extortion group 'ShinyHunters' claimed to have breached the Federal Bureau of Investigation and stolen data on a huge number of its employees. ShinyHunters was named by Maiden as a group they wanted to go after.

In Australia advanced models broke out of OpenAI testbeds to get into health, justice and other government sites off their own bat, in what some researchers say is the first autonomous hack of government sites.

But OpenAI did not tell the government for weeks, and it is reported to be looking at legal options to punish OpenAI.

The NZ Government initially said only it was well aware of the issues of frontier or advanced AI and the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) was working on it.

Digitising Minister Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

When asked again by RNZ if he had considered what the Australia attack meant for New Zealand and if he would approach the big AI developers, Digitising Minister Paul Goldsmith said, "NCSC is in contact with its Australian counterparts about the Open AI incident.

"The NCSC is in contact with frontier AI companies and will be seeking assurance that any incidents affecting New Zealand government agencies are immediately reported to the affected agency and to the NCSC."

How bounties work

Maiden said the CyberCrime Bounty Programme could take the offer of a bounty from anyone - after some vetting - not necessarily a hacking victim but, say, from someone wanting to do a bit of good, as is the case with the Inc Ransom offer.

The programme then received anonymous tipoffs to identify the cyber criminals personally, and if they are prosecuted it paid out the tipster.

A company supporting it, Fortinet - Maiden is chief security officer for Fortinet Australia - pulled the tips together and assessed them before they go to police.

The scheme had echoes of FBI 'Most Wanted' posters but went further so that the likes of New Zealand organisations targeted by hackers had a means to support bounties to hit back, Maiden said.

"It raises some interesting questions for New Zealand," said Crime Stoppers.

"International ransomware groups can operate across borders and jurisdictions that local authorities cannot easily follow - will this kind of public-private model help close those gaps?"

Crime Stoppers International's chief security officer Glenn Maiden. Supplied / Crime Stoppers International

Prosecuting criminals in some countries might prove tough, said Maiden.

But it was already working with Europol and Interpol against non-cyber criminal groups in eastern Europe, so had experience.

"So it's not always a failure but it definitely is difficult."

As to the OpenAI Australia hack, RNZ asked the NCSC and Health NZ if they knew of similar incidents here. The NCSC did not say.

Goldsmith said the Government was already working with a number of partners and companies on the application of advanced AI tools, and was "actively strengthening our defences".

Health NZ said it was not aware of any instances of autonomous AI agents or AI companies gaining unauthorised access to Health NZ systems.

"Artificial intelligence is a rapidly evolving area, and we continually review our cyber security posture and defences to ensure they remain appropriate to the changing threat environment.

World.title: Country Life:150 years of Tinui School
World.content:
Back in 1876, children at Tinui School would make their way to school on horseback, now they ride in utes and SUVs.

Bright modern classrooms, walls adorned with children's artwork and education materials - all was on show on a sunny spring day when the school threw open its doors to welcome students past and present to celebrate 150 years.

Like the school itself, Tinui has changed a lot in that time, with a smaller school roll a reflection of changing land use.

Audio player for " 150 years of Tinui School " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/country/1583272%2Fcountry-life-150-years-of-tinui-school

150 years of Tinui School Country Life Download MP3 21m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

European settler farmers began moving into Tinui in the 1850s, and by the 1870s the village was established, and the first school was founded in 1876 - a combination master's residence and boarding school.

Attendance back then was spotty, local historian Caryl Forrest told Country Life.

"There was still a problem that went on for a very long time with children being [absent] when they did a big muster prior to shearing and during shearing. Boys of about 11 and 12 were expected to be on the farm helping.

"Farming was very labour intensive. They had really, really big paddocks compared with today."

Close to 200 people attended the weekend's celebrations, with multiple activities held over the three days - from class pictures across the decades, to drinks, dinners and of course a Sunday church service. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Former students gathered for the reunion and to have their class picture taken. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

That changed with the establishment of the rehab farms after the war, when the government purchased blocks of land from larger stations to offer to returned servicemen, whose names were drawn from a ballot.

Ian Perry's father was one of those who further developed the district, breaking in a new farm named Orere.

"My father was a rehab farmer here, and our family's been here ever since.

"These people put in the paddocks, broke them up. These people were going onto farms without houses, probably two or three paddocks, no stock, so it was a huge challenge."

Ian Perry's father was one of the returned servicemen who helped develop the surrounding farmland. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

At the end of the weekend a plaque was being unveiled to commemorate these early families, listing the 20 original rehab farmers, their wives, the farm names and locations, and where the men served.

"They contributed significantly to the social and the economic fabric of this district," Perry said.

A former pupil himself, he said the school had long been the heart of the community.

"That's changed significantly over the past probably 20 or 30 years with what's happened in agriculture, but the school still remains a buoyant part of the community.

"So we're celebrating 150 years and it's fantastic to have everybody here together and enjoy each other's company and reminisce about a lot of the times gone by."

Reverend Steve Thomson of Tinui's appropriately named, Church of the Good Shepherd. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Reverend Steve Thomson also noted the changes in the community.

He first came to the area in 1977, working the land his wife's family had farmed for generations, and later working closely with the neighbours through the Rural Support Trust and, as the Reverend at Tinui's appropriately named, Church of the Good Shepherd.

He told Country Life it had been an "amazing place" to bring up his children who all attended Tinui School.

"I've seen the pine trees move into the area and basically destroy the school. [It's] all planting now and nowhere near the farms around now that there was 30 or 40 years ago."

His own farm was sold into pine trees so he understands the tension well.

"I just think that communities like this are the backbone of this country. I think that's what we need more of today, is communities like this.

"Unfortunately they're getting smaller, but just look at all the people around here, they come from all around the world, the people that have come back today and all of them have got good jobs and it's just very special."

At 93, Phyllis French, née Cameron, is perhaps the oldest former student present. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The Tinui Hall featured photos and histories from past pupils. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Close to 200 people attended the weekend's celebrations, with multiple activities held over the three days - from class pictures across the decades, to drinks, dinners and, of course, a Sunday church service.

It's clear the school, and its community, mean as much to those who've lived there for generations as well as newcomers to the district, like former teacher and principal Duncan Smith who was at the school in the late 1980s.

Students flocked around him to look over his collection of photos and handwritten lesson plans from his teaching days, breaking into song when they saw the familiar words.

"We loved it," he said of his family's experience in the small farming community.

"We were brought into it for them to chuckle at our naivety, but we learnt the skills and did the processes and felt as if we were farmers."

Former teacher and principal Duncan Smith. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Now retired as an artist in Whanganui, Smith said he did some of his best work in the quiet hours of the night before teaching.

He said it had taught him how special country schools were.

"This seems to have been one of the few country schools that has three roads going off it and as the other country schools closed, then it's probably become a little bit special but I think that so much has changed in rural character that we were in a prime time."

Jenny Balfour who helped organise the weekend's festivities is another import - from Auckland no less.

The school was refurbished after being badly damaged during Cyclone Gabrielle. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Walls covered in children's artwork, it's a far cry from the half a metre high silt left behind which filled the classrooms. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

However, her roots run deep as her husband attended the now closed Mangapakeha School nearby and she worked at Tinui School's office from 2000 to 2015, including helping organise its 125th celebrations.

She said it was a great place to live and it had been special seeing so many people come back to celebrate.

"[I'm] really, really thrilled that we've had so many people and to just watch everybody talking and chatting and reminiscing and all those things, it's just amazing.

"When I was here there were about 70 children and now we only have about 20 and the impact of forestry, and a lot of the houses have gone to other people who do not have children.

"It really saddens me because it was such a thriving [community]... we are still thriving and we've got a lovely new principal who's doing her best here."

That principal is Amanda Aitken, who told Country Life she had big visions for the school.

Post-cyclone, the then 40 or so students continued to learn in makeshift classrooms in the hall up the road, before moving back into the refurbished classrooms.

"I mean, a lot of schools you're going to, they're quite outdated and behind the times, but we're really lucky.

"Everything's sort of new and modern and they don't go without here, that's for sure," Aitken said, finding the silver lining in the flood experience.

"We're very lucky to have such a nice school, especially out in these rural schools. Often they get a bit forgotten about."

Current Tinui School principal Amanda Aitken at the school bell. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

She's taught in a few schools and knows they're something special.

One of the big advantages is the lower teacher-to-student ratio. Another, she said, was the intergenerational connections between the families.

"One of the really cool things here is, you know, that's the relationships you get with these sorts of schools. Everybody knows everyone - we know the nanas, the grans, they all come in for reading."

Her hopes for the future?

"These little rural schools tend to disappear, but I don't think we'll go anywhere. I'd love to hope you'll see me in one of those photos in 150 years, and they'll be, 'oh, that was her 150 years ago'.

"I'd love to hope that it's still a cool, thriving little rural school, because they're something different, country kids."

World.title: Teen in government's bootcamp charged over two armed robberies
World.content:
A teenager taking part in the government's bootcamp for young offenders has been charged over two-armed robberies while he was on the community part of the voluntary programme, RNZ can reveal.

A rangatahi (young person) who was in the community phase of the second Military Style Academy (MSA) pilot was arrested following two-armed robberies earlier this month, and faces new charges of aggravated robbery with an offensive weapon, as well as unlawfully taking a motor vehicle.

A community provider connected to the programme says it should be emphasised these kids are "persistent offenders".

"These are the ones that everything's been offered to them in the community ... and then they continue to offend and seriously offend."

It comes after the government's bootcamp legislation passed its final legislative hurdle in Parliament, and after the Minister confirmed in August that two other participants had already left voluntarily during the in-residence phase.

The second intake of 10 youths at the military style academy began in March with the transition from residential into the community phase taking place in July, as part of a second pilot that took place ahead of the legislation being passed.

The third reading for the Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill took place last week, with Minister in charge Karen Chhour saying the legislation would "help create less victims and make our communities safer".

Karen Chhour RNZ/Marika Khabazi

The legislation gives the Youth Court the power to sentence serious young offenders to bootcamps. The pilot programmes had been voluntary.

RNZ approached the police about two separate robberies, one in Rotorua and one in Waitara, about a week apart.

A statement from Police confirmed they'd been called to an incident in Rotorua where a group of masked offenders entered a store armed with weapons, smashed display cabinets and stole items before leaving the area in two stolen vehicles. There were no reports of injuries.

Another statement from police confirmed three people were arrested in Waitara after a report of assault and robbery nearly a week later. A pursuit commenced before being abandoned, with three people later taken into custody.

"Two were charged with aggravated robbery with an offensive weapon and unlawfully taking a motor vehicle.

"They will go through a youth justice process. Enquiries are ongoing," police said.

Asked by RNZ about the charges Oranga Tamariki (OT) deputy chief executive Dean Winter said given there was a police investigation underway with matters before the youth court, "we are unable to comment on this matter."

Minister for Children Karen Chhour was also asked, but a spokesperson for the minister said it would be inappropriate to respond in this instance as "all offending is alleged until found otherwise by a court".

But Labour's spokesperson for children Willow-Jean Prime told RNZ "enough is enough".

Prime said the majority of participants went on to reoffend in the pilot, and now in the second iteration of the programme, there was more offending and participants voluntarily leaving.

"The re-offending rate for National's boot camps is about the same as the rest of the youth justice system. It's a wasteful political experiment and takes us back down a path of harm.

"This is what Christopher Luxon has made Kiwis pay tens of millions for by turning this chaos into law just last week."

Labour has promised to scrap the bootcamps if elected and invest in "evidence-based and trauma-informed wraparound approaches that are proven to work for young people".

Willow-Jean Prime. VNP / Phil Smith

Community provider

The head of a community organisation that has been involved in the MSA spoke to RNZ, on condition of anonymity.

He was frustrated with the use of the word 'military' to describe what he called an "intensive wraparound programmme in residence".

"The programme gets completely slated because of the use of the word military.

"There's obviously some political reason to use the word military because it's not. It's not actually a military programme at all."

He described the in residence component as having intensive support, therapy, counselling, "that should be standard practice" in youth residence, "but it's not because it's obviously expensive".

The in-residence programme reduced victimisation "hugely" because these kids who were doing "lots of crime" were now off the street.

"They are doing crime every single day of the week," he said, wanting to reiterate the word "persistent".

"These are persistent youth offenders who have failed community intervention," adding they continue to be prolific offenders.

He said the mandatory sentencing now available to the Youth Court was a good thing for this specific cohort because it was a targeted intervention.

They couldn't re-offend while they were effectively locked up, "...how many kids you know offend when they're in residence? None of them".

But the reoffending by the MSA participant this month took place while they were in the community phase of the programme.

That was a key issue.

"What failed last time," he said in relation to the first pilot, "was when they were placed back in the community. The community placements for some of the kids were awful".

He said it really mattered where the kids went after being in-residence, because for some of those young people they might be returning to families with drug addiction or gang affiliations.

"My feedback from last time was that there wasn't a lot of thought, or it was left till the last minute," and bad selections were made.

"This time, I think they put a lot more thought into the placements."

He likened it to drug rehabilitation, and being offered a residential placement where you remain clean for that period of time. But the question was whether someone could stay drug free a year later with very little support, he said.

"How does that support then get reinforced once you're actually back out in the community."

When it came to reoffending he said "if you had 10 drug addicts going to rehab, how many of them do you think would reoffend within a month of getting out".

Asked if he thought the MSA programme was successful, he said they'd been developed to address "what is clearly a need within the youth justice system and within society".

Normally, these young people would go to prison, where they wouldn't have intensive support he said.

Asked what went wrong for this young person, he said you'd have to question how much trauma had they had in their life, how young they were when they first started offending, their family background, whether there are gangs involved or family harm, and whether the young person was emotionally unregulated, "There's a whole list of things."

In response, OT told RNZ the second programme had built on the first, including a full evaluation that showed the the transition to community period, the first months after leaving the residence, was the "most high-risk for rangatahi to re-offend, whilst their new skills, habits and behaviours are still embedding".

World.title: Saturday matinee World of WearableArt show cancelled after crew member's death
World.content:
A second World of WearableArt performance has been cancelled following the death of a crew member.

Emergency services responded to reports of a medical event at the TSB Arena on Wellington's waterfront at 10.15am on Friday. Police said medical assistance was rendered but the person did not survive.

WOW said they were a beloved and valued member of its team and Friday night's performance was cancelled.

In an update just after midnight on Saturday, chief executive Meg Williams confirmed Saturday's matinee performance would also not go ahead.

"Following the tragic death of a beloved and specialised crew member, World of WearableArt (WOW) has made the difficult decision to cancel a second performance - the 2.30pm Saturday 26 September matinee," she said in a statement.

"While the result of a medical event - and the production has extensive contingency plans in place - we are dealing with an exceptional set of circumstances."

Williams said the crew member worked in a highly specialised area of production, with "a close-knit team who are deeply affected by this loss".

"Because of this, we have this [Friday] afternoon identified a need to make changes to the behind-the-scenes operation of the show to enable it to continue safely for the remainder of the season."

The team would be working on those adjustments during the day, she said, ahead of the scheduled performance that night.

Impacted ticket buyers had been contacted with information about arranging a transfer to another performance or a refund, Williams said.

"We understand there is deep disruption and disappointment to many WOW fans as a result of cancellation and are so very sorry. This has been an extremely difficult decision to again make," Williams said.

"Our thoughts and support continue to be with the crew member's family and the wider WOW whānau.

"We also extend our immense gratitude to the outpouring of aroha and support we are receiving. It means the absolute world to us at this extremely difficult time."

On Friday, a spokesperson for WorkSafe said it was carrying out initial inquiries.

He has a bandana, he has a collar, he has a prosthetic leg on his front leg. So all these things have to be maintained, have to be broken down, have to be coloured, have to be fixed."

World.title: Victim of Te Awamutu train incident was a young person
World.content:
A young person was the victim of a "tragic" train incident over the weekend, the Waipā District Council revealed.

The person died after the incident at Te Awamutu train stop on Sunday night.

Emergency services had rushed to the Waikato railway station around 6.20pm and said the person had "died at the scene".

The Waipā District Council said in a Facebook post it was young person that had a "tragic and untimely passing".

It also shared the details of a vigil to be held at Anchor Park in Te Awamutu on Sunday 11:30am.

"Everyone is welcome to attend and take a moment to remember, reflect and stand together.

"Our thoughts are with the whānau and all those affected at this difficult time."

Embedded content removed for printing https://www.facebook.com/WaipaDistrictCouncil/posts/pfbid02V7NAPEamf2r2yqUWjrcfqoUz8bZQiBxbQwmxPdZWbwoN9huy1tbvcYy9m6eFGn58l

A passenger, who RNZ agreed not to name, had said at the time it was something she would never forget.

"We weren't told what happened, but looking at the trauma of the bystanders... the trauma of staff, something I'll never forget."

She said she heard people yelling "stop" as the train left the station before it came to a halt.

The staff were extraordinary, she said, keeping passengers hydrated and informed as much as possible.

Senior Sergeant John McCarthy had previously said police were "providing support to whānau and those who acted immediately to try to help.

"Chief investigator of accidents Louise Cook said following the incident it had appointed a team of investigators who were now gathering evidence.

"Our investigators will focus initially on establishing what happened and identifying any evidence that could assist the inquiry. Our first priority is to gather evidence while it is available.

World.title: Marmite smears, live locusts to celebrate Orana Wildlife Park's 50th birthday
World.content:
Gibbons at Christchurch's Orana Wildlife Park have been treated to smears of Marmite and peanut butter on poles, and gift-wrapped boxes of cooked corn and live locusts, as part of the zoo's 50th birthday celebrations.

Festivities marking five decades since the park's opening on 25 September, 1976 came days after the cash-strapped park received a $1.2 million lifeline from ratepayers, with neighbouring councils also urged to chip in to secure its future.

Orana Wildlife Park chief executive Rachel Haydon said the zoo's drive-through safari, which ran from 1976-95, was still a big talking point.

"I do love people's stories of claw marks on the Cortina hood and things like that," she said. "Let's say, in our vision for our future, we are aiming to bring back a different version of a drive-through, so that still speaks to that nostalgia, but thinks about safety through a modern lens as well."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405604917112

Haydon said that different version of the drive-through would be part of a masterplan design, due be released in coming months, as the park grapples with financial difficulties.

An independent analysis by consultants BDO estimated a funding shortfall of $4.1 million for 2026/27 would increase to approximately $4.6-5.6 million each year for the following five years.

Earlier in September, park managers warned that the zoo might have to close without a cash injection.

On Wednesday Christchurch City Council agreed to contribute $1.2 million, as long as Orana approached other organisations for contributions, including neighbouring councils.

Haydon said Orana was grateful to the city council and had employed a fundraising and partnership manager.

"We have begun engagement with Selwyn and Waimakariri [District Councils]. No hard-and-fast plans yet, but we are organising times to hope to present and see what is possible."

Haydon said she understood councils faced tough funding decisions, but feedback showed that Orana park was valued by visitors.

Orana Wildlife Park celebrates its 50th anniversary. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"I'm blown away by the emails and words people have sent through to me and the team about what the park means to them," she said.

On Friday, London holidaymakers Ryan and Liz Simes paid a visit to Orana Wildlife Park, with three-year-old son Reuben.

Ryan Simes grew up in Christchurch and said it was a nostalgic trip back to the park, which he hoped can climb out of a financial hole.

"I'm sure there are plenty of billionaires in the country who could reduce their lifestyle by 0.001 percent and it would cover it for years to come," he said. "The government could probably take their hands out as well, instead of reducing everything for everyone."

A historic image of lions in the carpark of Orana Wildlife Park as it celebrates 50 years. ORANA WILDLIFE PARK / SUPPLIED

On a visit from Sheffield in the Selwyn district, Jess Herring was celebrating son Archie's third birthday. She was not opposed to other councils financially backing Orana Wildlife Park.

"We all learn a lot about conservation coming here and a lot of children don't get the opportunity see these animals otherwise," she said. "I've been coming since I was a little child.

"It's such an integral part of Christchurch and such a big attraction, it would be a shame to see it go."

World.title: Two people seriously burned, one in custody, after family harm incident in Northland’s Whangārei
World.content:
Two people have been seriously burned in Northland during a family harm incident.

Police said the incident happened in Whangārei on Friday evening and one of those injured was in police custody.

St John said it sent two ambulances to the scene and one person was flown to the serious burns unit at Auckland's Middlemore Hospital. The other person had been taken to Whangārei Hospital.

World.title: Late Brazil goal denies Socceroos famous win after stunning Irankunda free kick
World.content:
Nestory Irankunda's stunning free kick had the Socceroos just seconds away from a famous victory against Brazil in Townsville.

However, Brazilian substitute Rayan slammed a header in off the underside of the crossbar in the 95th-minute to salvage a 1-1 draw, dashing the Socceroos hopes of recording just a second ever victory against the Seleção.

Irankunda later told Channel 10 that his goal was "beautiful" and it would be hard to disagree.

Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti bemoaned what he described as a "not so good" pitch that made it hard to play good football.

But Irankunda's goal was everything that is beautiful about the game.

Lining up a free kick 20 metres from goal, Irankunda punched the ball over the four-man wall, and into the top corner of the goal.

"I mean, good goal, good goal," the 20-year-old told Channel 10.

"I've done it before and to do it again today against a top team in Brazil, it's amazing."

The goal, and lead, was exactly what the Socceroos deserved after a superb first half, running the number five-ranked Brazilians ragged through midfield and creating a number of chances.

Brazil looked shaky and uncertain in possession, turning over the ball in dangerous areas in a throwback to the worst aspects of their faltering 2026 World Cup campaign.

"I think we should do so much, much better," Bruno Guimarães said,

"The pitch was a little bit difficult … we couldn't pass the ball properly.

"We got a draw and I'm hopeful we can perform better in the next game, because the level that we have in the squad, we can definitely play better."

Both Australia's fullbacks found themselves in acres of space, rushing forward and laying the ball off to attacking threats Tete Yengi and Irankunda, who forced a fine save from Hugo Souza with a 20-metre driven shot inside the opening 10 minutes.

Nestory Irankunda had a fine effort saved early in the first half. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Brazil grew into the game towards the end of the half, even putting the ball in the back of the net in first half stoppage time when Estêvão slotted home after Harry Souttar was caught in possession.

However, VAR ruled that Bruno Guimarães had grabbed the giant centre back's leg, leading to the goal being overturned.

Brazil also felt they could have had a penalty when Lucas Herrington was seen to grab a fistful of Endrick's shirt as he raced into the penalty area.

In the second half Brazil continued to build the pressure right up until the moment Irankunda turned on the style with his magical free kick.

The remaining 20 minutes saw the Socceroos retreat deeper and deeper into their shells, with all 11 players within 20 metres of the goal line at times as Brazil camped on the edge of the penalty area.

Souttar and Herrington both made tremendous blocks in outstanding performances, but neither could stop a bullet header from Rayan, which kicked up off the pitch and through the palms of Pat Beach, going in off the base of the crossbar.

The two teams will resume hostilities in Tuesday night at Brisbane's Lang Park.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Red-hot Roosters roar into NRL grand final
World.content:
Sydney Roosters are through to their first NRL grand final in seven years after Mark Nawaqanitawase genius and a miracle Sam Walker injury comeback inspired a 36-20 demolition of the Dolphins.

The Roosters shot out to a 16-0 lead inside 27 minutes in front of a sold-out preliminary final crowd of 52,286 at Lang Park on Friday night.

Their defensive grit on the tryline, a feature of their finals campaign, limited the damage from a mini-Dolphins comeback, but two-try hero Nawaqanitawase has a box of unlimited magic tricks that he unfurled with a wow factor rarely seen on a rugby league field.

The Dolphins had won eight straight games to reach their first preliminary final, a wonderful achievement, but on this occasion it was the Roosters' big-game players who stood tallest.

Walker returned in a record-equalling 27 days from a syndesmosis injury to orchestrate the backline in a masterclass to set up a decider clash with either Penrith or Newcastle.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson will be angling for his fourth premiership win in as many attempts.

An error or a moment of magic was needed to turn an early set-for-set stalemate, and the paranormal Nawaqanitawase provided it in the 18th minute.

The rugby-bound revelation's pivotal moment was pure instinct and skill backed with supreme confidence.

Dolphins centre Herbie Farnworth hesitated with his pass for what would have been a Dolphins try had it hit the mark. The man known as "Marky Mark" swooped, raced 90m and the Roosters never looked back.

"Big players make big plays in big games," Billy Slater said on Channel Nine commentary.

Dolphins bench impact man Kurt Donoghoe dropped the ball when he came on and then missed a tackle for a rampant Victor Radley to score.

Walker's sublime lob for jumping Daniel Tupou had been well rehearsed and was perfectly executed.

The Roosters ran up an early lead they never surrendered. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts )

The Roosters lost bench rake Connor Watson to a category one HIA, upgraded by the independent doctor, in the first half and the St George Illawarra-bound utility will miss the grand final.

Dolphins winger Jamayne Isaako scored tries either side of halftime, but Nawaqanitawase collected a kick and flicked it back for Robert Toia to crash over.

When Nawaqanitawase bulldozed over for his second and Walker sliced through, it was all over for the hosts.

AAP

World.title: Eagles keep Dons winless, Dogs put Power on the brink
World.content:
Ella Roberts has celebrated her 50-game AFLW milestone in grand style, producing a typically brave effort as West Coast survived a frenetic Essendon comeback to post a 10-point win at Windy Hill.

The Eagles led by as much as 34 points during the third quarter of Friday's match and the margin was still 28 points at the final change, with Essendon scoring just two goals up until that moment.

But any thoughts of West Coast simply cruising to victory were extinguished as Essendon launched wave after wave of attack in the last quarter to put the Eagles under all sorts of pressure.

In the end, it was Essendon's missed chances that resulted in them falling just short, with the Bombers kicking 2.7 to 0.1 in the final quarter as West Coast clung on for the 6.9 (45) to 4.11 (35) win.

Roberts starred on her special day with 31 disposals, four clearances, one goal assist, nine tackles and 717m gained, while Jaide Britton kicked two goals and Amy Franklin kicked 1.3 and took six marks in a powerful display.

Maddy Prespakis (27 disposals, 466m gained) and Steph Wales (20 disposals, one goal) fought hard for the Bombers, who slumped to a 0–7 record.

West Coast started their season with four losses on the trot, but are now back in the finals mix at 3–4 following three consecutive wins.

Over at Whitten Oval, the Western Bulldogs improved to 5–2 with a 13-point win over lowly Port Adelaide (2–5).

Bulldogs forward Heidi Woodley was the star in the 10.2 (62) to 8.1 (49) win, kicking a career-high four goals from 18 disposals.

Ellie Hampson kicked three goals to go along with a goal assist in her Port debut, while Shineah Goody chipped in with two majors and Matilda Scholz had a huge day in the ruck with 22 disposals, 40 hit-outs and five clearances.

But the Bulldogs' deadly accurate return of 7.0 in the second half meant Port were never able to claw back the 13-point half-time deficit.

In the afternoon game at Princes Park, Carlton romped to a comfortable 11.10 (76) to 3.3 (21) win over Richmond.

Later, North Melbourne bounced back from their first AFLW loss in more than 1000 days, overcoming a horrid first quarter to hammer previously unbeaten Melbourne by 31 points.

Coming off a first defeat in 35 games, North overturned a 17-point quarter-time deficit to win 10.5 (65 to 5.4 (34) at Ikon Park on Friday.

With both teams now having a 7-1 win-loss record, victory lifted North above Melbourne into top spot on percentage.

AAP

World.title: 'Cynical' Freo coach bemoans how long AFL took with Neale reprieve
World.content:
Brisbane coach Chris Fagan doubted Lachie Neale would be cleared for the AFL grand final, as his "cynical" Fremantle counterpart Justin Longmuir took umbrage with the lengthy process.

But both coaches are happy with the end outcome, with Fagan declaring Neale's availability "good for footy".

The dual Brownlow Medal winner will feature in the premiership decider against Fremantle — his former club — at the MCG on Saturday after having a one-game ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan downgraded in a drama-filled hearing on Thursday.

Neale was instead fined $10,000 as the appeals board gave the four-time All Australian midfielder the ultimate reprieve due to having never previously been suspended in his decorated 320-game AFL career.

"I didn't think he would (get off)," Fagan told reporters on Friday.

"It was a bit like last year, I didn't think he was going to play last year until the day before the game when he got through a fitness test.

"So it's sort of history repeating itself, just in a different way. Good for footy I reckon but we were pretty much ready for him not to be playing, I must admit."

Brisbane swayed the appeals board that the tribunal had made an error of law in not considering the exceptional and compelling circumstances of Neale's past record.

Longmuir expected Neale to be cleared all along, although thought the decision would have come earlier in the week.

"I'm a bit cynical with these things. Sometimes I feel like that's the outcome that gets reached a little bit later than what I thought it would get reached," the Dockers coach said.

"We prepared for Brisbane's best and he's clearly in their best team. Even if he didn't play, we felt like someone else would have had to step up and they've got a lot of those 'someone else's' that are probably searching for midfield time."

Longmuir later added: "If players who have great records, who have contributed so much to our game, get a bit of leeway at certain times, I don't think that's a bad thing for the game".

Defender Noah Answerth, injured in Brisbane's qualifying final loss three weeks ago, was available and would have returned had Neale been suspended, but misses out.

"Coaches aren't supposed to have favourite players but he's (Answerth) one of mine," Fagan said.

The AFL's gut feel to Neale's gut punch leaves fans dazed and confused It was the AFL's Folarin Balogun moment, and the decision to let Lachie Neale play in the grand final has left many seeing red.

"If Lachie hadn't have played, Noah would have come into the team and Jaspa Fletcher would have pushed up onto a wing."

For the second year in a row, Neale has been the headline story of grand final week.

Last year, the 33-year-old famously overcame a calf injury that appeared season-ending to play a second-half super-sub role in the Lions' stunning demolition of Geelong.

Neale's fourth-straight grand final will almost certainly be his last for Brisbane, with a move to Collingwood looming in the off-season.

"Who says it's my last?" Neale replied to a question about his future.

With rain expected on Saturday, Neale will figure prominently as one of the Lions' best wet-weather players.

Brisbane take an unchanged team into the grand final as they attempt to become just the third side in the last 69 years to complete an AFL premiership three-peat.

And should they win, it would be the second three-peat in their history, following 2001-2003, and it would see them join Melbourne (1939-41 and 1955-57) as one of the only two teams to record the feat twice.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Fagan's future undecided as Lions focus on making grand final history
World.content:
Chris Fagan will again wait until after the grand final to confirm his future as he stands poised to join one of AFL coaching's most select clubs.

There has been speculation over the last few days about whether Saturday could be it for the two-time Brisbane premiership coach.

While Fagan said nothing had changed from the last couple of years — he will speak with Lions hierarchy once the season is over — the 65-year-old acknowledged on Friday that he had been in the role for a decade.

If Brisbane beats Fremantle on Saturday at the MCG, Fagan will become only the seventh VFL/AFL coach to mastermind a premiership three-peat.

"I'm only worried about the game tomorrow," Fagan said at the pre-game media conference.

"Every year, for the last two or three years, I've had a chat with our CEO and president about when's the right time for me to finish up.

"This is my 10th year, so I've been going for a while. I will get through this game and probably have the usual chat I've had every other year."

Chris Fagan has led the Lions to four straight grand finals. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Fagan's long-time confidant Leigh Matthews, who coached the Lions to their 2001-03 three-peat, and former Brisbane captain Jonathan Brown discussed Fagan's future earlier this week.

Brown suspected Fagan would want to try for four in a row if the Lions won. While Matthews said coaching was a lifestyle and Fagan might decide at some point he did not want to do it anymore.

"It's fair enough to speculate about it, but I honestly don't know right at this point in time whether I will keep going or not," Fagan said.

"I was like that last year and the year before, so we just have to work out the right time to go.

"It's not the big issue; we have to play a big game tomorrow."

Justin Longmuir says he is hoping to emulate Chris Fagan's long-term success. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

As Fagan and the Lions try to win another premiership, Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir and his team are looking to win the club's first flag.

Sitting next to Fagan, Longmuir said the goal was to make sure that whatever happened on Saturday, it was only the start of a successful Dockers era.

"I've thought about this moment for a number of years," Longmuir said about the prospect of Fremantle winning the premiership.

"It would fill me with great pride to be able to do that. But win or lose tomorrow, it's not the end of the journey.

"We want to create something that 'Fages' has created, where you're contending for a number of years."

AAP

World.title: Front-running Freo ready to claim first flag
World.content:
Football fans unite in glory, but the bonds of fandom are often forged in failure.

It is fair to say that Fremantle fans have suffered more than most since their club's entry to the AFL. It's also fair to say that, as a result, Dockers fans are some of the most passionate and dedicated in the league. It's why something like Wharfie Time is endearing instead of cheesy. The Purple Army is something to believe in.

The Fremantle experience has often been one of struggle. Struggling against the bigger brother in blue and yellow. Struggling against the tyranny of distance in a league based on the other side of the continent. Struggling against the weight of its own history.

The anchor is sometimes less a motif of their moniker and instead a weight tethering their expectations.

But this year everything seems different. This year Fremantle has led from the front, often without looking back.

Even as the pack came for the Dockers, they didn't fold under the pressure. Instead, they buckled down and somehow got better.

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir explained last week.

"So we all know what's on the line, but we've just got to make sure that we give our best at each moment, and the next moment's the most important one."

The Dockers showed a resilience often only attached to the best of teams. It's also one baked into the identity of their side.

Fremantle aren't just stocked with high-draft picks. The Dockers are also filled with players overlooked and discarded by others. Almost half of the side that will run out on Saturday fits into those categories, with a few rookies to boot. If these players had given up at the first rejection, they wouldn't be in the league.

More pertinently, Fremantle wouldn't be in the big dance without many of these names.

If Fremantle's fandom and side are somewhat unconventional, its success on the field is anything but. Like many successful teams of years' past, they have been built on a solid defensive base, with enough star power to shine through when needed. Like many great teams, they are more than the sum of their parts.

Like many great teams, they play their best footy when it matters most. Last week, Fremantle put together arguably the best quarter of its season to make the grand final.

"We played our best footy in the last quarter when everything was against us … I'm just so proud of everyone," captain Alex Pearce said in the immediate wake of last week's victory.

Thirteen years after their first grand final, the Dockers finally seem primed to break their premiership drought. In their way stands a side featuring the only remaining Fremantle player from that 2013 loss: Lachie Neale.

Strength in defence

Alex Pearce (right) is the lynchpin of a formidable defensive unit for Fremantle. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Often the leaders of a side dictate the identity and style of a side.

Led ably by captain and All-Australian Alex Pearce, Fremantle's backline may not be as star-studded as other defensive units around the league, but it is as sturdy as any. They scramble, hustle and fight through all four quarters. Regularly through the year teams fell away as the Dockers held strong.

The Dockers have had the league's most consistently good defence across all facets of the game. Some backlines drop their heads when the tide starts to turn — not Fremantle.

Fremantle excels at defending before danger begins. Its midfield works hard to prevent clean exits from stoppages and contests around the ground. Although the Dockers don't have the best clearance differential or ability to win ground balls in the mid-arc, they are exceptional at preventing opposition teams from scoring from these sources.

When they lose possession in their front half, the Dockers stay eager to get the ball in their hands. They are the best side in the league at winning the ball back in the middle third of the ground.

If the ball does end up inside their defensive 50, no side is better at repelling opposition forwards. Miserly is an understatement about how Fremantle defends. It is the biggest reason that the Dockers are still alive in season 2026.

When they win the ball back, they can turn on the jets and blow opposition sides away.

The cherry on top

Players such as Luke Jackson (left) and Shai Bolton (right) ensure Fremantle can beat teams offensively as well as defensively. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Few fans turn up to the footy for stout defence. It's the action at the other end that hypnotises.

Despite their defensive DNA, Freo are not lacking for weapons of their own. They turn defence into attack at the drop of a hat thanks to a plethora of creative players.

Fremantle can put on a show like few others when everything is firing, possessing the ability to pile goal after goal on the scoreboard. While their defence is often understated, their attack is anything but.

Few players generate more highlights than Shai Bolton, with the former Mark of the Year winner routinely getting Purple fans off the edge of their seats. Bolton isn't alone however.

The Dockers side is stocked with players that use the ball well.

Murphy Reid has quickly cemented himself as an attacking line breaker, while Caleb Serong, Jordan Clark and Corey Wagner gain ground with ease.

Luke Jackson also proves a challenge for any opponent as the most capable ruck at ground level in the league. Jackson has the most score involvements of any ruck this year.

The Dockers often attack in straight lines, and use the tallest timber in the league to their advantage.

But when sides like Sydney take those avenues away, Fremantle doesn't shy away from changing angles of attack and look laterally as well.

That ability to win aerial contests has another benefit. It tends to encourage opposition players to fly more often than they should, leaving Fremantle with an outnumber at ground level. That allows even more room for the ground gang to work in.

Up forward, the Dockers can beat you in any number of ways. The likes of Hye Amiss, Patrick Voss and Josh Treacy can take clunks and convert them into sure scores. At ground level, Michael Frederick, Isaiah Dudley and Shai Bolton regularly hit the scoreboard and strike fear into the hearts of opposition small defenders.

Their big men love a bomb from the top of the arc, but Freo don't tend to score a lot from out wide. That makes Hayden Young's preliminary final heroics all the more notable.

Perhaps Fremantle's biggest strength is their evenness across the board. Against Hawthorn it wasn't just the stars like Bolton and Luke Jackson that stood up late, but also players like Judd McVee and Frederick. It is clear that there's belief in this team, and dedication to a united cause.

The Final Challenge

Lachie Neale (centre) and the Brisbane Lions are standing between Fremantle and its maiden premiership. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Although Fremantle has been the best side across the year, it isn't coming into the grand final at the peak of its mid-season powers. The Dockers have won just three quarters in their three finals so far — a feat no other team has achieved before.

The Dockers have struggled late in the year when the ball has hit the deck against good sides, and some of the best midfields have overwhelmed their attacking midfield unit. These may sound like minor issues, but to win a grand final against the two-time defending champions, everything has to be on point.

But the Lions are a side that the Dockers have vanquished through the year. In round 12, the Dockers eased to a 25-point win in one of their most impressive wins of the year. The Dockers absorbed the Lions' clearance dominance while preventing them from getting the upper hand in the marking battle. Fremantle worked out a way to penetrate the Lions' whole ground defence, scoring a massive 52 points from their defensive half.

But it was also a Brisbane side that Longmuir acknowledged wasn't at their best coming into the game.

Fremantle got the better of Brisbane in the only meeting between the two sides during the home-and-away season this year. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

"We felt like there were some opportunities there. You know, Fages [Lions coach Chris Fagan] would come in here and say they're not in the greatest form," he said.

"I just don't want to be disrespectful with that because they've been in the last three grand finals."

Longmuir and Fagan both know that premierships aren't won in May. The early season Lions are vastly different to the side that Fremantle has to beat in the grand final.

But there's hope in the West that the result will be the same and that the Dockers three-decade drought will be over.

World.title: Retiring Dolphin lauded as one of NRL's toughest ahead of prelim final
World.content:
Ray Stone has claims to being the toughest man in the NRL.

Not that the Dolphins' warrior would care two hoots for the title as he nears retirement at the end of the 2026 season at the tender age of 29.

But there was a reason coach Kristian Woolf singled him out at last year's presentation night for playing the last six rounds with a broken hand and final 15 rounds with needles in both shoulders.

He had off-season shoulder surgery after pushing himself to play when the Dolphins had multiple forwards on the injured list.

Stone is one of those players who performs when busted. When fit and relatively injury-free, though, he is even more dangerous.

"There are a lot of tough men who play our game but he is in the top group," Woolf said.

"It is not just his toughness, it's his commitment to the team that I really admire.

"He is just a guy who refuses to let his teammates down. It doesn't matter if it is playing injured, he is making an effort on a kick-chase, getting into a tackle or a carry.

"I love his hit-ups off the kick-off. I get a kick out of watching those because he runs so hard. He is just committed to the team. That is what we are going to miss."

Stone has been linked to a boxing career but AAP understands he has obtained multiple tickets in trade areas and will only get in a ring if he sees fit. He can hold them up, as the saying goes.

Finals battle between an unstoppable force and an immovable object Brian To'o and Greg Marzhew have never met a rugby league problem they couldn't solve by running over it and now the two wrecking balls will go head-to-head with an NRL grand final berth on the line.

"It is probably based on family time for me," Stone said, when asked why he was calling time.

"The kids are getting a bit older and I am quite busy on weekends so I want to be a part of that."

Woolf wanted him on deck in 2027.

"I have spoken to him a number of times and asked if I could change his mind but he has got other things in life he wants to do," the coach said.

"I respect that about him. He knows what he wants. He has pushed himself through the pain."

Stone was the second player signed at the Dolphins after starting his NRL career at Parramatta, where he played 31 matches in five seasons. At the Dolphins, he has notched 81 games in four years.

Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf has tried his very best to convince Stone to play on next season.

"The reason I came up here was for opportunity," he said.

"I was in and out of first-grade at Parramatta where we had a strong team and I spoke to Wayne Bennett about coming here and he said I'd be more of a consistent first-grader."

The warhorse, who plays mostly off the bench, has scored eight tries for the Dolphins but, like an old-school footy player of the past, he doesn't smile after any.

"It's not something I stress about," Stone said, through gritted teeth.

"I like to leave all my celebrating until after the game when the boys have got the result."

The Dolphins have won 16 of their last 18 matches coming into Friday night's NRL preliminary final. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He's done plenty of that this year, with the Dolphins winning 16 of their last 18 matches ahead of the preliminary final against Sydney Roosters.

"This year I've been a lot healthier and the squad has too, which has definitely helped our middle rotation," Stone said.

"Last year, pretty much our whole starting pack was in rehab. The minutes have been distributed a lot more which has helped me stay healthy."

Woolf is just glad to have Stone in the team after he missed the early rounds with his shoulder recovery.

"We did miss him too. He is a small man in a big man's world who plays so tough," Woolf said.

"He is loved, respected and will be missed next year.

"He is going to leave a legacy that people don't realise. There are no discipline issues around Ray. He turns up and gets his job done every day of every week."

AAP

World.title: Brazil’s big-name squad meets mega hype from soccer fanatics
World.content:
As some of the world's most famous football players arrive in a city known for its love of another football code, soccer fans hope the hype might change people's minds.

The Brazilian soccer team landed in Townsville yesterday ahead of their friendly clash with the Socceroos tonight at North Queensland Stadium.

Legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti brought a squad of big names, including Vinícius Júnior and captain Marquinhos, whose combined yearly salaries are estimated at more than $55 million.

Brazilian superstar Vinícius Júnior met with fans in Townsville to sign autographs. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

For the city's small and vibrant Brazilian community, their arrival has been a cause for celebration.

Enthusiastic fans wore jerseys and held signs, screaming out to the star-studded team, after they touched down in Townsville.

"We love to party, we love dancing, and we like to cheer for our soccer team," Tatiane Pinheiro said.

"Very loud, very excited, everyone is going to be so excited to watch the game."

Football fanatics came from far and wide to welcome both the Brazil and Socceroos teams. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

The friendly match is one of two games in the series, with the other scheduled for Brisbane on September 29.

It will be the 12th time the Socceroos and Brazil have met since their first match-up in 1988.

Australia has beaten the five-time World Cup champions just once, in 2001.

But a lopsided head-to-head has not tainted the excitement in Townsville, which has been decked out in green and gold in anticipation of the international game.

Brazilian community fires up

Ms Pinheiro, a Townsville resident and Brazilian national, said she was excited to welcome crowds of Brazilians from around the country to her city.

Tatiane Pinheiro expects to meet Brazilian fans who have flown in from around the country. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

"Everyone that we know from other cities is coming to watch the big game," she said.

Organisers said more than half of the sell-out crowd of 25,000 were visitors from outside of Townsville.

Louise Monteiro (right) came with friends and family to greet the Brazilian team in her new hometown of Townsville. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Louise Monteiro and her family recently moved to Townsville, and she is originally from Brazil.

She said it was difficult for her to decide which team to support.

"I think I'll always support Brazil first," she said.

"If Socceroos play against another team, I'll be supporting Socceroos."

Socceroos vs Brazil, everything you need to know Everything you need to know as the youthful Socceroos take on a Brazil team on the rebuild under legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti in Queensland, with international friendlies in Townsville and Brisbane.

Townsville Brazilian community leader Ronie Reed said the occasion trumped every event she'd ever seen in Townsville.

She said the hype among her community had been building since the announcement, including gathering for pre-game events.

"The supporter part of Brazilian football is such a big thing," she said.

"All the Brazilians are so excited to go and support the team and just to be there."

Brazilian community leader Ronie Reed said the local community has been very excited about the game. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

Ms Reed has lived in Townsville for 14 years and organises many local events for the South American community, which is often made up of the many backpackers who visit North Queensland.

"We want to show our presence; we want to show the impact that we have," she said.

"We want everyone to know how good it is to have this community here."

The Brazilian team lined up for a photo in front of Cleveland Bay. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

A street party and festival in the city starts at 3pm, before entertainers and musicians lead the crowd to the stadium.

A different type of football

North Queensland Stadium is home to the NRL's North Queensland Cowboys, but soccer fan and local player Mark Gadzikwa hopes Brazil's appearance and performance at the stadium could help curb a "lack of interest" in the round-ball game.

Townsville resident Mark Gadzikwa is both a rugby league and soccer fan. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

"Brazil has always meant football; there's no better team to do it," he said.

" When you think of football, you think of Brazil. "

Anotida Sandengu has watched soccer since he was five, but this will be his first time watching a team as skilful as Brazil.

Mr Sandengu said he was surprised Townsville was chosen for the international match, which was announced after the World Cup in June.

Townsville locals Anotida Sandengu and Jobe Waring. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

"I wouldn't have called it; I remember I heard the news around the World Cup when everyone was watching soccer," he said.

"It was just really exciting. This is a once-in-a-lifetime event; it probably won't ever happen again." Brazil is the most successful team at the FIFA World Cup, having won five times.

The Socceroos last met Brazil for a friendly game in Melbourne in 2017, where they lost 4-0.

Kick-off in Townsville is 8pm.

Tech.title: Phones don’t have lights
Tech.content:
Mark Zuckerberg has a new defense of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses: They’re actually doing more to signal they’re taking a photo than phones do. He’s brought this up in at least two recent interviews, noting that the glasses have a light that comes on to signal when a photo is being taken, while phones do not. In one of the interviews, Joanna Stern notes that, while phones do not always emit a light, someone does have to hold a phone up in the air, which is itself pretty noticeable.

On today’s Vergecast, we’re talking about Meta Connect, the Muse AI assistant, all the new smart glasses hardware, and Zuckerberg’s response to the privacy uproar around wearable cameras. First, we spend time diving into Muse, which has quickly turned the vibes around on Meta’s progress in AI by making agentic features vastly more accessible than others have in the past. That ties right into Meta’s glasses problem and the question of whether people will trust Meta enough with their privacy to link all their services up to Muse.

There’s also a ton of hardware to discuss. We have thoughts on the new audio-only Ray-Ban Meta glasses and the new Meta VR Glasses. Then it’s onto Googlebooks, which arrived this week with surprisingly refined hardware and compelling integrations between desktop and mobile. It’s going to be a big hurdle to convince people to switch from Windows, but the laptops are full of interesting enough ideas that we’re excited to check them out.

Finally, everyone’s favorite podcast within a podcast returns after a brief hiatus. And then it’s on to the Lightning Round, where we’re discussing the Paramount settlement, YouTube’s embrace of AI tools, the state of Xbox, and Rode hooking its users up with 4K.
