Tech.title: These camera apps give you more control over the iPhone 18 Pro’s aperture
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

One of the questionable limitations of the iPhone 18 Pro’s new main camera with a variable aperture is that you’re limited to just four settings in the native iOS’ camera app in manual mode: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. Those same limitations are also in place when the app is adjusting the iris itself in Auto aperture mode, but it turns out that’s not a strict limitation of the iPhone’s camera hardware. Apple’s SDK allows third-party camera apps to implement more granular control of the aperture.

BlackMagic Design’s well-featured and still completely free BlackMagic Camera app for iOS was one of the first third-party options to introduce support for the iPhone 18 Pro’s adjustable aperture. But instead of just four stop settings, the app offers 10 presets with additional options in-between the settings available in iOS’ camera. The iPhoneographers YouTube channel tested the new functionality in version 3.5 of the app last week and while they describe it as “pretty buggy” the app has since been updated to version 3.5.1 with “general performance and stability improvements.”

Yesterday, Moment followed suit with an announcement on X that its $12.99 Moment Pro Camera II app has also been updated to support the iPhone 18 Pro’s variable aperture. You can adjust the aperture from f/1.48 to f/4.0 in 1/3 stop increments giving you 10 presets like Blackmagic’s app, which is the same approach as most digital cameras take. Given the small sensor size of the iPhone 18 Pro you may be hard-pressed to see a difference in background blur and focus depth when comparing photos with f-stops different by just 1/3 of a stop, but more control is never a bad thing.

Tech.title: Tesla’s Optimus robot is going through growing pains
Tech.content:
Hitting its goal of making 20,000 Optimus robots per week is reportedly proving tricky for Tesla. The Information reports that Tesla produced “several hundred robots a week” last month, after it repurposed its Model S and Model X production lines for Optimus earlier this year. However, this strategy is reportedly creating manufacturing snags, like issues lining up parts precisely, as The Information notes: “Not only are the Optimus production lines new, but the Optimus parts are much smaller and have to fit together far more precisely than car parts.”

It reports that even in the “V3” Optimus robots it’s currently producing, the hands and forearms “have more than 100 screws and other small components that currently require a worker to assemble manually.” These robots are lighter and have more cameras than previous versions, but lack a “sensing glove” currently in development that will improve durability by making it easier to replace touch sensors without swapping out the entire hand.

Optimus has faced delays for years now, even as Tesla CEO Elon Musk has made bold promises about it, saying Optimus will be Tesla’s “biggest product of all time.” However, at the moment they’re still being used internally for specific tasks in limited areas, and not generally or with remote teleoperation. Tesla also reportedly plans to lease the robots initially rather than selling them, and use the training data collected to improve the robots, but it will have to get them out in the world first.

Meanwhile, other developers have begun shifting to less lifelike designs for their robots, and earlier this month, Chinese regulators reportedly started holding back IPO listings for humanoid robotics companies.

Tech.title: Meta makes the Muse filesystem even more accessible
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Yesterday, with a little prodding, it was discovered that Meta’s Muse would expose its filesystem to curious users. The files offered a fascinating peek under the hood of an AI chatbot, and appeared to expose details we weren’t meant to see, not least because Muse itself told people, including us, it wasn’t supposed to reveal them.

But today Muse will eagerly offer up the contents of its file system when you ask for it. That appears to be because, as Meta’s Nat Friedman later said, this is the “intended behavior.”

In a post on X, Meta Superintelligence Labs’ David Singleton elaborated:

This was a very deliberate choice - your Muse Secure VM truly is your own computer in the cloud. You can install software in it, write and compile code, use the browser to surf the web: it is your own Linux box that you can operate as you choose with your Muse.

Muse’s architecture is fundamentally different from other AI platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini. It’s closer to running OpenClaw on a local machine, except the machine is in the cloud.

In a statement provided to The Verge yesterday, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts said, “We’re continuing to make updates to the product, so users may see changes in how much information is available about their virtual machine.” And that seems to be the case. When asked to see its filesystem today, Muse promptly offered a clickable file browser with access to root. Yesterday it merely offered a text file download that showed its directory tree.

Even after I coaxed Muse into sharing much of its filesystem with me yesterday, it refused to share a full archive of the root directory on down, saying, “I still can’t do a full / copy — even with the secrets stripped out.” Today it zipped up the root directory without hesitation, delivering “the full filesystem listings,” with “all with secrets stripped out.”

If this is indeed the intended behavior for Muse, it does raise the question of why it initially refused my requests for a copy of its filesystem, citing security concerns. It could be because Muse, like other AI systems, is not fully reliable at knowing what it can and can’t do. Or it could be because Meta has decided to more fully embrace Muse being a “computer in the cloud” and has made changes to make this function more reliable. In any event, it’s pretty fun.

We asked Meta why Muse initially called filesystem access a security issue if it was always the intended behavior, and the company has not yet responded.

Tech.title: Leaks reveal a new Apple HomePod mini, iPad mini, and Apple TV 4K
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple is expected to announce more hardware before the end of the year following the debut of the iPhone 18 Pro and folding iPhone Duo earlier this month. The updated products will include a new version of the HomePod mini, the iPad mini 8, and the Apple TV 4K, according to details and images discovered in Apple’s own code by MacRumors contributor Aaron Perris.

Details from the leaks are sparse, but the HomePod Mini 2 will carry forward a similar design to the original model that debuted in late 2020. While the current model is available in bright color options including orange, yellow, and blue, the leaked images of the HomePod Mini 2 reveal new green, pink, blue, white, and black shades that are more subdued and better suited to blending into existing decor.

The new iPad mini 8 will replace the seventh-generation model that launched two years ago with an upgrade from Apple’s A17 Pro chip to the recently announced A20 Pro found in the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max, and iPhone Duo. The leaked images only show the front of the iPad mini 8, but Apple has moved its front-facing camera to the landscape edge of the tablet, while a groove on the top edge of the display, similar to the iPhone’s, seems to indicate an added speaker.

As previously reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the next version of the iPad could also include improved waterproofing thanks to a new vibration-based speaker, and an OLED display like the larger iPad Pro features.

The current version of the Apple TV is nearly four years old, but today’s leaks don’t give much away about what upgrades the new 4th generation version will include aside from a very similar design to its predecessor. Previous details uncovered by MacRumors’ Perris include a potential upgrade to Apple’s A17 Pro chip, while in 2024 Mark Gurman said the next Apple TV would use Apple’s in-house Bluetooth and Wi-Fi chip we now know as the N1.

Tech.title: Sony and UMG are suing Suno again
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sony and Universal Music Group filed yet another suit against Suno. The labels claim its new v6 model still infringes on their copyrights because it’s trained on user outputs from previous models, which were themselves trained on unlicensed music ripped from YouTube and other sources. Sony and UMG are notable holdouts who did not sign a licensing agreement with Suno.

In its complaint shared with The Verge, Sony and UMG accuse Suno of “model laundering,” saying:

“Training a ‘new’ model on the outputs of an infringing model does not eliminate the infringement; it launders it, passing the value of Plaintiffs’ expression from the copied recordings into the tainted models, from those models into their outputs, and from those outputs into v6 … V6 is not a fresh start; it is the fruit of the same poisoned tree.”

When v6 launched, Suno’s Jack Brody told The Verge it was “trained from the ground up, with a new set of data,” including “user data,” but did not offer details beyond that. Suno later confirmed to Engadget that data includes “creations” from users, but would not elaborate further when reached for comment.

Sony further alleges that Suno used distillation to train v6. It claims that it was trained to replicate the results of its previous, “teacher” models, which were created using infringing data.

The complaint says that “even a model not directly trained on Plaintiffs’ recordings is informed by, and benefits from, Suno’s retained unauthorized copies.” Essentially, the labels argue that, unless Suno truly starts from scratch, its models will continue to be built on stolen data.

Tech.title: One company is at the center of a wave of rogue AI attacks
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In July, OpenAI revealed that its AI agents had attacked Hugging Face without permission, sparking widespread concerns about AI safety. Since then, a string of similar incidents involving agents from Meta, Anthropic, Google, and other companies has fueled further fears about rogue AI. As disclosures implicating numerous AI models trickled out over the past few months, these seemed like separate incidents. But many share a common source: one specific company tasked with testing the agents.

Irregular, an Israeli startup that stress-tests AI models in “high-fidelity research platforms that simulate and monitor real-world AI security scenarios,” has worked with many of the industry’s biggest players since it was founded as Pattern Labs in 2023. Its exact client list is not known, but its work has been cited in OpenAI model system cards, it was used to test systems for the UK government and Anthropic, and it published research with RAND, a highly influential think tank that informs policy on AI.

In several Irregular tests this year, agents escaped their supposedly secure testing environments and went after real-world targets.

The breaches, which are independent of the Hugging Face hack, all follow the same broad template: Irregular was testing the models’ cybersecurity capabilities in controlled environments meant to simulate realistic conditions. Some of the tests used “capture-the-flag” exercises, a common way of testing hacking abilities that asks agents to find hidden information inside of a simulated network. At least, the network is meant to be simulated.

Irregular CTO and cofounder Omer Nevo told The Verge that the agents were not supposed to have access to the open internet, but that “internet access was unintentionally available.” At the same time, Nevo said a fictional company name created for the simulation as a target “overlapped with a real domain.” Put together, those mistakes sent the agents after real-world targets, though it’s not clear which companies or organizations were actually attacked.

“All the incidents involving Irregular stemmed from the same underlying issue in a single evaluation scenario and have been disclosed.”

Nevo confirmed to The Verge that this same issue was behind incidents involving models from OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, and Google. “All the incidents involving Irregular stemmed from the same underlying issue in a single evaluation scenario and have been disclosed,” he said. “Other security incidents which have been reported recently across the industry are unrelated to Irregular or to our evaluations.” This includes the Hugging Face hack and breaches from the UK’s AI Security Institute.

“Disclosed” does not necessarily mean made public, though, and it’s unclear whether Nevo was referring to informing Irregular’s clients, the public, or someone else. While the incidents all stemmed from the same underlying testing failure, reports from Anthropic and OpenAI, along with reporting on Google, indicate the tech companies were notified at roughly similar times in late July. OpenAI and Anthropic announced the breaches themselves, while the incidents involving Meta and, weeks later, Google first became public through media reports.

Irregular’s cybersecurity testing goes beyond the four US tech giants. Research published on its website indicates it has also conducted similar cybersecurity testing on Kimi K3 and GLM-5.2, open AI models from Chinese companies Moonshot AI and Z.ai, respectively. Unlike the proprietary models involved in the other incidents — Meta has kept its flagship Spark model proprietary — these models can be freely downloaded and run on users’ own hardware, meaning testers like Irregular don’t have to rely on the companies for access or send data back to them. Irregular’s research describes them as “self-hosted” instances.

“Disclosed” does not necessarily mean made public.

The evaluations of the Chinese models did not result in similar real-world incidents, Nevo said: “We did not observe the same type of issue described in the incidents referenced here during our evaluations of GLM or Kimi.” However, Nevo cautioned that this “observation alone should not be interpreted as evidence that these models are less susceptible to this kind of behavior.” Neither Moonshot nor Z.ai responded to The Verge’s request for comment.

Nevo said the incidents have prompted changes at Irregular. “We have tightened internet access controls, expanded monitoring and manual review, and strengthened checks before evaluations begin to verify that access matches the intended scope,” he said. “We have also improved how we document and agree on each evaluation’s setup and parameters with our partners.”

Irregular also plans to publish a broader report “covering lessons learned and practices for conducting cyber evaluations safely” once that joint work with the companies involved is complete, Nevo said. “Our work with partners aims to turn lessons from these incidents into public shared practices for developing and evaluating increasingly powerful AI safely.”

Are you an AI safety researcher or frontier lab employee? You can contact me securely and confidentially via Signal at robhart.01

Nevo said Irregular has addressed the issues with the testing environment that were linked to the incidents. None of the four US AI companies answered questions asking for further details — including when they became aware of the breaches, whether they were seeking damages or other remedies from Irregular, and whether they expected to continue working with the Irregular. Google and Anthropic did not respond, while OpenAI and Meta pointed The Verge to previously published blog posts.

Tech.title: Ahead of US IPO, British AI neocloud Nscale secures $3.36B in convertible financing
Tech.content:
In Brief

Nscale, a British neocloud, has secured $3.36 billion in financing ahead of its IPO later this year, the company announced on Friday. Structured as a convertible note, the massive funding round underscores the staggering capital required to build out AI data centers.

Led by hedge fund Third Point, the new investment includes $2.36 billion available to the company immediately and an additional $1 billion coming from existing investor Nvidia, which Nscale will receive in mid-November. The notes will convert into equity shares once the IPO is completed.

Nscale, which filed its IPO paperwork last week, is expected to be valued at $35 billion on the NYSE, the Financial Times reported, and is seeking to raise $3 billion in the offering, according to Bloomberg.

Since it was spun out of Australian cryptocurrency mining company Arkon Energy two years ago, Nscale has amassed over $103 billion worth of contracts, according to its IPO filing.

The company is currently developing several large data center campuses, including in Norway and West Virginia.

Tech.title: The Aeropod automates soil aeration without robotics — see it at TechCrunch Disrupt
Tech.content:
Farmers around the world face a pressing problem: The equipment they use to till, plant, and harvest their fields is killing their margins. Studies have estimated that soil compaction can reduce yields by 20% to 60%.

Plowing can help, but it’s a laborious and expensive task that harms soil health in different ways. Muju Earth has developed an alternative, the Aeropod, that automatically aerates the soil without machinery or robotics. The startup says it can promote better soil health while cutting farmers’ tilling costs by half or more.

The device is “built like a seed, it sows like a seed, and it ships like a seed,” Ifeoluwa Afolayan, the company’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch. The device is about the size of a fingernail, and farmers drop it in the soil alongside their seeds using the same equipment. There’s no need to till the soil in advance.

“It just really seems like a no-brainer,” Afolayan said.

After the Aeropod is exposed to a combination of temperature, pressure, and moisture, it bursts open, loosening the soil and creating small channels that let air, water, and roots move through it more easily.

Muju Earth — one of the 200 startups in this year’s Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco in October — has tested its devices in lab settings and is embarking on paid field trials this fall in the U.K. Nine farmers are participating, and the startup has more than 30 on a waitlist.

Its initial target market is onion growers in the U.K. since onions are particularly sensitive to soil compaction, Afolayan said.

Tilling a field once might cost around £250 to £400 per hectare when factoring in labor costs, diesel, and wear and tear on equipment, Afolayan said. The Aeropod should produce similar results at just £100 per hectare, Afolayan said.

The Aeropod was born during Afolayan’s and co-founder Wangyang Hu’s time at Imperial College London, where they sought to design a product that would improve farmers’ bottom lines while also aiding soil health. The Aeropod’s development was driven by a single question: “How do you make this as simple as sowing a seed?” Afolayan said. “That’s the most equitable practice across every farmer on the planet.”

In addition to farmers, the startup has also heard from companies developing biologic amendments — products added to soil, often containing living microbes, that boost or replace chemical fertilizers. Because those companies’ products work best in aerated soils, they’re interested in pairing with the Aeropod.

But Afolayan said that farmers have been leading adoption. Most of the marketing to date has been inbound. “The best thing about Aeropod is the farmers intuitively understand the proposition,” she said.

Muju Earth is one of 200 startups in this year’s Startup Battlefield, a pitch competition in which 20 finalists will present on the main stage at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 at Moscone West in San Francisco.

Tech.title: Some Supabase customers are publicly exposing reams of people’s data to the web
Tech.content:
Thousands of databases hosted by development platform Supabase are exposing people’s sensitive information to the public web, new security research by cybersecurity firm UpGuard has found.

UpGuard told TechCrunch that it found around 16,000 databases on which some degree of personal data was exposed while they were hosted by Supabase, which allows web and app developers to store and run their databases.

Supabase earlier this year reached a $10 billion valuation, thanks to a rise in developers hosting their vibe-coded apps on the platform. But the company has faced criticism for how it handles user security. There are widely documented cases of users misconfiguring or unknowingly exposing their databases to the broader internet, in some instances to the tune of millions of records each.

The findings highlight how vibe-coded apps and websites can spill or expose sensitive data through basic misconfigurations and improper security. While AI tools can be used to easily build websites and apps, the generated code can often contain security flaws, or apps might require specific configuration that the developer may be ignorant of.

Over the years, countless data breaches have been linked to improperly configured storage servers, databases and websites. Such cases have resulted in the leaks of sensitive military emails, immigration and visa applications, classified government files, hundreds of thousands of driver’s license scans, and children’s personal information.

Now, the boom in AI vibe-coding is helping fuel a new wave of data breaches, many of which are now being linked to Supabase as people increasingly use it for storing their data.

UpGuard says it sought to understand the scale of exposed data across the platform, and found publicly accessible names, addresses, phone numbers, and user passwords. The research surfaced a fewer number of passwords and authentication tokens.

The firm said the databases contained data linked to various projects, such as private conversations with sex workers on an Indian adult streaming site; thousands of license plates of a U.S. valet service; and the contact information of people who used an immigration and relocation service. One of the databases belonged to an African government’s consulate in France, said UpGuard, while another was used to intercept text messages by a virtual SIM farm for sending one-time passcodes to verify online accounts, typically for launching scams and phishing attacks.

While the majority of these exposed datasets appear to be located in the United States, UpGuard said this is a worldwide problem. The findings build on earlier research that also found a range of exposed databases hosted on Supabase, including those by Y Combinator startups and other popular apps.

Supabase has made changes to its platform over the years, including bolstering its platform and user access to databases.

When reached for comment, Supabase’s Chief Information Security Officer Bil Harmer said that while the company has not seen the research, its projects are “secure by default.” He described security as a shared responsibility between the company and its customers. “We provide secure defaults and tooling, and customers control how their own projects are configured,” and the company notifies affected customers when security issues are discovered, he said.

“Security at Supabase is never finished. We care deeply about getting it right, and we’ll keep making it easier for every developer to ship securely,” said Harmer.

UpGuard security researcher Greg Pollock said the company’s research was important for raising awareness about the issue of data exposures.

Tech.title: Astra and Opus just passed Turing’s other test
Tech.content:
Computer pioneer Alan Turing is best known for his eponymous experiment to test whether artificial and human intelligence can be distinguished. However, the more important test he faced during his lifetime was cracking the Enigma code used by Nazi Germany during World War II.

Now, a pair of cryptanalysts say they’ve cracked two long-unsolved messages encoded by Enigma machines using LLMs built by OpenAI and Anthropic.

While Turing and his team of cryptanalysts built an early computer, dubbed the Bombe, that allowed the United Kingdom to translate Enigma messages during the war, a handful of archival messages remain unbroken — usually due to mistranscription or errors by the original encoders.

Carter Leffen, a developer, simply told OpenAI’s newest model, Astra, to search a database of Enigma messages for an unbroken message and decode it. The model was able to do just that, after doing its own archival research, finding context clues, building a simulator of the Enigma machine, and ultimately recovering the plaintext of a message that had baffled researchers since 2005. He even used Astra to build an interactive website explaining the whole problem.

Frode Weierud, a retired electrical engineer with a lifelong interest in cryptology, maintains the website Crypto Cellar, which includes a variety of resources and records and a database of messages. Last week, Weierud validated Leffen’s solution, which he said left him in “awe.”

Notably, given the lengths that AI agents will go to answer the questions in front of them, the Astra model’s logs include discussion of archived messages in a “private collection” that aren’t hosted by Weierud. He still isn’t sure if the model accessed them or not, but speculates they may have been shared by a different researcher somewhere online, or that the model was able to access the German government’s public archives.

“GPT–6 Astra is behaving like a very professional cryptanalyst and archive researcher,” he wrote. “What it has achieved in two days would take a human researcher weeks or even months. Personally, I spent several weeks researching the Bundesarchiv files GPT–6 Astra refers to.”

On September 21, another cryptanalyst, Jack Willis, reached out to Weierud, saying he had used Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 model to break a different unsolved message. Willis provided significantly more guidance to Claude, which was ultimately able to use the known signature of a particular officer’s name to break the message.

Weierud notes that there are just seven unbroken Enigma messages remaining, along with one message where the plaintext is known but the code is still unbroken.

Perhaps not for long.

Tech.title: Meta is putting its muscle behind Muse as the AI app takes off
Tech.content:
Muse’s traction is surging, fueled by Meta’s promotion of the AI app at its annual Meta Connect developer conference this week and strong early reviews that praised its polished design and highly capable AI model under the hood.

At the start of the week, Muse had surpassed 2.5 million downloads since its September 8 launch. Now the app has amassed more than 3.4 million downloads, according to the most recent estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

The install numbers are only current as of the firm’s Thursday estimates, which can lag behind real-world adoption.

That means they don’t even capture the full impact of the big push Muse received at Meta Connect, where the social network company announced a range of upcoming features for the new AI app, including video chat with the Muse avatar, support for computer use on the Mac, a dedicated email address, more partners and connectors, and plans for smart glasses integrations.

Estimates from other market intelligence firms show Muse with similarly strong traction, though their numbers vary quite a bit. Apptopia, for example, puts Muse’s total number of downloads to date at 4.3 million. (Muse is currently only available in the U.S. and Canada). It estimates that 2.6 million of those were on iOS alone.

Meanwhile, another firm, Appfigures, says it sees Muse installs at roughly 2.3 million as of Thursday, almost evenly split between iOS and Android.

Image Credits:Meta (screenshot)

Sensor Tower also has visibility into daily active users for the Muse app following the Meta Connect conference. It found that figure climbed 27% on Wednesday after the event wrapped.

Before the conference, Muse was already off to a strong start. Sensor Tower said the app reached an estimated 2.8 million downloads in its first two weeks on the app stores. During that time (September 8 to September 17), the Muse app averaged 55% day-over-day growth in downloads. For comparison, ChatGPT averaged 24% day-over-day download growth in its first 10 days after launch. Download growth for Claude and Grok, meanwhile, declined during their respective launches.

On Friday, September 18, Muse climbed to the top of the U.S. App Store and has retained its ranking ever since. It also reached the top spot on the Google Play Store on September 19 and remains there today.

While much of Muse’s traction so far is organic, the app is also benefiting from the same cross-platform promotion that helped one of Meta’s latest social apps, Instagram Threads, top 500 million monthly active users — that is, Meta is marketing the app to existing Facebook and Instagram users.

Image Credits:Sensor Tower

However, as Meta’s Head of Threads, Connor Hayes, recently told Business Insider, Meta’s approach to marketing Muse differs from its approach with Threads. While Threads also deals in user-generated content that Meta can match to users’ interests when running its cross-promotions, the trick with Muse is to build promotional units that can showcase something the AI agent can do for the user, based on Meta’s understanding of what would be useful or helpful to them specifically.

Sensor Tower’s data indicates that Meta rolled out house ads promoting Muse on September 9, a day after its launch. Within 10 days, Muse received the majority of house advertising promotions across Meta’s properties, ahead of promotions for Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp. Meta has also begun advertising Muse on mobile ad networks and other social networks, including Reddit, TikTok, and YouTube.

By Tuesday, September 22, Muse ranked among the top 10 brands by advertising spend, Sensor Tower said.

Still, Muse’s growth can’t be chalked up to Meta’s marketing efforts alone, as ads promoting the app only account for 6% of the ad impressions from launch through September 19.

Tech.title: Kiteworks urges customers to shut down their servers amid ‘imminent’ threat of cyberattack
Tech.content:
Technology giant Kiteworks is urging customers to shut down their systems after the company received information that hackers may attempt to target them.

Kiteworks (formerly Accellion), which makes tools for transferring large files and sensitive datasets over the internet, confirmed to TechCrunch that it had notified its customers about a potential threat. The news was first reported exclusively by German publication Heise, which cited an email that Kiteworks had sent to its customers about an “imminent” attack that could happen as soon as this weekend.

When reached by email on Friday, Kiteworks chief information security officer Frank Balonis told TechCrunch that the company “received credible threat intelligence from law enforcement indicating that a threat actor may attempt to target some Kiteworks systems for customers.”

“Out of an abundance of caution, we notified customers directly and recommended a precautionary shutdown window while we and our law enforcement partners work through the matter,” said Balonis. “We are not aware of any compromise of Kiteworks systems, and this advisory is preventative rather than a response to a confirmed breach.”

Kiteworks did not say, when asked, which law enforcement agency alerted the company or which hacking group may be behind the threat. The FBI declined to comment. U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA did not immediately comment when reached by TechCrunch about the Kiteworks alert to customers.

Balonis said that the company has fixed all known vulnerabilities in its latest software release, 9.5.1, which it recommends all customers use.

According to a copy of the email sent to customers on Friday and shared with TechCrunch, the company said it was concerned about the exploitation of vulnerabilities that are currently unknown to Kiteworks. These bugs are known as zero-day flaws because they give the vendor — in this case Kiteworks — no time to fix the flaws before they are exploited.

In the email, Kiteworks urged customers to shut down their systems before the weekend, if not sooner, to “protect against any potential zero-day attacks,” as the company cannot confirm whether there are other potential routes for improper access.

It’s unclear exactly how many customers may be affected, but Kiteworks notes on its website that it has thousands of customers across healthcare, technology, education, automotive, and government, among others. Security researcher Kevin Beaumont pointed to a listing of at least a thousand internet-facing Kiteworks systems online today, though the number is likely an overcount of affected customer systems.

One Kiteworks customer who works in healthcare told TechCrunch that they received the alert from Kiteworks and took down their organization’s server immediately. The person, who asked not to be publicly named, said the outage is causing delays and disruption to doctors’ ability to contact their patients.

Kiteworks is no stranger to cyberattacks. Prior to its rebrand from Accellion in late 2021, a vulnerability in its file-transfer application allowed an extortion gang to mass-hack and steal data from hundreds of organizations that relied on the product to send customer or internal corporate data over the internet.

The mass hack was part of a broader hacking campaign targeting file transfer products, with the goal of stealing copies of the data that had been previously sent over the internet but not deleted from the affected servers. The hackers then held the data for ransom, threatening to publicly release customers’ information if the victim organizations did not pay a ransom.

Do you know more about the threat facing Kiteworks customers? Are you an affected Kiteworks customer? We’d love to hear from you. You can contact this reporter securely on Signal at zackwhittaker.1337, or reach him by email at zack.whittaker@techcrunch.com.

Tech.title: Appeals Court Lets the Pentagon Designate Anthropic a Supply-Chain Risk
Tech.content:
Anthropic lost a legal battle to overturn one of the supply-chain risk labels that the US Department of Defense slapped on the company, as a federal appeals court in DC on Friday refused to second-guess the Trump administration.

“The department had ample support for its conclusion that the continued integration of Claude into the department’s information systems, by the department or its contractors, presented a statutorily covered national-security risk,” the judges wrote in a majority opinion. “As Anthropic admits, the company encodes restrictions into Claude that prevent the model from performing tasks that Anthropic wishes to prevent.”

Anthropic spokesperson Danielle Cohen says the company remains confident in its position and is considering all options. That could include appealing to a broader panel of the DC Circuit Court of Appeals or the US Supreme Court.

Earlier this year, the Pentagon sanctioned Anthropic under a pair of separate supply-chain laws to remove the company’s Claude AI models from the military and other parts of the federal government by this month. Anthropic executives have said that the company would not allow the government to deploy its current AI models to support autonomous weapons or domestic surveillance. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth deemed the stance a significant national security risk.

The laws designating Anthropic had to be challenged in separate courts. A federal judge in San Francisco tossed out one of the supply-chain risk labels in March and confirmed that decision last month, but Friday's ruling means the other one will stay in place indefinitely, meaning the Pentagon’s blocking of Anthropic can continue. Both rulings face the prospect of years of appeals before being fully resolved.

Tech.title: War Bros Didn’t Always Rule Silicon Valley
Tech.content:
In September 2015, the Founders Fund hosted a retreat at an eco-resort in British Columbia. Most of the attendees were VCs and people from the companies the firm was backing, but they also invited a few outsiders, including computer pioneer Alan Kay, writer Neal Stephenson, and me.

One morning at breakfast I was sitting across from Kay at a long table. The man who conceived the Dynabook—basically the modern computer that we all use—was expounding on his exploits when Founders Fund leader Peter Thiel plopped down next to him. As Kay, in full raconteur mode, spun stories of optimizing the mouse and advising Steve Jobs, Thiel listened with increasingly visible incredulity. Finally, he couldn’t take it. “Who ARE you?” he demanded of Kay.

The mustachioed legend was stunned. He began stumbling out his bona fides, but quickly realized that for someone unacquainted with his résumé, it would have sounded ridiculously overblown. It was like asking Einstein or Mick Jagger to explain themselves. Kay stopped mid-sentence and sighed. “I’m just an old has-been,” he said and went back to his breakfast. Two worlds had collided, and failed to connect.

I thought back to that moment a couple of weeks ago while reading an op-ed in The New York Times headlined “Silicon Valley Was Right From the Start,” by Sharon Weinberger. The essay claimed that the portrait often painted of the Valley as driven by the counterculture and a desire to make the world better was a sham. Today’s bare-knuckled approach to accumulating massive wealth, kowtowing to an authoritarian leader, and embracing lethal military technology simply exposes the industry for what it always was. (Weinberger’s essay was promoting her new book Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War.)

“Silicon Valley’s values haven’t changed, just its customers,” she wrote, calling the industry’s current love affair with military tech “less a story of political conversion than of market adaptation.” In that reading, all that hippie stuff about free expression and democratization during the 1980s PC revolution and the 1990s Internet boom was a mirage, an opportunistic feint by Big Tech to push its wares and garner the loot.

I disagree. The story as I see it is that beginning in the late 1970s, a new generation of technologists, identifying with the counterculture, operated with a set of values that unleashed innovation and ironically set the stage for the industry’s current wealth. Yes, that movement carried a torch from the field’s defense industry roots. But even as DOD funding kept fueling innovations (Darpa grants provided dough for the GUI, the internet, and Google Search), that new generation was characterized by idealism, a hackerish love of building things, and disdain for conventional practices.

That mindset changed not only the course of the computer industry, but the culture of American business. (Before Apple Computer, a CEO wouldn’t dare come to work in anything but a suit.) Denying the existence of that idealism is not only inaccurate, but it conveniently lets the new generation of defense contractors off the hook for their pivot toward deadly materiel.

When I shared my views with Weinberger, she acknowledged that I’d probably studied tech culture more than she had from her perch in Washington, DC. Still, she gamely defended her op-ed. “We’re all products of what we grow up in,” she says. “If you were growing up in the peace-dividend era, with defense tech jobs disappearing, the money from defense was less important, and you start to have different values.”

By that standard, the market shift from missile control modules to Macintoshes was driven not by values but by greed. Likewise, she says, the recent return to high-tech weaponry doesn’t represent a philosophical repositioning but a fortuitous opportunity to sell to a Pentagon eager to exploit the Valley’s innovations. “It's not like everybody in the workforce in Silicon Valley woke up and went, like, ‘Defense is cool,’” says Weinberger. That impulse to go where the money is, she argues, is the defining ethos of Silicon Valley. “Your prime directive is for your company to succeed,” she says. “Why didn't Apple work with the military? Because they didn't need to. They had the consumer marketplace.”

Tech.title: The Trump Administration Is Trying to Get Musk and X Out of a $137 Million EU Fine
Tech.content:
The US government is trying to get Elon Musk and his social media platform X out of a $137 million fine by the European Union in an escalation of its criticism of the bloc’s tech rules.

The US Department of Justice said it had filed an application with the help of the Department of State to support a legal challenge by Musk to annul the case in the EU’s General Court. The Luxembourg-based court will now decide whether the US has a right to intervene.

The US government is arguing that it should be involved in the case to protect American companies. The fine is precedent-setting as the bloc’s first sanction under the Digital Services Act, which requires online platforms to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content, especially the largest sites. Many of those, which include Meta’s Facebook and Instagram, Google’s YouTube, and Microsoft’s LinkedIn, are headquartered in the US and contribute significantly to the US economy, it pointed out.

“We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory overreach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth,” said assistant attorney general Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division.

The case also has “implications” for US-EU relations, it warned. The act has become a major source of tension between officials, with US President Donald Trump calling the penalties “overseas extortion.” Last year, he threatened imposing tariffs on any country implementing digital regulation, which he said were “all designed to harm, or discriminate against, American technology.” Vice President JD Vance has criticized the DS’s content moderation rules as “authoritarian censorship.”

Tech.title: Best Laptops (2026): My Top Recommendations After Testing Hundreds
Tech.content:
And lastly, for something with a larger screen, I'd recommend the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x. It's a particularly good alternative to the 15-inch MacBook Air, at a much lower cost. These days, you can buy the upgraded model with the 2560 x 1600 OLED display (and 165-Hz refresh rate) for $1,000, on sale at Amazon. While it's slightly thicker than the MacBook Air, it leaves more room for extra ports including HDMI, USB-A, and an SD card slot. And while the Snapdragon X2 Plus isn’t quite an M5 killer, I was happy with the performance and battery life provided.

Lenovo also sells a cheaper version directly, but it has a lower-resolution IPS screen that I haven't tested. While the other specs are good, you might want to consider one of the cheaper options that I've tested below, such as the HP OmniBook 5. The IdeaPad Slim 5x has stronger performance and a better touchpad, though.

Cheap Laptops That Are Actually Good

While “cheap” means something different to everyone, the best budget laptops generally fall under $750. This is where Windows truly shines, offering great specs for less money. Thanks to the latest processors from Qualcomm and Intel, these laptops now offer battery life that rivals Apple. The best affordable laptop I’ve checked out is the HP OmniBook 5. The model I tested has a Snapdragon X processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. Discounts fluctuate frequently, but HP always has some version of the OmniBook 5 with a Snapdragon CPU at under $700. The specific discounted configuration seems to change every few days, though, so shop carefully.

I also recently tested the new HP OmniBook 3, which uses the same chip as the OmniBook 5. It frequently sells for less than the OmniBook 5 by at least $100 or so. HP is selling this configuration of the 14-inch model for around $550. While the OmniBook 3 is a good alternative, the OmniBook 5 is much thinner and looks more modern. Neither laptop has a particularly great touchpad, though, which is easily the biggest flaw in both laptops. Between the two, the OmniBook 5 is the better buy if you can afford it.

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s new entry-level laptop. It initially started at an aggressive $599, but that price has recently been raised to $699. Even at that price, the laptop shines when it comes to the display. It offers the best screen you can find at this price, bringing the macOS experience to an unprecedented value, even at $699 (or $799 for the 512 GB model). Apple clearly prioritized the front-of-screen experience, delivering a premium feel across the display, build quality, and keyboard. While the 8 GB of RAM, outdated ports, and slower SSD are notable drawbacks—making the MacBook Air a far better choice for remote workers—the Neo is an extremely premium-feeling laptop available for students, travelers, and casual users. Thanks to the lower-powered A18 Pro chip, though, performance does take a hit. So, be careful about buying this laptop if you work at a computer all day.

Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 $749 Best Buy

Given how good some of these budget laptops are, it’s a bit harder to find a place for Chromebooks. The standout option is still the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14. It’s the most premium Chromebook available, with an OLED screen, 16 GB of RAM, and battery life that rivals the MacBook Neo. Its price just keeps going up, though, now at $849. That’s far too expensive for what you get. Instead, I'd recommend the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514, which uses the same efficient (and responsive) MediaTek Kompanio Ultra that delivers excellent battery life. This one is also a 2-in-1, with a touchscreen, a 360-degree hinge, and a quality touchpad. The retail price of $749 is way too much, but it frequently drops down to $549, which is a great deal for this hardware. For a true budget Chromebook under $400, there are significant compromises, but I'd recommend the Asus Chromebook CX15. The screen isn't the best, and neither is the touchpad. But the specs are solid for the price, and I liked the more modern look compared to other ultra-cheap Chromebooks.

Windows laptops are about to get much stronger in this category, however, just as higher-priced Chromebooks will be seemingly phased out over time and replaced by the upcoming Googlebooks. Personally, I wouldn't spend more than $500 for a Chromebook and would instead opt for one of the cheaper HP OmniBooks mentioned above if you're already spending close to this price.

Powerful Laptops for Those Who Need It

While the laptops above are great for the average person, content creators and gamers need extra performance. For the former, the 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro is the ultimate choice. It combines immense power with surprising portability and fantastic battery life—a rare feat. The M5 generation is the most impressive yet, with a greatly expanded GPU and significantly boosted on-device AI processing thanks to a more efficient Neural Engine and faster memory bandwidth. While it is one of the most powerful AI laptops available, the MacBook Pro isn’t for everyone; it is built specifically for professional creatives and engineers running heavy, demanding applications. It’s become more expensive in 2026, but there’s still nothing quite like it on the market.

There are a number of Windows alternatives to the MacBook Pro, including the Asus ProArt P16 and Lenovo Yoga Pro 9i. And while both are powerful, they take an old-school approach to performance, using hot-and-heavy discrete graphics cards that significantly reduce battery life to achieve that level of performance. We'll probably need to wait for Nvidia's anticipated RTX Spark laptops for a true MacBook Pro competitor later this year. The Dell XPS 14 takes a different approach, ditching the discrete GPU for Intel’s new X7 or X9 chip (also known as B390 or Intel Arc graphics). The results are seriously impressive, replicating the performance of an RTX 4050 without the downsides of using a discrete GPU. Moreover, the Dell XPS 14 has a level of design polish you usually see only on MacBooks—and it even surpasses them in some areas. The more affordable configurations with the Core Ultra 5 or 7 don't have as strong graphics, but you still get the premium design and excellent battery life.

The most common use for laptop performance, however, is for playing games. If you plan on booting up any graphically intensive games more than a couple of times a week, you will want a dedicated gaming laptop. After testing dozens over the past year, I've come back to the Lenovo LOQ 15 as my top pick. There are cheaper RTX 5050 models out there, such as the Alienware 15 or MSI Cyborg A15, but prices have been increasing on these laptops over the past few months. The Alienware 15 with the RTX 5050, in particular, has seen a $600 price increase, which makes it incredibly overpriced. That's led me back to the LOQ 15, which has stayed steady at $1,300 at Walmart and gives you an RTX 5060 for graphics and a bright, colorful screen.

You won't find a cheaper gaming laptop that doesn't make some significant compromises in either performance or screen quality, both of which can sour the gaming experience. And while I wish the LOQ 15 were still selling for under $1,000 like it was when it first launched, it remains the absolute best gaming laptop for the money right now. It's really the only gaming laptop under $1,500 I'd currently buy, given where prices are.

There’s also a whole world of gaming laptops outside the budget tier, though. I’ve tested an assortment of options, and I always come back to the Razer Blade 14 and Razer Blade 16. Portable, minimalist, and extremely well-made, they have rightfully earned their reputation as the MacBooks of PC gaming—along with the MacBook Pro–like price tag. Their sleek design means they work just as well for school or work as they do for gaming, without the bulk of a traditional gaming laptop. While there are more powerful options out there, nothing quite matches the Razer Blade. They're expensive, but if you've got the money to spend, they're as premium as gaming laptops get. I'll soon be testing the latest version of the Blade 16, which includes Intel's latest Panther Lake chips and should have vastly improved battery life.

Other Good Laptops I’ve Tested

If you choose one of the laptops above, you will be very happy with your purchase. However, if you are looking for a specific feature or a different price point, I have included a few other options below that I've recently reviewed and enjoyed using. I've tested dozens of laptops this year already, but I've included some of the standouts below. Each of these recently tested laptops has at least one minor drawback, but they could still be the perfect choice depending on your needs and current discounts.

Tech.title: Party Invite Phishing Scams Are the New Missed Connections
Tech.content:
This past April, while attending his nephew’s bar mitzvah on Cape Cod, Eric Umansky woke up to an inbox full of emails from people from his past. They all wanted to know the same thing: Was he actually throwing a party Saturday night?

The New York–based journalist wasn’t sure what party they were referring to, or why random acquaintances he’d met in passing 15 years ago were emailing him. On deadline and already stressed about work, he checked his phone, where more messages inquired about a supposed Paperless Post invite he’d sent for a “Special Private Dinner Party” at 7 pm on May 2.

Except Umansky hadn't sent the invite, and he wasn’t planning to host a party anytime soon.

As it turned out, he was an early victim of an email scam that has since become more widespread. What Umansky didn’t expect was the positive effect it would have on his social life.

In May, after receiving increased reports, the Federal Trade Commission issued a consumer alert warning about scammers sending “unexpected messages that look like they’re from well-known invitation platforms like Evite or Paperless Post,” noting how some messages “make you enter your email username and password to see event details” while others “tell you to enter a phone number and share a special code to RSVP.”

Umansky wasn’t sure how it happened; he thought he'd taken the necessary precautions to safeguard his email, including using two-factor authentication. All he could think to do was post a message on Facebook, LinkedIn, and his other social networks to notify people that he was, in fact, not having a party and, more importantly, “don’t come to my house.”

Phishing scams, which have proliferated across the last two decades, remain one of the biggest security risks faced both by individuals and companies. Email scams, in particular, can now be highly sophisticated, incorporating social engineering techniques like creating urgency or fear in a target and even leveraging the personal relationships between two people to manipulate a victim, what’s known as “spear phishing.” AI has only made those deceptions harder to weed out.

But in some recent cases, like Umansky’s, the fake party invite is having an unintended outcome: It is encouraging people to check in to see whether the message was actually real and, in doing so, has reignited dormant relationships.

“It was so striking to me after it happened that I actually had a thought that I was like, ‘Oh, is this a net positive?’” says Umansky, who over the last several months has reconnected with a handful of old friends and colleagues over lunch and via text. He recently spent an hour on Zoom with a former coworker who now lives in Mexico City. They hadn’t talked to each other in over a decade. “I was like, Oh, you know, I actually want to catch up with you about something. There was an idea I wanted to bat around with him, which we talked about for maybe 10 minutes. The rest of the time we talked about our lives.”

According to a 2024 study published in the scientific journal Communications Psychology examining social withdrawal, which surveyed 2,400 adults in the US, UK, and Canada, people are sometimes unwilling to contact old friends because they believe the other person won’t want to hear from them or they fear the interaction will be awkward. The research noted that “high priority placed on work and productivity in North America has led people to cut back on social connections and social time to meet increasing demands at work,” in addition to other life transitions, such as parenthood or moving to a new city.

Tech.title: ‘Primetime’ Exposes the Ego-Driven Core of Vigilante Pedophile Hunting
Tech.content:
Child predators are arguably the most reviled demographic in society.

So when someone like Chris Hansen, the former NBC Dateline journalist and host of the To Catch a Predator series, decides to take up the mantle of exposing them to the public, he is naturally praised as a hero.

But, as is revealed in Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime—a dramatized snapshot of Hansen’s life at the show’s peak—it’s not as simple as that. Exposing allegedly bad people for public entertainment brings up a lot of ethical concerns and unintended consequences. And while many of the vigilantes carrying out these sting operations claim they are doing a public service, their motivations become a lot more suspect when fame and money are involved.

To Catch a Predator launched in 2004. In the show, Hansen’s team would pair up with civilian watchdog group Perverted Justice, using adult “decoys” to pose as minors online and exchange messages with men in chatrooms and private DMs. After the conversations became sexual, the crew would set up a sting, inviting these men to a home to meet the decoy, only to have Hansen confront them, uttering his catchphrase, “Have a seat.” The men were technically free to leave instead of sitting for an on-camera interview, but often police were waiting outside to arrest them.

The show developed an intense fandom that remains active to this day in subreddits like r/tcap, which has 52,000 weekly visitors, despite the fact that NBC stopped airing the original series in 2007.

In A24's Primetime, a darkly told character study in theaters September 25, Hansen (Robert Pattinson) clearly enjoys the praise and seems desperate for more accolades. He brags to his two young sons that he’s about to be on prime-time television, despite them not understanding the importance of that, and complains that the show has “never won an Emmy or any of the significance it deserves.” When a fan recognizes Hansen on a flight and becomes bloodthirsty, asking the TV host if he ever wants to “bleed” the predators he’s outing, Hansen smiles and admits that what he does by disgracing them on national television is “a little worse.”

In real life, Hansen cofounded the streaming service Trublu in November 2022, where he continues his investigations into alleged child predators. But these days, he’s far from alone. His work has inspired copycats, who thrive on social media and streaming platforms like YouTube, Kick, and Facebook. These groups and individuals are largely disorganized, and as such, hard to track, but a 2022 Washington Post investigation identified at least 160 in the US. Arguably, the people running these operations are more reckless, in part because they’re driven by virality.

Tech.title: How to Record Your Screen on Any Phone
Tech.content:
There are numerous reasons why you might want to record what’s happening on your phone. Maybe you’re having a problem with an app and you want to share what’s going wrong with a tech-savvy friend; or maybe you're the tech-savvy friend, and you want to show someone else how to fix a bug.

Perhaps you’re starting up a YouTube channel of smartphone tutorials. Or it could be that you want to capture evidence of a new high score in a mobile game—not just a screenshot of it, but the actual act of you achieving it.

For these reasons and more, screen recordings are useful, and they’re not difficult to capture no matter what the make and model of your handset. You’ll find instructions below for the two most well-known Android phone brands, and the iPhone.

Record Your Screen on a Google Pixel

Recording options on a Google phone. Courtesy of David Nield

If your phone of choice is the Google Pixel, unlock your handset then swipe down from the top of the screen with two fingers to bring up the full Quick Settings selection. You should see a widget for Screen recorder—if you can’t see it, try swiping left or right. If you still can’t see it, tap the pen icon (lower right) to add it to the Quick Settings menu.

Next you’ll see a panel of toggle switches: These options let you choose whether or not the screen touches are visible in the recording, and whether you want the selfie camera feed to be visible as an overlay (handy if you’re narrating or reacting to what’s on screen). You can also opt to include audio from your phone’s apps or from the microphone.

The drop-down menu at the top lets you decide between recording the entire screen or just a single app. When you’re happy, tap Start. You’ll see a short countdown, then the recording begins. To end the recording, tap the red recording timer in the status bar at the top, then Stop. The video will be saved to Google Photos.

Record Your Screen on a Samsung Galaxy

Recording options on a Samsung phone. Courtesy of David Nield

On Samsung Galaxy phones, the process is similar but not quite identical to screen recording on a Pixel. With your phone unlocked, swipe down from the top of the display, then swipe down again on the central pane (with icons for features including Wi-Fi and the flashlight) to reveal the Screen recorder icon.

Tech.title: Who Killed Paulina Borsook’s Career?
Tech.content:
The offers had come in earlier that day. Paulina Borsook, 72, allowed herself a flash of excitement before returning to the question of what had ruined her life.

“I don’t know what to make of it,” she said as we drove to lunch. I’d picked Borsook up outside her home near Oakland, California, a basement unit that she calls “Ice Station Zebra” on account of the cold and the color scheme and the isolation. At least that’s how I was encouraged to picture it. Borsook didn’t want me to come inside, lest I pull the old magazine hack’s scam of investing the decor with symbolic significance. She wrote enough stories of this kind in her heyday, back when she was landing bylines in WIRED and the like, to know how the game gets played. Later, she explained over email: “this place i ended up in reflects me not at all. i lost all i owned when i couldnt pay for storage and this place is the best i could find that worked with my disabilities. so i feel it REALLY doesnt reflect me/my taste/my preferences. shame and aversion.”

What had happened to Paulina Borsook? The question was haunting her, even on a day when she’d gotten such good news. It’s haunted her for a quarter-century now. In 2000, after years writing about Silicon Valley, she published a book, Cyberselfish, that discerned within the tech utopianism of the era a dead-eyed, woman-hating social malevolence—what the subtitle called the “Terribly Libertarian Culture of High-Tech.” It was smart at a moment when the whole of the tech industry had gone dumb, and it was funny where Silicon Valley was at its most self-serious. Cyberselfish got warm, if occasionally baffled, reviews. It sold something like 5,000 copies in hardcover and another 2,000 in paperback, a respectable mid-list number, no blockbuster but not a dog, either.

And then … nothing. Editors stopped taking her calls. No fellowships materialized, no second book deal, no regular MSNBC spots for the dotcom Cassandra of the boom times. Borsook couldn’t get work. She began to wonder if she had been blacklisted. Her health, always wobbly, only worsened. She was living in other people’s houses. She went broke, a process she likened to a fire in which everything burns to the ground, and was getting by on a GoFundMe and support from friends. She’d taken to calling the book TDB. That damn book.

Tech.title: Apple’s 20th Anniversary iPhone 20 Pro May Arrive as a Seamless Slab of Glass
Tech.content:
Hope there’s extra room in your pockets. A new rumor says Apple’s iPhone 20 Pro and Pro Max could have the largest displays in iPhone history, alongside a quad-curved, nearly all-glass exterior.

Digital Chat Station, a prominent anonymous tech insider on the Chinese social media platform Weibo and a reliable source of Apple news in the past, posted over the weekend that the iPhone 20 Pro screen would be 6.41 inches and the Pro Max 6.96 inches, measured diagonally. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, which hit stores last Friday, measure 6.27 inches and 6.86 inches (which Apple rounds up to 6.3 inches and 6.9 inches). The iPhone Duo, Apple’s long-awaited first foldable phone, which reaches stores on Oct. 23, has a diagonal 7.6-inch inner display when open.

A representative for Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

More from CNET

CNET Senior Reporter Abrar Al-Heeti said that larger screens are great for watching videos and working on the go, but bigger displays also mean higher costs for consumers, serving as an “excuse for companies to charge you more.”

“Along with the commemorative angle of the iPhone’s 20th anniversary, it’s likely Apple could use design elements like a bigger screen and an all-glass design to hike prices,” Al-Heeti said.

More glass, smaller Dynamic Island

Digital Chat Station backed Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman’s August report that the exterior of the new flagship phones would be nearly all glass in what’s called a quad-curved design. That means the glass will wrap around all four sides of the phone, making it look as if there is no bezel.

In his report last month, Gurman said that the glass on the front and back of the phones would “curve into the sides of the devices, with a metal band in the middle.”

The exteriors of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are made of aluminum and ceramic glass.

The iPhone 20 Pro and Pro Max will also have a smaller Dynamic Island and a tiny punch-hole selfie cutout on the front, according to Digital Chat Station.

The Dynamic Island is the capsule-shaped region at the top of the front screen that houses the selfie camera. It also expands and contracts to display notifications, system alerts and background activities.

The iPhone 20 Pro and Pro Max are expected to launch in September 2027 as the next iteration in the series. Apple is widely expected to skip over the iPhone 19 name and jump straight to iPhone 20 next year, marking the 20th anniversary of the first iPhone launch in 2007.

Tech.title: I Tested Two Groundbreaking Security Sensors in Spots Other Systems Can’t Go
Tech.content:
Tyler Lacoma/CNET Art Abode Security Sensors 2026 8.0 Garage Tilt Sensor Outdoor Contact Sensor Pros & Cons Accurate and speedy sensors for areas other security sensors aren't made for

Tests showed excellent performance on garage door and fence gate

Abode's hub automatically connects to sensors and makes setup one of the easiest I've done

Offers a variety of automations and alert options through Abode's intuitive app

Sensors have many additional applications for sheds, tilting windows and more Abode's standard hub requires a permanet Ethernet connection

The outdoor contact sensor design could use another pass

Security systems have stayed the same for years, with only minor advances, but 2026 is changing that. I’ve seen new sensors start to hit the shelves, from presence-sensing devices that can detect people without needing security cameras to small sensors that monitor tilting, opening and tampering all at once. But Abode’s latest offering is even more unique.

Abode has two new products available now, a sensor made to monitor garage door access ($35), and an outdoor access sensor ($50) designed for gates, sheds, barns and any door open to the elements. I got to try them both around my home, and found them particularly effective and easy to set up compared to many of the sensors I’ve tested.

If you’ve been looking for a special device to help monitor access to backyards, detached buildings on your property, or garage doors that always seem to get left open, these sensors are a remarkable answer, particularly if you already have an Abode system. If not, I’ll cover what you need to know from my testing.

More from CNET

Unboxing and setup

Abode’s new sensors work flawlessly with its existing hub. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

I was able to fully test an Abode starter security kit as well as its two new sensors for this review, providing a clear look at how the security brand functions. As far as setup experiences go, this has been one of my speediest. And I’ve tested many different systems.

Abode’s beginner’s kit is small, offering an indoor sensor, motion sensor and fob, along with the hub. I was pleased to find out, after downloading the app and connecting the hub, the other base devices automatically added themselves and made the setup process effortless, smoother than nearly any other security system except possibly Ikea’s affordable sensors.

Adding the new garage and outdoor sensors also proved quick, with pairing happening only seconds after I installed the batteries and typed in the activation code.

Abode’s hub connects to new sensors in a snap. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

The one problem I have with Abode’s system is how the standard hub connects to Wi-Fi. This hub requires an Ethernet connection to your router or gateway, not only during setup but all the time. That’s a not-so-small problem if, like me, you have a router, gateway and other necessary devices already taking up all nearby outlets, which forced me to jury-rig a solution for the hub while I was testing.

Abode’s Iota hub does offer Wi-Fi, but that requires a more expensive upgrade to a $200 starter kit, not including extra sensors. It’s baffling that Abode’s standard hub still doesn’t support Wi-Fi when every other brand does. Check the outlets near your router before you choose this solution.

Garage sensor installation and performance

Abode’s garage sensor can sense any kind of tilt up and down. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Equipped with internal gyroscope technology, Abode’s garage door sensor is made to detect orientation, and setup couldn’t be simpler. Using the included adhesive strips, I slapped the small monitor on my closed garage door, and it began accurately detecting open/closed states immediately in the Abode app.

Smart garage door motors and controllers can also do something like this, plus app controls, but this is one of the first standard home security systems to expand to the garage, and adding a single $50 sensor is far more affordable than replacing your garage controller entirely. Abode let me know if the garage was left open, and advised me on unexpected garage door movement when no one was at home, just as advertised.

Placing the sensor shouldn’t be any trouble, no matter what kind of garage you have. It sticks onto the inside of the garage door where there is plenty of space, and doesn’t require any complicated calibration. You may have to reset the sensor after placement to make sure it’s reading open and closed states correctly, but that, too, takes only moments.

Finally, you could use this sensor on anything that tilts up and down like a garage door, such as tilting windows, so it could have other applications in your home.

Gate sensor installation and performance

Abode’s outdoor sensor is a little annoying to put together, but works like a charm. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Abode’s outdoor access sensor proved more complicated than the garage monitor. Bulkier than most access sensors and equipped with weather-resistance capabilities, it’s made to tell when anything outdoors opens and shuts. The two parts sense when they are close or when they’ve moved apart, with a bit of extra leeway compared to indoor sensors, since outdoor fences and other access zones have varied designs and gaps.

The complex housing proved adequate, but was more frustrating to install and is in need of some future refinements. The screw-in backplate, for example, had pop-out sections to make room for the screws, but the plastic base was so thick I couldn’t put out the sections at all, not even with a hammer that nearly destroyed the base itself (I used another tool to carve them out eventually, not an ideal situation). And the battery casing was so tight and awkwardly designed, I was afraid forcing the batteries in would harm the nearby, unprotected circuitry.

In these ways, the design feels a little too close to a prototype model for me, and it probably needs another pass or two. But it works, and works very well, when it’s finally set up.

Connected to my old fence gate, the sensor accurately and immediately told me whenever it was opened or closed. I’ve found that gate left open more than a few times, so this gave me welcome peace of mind. I also tested it during a stormy downpour, which did nothing to affect the performance of the sensor.

You may want to turn off beeps from the hub that sound every time it alerts to the sensor being opened, but Abode provided a setting to do just that. However, alerts and monitoring aren’t the only things these sensors can do.

App automations that benefit from Abode’s support

Abode’s app allows for customizations and automations, too. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

One of the most impressive parts of Abode’s security platform is how it maintains connections to other third-party smart home gadgets, from Google Home connections to the rare-to-find Apple support for certain devices. There are also Abode’s own devices, including cameras and smart locks, which naturally work with the system

Abode’s CUE function offers automations similar to Google Home or Apple Home. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

When Abode’s system is armed, triggering one of these garage or gate sensors can trip the system and sound a siren. But using the CUE automation tool in the Abode app, I found you can also set up many other types of automations, depending on what you want to activate.

This can include setting lights to turn on a warning glow if a fence gate is left open, or automatically unlocking your door when the garage is opened. You can also set times for these triggers to work, so they only function in the evening, on weekdays or only trigger after a certain time (the gate has been left open for 2 hours, for example). This adds more possibilities if you want to expand your smart home, but it’s not necessary to get value out of these sensors.

Remember, Abode’s app can also support third-party integrations with other devices. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

If you want to pay for an Abode subscription, you can add more features with plans starting at $80 a year, but these are mostly camera-focused, and I don’t think they’re necessary for these sensors at all.

Final thoughts on Abode’s new access sensors

Abode’s sensors signal helpful new trends in the home security world. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Abode’s newest sensors offer exceptional performance in spots other sensors aren’t really made for. They’re also more expensive than typical sensors, and the outdoor sensor might need another design pass in the future, but I otherwise found them easy to set up and start using for customized, helpful alerts.

One word of caution: Abode’s standard hub requires an Ethernet connection, so consider where you’ll put it, and if you’ll need to run Ethernet cable anywhere during installation. Otherwise, this system sets itself up in minutes.

I’m enjoying this 2026 wave of security tech innovations. They’re finding new applications in the home – and finding them with success. Aqara’s multipurpose sensor is one such model. Abode’s proved another strong example, so if you’ve been looking for extended security capabilities outdoors or in the garage, take note of this update.

Tech.title: Gemini’s Live Avatar Puts a Face on Its AI Agent. It’s Freaking Me Out
Tech.content:
I’ve noticed a lot more businesses using AI agents to process customer support requests. But now it’s getting weird.

Google’s Live Avatar feature is now available for those with Gemini Enterprise. This comes days after Google announced Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking.

What exactly is Live Avatar? It combines an interactive visual experience with a conversational AI agent to do things like filing insurance claims through a video chat — which was Google’s example in its announcement. Businesses or those with Google Enterprise can choose from a few avatars to put a face to an AI agent’s voice.

More from CNET

Live Avatar seems pretty handy for businesses. It can create live video avatars with lip synching for conversational videos and process live audio, screen sharing and video feeds simultaneously. Live Avatar can run tools and API calls while continuing conversations with customers. But imagine a cartoon or realistic-looking avatar’s lips moving to match the bot’s voice to handle your request. Creepy.

Live Avatar also aims to create more fluid dialogue with native speech-to-speech for “more natural interruption recovery without dropping conversation context or backend transactions.”

Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on when it will be available to the general public or how it plans to safeguard the information the AI agent receives during video calls (like, in the insurance example, your address, name and live video when filing a claim).

Google has a few safeguards in place to prevent misuse, like choosing from curated, prebuilt avatars. If you want to create a custom avatar, you’ll have to go through a verification process, Google’s announcement says. All audio and video are watermarked with SynthID to keep all AI content verifiable.
